entry.title: Rule's big day, some sloppiness and a new QB look: Amie Just's takes from Nebraska vs. Ohio - Omaha World-Herald
entry.body: Here are Amie Just’s quick takes from Nebraska’s 49-21 season-opening victory over Ohio: * * * Loved Jamal Rule Running back Jamal Rule may be a true freshman, but he’s ready for the moment. The North Carolina native scored two touchdowns before halftime in his Husker debut: a 1-yard rushing score on Nebraska’s opening drive and a 24-yard reception touchdown on third-and-4. By the game’s end, Rule was Nebraska’s leading rusher — compiling 122 yards rushing on 15 carries with 47 yards receiving on two receptions. Pretty special for Rule to have a performance like that with Emmett Johnson in the building. Mehki Nelson’s touchdowns People are also reading… Another running back who’s battling for the starting job showed that he has the potential for greatness, too. Nelson had two touchdowns on Saturday, too — a 29-yard rushing score in the third quarter and a 51-yard receiving touchdown in the fourth quarter. Nelson finished the game with 10 carries for 64 yards rushing and two receptions for 65 yards receiving. Frank Solich recognition Well before kickoff on Saturday, Nebraska vs. Ohio was informally dubbed “the Frank Solich Bowl” due to the former Lincoln Southeast coach’s coaching careers at both universities. Solich — while wearing a nondescript white polo – was recognized before the game as part of the 2026 Nebraska Football Hall of Fame Class, and flipped the coin for the coin toss. A classy touch by Nebraska. Single-digit guys The new class of single-digit Huskers was revealed on Saturday, and there are 11 new members of that fraternity: No. 3 receiver Kwazi Gilmer, No. 5 Anthony Jones Jr., No. 7 cornerback Andrew Marshall, No. 8 Donovan Jones and No. 8 tight end Luke Lindenmeyer. Congrats are in order for these fellas. Fans If you stayed for the whole game, pat yourself on the back. It was hot as blazes outside, with a feels-like temperature of 130 degrees on the turf itself. Metal bleachers in this heat? Liked Anthony Colandrea If you’re just a box score-watcher, Colandrea’s line won’t jump off the page. But if you actually watched the game, you saw some zippy throws that had plenty of promise, but ultimately were dropped. On the second play of the second half, he was dinged for intentional grounding — setting up an impossible third-and-31. But on the next drive, Colandrea commanded an 11-play, 73-yard drive that, after a rushing touchdown from Colandrea himself, gave Nebraska an 8-point lead. One notable thing: Colandrea — who possesses plenty of speed — didn’t have a designed run or true scramble play until late in the second quarter, when he pulled in the ball on second-and-10 and ran through traffic for an 11-yard gain. He had a few other successful scrambles, too. In his first start for Nebraska, Colandrea completed 18 of his 32 passes for 275 with three touchdowns and no interceptions. On the ground, he added 10 carries for a total of 23 yards. Let down by Sloppiness Nothing is ever perfect in season openers, but the sloppiness Nebraska showed at points on Saturday was notable. The fumbled hand-off on the first drive for Nebraska could have been costly, but the Huskers managed to bounce back and find the end zone later in the series — thanks to big plays by receivers Kwazi Gilmer and Jacory Barney Jr. before Rule punched in the touchdown from inches out. Before the first quarter was over, Nebraska had racked up four penalties for 15 yards — a 5-yard special teams offside penalty on Rex Guthrie, a 5-yard defensive offside on Jahsear Whittington, and two false starts for 5 yards apiece on right guard Brendan Black. The latter two derailed Nebraska’s third drive of the game and turned third-and-11 into third-and-16. Not too many plays in the playbook for Dana Holgorsen for third-and-16… and on third-and-16, Colandrea was sacked for a loss of 7 yards by Omaha’s own Isaac Ackerman. Nebraska kickstarted the second quarter with a big penalty, too. Ohio faced third-and-8, and the Bobcats couldn’t connect because of the Blackshirts’ smothering pass rush — but Williams Nwaneri was popped for a facemask, and Ohio went on to add another field goal to the tally. On the ensuing kickoff, Nebraska return man Nyziah Hunter inexplicably doubled back and ended up having an 8-yard return instead of what could have been a 30-yard return. Moments later, Colandrea threw a bullet toward Gilmer, and Gilmer couldn’t reel it in. If Gilmer had snagged it, the UCLA transfer would have room to run for days. Another penalty — a questionable “block in the back” flag on Barney — negated a second-quarter, 57-yard touchdown for Hunter. In total, Nebraska was penalized nine times for 65 yards. Loathed Middle eight The middle eight – otherwise known as the final four minutes of the second quarter and the first four minutes of the third quarter — minutes for Nebraska went about as poorly as one can expect without a turnover. The final drive for Nebraska of the first half was empty calories: 10 plays for 29 yards that lasted a little more than 2 minutes. At the end of it, though? A turnover on downs at the Ohio 45-yard line. The thinking there is: if Nebraska can score before halftime and again to open the second half, that breaks the game open. I respect the confidence to go for it. But the execution left plenty to be desired. The first drive for Nebraska of the second half? Precisely the opposite of what you want: a rush for a loss of 3 yards to open the quarter followed by an intentional grounding penalty on Colandrea for the equivalent of an 18-yard sack to set up third-and-31. Nebraska did have forward progress on that ensuing play, but 7 yards wasn’t nearly enough to move the chains. Opening defensive drive It took one play for Ohio to take advantage of a (likely) miscommunication-related busted coverage. Ohio receiver Riley Neer was uncovered on the Bobcats’ opening play and made Nebraska pay by darting downfield for 68 yards — 50 or so of which came after the catch. Two plays later, Neer caught a 4-yard pass to give Ohio the early 7-0 lead. Owen Chambliss’ absence One of the Huskers who transferred into Nebraska with a lot of excitement around him was linebacker Owen Chambliss. 0 was nicked up late in camp, he didn’t play on Saturday. Nebraska could have really benefitted from his talent against Ohio. Missing Darlington One of the best things about halftime in Memorial Stadium’s press box was the conversations with Nebraska coaching legend George Darlington. He never pulled any punches with his opinions, and he always found a relevant story from his coaching days to tell. Sometimes his unfiltered thoughts made it into my (and Tom Shatel’s) game columns. To not have him with us? On Saturday at halftime, I found myself wondering what Darlington would say about the Blackshirts’ opening series. I know he would have been shaking his head. But his comments about it? Only the man himself would know what he was going to say.

entry.title: Dodgers Notes: Ohtani, Rushing, Hernandez, Wrobleski - MLB Trade Rumors
entry.body: While he hasn’t been put on the injured list yet, Shohei Ohtani remained out of the Dodgers’ lineup on Saturday against the Nationals. He’s now missed three straight games. Manager Dave Roberts told reporters, including Katie Woo of The Athletic, that the team will evaluate Ohtani on Sunday. “My expectation is he’s going to hit today in the cage,” Roberts said. “I think that once he hits, how he comes out of it will be telling for tomorrow.” IL stints can be backdated up to three days, so it makes sense that a final decision would come tomorrow. Ohtani’s status as a two-way player complicates matters. He’ll be required to go on the 15-day IL, not the 10-day IL. The Dodgers will be without his bat for an extended stretch if he heads to the injured list. Ohtani struck out four times in his most recent appearance on Wednesday against the Cardinals. Roberts told reporters after that game that the slugger didn’t look like himself, and the team would consider giving him a day off. What started as a rest day has now extended into Ohtani’s longest absence from the lineup in his Dodgers tenure. It was less than a week ago that Ohtani was trending toward a return to the mound as part of a tandem approach with Tyler Glasnow. That appearance never came to fruition. Each passing day of nagging injuries makes it less likely that Ohtani will contribute as a pitcher down the stretch. Here are a few more items from the Dodgers… - Ohtani wasn’t the only one out of the lineup on Saturday. Max Muncy and Dalton Rushing were both scratched. Muncy is dealing with an illness. Rushing was removed from the starting nine with right elbow soreness. It’s a worrisome development for Rushing, who is playing through a UCL tear. He hasn’t been cleared to play the field, but he’s pinch-hit in every game since coming off the IL. Tonight would’ve been his first start since being activated. - Teoscar Hernandez has recently gone back to a batting stance that includes a toe tap, notes Bill Plunkett of the Orange County Register. It’s helped the outfielder get back on track at the plate. “Everything is clicking,” Hernandez said. I’m seeing the ball better so better decisions, better contact, better at-bats. Everything is the way it should be.” Hernandez was 13-for-34 with four extra-base hits over his last 10 games heading into Saturday. - Roberts tabbed Justin Wrobleski to handle the bulk of the innings in Sunday’s series finale against the Nationals, relays Plunkett. The lefty allowed three runs (two earned) over two innings in his first appearance off the injured list on Tuesday. Wrobleski had a minimum stint on the IL with forearm inflammation. Bobby Miller was also activated off the 60-day IL today and could factor into Sunday’s plans. - Emmet Sheehan is an option to start Monday’s game against the Reds, per Plunkett. Sheehan spent most of August in the minors. He’s pitched well at Triple-A, allowing three earned runs over four outings. Sheehan has 24 strikeouts in 18 innings with Oklahoma City. He has a 5.29 ERA in the majors this year, but the solid stretch in the minors may afford him another opportunity with the big-league club. Photo courtesy of Kiyoshi Mio, Imagn Images

entry.title: 3 takeaways from BYU’s dominant win over Utah Tech - Deseret News
entry.body: BYU left no doubt in its season opener. The Cougars kicked off their 2026 campaign with an emphatic 63-7 win over Utah Tech Saturday at LaVell Edwards Stadium, leading 42-0 at halftime and never looking back. 3 takeaways Legend Glasker was legendary. No player garnered more fall camp buzz at BYU than Glasker, and in his first college game, the freshman receiver out of Lehi High more than lived up to the hype. Glasker’s first career touch resulted in a 9-yard rushing score. His first catch became a 26-yard touchdown, and he’d find the end zone again later on a 33-yard haul. In all, Glasker racked up 81 total yards on five touches, tripling Utah Tech’s team touchdown total on his own. With Glasker’s versatile skillset, he could easily become a new favorite target for Bear Bachmeier and the alpha within BYU’s receiver room. Perhaps Saturday against Utah Tech is just a sample of what else is to come. Kelly Poppinga’s defense (mostly) showed well. When the Cougar starters were on the field, Utah Tech was clearly overwhelmed — Tre Alexander grabbed an interception on the first play of the game, after all. In fact, after one quarter, BYU had more takeaways (two) than first downs allowed (one), and the Cougars surrendered just 52 yards in the first half. After halftime, however, Utah Tech fared much better against the BYU backups, orchestrating a 15-play touchdown drive and another 14-play series that ended with a goal line interception. Utah Tech went 5 of 7 on fourth down in the second half after going 0 for 6 before halftime. Additionally, the Trailblazers nearly doubled their yards per play average (2.2 to 4.1) from the first to second half. But as previously mentioned, BYU’s starters were excellent when they were on the field. Alexander and Evan Johnson each snagged an interception, Siale Esera had a sack, Tausili Akana recovered a fumble and Cade Uluave had two tackles for loss. The late slump for BYU’s defense shouldn’t sound any alarm bells. The Cougars were playing third and fourth-string players in a game that was well out of reach. When things mattered most, Poppinga’s unit did its job and did it well. Next week against Arizona will give us all a better idea of how good the defense truly is. BYU took care of business offensively. The Cougars are a top-15 team nationally. Utah Tech was a week removed from losing 54-0 to a fellow FCS squad. Anything less than a lopsided blowout would be quite disappointing for BYU. Luckily for Kalani Sitake’s crew, the Cougars did exactly what they were supposed to in notching a 56-point victory. They posted 521 yards of total offense, averaging 7.7 yards per play, committing no turnovers and only being forced to punt once. Bachmeier picked up right where he left off, completing 16 of 20 passes for 198 yards and three touchdowns while running for another score as well. Led by LJ Martin and freshman Devaughn Eka, BYU ran for 308 yards at nearly seven yards a pop, with five different players — Bachmeier, Eka, Glasker, Preston Rex and Journee Tonga — finding the end zone. Additionally, some of BYU’s special teams uncertainty cooled off a bit as Cannon DeVries emerged as a potential weapon in the return game, bringing a kickoff back 100 yards for a touchdown and averaging 37 yards per punt return as well.

entry.title: Mariska Hargitay Wins Two Emmys For ‘My Mom Jayne,’ Thanks Gloria Steinem From Stage - deadline.com
entry.body: Mariska Hargitay is warming up to host the televised Primetime Emmy Awards in the best way imaginable – by winning two Emmys for her documentary My Mom Jayne. The HBO film in which Hargitay explores the life and career of her late mother, the actress Jayne Mansfield, as well as a mystery over Mariska’s biological father, won Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special. Hargitay also claimed the Emmy for Outstanding Directing for a Documentary/Nonfiction Program. The honors came as the 78th Annual Primetime Emmy Awards kicked off Saturday night in Los Angeles with what were formerly called the Creative Arts Emmys. The show will continue Sunday evening from the Peacock Theater downtown, leading up to the televised Primetime Emmys on Monday, September 14 (airing on NBC and the Peacock streaming platform). Accepting the award for Documentary or Nonfiction Special, Hargitay acknowledged the feminist icon Gloria Steinem, who died Wednesday at the age of 92. Watch on Deadline “My hero and friend Gloria Steinem recently said, ‘Please tell your own story,’” Hargitay shared. “The most important thing we can do for each other is to know each other through stories. I got to know my mother through telling the story. It’s a gift that’s indescribable.” Accepting the trophy for directing, Hargitay commented, “I’m utterly overwhelmed. I just wanted to share with you that it took me a while when I decided to make this film during the pandemic. It took me a while to realize that this was my story to tell. I could direct it.” And she alluded again to Steinem’s counsel to women about “telling your own story,” saying, “I just want that invitation to go out, especially to women. I’m so excited to explore and discover and innovate new ways of telling stories from half of the earth’s population because we don’t hear from you enough. I can’t wait to get to know you.” It’s been an extraordinary year-plus for Hargitay, who is entering the 28th season as the star of Law & Order: SVU. In addition to premiering My Mom Jayne, she made her Broadway debut in Every Brilliant Thing, and then agreed to take on the challenge of hosting the Primetime Emmy Awards. “Dreaming is actually part of planning,” Hargitay said backstage at the Emmys after her two wins. “I’m at a place in my life where I just say yes, I said yes to Broadway, and I said yes to hosting the Emmys. When they called me, they thought it was a joke. It’s a year of firsts and a year of saying yes. Not limiting myself or not being governed by fear. What if it all works out? That’s the process of art. I’m in that place right now, I’ll figure it out. I’m really happy right now.” In the Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Special category, My Mom Jayne triumphed over John Candy: I Like Me; Marty, Life Is Short; Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!, and Ocean with David Attenborough (the latter film won Outstanding Cinematography for a Nonfiction Program and Outstanding Sound Editing For A Nonfiction Or Reality Program). In the documentary directing category, Hargitay was up against Lawrence Kasdan of Marty, Life Is Short; Judd Apatow and Michael Bonfiglio of Mel Brooks: The 99 Year Old Man!; Alexandria Stapelton for Sean Combs: The Reckoning, and Rebecca Miller for Mr. Miller, however, isn’t going home empty-handed. Her five-part docuseries about legendary filmmaker Martin Scorsese won the marquee category of Outstanding Documentary or Nonfiction Series. Robert De Niro, Leonardo DiCaprio, Jodie Foster, screenwriters Paul Schrader and Nicholas Pileggi, Spike Lee, and Daniel Day-Lewis (Miller’s husband) are among the luminaries who appear in the series. Scorsese himself sat down for intimate interviews in which he addressed his career highs and some early lows, his complicated romantic life, and his upbringing as an asthmatic child in New York City.

entry.title: Lee Chang-dong, Jeon Do-yeon and Sul Kyung-gu on Class, Desire and Reunion in Venice Competition Drama ‘Possible Love’
entry.body: Every great love story, in Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong‘s telling, is secretly a story about love that cannot happen — class, status or fate standing in the way. His new film dares to ask the opposite question, and it took him the better part of two decades, one abandoned script about a 2009 workers’ strike and a single idea from his co-writer to find an answer worth filming. “When we think about a love story, usually the most typical love story we think about is love that cannot come true,” Lee says about Venice competition title “Possible Love,” his first feature since 2018’s “Burning.” “So to simply put it, you could say that all of these love stories are called impossible love, so to speak.” “Possible Love” follows Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon), who works at a mask factory while dealing with the fallout of her husband Ho-seok’s (Sul Kyung-gu) layoff and the strike that followed it. A funeral draws the couple into contact with Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong), a filmmaker shooting a documentary about laid-off workers, and her husband Sang-woo (Zo In-sung); they are a couple whose money and detachment set them apart from Mi-ok and Ho-seok’s daily struggle. Once Mi-ok signs on to be filmed, a bond forms with Ye-ji, while something harder to name pulls her toward the unreadable Sang-woo, and the two households’ collision starts to crack open both marriages. Zo and Cho are working with Lee for the first time. Popular on Variety The mass layoff at the center of the film happened at a major Korean company in 2009, followed by a 70-day strike and a violent crackdown by authorities. Lee began developing a fictional treatment soon after but could not finish it. “Every time I create a film, what I need is a conviction that this story is worth telling in the format of a film,” he says, adding that he could never settle whether turning real workers’ pain into fiction, rather than documentary, would mean anything to him, to audiences or to cinema itself. The story only came back to life once his co-writer, Oh Jung-mi, suggested pairing it with the story of a filmmaker. “Because it is told adjacent to my own story as a filmmaker, I could be more honest in the storytelling,” Lee says, describing the addition as a new layer that gave him a way back in. That doubling lets him ask a question he says has followed him since his years as a novelist, long before he started directing. “When we deal with the lives of other people, are we worthy of telling their story, and are we not only using it for our own purposes? This is something that always I had in mind,” he says, adding that the question belongs to all filmmaking, not only documentaries, and that he wanted “Possible Love” to put it to the audience as much as to himself. He locates the film’s title in the same territory. “In our film, ‘Possible Love,’ as you can see in the title, it asks a question: what is love that is possible?” he says, noting that the love in question reaches beyond the romantic, to Ye-ji’s pull toward the people she films and to Ho-seok and Mi-ok’s marriage. On the distance between the two couples, he resists calling it simple class conflict: “Now we live at a time where class is really no longer just class,” he says, pointing to Sang-woo as someone who “deals with the amount of wealth and capital that is unfathomable by people like Mi-ok and Ho-seok.” Lee also traces the story to the 10th commandment, “thou shalt not covet,” and to Kieślowski’s “Dekalog 10.” “The former nine [commandments] all are about human actions. However, this very last one is about the human heart,” he says, framing the film’s real question as how much resistance to coveting is even possible “in this capitalist society we live today,” and noting that Ye-ji’s desire to claim other people’s lives for her documentary is its own version of the same impulse. Jeon, reuniting with Lee nearly 20 years after “Secret Sunshine,” found her way into Mi-ok through what they share rather than their circumstances. “I thought that the anxiety she harbors in her heart was something that I could relate to, because I also have that as well,” she says, describing Mi-ok as someone living with “a ticking time bomb in her heart.” She had read Mi-ok’s pull toward Sang-woo as desire on the page, then revised that once shooting began. “I came to think that it’s more about curiosity,” she says. She also connected with Mi-ok’s refusal to collapse under hardship, echoing something she says has been said about her own work as an actor. “I don’t think that she is going to crumble and just be sad,” Jeon says, calling the character someone who won’t “let go of hope.” Stepping back onto Lee’s set after two decades felt easier than she expected. Where “Secret Sunshine” had been “very intense,” she says this time “I felt so comfortable and so much at ease when I stepped onto the set.” She adds that “Possible Love” arrives at a point in her career when she has grown frustrated watching commercial appeal crowd out character work in the Korean industry, and that the project is “so significant for me at this juncture.” Sul, reuniting with Lee 24 years after “Oasis,” which won Lee the Venice Film Festival‘s best director prize in 2002, agreed to the project before reading a script. “I think just the name Lee Chang-dong means complete trust for me,” he says, adding that “Peppermint Candy,” their first film together, remains the role he still calls his most representative work. Getting back on set stirred the same nerves he felt making that film decades earlier. “I just feel like all of this is the power that director Lee holds,” he says. Playing Ho-seok’s silence, he says, was the harder task. He describes the character as carrying rage, guilt and shame after being laid off, his pride “thrown on the ground,” with only “silence and just glances” as tools, all beneath an outwardly unbothered exterior. Asked whether he saw himself in the role, Sul calls Ho-seok “a universal Korean man,” caught between a tough exterior and a wound he never lets show. He’s less certain how much that particular tension has shifted since “Peppermint Candy”: “It has been three decades, so I do think there has been some changes,” he says, though he stops short of generalizing about Korean masculinity broadly. Lee, asked about Korean cinema’s rise since his 1997 debut “Green Fish,” when he says international interest in Korean film was “close to none,” credits the industry’s current global standing to younger filmmakers, adding that how optimistic to be about its future “is a question not for me to discuss, but something that I do believe the younger filmmakers of today should be asking themselves.” “Possible Love” heads next to the Toronto, Busan and London film festivals. It opens theatrically on Oct. 23 before streaming on Netflix starting Nov.
entry.summary: Every great love story, in Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong’s telling, is secretly a story about love that cannot happen — class, status or fate standing in the way. His new film dares to ask the opposite question, and it took him the better part of two decades, one abandoned script about a 2009 workers’ strike […]

entry.title: Wim Wenders on Why He Made a Documentary About Architect Peter Zumthor, and How Brad Pitt Helped Get It Made
entry.body: Wim Wenders’ 3D documentary “From Inside Out,” which has its world premiere at the Venice Film Festival on Sunday, examines the work of Pritzker Prize-winning architect Peter Zumthor, paying particular attention to the design and construction of the David Geffen Galleries of the Los Angeles County Museum of Art. In the film, the result of a 14-year collaboration with the architect, Zumthor explains how he approaches the design of his buildings so that they are in harmony with their surroundings and serve the people who will use them. Wenders first came across Zumthor’s work when the architect took part in a competition for a gallery building in Berlin, opposite the Neues Museum. “It looked splendid but wasn’t built,” Wenders explains. Popular on Variety Among those appearing in the film are filmmakers Ava DuVernay and Werner Herzog, actress Ever Anderson, singer-songwriter Sophie Hunger, visual artist Tarek Atoui, and actress and dancer Aoi Yamada, who also appeared in Wenders’ “Perfect Days.” Brad Pitt serves as executive producer on the film. Variety submitted a series of questions to the director about the film, and publishes his written responses below: When did you first meet Peter Zumthor? As a commission for the 13th Architecture Biennale, I made a short film on him: “Notes From a Day in the Life of an Architect.” We got along great and decided to do “something real” together, a long feature film. What motivated you to make a film about him? I have loved architecture since my childhood and always wanted to know more about the work of an architect. Zumthor seemed like an ideal partner, as his work is truly rethinking the very basis of what architecture is or can be. What was it about his architecture that made it a suitable subject for a film? The fact that Zumthor works in quite a radical way. He spends more time on each building than most of his colleagues, both in the design and the construction process. Like other artists, he feels that a building is not done or finished with the approved plans, but that it is shaped only in its construction process. As a filmmaker, I share that approach. Why did you choose to shoot it as a 3D film? No visual language would be more suitable for architecture than 3D. Can you speak about the role of the people in the film? They are not “actors.” They are real people who visit the buildings by Peter Zumthor or live in them. They see these places, and the audience sees and experiences them through their eyes. Was the construction of the David Geffen Galleries pivotal to the film? We had already started the film when the building of the new LACMA became real and was no longer just a project. Peter and I agreed that the film should definitely include this milestone in his career, and what was already a “long-term observation” now became even longer. I also met Brad Pitt at that moment, as he had been an ardent defender of Zumthor’s building, even in front of the City Council, and he agreed to help make the film. Can you explain how Zumthor contributed to the making of the film? We shot countless times with Zumthor over a period of 14 years, both in his office in Switzerland as well as all over the world. He always made himself available for our film, opened his archives and answered each and every one of my questions.

entry.title: Dev Benegal’s Judith Blum Reddy Doc ‘Everything Is Not OK’ Acquired by Watermelon Pictures, Annemarie Jacir Aboard as EP (EXCLUSIVE)
entry.body: Watermelon Pictures has acquired “Everything Is Not OK,” a documentary from director Dev Benegal chronicling the life of artist Judith Blum Reddy. The film will stream exclusively on Watermelon+, the distributor’s streaming platform. The producing team pairs Benegal with Min(d) Studio’s Maya S. Patel and Neeraj Jain, while Annemarie Jacir (“Palestine 36”) has signed on as executive producer. “Everything Is Not OK” follows Reddy, whose work as an artist has been shaped by the Holocaust and by displacements that carried her from New York to Paris and ultimately India. The documentary threads Reddy’s story together with those of fellow artists Nil Yalter, Zarina and Camille Billops, each of whom channeled displacement into their art. Palestinian, Kashmiri and Indian poets are interwoven throughout, framing the film as a meditation on remembering what has been erased from home and pushing back once staying quiet stops being an option. Popular on Variety “For Judy, making art is an act of confrontation. A refusal to let erasure win,” Benegal said. “‘Everything Is Not OK’ is not only a portrait of an artist — it is a meditation on what it means to create, remember and resist through art when silence is no longer an option.” Jacir signed on as executive producer after connecting with the film’s exploration of memory and resistance. “In a moment when the world tilts towards intolerance, Judy’s story is a reminder that memory refuses to disappear and art can still be an act of resistance,” Jacir said. Jacir and actor Adam Bakri both lend their voices to the film’s readings of revolutionary poetry. Benegal is also known for directing “English, August” and “Road, Movie.” A restored version of “English, August,” undertaken by the Film Heritage Foundation, is playing at the Venice Film Festival. The 1994 film is based on Upamanyu Chatterjee’s novel “English, August: An Indian Story” and stars Rahul Bose. The creative team behind “Everything Is Not OK” includes Jain doubling as producer and additional cinematography; Patel as producer; Dhruv Goel composing the music; Jean-Luc Panda as cinematographer; Mona Gesbel as editor; Anurag Jadhao on sound design; and Rob Sciarratta as colorist. Watermelon Pictures launched in 2024. Its distribution and production credits include “From Ground Zero” and “All That’s Left of You” alongside “Palestine 36,” all three shortlisted in the Academy Award’s international feature category, plus the Oscar-nominated “The Voice of Hind Rajab.” Hamza Ali and co-founder Badie Ali brought the Watermelon+ platform online in May 2025, positioning it as the largest single collection of Palestinian film ever assembled in one place. entry.title: San Sebastian, Busan-Bound Taiwanese Coming-of-Age Drama ‘Will You Still Be My Friend’ Boarded for Sales by Moveria, Trailer Unveiled (EXCLUSIVE)
entry.body: Paris-based Moveria has boarded international sales on Taiwanese filmmaker Lu Po-Shun’s debut feature “Will You Still Be My Friend,” which is set for a berth in San Sebastián’s New Directors sidebar before travelling on to the Busan International Film Festival. A Taiwan-Singapore co-production, the film follows two young boys, played by Jaden Wang and Aloysius Looi, whose bond comes under strain as tensions build between their families and the surrounding rural community. Rounding out the cast are Lung Tien Hsiang, Lu Yi-Ching, Andie Chen, Kate Pang and Xing Chang. A trailer has been unveiled. Popular on Variety Eric Chou Tseng-Chen and Yu-Hao Su produced the film through Taiwan-based InLight Film Studio and Verdant Peak Films. At San Sebastián, the film is also in contention for the Sebastiane Award, an honor for films exploring LGBTQIA+ themes and experiences. In the story, an escalating feud in a rural Taiwanese village forces a boy to shield his secret friendship with his Singapore-raised best friend from the adult conflicts threatening to divide them, even as he privately begins to question his own feelings for his friend. “What I really connected with is the relationship between the two boys,” said Yasmin Porangaba, Moveria’s head of sales and acquisition. “When they’re alone, everything feels simple, light and natural. It’s like they have this little world of their own, almost like a secret, because the people around them don’t really get them. Around their families and friends, they have to fit into certain roles, while their time together feels like a space where none of that matters. “I also love that the film never defines what they are to each other. They’re too young to really make sense of it themselves, and I like that the film leaves that open. They know how to be there for each other, forgive each other and just move forward in a way that feels surprisingly mature. The two boys are amazing together, the film is beautiful, and that’s really what made us want to represent it.” The film has already built an international industry profile through selections including Ties That Bind, the Golden Horse Film Project Promotion, EFM Far East in Progress and HAF Goes to Cannes at the Cannes Film Market. Lu’s short film “Wild Tides” earlier earned him the best director prize at the Taipei Film Awards. He also directed the segment “Way Home” in the 2018 anthology film “Ten Years Taiwan,” part of Busan’s A Window on Asian Cinema lineup. “Will You Still Be My Friend” is his first feature as director. Producer Eric Chou Tseng-Chen brings experience in sales, acquisitions, project management and festival promotion on the international circuit, and co-produced “Get the Hell Out,” which had its bow in the Midnight Madness lineup at Toronto in 2020. Yu-Hao Su has produced credits such as Shatara Michelle Ford’s “Test Pattern,” a Film Independent Spirit Award and Gotham Award nominee, as well as “Fragrance of the First Flower.” Su also executive produced Ford’s “Dreams in Nightmares,” which screened in Berlinale’s Panorama section. InLight Film Studio, a Taiwan-based outfit, spans film and visual art projects, while Verdant Peak Films is dedicated to bringing Taiwanese stories to global audiences and developing international co-productions. Verdant Peak’s recent credits include “Dreams in Nightmares.” Moveria, headquartered in Paris, operates as an independent production and sales outfit for international markets.

entry.title: Tupac trial spotlights decades of US police failures in solving the case - The Guardian
entry.body: While Las Vegas sent two detectives to Compton and they did interview Anderson, nothing came of the interview, Ladd testified. The trial was not the first time the former Compton detective has spoken publicly about the Shakur case: Ladd went public about his frustrations with how Las Vegas police handled the case in a 2002 Los Angeles Times investigation, saying that Compton police had told Las Vegas police a week after the attack that they believed Anderson was the shooter, but that the Las Vegas police rejected the theory. When Compton police gave Las Vegas police a chance to interview Anderson and other gang members they believed to be involved in Shakur’s murder, “Las Vegas expressed no interest whatsoever in talking to any of them,” Ladd said in 2002, saying that their interview with Anderson lasted only 20 minutes. Anderson was publicly identified as a potential suspect in Shakur’s killing less than a month after the shooting, and was widely rumored within Compton to be the one who killed the hip-hop icon. Anderson, his lawyer and his family repeatedly denied he was involved in the killing, but those close to him told the Guardian after his death that the allegations that he shot Shakur shaped his daily life, and that strangers would sometimes recognize him as Shakur’s killer. In 1997, while Anderson was still alive, Tupac’s mother, Afeni Shakur, filed a civil lawsuit accusing him of murdering her son.

entry.title: Andy Williams a.k.a. ‘The Butcher’ collapses at Enjoy Wrestling show - POST Wrestling
entry.body: The Butcher, suffered a medical event at an independent show on Saturday night, which led to the show’s cancellation. Williams was teaming with longtime partner The Blade (Jesse Guilmette) against TME for Enjoy Wrestling at Mr. Small’s Theatre in Millvale, Pennsylvania. Enjoy Wrestling has posted the following statement: Andy collapsed at the end of his match this evening. Our doctors on staff tended to him immediately, administering CPR until the ambulance arrived. We sent everyone home and are at the hospital now waiting for more information. Thanks to everyone who helped and has reached out POST Wrestling has heard from several people who attended the show and shared their eyewitness accounts of what happened. From Rich Fann, who attended the show: It was towards the end of the match. He seemed to be in a bit of dire straits, they went to a finish, and he was a little wobbly. Andy then went down, and Blade helped him up a bit and then tried to get folks to help – but no one saw at first. Once they saw, both the crew, the paramedics, and the crowd worked in unison. Cleared a path, paid attention to the calls on the mic, and then got him chest compressions, ice, and then the AED. Then they boarded and got him out of there. From a second person in attendance: He was in a match with Blade against TME which seemed to go short as he left the ring for Blade to take a pinfall. He then was outside for the remainder. I thought maybe he was concussed but my friend said he looked gassed. They paused the show for an intermission as Enjoy staff and fellow talent tried to help him. They moved him near an exit door. Nothing really happened for 15 or so minutes until police arrived and then EMTs 5-10 mins later when they announced the show was ending early. Fann noted on BlueSky that paramedics were in attendance for the show. We are continuing to monitor this story and sending our best to Andy Williams.

entry.title: Volcano eruption leaves 150,000 passengers stranded in Indonesia
entry.body: Volcano eruption leaves 150,000 passengers stranded in Indonesia - Published More than 150,000 passengers have been left stranded after a volcanic eruption forced Indonesian authorities to temporarily suspend operations at six airports. Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta International Airport was the first to be closed on Sunday morning after ash from Anak Krakatau was detected in airspace near the airport. Transport minister Dudy Purwagandhi said so far 467 flights have been affected and asked airlines to consider diverting some flights to other airports. The volcano had started erupting late on Friday night, generating continuous seismic activity, lava fountains, and booming sounds across surrounding regions. Two more eruptions happened early on Sunday, authorities said. The transport ministry said the pause in operations mainly affected flights to and from Singapore, also other international routes including Doha, Sydney and Kuala Lumpur. Purwagandhi said the decision to temporarily close more airports was made after tests found that volcanic ash had spread towards West Java. He urged airlines to speed up processes for refunding tickets for passengers who have been affected by flight cancellations, and for airlines to provide timely information to those with upcoming flights to avoid overcrowding at airports. According to Indonesia's meteorological agency BMKG, ash reached as far as 20,000ft (6,000m) on Java on east of the volcano, and 50,000ft (15,000m) west of the volcano on the Sumatra side. Authorities have confirmed there is no tsunami warning linked to the recent activity of the volcano, which is in the Sunda Strait between the islands of Java and Sumatra. The health minister has urged residents in affected areas to stay indoors and wear face masks to protect against respiratory, eye, and skin risks. According to local newspaper Kompas, several schools cancelled activities on Saturday after students and residents reported eye irritations from the ash, while some fishermen had cancelled fishing trips at sea similarly reporting sore eyes. One resident, Aldi Candra Prayogi, told the outlet that he felt since Friday evening and it felt like "small grains of sand had gotten into my eyes", and that he needs to use eye drops to ease the irritation. The dust is so thick that he has to sweep the front yard of his house every five minutes, he also said. Anak Krakatau, which means Child of Krakatoa, has been sporadically active since it emerged from the sea at the beginning of last century in the caldera formed after the 1883 eruption of Mount Krakatoa. The volcano - also known as Anak Krakatoa - collapsed in December 2018, triggering a huge tsunami which killed over 400 people, and displaced and injured thousands more on the nearby coastlines of Sumatra and Java. Scientists found that some of the chunks of rock that slid from the volcano when it collapsed were about 70-90m high. Indonesia sits on the Pacific Ring of Fire, where there is high volcanic and seismic activity because of a line of frequent earthquakes and volcanic eruptions that circles virtually the entire Pacific rim. Related topics - Published2 October 2019 - Published24 December 2018
entry.summary: More than 150,000 airline passengers are stranded after ash was detected in airspace near Jakarta following the eruptions.

entry.title: German voters head to polls as far-right AfD party eyes historic state win - Al Jazeera
entry.body: Germans vote in eastern state as far-right AfD eyes power Saxony-Anhalt elections could see AfD become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since WWII. Voting is under way in the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt that could see the Alternative for Germany (AfD) become the first far-right party to take power at a state level since World War II. Recent surveys place AfD at 40 percent, ahead of the centre-right Christian Democrats (CDU) at 23 percent. Recommended Stories list of 3 items - list 1 of 3Germany’s far right AfD eyes election breakthrough in Saxony-Anhalt - list 2 of 3Germany’s far-right AfD eyes historic first in state election - list 3 of 3Thousands protest in Germany as far-right AfD party meets AfD has led comfortably in the pre-election opinion polls for months and has a chance at winning an absolute majority if several smaller parties fail to clear the 5 percent threshold to enter the parliament. A CDU-led administration under incumbent state premier Sven Schulze is the most likely outcome if the AfD does not win a majority. Weeks of coalition talks could follow the vote, depending on which parties surpass the 5 percent minimum. AfD candidate Ulrich Siegmund, who was previously a member of the CDU, predicted gaining an absolute majority that would lead the anti-establishment party to national victory in 2029. He was named “Germany’s most dangerous man” by the influential magazine Der Spiegel. “It was the others who erected the firewalls,” he told German tabloid Bild. “If no one wants to work with us, then we’ll just have to do it alone.” An absolute majority would allow AfD to bypass mainstream parties’ “firewall” noncooperation policy, which the far-right party has already done at the local level. For the AfD, the Saxony-Anhalt elections are a stepping stone towards its larger ambition: securing national power in the 2029 federal elections. The CDU is led by deeply unpopular German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. At a local campaign rally in Lower Saxony a week before the election, Merz urged other politicians to engage with AfD more effectively. “We must address the issues at hand. We must also address our choice of words,” Merz said, referring to a statement by the AfD’s state leader in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Reichardt. Reichardt previously told the AfD’s youth organisation that Germany had become “a lazy, anti-social bum reeking of dope”. Thousands of demonstrators gathered for a festival in support of democracy the night before the crucial election. Rally organisers estimated that between 15,000 and 20,000 people attended the demonstration. Initial results are expected at about 16:00 GMT (6pm local time) on Sunday.
entry.summary: German voters head to polls as far-right AfD party eyes historic state win Al Jazeera Germany’s far-right AfD is poised for power – and split on whether to cozy up to Trump CNN Far-right AfD predicted to win big in crucial German state election The Guardian The Ex-Salesman Bringing the Far Right to the Cusp of Power in Germany The New York Times ‘We Can Only Win’: The Rise of the Far Right in Eastern Germany Bloomberg.com

entry.title: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover
entry.body: Nigel Farage tells BBC he 'wasn't listening' during foreign donor talks filmed undercover - Published Nigel Farage has said he "frankly wasn't listening" during a conversation with his former chief of staff and an undercover reporter discussing what appears to have been a scheme to funnel foreign money to Reform UK. His former chief of staff Dan Jukes and ex-head of policy James Orr have both been removed from their jobs after an investigation recorded them talking about how to get money to the party from an American donor and asking a fake company to pay for polling. Jukes has denied doing anything wrong. Orr has told Sky News he will co-operate fully with Reform's internal investigation. In an interview with the BBC, the Reform leader said he was not listening to the discussion and revealed his family are "begging" him to leave his job amid increasing pressure. In a film by Verbatim Investigations and Channel 4 News, Farage and Jukes were present during a conversation in which it is suggested the US donor gives Â£500,000 to Reform through his UK-based son. Under electoral law, donors to UK political parties must be a UK registered voter, or a company registered in the UK, so cannot give money from abroad through a British resident. The proposed donation was never made as it was part of an undercover sting, but that it was seemingly entertained has sparked questions. When asked about the exchange by reporters at Reform's party conference on Friday, Farage said he was questioning whether the arrangement was above board. In an interview to be broadcast on Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg, he has now said: "I am not a compliance officer. I was in the middle of canvassing in the Clacton by-election. I frankly wasn't even listening." "I was told there was a global family office based in London, so the money could have come from Singapore," he said of the conversation in the Channel 4 film. "The money could come from all over the world, you know. Income could have came from all over the world into a family office based in London. I know donation law better than anybody. "Frankly, the two individuals involved here have never been involved in fundraising before and they shouldn't have been involved directly in fundraising. They should have done basic checks and nobody, nobody should be brought to me, unless they've been vetted from." The row over the Channel 4 film has threatened to capsize Reform's conference, with Labour and the Liberal Democrats calling on the Metropolitan Police to investigate the claims. The force is assessing whether or not to investigate. Jukes and Orr - both senior figures in Farage's inner circle - have stood down pending the outcome of the party's internal investigation, but political opponents are demanding that Farage is investigated and takes accountability. Farage categorically denied that Reform had ever taken money from a foreign entity by channelling it through a UK donor. But as pressure ramps up on Farage in the latest crisis to rock Reform, he also told the BBC that "for the first time", he does not have his family's support to be in politics. "They would rather I packed it up and walked away," he said. He added he had not considered standing down, but "when you've got your family begging you to, it's not easy". Farage also condemned the hundreds of masked "stop the boats" protesters who descended on the Port of Dover on Saturday morning, causing major travel disruption. Farage said he "deplored" anyone wearing masks or balaclavas at public demonstrations. He added: "You should not be allowed to be masked up, balaclava-ed up and go out and protest on the streets of our country. It is wrong at every level. So I deplore what is happening in Dover today." Speaking after watching the interview, Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds said: "For a political party that don't like foreigners much they do seem to have a soft spot for foreign cash. "We have rules in this country about how our democracy works and everyone has to stick to them." He added: "I think you see someone struggling to decide whether they're really serious about trying to run for power or want to keep the protest going." Analysis: Farage may have to pay more attention There's no question the allegations in the Channel 4 film have been embarrassing for Reform, and disrupted what they hoped would be a conference about their plans for office if they win the next General Election. Everywhere around the huge, draughty exhibition hall in Birmingham are giant posters and placards saying, "Reform - the first 100 days". They wanted to herald their deal with a serious contender to be the next French President, Jordan Bardella, to deal with small boats. They were keen to highlight the promise to cut income tax if they win the election, scheduled to be in 2029. They wanted to talk about their proposals for education, welfare, planning, and the rest. Party members, delighted to have a reason to get together, have taken part in those sessions, applauded and cheered in the hall; gone wild for Farage on stage. But for the rest of the country, most of the noise from the conference will have been the huge and awkward story about the toxic mix of politics and money. What is harder to assess is the impact this mess will have on Farage's standing with the public, after a tricky summer and a recent poll slump. At the top of the party there is a quiet admission that what has happened here is a genuine mistake. One senior figure told me they could brush off other claims of murky funding, confident nothing had gone wrong - but they conceded these claims do matter, and that for a certain vital percentage of voters, it would "cause them to ask questions". No one is pretending it's just what Farage tried to joke was a "little, local difficulty". And there is a private acknowledgement that stories like this can be off putting to voters beyond Reform's no doubt very enthusiastic base. Another party source told me they were "totally blindsided" by the revelations; stunned "there'd just been no diligence" and in disbelief at how Jukes and Orr, who both say they'd done nothing wrong, seem to have behaved. A different member of the party's top team said, "hopefully, it's just growing pains". In other words, Reform's developed so fast that sometimes mistakes are made. But they told me: "The party has to step up â sometimes the people that got us here, aren't the people for the next stage". Among Farage's fans at the conference, I found different views. One member was convinced the party is treated unfairly: "It's the blob, it's all against him," she said. But another young Reform enthusiast rejected that, telling me: "It's all documented and there on camera â Nigel has to be more careful about what party members say." But there is a sense of "here we go again". When I asked another member what they thought of the financial scandal, a weary answer, "Which one?" This time last year in the same conference complex, Reform felt like they were simply sweeping all before them. Twelve months on, they are having to work harder, the scrutiny is more intense, and the pressure only growing. Farage's claim that he "wasn't listening" to the conversation was telling â to get to power without more of these kinds of serious embarrassments, he may have to pay more attention to what is going on. entry.summary: The Reform leader also told the BBC's Laura Kuenssberg that his family are "begging" him to leave his job.

entry.title: Taylor's place among greats set in stone after extraordinary swansong
entry.body: Fierce inside the ring yet unassuming outside of it - even factoring in an impulse-buy speedboat, since sold - superlatives such as trailblazer, icon and Ireland's greatest sportsperson are not hyperbolic, for Taylor's status as a legend is in no way cliched. She has indicated she will remain in the sport, but for now, there is time to savour an extraordinary career, with her place among boxing's greats set in stone. Irish boxing is going to be a lesser place. "I'm retired now so I can eat what I want, but I'm just going to enjoy a nice celebration and look back on a dream ending to a dream career. "My story is the story of everyone in this room: we all have our ups and downs. I think people resonate with your vulnerabilities and your successes - saw me cope with the heartbreak of Rio, the Chantelle Cameron loss and personal difficulties.
entry.summary: Fairytale endings in boxing are a rarity, but Irish icon Katie Taylor sails off into the sunset after the most perfect of farewells at Dublin's towering Croke Park.

entry.title: Ukraine war briefing: Zelenskyy links Russian strikes on Kyiv airports to US envoys' visit - The Guardian
entry.body: - Russian attacks on Kyiv and Boryspil international airports were “clearly” a reaction to the possibility of the US negotiators flying to Kyiv after talks in Moscow, the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has said. On Saturday, Zelenskyy said Kyiv had “taken note of this Russian move, and next week we will adjust our operation accordingly regarding Russian airspace, which has become dangerous because of our drones and missiles in the sky. Of course, there are and will be no threats to diplomacy from our side.” Both airports service the Ukrainian capital. - There was no comment from the US envoys, Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff, who were visiting Moscow for the first time since January. They flew out of Moscow soon after the talks and were due to meet Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Sunday. The Kremlin’s tone appeared unchanged. After three hours of talks, an aide to Vladimir Putin, Yuri Ushakov, said the Russian president had told the US pair that Russia was making “real progress” on the battlefield, was confident of achieving its goals, and stressed the necessity of addressing “all the root causes of the conflict”. Ushakov said the Americans had “outlined a number of ideas regarding possible avenues for a settlement”, but he did not say what those ideas were. - The air war between Russia and Ukraine has intensified as troops have struggled to make progress along the 1,250km (775-mile) frontline. Russia has recently been using fast-flying, jet-powered drones, and the recurring wail of air raid sirens has become part of daily life in Kyiv. Kremlin spokesperson Dmitry Peskov posted online that Putin had ordered the military not to strike Kyiv for three days, starting at midnight on Saturday. However, he said Russia had not yet agreed to a broader three-day ceasefire. Zelenskyy has said Ukraine is prepared to refrain from strikes on Moscow through to Monday. - Russian attacks killed five employees and wounded five others at an industrial facility in the Dnipropetrovsk region, said the local military administration head, Oleksandr Hanzha. “A locksmith, an electrician, a plumber and a machinist. They were simply working their shift. They were doing their job when enemy missiles cut off their lives.” Russia’s defence ministry said it had carried out strikes on two metallurgical plants that it claimed were sites for military production. - A 62-year-old man was wounded, and several homes and an apartment building damaged, in a separate attack on the region’s Nikopol district, Hanzha said. The city of Dnipro and the nearby Pidhorodne community were among the areas hit. One person died and five other were injured, including two men who were hospitalised in serious condition. A sixth civilian was injured in an attack on the Nikopol district. - Other deadly Russian attacks took place in Chuhuiv in Ukraine’s eastern Kharkiv region, on the Bucha district of Ukraine’s Kyiv region, and on a shopping centre in the southern Mykolaiv region. In Russia’s Belrogod region on the border with Ukraine, two people were killed and three others wounded by Ukrainian attacks on Saturday, local authorities said. Russia launched ballistic missiles from its Rostov and Voronezh regions and deployed 167 attack drones, Ukraine’s air force said on Saturday.

entry.title: US envoys hold talks with Zelensky in Kyiv after meeting Putin
entry.body: US envoys hold talks with Zelensky in Kyiv after meeting Putin - Published Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelensky has held a first round of talks in Kyiv with Donald Trump's top envoys, in their first visit since Russia's full-scale invasion. Steve Witkoff, sitting opposite the Ukrainian leader, told reporters the US team felt "encouraged" by what he called a "substantive" and important discussion. Jared Kushner said the US president had instructed them to find a way to end the war and "create the right conditions for a long-term, durable peace". Ahead of the meeting, Zelensky said Ukraine was ready to talk about bringing "the end of the war closer". But he said security guarantees would be required as well as a dignified post-war peace. - The 'thorny' issues that threaten to derail a Russia-Ukraine peace deal - Published30 December 2025 Kushner told the Ukrainian president that Trump was "very determined to see an end of this war", and thanked the UK, Germany and France for their efforts in trying to achieve peace. Witkoff added that the US negotiators would continue for "as long as it takes", praising Zelensky for his "unsurpassed" hospitality on their trip. The Ukrainian leader earlier greeted Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's St Sophia Cathedral, near where a Russian drone hit the headquarters of Ukraine's security services on Friday. On Saturday, the two envoys met Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow for talks on ending the war that were described as "frank" and "constructive" by the Kremlin. The envoys travelled to Kyiv by train after flying to Poland â Zelensky told the media that it was not possible for them to land their plane despite preparations. Putin and Zelensky agreed to halt strikes on each other's capitals for three days while the negotiators carry out their trip. While Witkoff and Kushner were in talks at the Kremlin on Saturday, Zelensky said he and his team were "ready for a substantive conversation". On Sunday, Zelensky wrote on social media that his country "has always been and will remain constructive". "We are interested in bringing the end of the war closer. "A dignified character of the postwar peace is needed. Our proposals are ready," he said. Overnight, Russian and Ukrainian forces continued to exchange strikes, with Ukraine confirming they struck an oil refinery, an airfield, and two air defence systems. The country's defence ministry said they targeted the Ryazan oil refinery, which supplies the Russian army, and an airfield in Rostov-on-Don. Earlier, Ukraine's Air Force reported that Russia attacked Ukraine with 108 long-range drones and small cruise missiles. The country's air defences downed 82 drones and six missiles, but 11 locations were hit, with debris falling at a further seven sites. Saturday's talks in Moscow lasted three hours and were held behind closed doors in Putin's official residence in the heart of the Russian capital, according to Russian state media. Details are still emerging, but both sides have given broadly positive remarks without going into specifics. Putin adviser Yuri Ushakov described the talks as "constructive, extremely frank". "The talks were not limited to an exchange of views on resolving the Ukrainian crisis - economic issues and potential major, mutually beneficial Russian-American projects were discussed in considerable detail," he said. Ushakov also said "note was made of the Russian army's tangible advances in the combat zone" and that there was acknowledgement that talks needed to address "the root causes of the conflict". Despite an escalation of Russian missile and drone strikes on Ukrainian cities including Kyiv, Russian ground forces have made very slow advances for most of the conflict, incurring enormous casualties. Russia still controls about one-fifth of Ukrainian territory - areas that it seized back in 2022. The talks come after Russia and Ukraine have intensified aerial attacks in recent months. Ukraine says it has struggled to repel ballistic missile attacks due to a lack of interceptor missiles, while Kyiv has focused its strikes on Russian economic infrastructure targets, notably oil installations.
entry.summary: Steve Witkoff tells reporters the US team feels "encouraged" by a "substantive" and important discussion.

entry.title: Indonesia volcano eruption cancels hundreds of flights in major airport hub - CBS News
entry.body: Indonesia volcano eruption cancels hundreds of flights in major airport hub A volcano eruption in Indonesia on Sunday has forced the cancellation of all flights at the capital city's airport as volcanic ash drifted across the western parts of the country. No casualties were reported and no evacuation orders were issued as the nearest settlement is more than 10 miles away, but authorities warned people to stay at least 2 miles clear of the crater. Footage filmed from a fishing boat at sea showed lava shooting up from the volcano into the air. Indonesia's Geological Agency said the volcanic island located in Indonesia's Sunda Strait between the main Java and Sumatra islands had showed signs of activity since Friday before erupting for 30 seconds in the early hours of Sunday. Volcanic ash spread across parts of Jakarta and Lampung province on Sumatra's southern tip, Indonesia's Center for Volcanology and Geological Hazard Mitigation said. AirNav Indonesia closed airspace around Soekarno-Hatta and Halim Perdanakusuma airports in Jakarta, as well as four other airports, including Radin Inten II Airport in Lampung, because of volcanic ash. By mid-afternoon local time in Jakarta, the closure had affected 516 flight movements, with 202 in Jakarta's Soekarno-Hatta airport alone that affected about 22,800 passengers, on Sunday. "Safety remains our top priority in every operational decision," Lukman F. Laisa, Ministry of Transportation director general of civil aviation, said in a statement. He warned flight schedules could face cascading disruptions affecting aircraft rotations, fleet availability and terminal capacity as airlines work to restore operations. The name of the volcano Anak Krakatau, means "child of Krakatau," which is the offspring of the famous Krakatau, whose monumental 1883 eruption triggered a period of global cooling. The eruption caused a tsunami in 2018 that killed at least 430 people in Sumatra and Java. Researchers believe volcanic activity triggered an underwater landslide and caused a large chunk of Anak Krakatau's southwest slope to collapse and displace a large volume of water. Scientists said Anak Krakatau island was only about a quarter of its original size after that eruption.
entry.summary: Indonesia volcano eruption cancels hundreds of flights in major airport hub CBS News Anak Krakatau: Volcano eruption closes six Indonesian airports BBC Volcanic island in Indonesia erupts, forcing the cancellation of hundreds of flights PBS Indonesia's main airport suspends operations after volcanic eruption Yahoo Volcanic eruption halts flights at Jakarta and seven other Indonesian airports The Guardian

entry.title: Russia’s Lavrov Calls Accusations of Moscow’s Involvement in Leipzig Drone Incident ‘Start of Real War - themoscowtimes.com
entry.body: Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Sunday that the accusations levelled at Moscow by the West that it was involved in the drone incident at Germany's Leipzig airport were, "by and large, the start of a real war," state news agency TASS reported. "All these statements by Merz about making Germany the leading military power in Europe once again — they are being put into practice. He is, in effect, declaring war on us," Lavrov said, referring to German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The German government said on Sept. 1 that it had concluded that Russia was responsible for an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport last month and ordered a series of measures in response, including the closure of a consulate and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin. Russia dismissed the German accusations as baseless, accusing Berlin of planting evidence to frame Russia for the attack. entry.title: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi - BBC
entry.body: Dozens feared trapped in collapsed building in Delhi A residential building in the Indian capital Delhi has collapsed with dozens of students feared trapped inside. Eyewitnesses told local media that as many as 50 people were inside the five-storey building in the Satya Niketan neighbourhood of south-west Delhi when it came down around 13:30 local time (08:00 GMT) on Sunday. At least one person was killed and two others are in a critical condition, NDTV reports, citing local police. Six people were said to have been rescued so far. There had been construction work going on in the basement of the building, Hostel Daze, which sits a short distance from the Delhi University campus. Many of the students staying there were thought to be in their rooms at the time of the collapse as there were no lessons on Sunday. A legislative assembly member said at the scene that some of the trapped students had been making calls from under the rubble. Eyewitnesses told local media that another building beside the hostel had also collapsed. Chief Minister of Delhi Rekha Gupta said an adjacent building had been evacuated "as a precautionary measure". "Every possible effort is being made to safely rescue those trapped," she added. Delhi Police said the building had only been 40 or 50 years old. The owner of a nearby shop told news agency ANI that it was under a 100-year lease and that the leaseholder had undertaken excavation work in the basement to increase their income. "They strengthened the upper building, but the pillars below were weak," he said, noting that the construction workers had also been buried. The National Students' Union of India called on the government to investigate the cause of the collapse and hold anyone found responsible to account. "Negligence with the safety of students and common people will not be tolerated at any cost," it said. Police are searching for the owner of the building, Times of India reports.
