entry.title: Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands - The Guardian
entry.body: Hawaii has declared a state of emergency as powerful Hurricane Lowell makes its way toward the islands, with the first impacts expected as soon as Monday. The storm is the third system in just over three weeks to threaten Hawaii during an active hurricane season in the central Pacific. Lowell remained a category 3 hurricane early on Sunday morning, packing winds of 125 miles per hour while moving north-west at six miles per hour. According to the forecast, Lowell will reach Hawaii as a category 2 hurricane. Its center could pass roughly 130 miles west of Ni’ihau or 170 miles west of Kauai between Monday evening and Tuesday morning. The threat comes amid unusually intense hurricane activity across the Pacific. As of Saturday, Hurricanes Karina, Lowell and Marie were all churning in the Pacific at the same time, marking the region’s first triple-hurricane stretch in a decade. The National Hurricane Center (NHC) was also monitoring a fourth potential system off the coast of Mexico. The Pacific averages only eight hurricanes per year, according to the NHC, making three simultaneous hurricanes highly unusual. Lowell’s projected offshore path is expected to keep the storm’s most dangerous winds away from Hawaii’s islands. But heavy rain, high surf and dangerous coastal conditions are still expected. A tropical storm warning is in effect for Kauai and Ni’ihau, where wind gusts above 39 miles per hour are possible over the next 48 hours. Lowell is the third storm in a matter of weeks to hit Hawaii as the climate crisis continues to increase the intensity and frequency of storms and other weather events. Tropical Storm Moke struck the southern part of Hawaii’s islands two weeks ago, bringing heavy rainfall and strong winds. That came just days after Hurricane Lala hit the region. The Hawaii governor Josh Green said Lala alone had caused at least $43m in infrastructure damage on the Big Island, along with another $4.6m in damage to homes. The escalating storm activity comes as the UN warns that this year’s El Niño is forecast to become the strongest on record in four decades. A statement released on Thursday described El Niño as being “supersized before our eyes”, adding that the world is in “the danger zone of extreme weather”. The latest data on the natural climate phenomenon shows a near 100% likelihood that the latest El Niño will continue through February 2027, the statement said. The stronger an El Niño becomes, the greater the chance it will significantly alter rainfall and temperature patterns around the world and help fuel extreme weather. The National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) has previously warned there is a 69% chance that this El Niño will be the strongest in 70 years.
entry.summary: Hawaii declares state of emergency as Hurricane Lowell approaches islands The Guardian Hurricane Lowell makes final turn toward Hawaii as islands brace for impacts CNN Hawaii residents told to expect tropical storm conditions as Hurricane Lowell passes to the west WFLA Kauai, Niihau under tropical storm warning as major Hurricane Lowell approaches Honolulu Star-Advertiser Hurricane Lowell threatens Hawaiian Islands with life-threatening surf NBC News

entry.title: Trump can’t stop changing the name of things and now has US state as his target - The Independent
entry.body: Trump can’t stop changing the name of things and now has US state as his target Trump wants to relabel New Mexico as New America days after changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake Ameria - Bookmark - CommentsGo to comments President Donald Trump has already changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico and Lake Ontario, and now he’s targeting a US state for a rebrand. Trump is spending the holiday weekend dreaming up his next demand to relabel America’s geography. He posted a map on Truth Social Sunday afternoon of New Mexico, but the word Mexico was crossed out and replaced with America. Relabeling the southwestern state on the U.S.-Mexico border as New America is reminiscent of an executive order he signed early in his second term, in which he changed the name of the Gulf of Mexico to the Gulf of America. In that January 2025 executive order titled “Restoring Names That Honor American Greatness,” Trump also changed the name of North America’s tallest peak, Denali in Alaska, back to Mount McKinley. Trump’s controversial relabeling of America’s geography didn’t stop there. The president signed an executive order late last month changing the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America amid an escalating trade war with Canada. Despite Trump repeatedly suggesting Canada become the nation’s 51st state, he recently told Fox News, “They think they’re a state, but they’re not a state. Why should we be subsidizing Canada?” Like Trump’s previous name changes on the U.S. map, his latest push to relabel New Mexico is sure to receive a wave of backlash. The group Republicans Against Trump was quick to post on X following Trump’s suggested name change of New Mexico, writing, “WTF is wrong with him?” When the president relabeled Lake Ontario, MapQuest refused to change its navigation app, writing on X, “We’re not changing it.” MapQuest then saw a surge in App Store rankings, with the company’s general manager Doug Berger saying, “We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they're familiar with. “Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app.” But tech giants Apple and Google caved to Trump, switching the name of Lake Ontario to Lake America for U.S. users of their maps apps, just as they did when the president demanded that the Gulf of Mexico be changed to the Gulf of America. Conservative journalist Eric Daugherty, however, was seemingly on board with the relabeling of New Mexico, writing on X, “This man is on a roll!” Trump’s ambitions to remake Washington, D.C., and the rest of the U.S. as he sees fit apparently go beyond the country, and even the world. Shortly after Trump’s post about relabeling New Mexico, he shared an image of the moon on Truth Social, with the caption “The moon is ours.” The 80-year-old leader has been heavily focused on his legacy during his second term, not just with changes to the map, but with renovations to the White House, including his massive and expensive ballroom, and the broader D.C. He’s also slapped his name and face on several buildings in the nation’s capital, most notably the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts. But a federal judge demanded his name be taken down from the center, and it was removed. Meanwhile, 73 percent of Americans say Trump hasn’t paid enough attention to the country’s most important problems, according to a CNN poll conducted by research firm SSRS and published in late July. entry.title: How MapQuest’s ‘Lake America’ stance sparked a massive App Store surge - Fox Business
entry.body: How MapQuest’s ‘Lake America’ stance sparked a massive App Store surge Hundreds of thousands of downloads sent MapQuest usage soaring to roughly 50 times its normal level MapQuest announced last week it had soared to the top of Apple's App Store navigation rankings following its decision to keep the former name of Lake America, Lake Ontario, on its maps. Hundreds of thousands of people downloaded the app after it reaffirmed it would continue using the historical names for lakes and gulfs, driving usage to roughly 50 times its normal level, according to MapQuest. The company said it was the No. 1 navigation app and the No. 8 free app overall in the U.S. Apple App Store as of 7 p.m. It also climbed to No. 2 among all free apps in Canada. "We took the same approach we did with the Gulf of Mexico: be part of the conversation, and give people an app that keeps the names they're familiar with," Doug Berger, general manager of MapQuest, said in a statement. APPLE MAPS RENAMES LAKE ONTARIO ‘LAKE AMERICA’ FOR US USERS AFTER TRUMP ORDER "Hundreds of thousands of people signaled to us this weekend that we got it right, by downloading our app," Berger added. The surge came after President Donald Trump ordered the body of water be renamed "Lake America." While Google Maps and Apple Maps adopted the change for U.S. users, MapQuest said it would continue displaying Lake Ontario, mirroring its earlier decision not to replace "Gulf of Mexico" with "Gulf of America." The company also expanded a feature allowing users to rename Lake Ontario within the app themselves, building on a tool it first launched for the Gulf of Mexico in February 2025. GOOGLE MAPS CHANGES LAKE ONTARIO TO ‘LAKE AMERICA’ FOR US USERS AFTER TRUMP ORDER: 'IT'S OFFICIAL!' Eric Yaverbaum, CEO of public relations firm Ericho Communications, told FOX Business the company capitalized on a cultural moment closely tied to its business. "What worked for them was they didn't force this," Yaverbaum said. "They're an expert at one thing: maps. They get to weigh in on one thing: maps." Yaverbaum said the viral attention presents MapQuest with an opportunity to revive its brand and reconnect with consumers. "You want to have a redo on your brand, you want to do a rebrand — boy, did they just open a big door," he said. GOOGLE MAPS UPDATE: GULF OF AMERICA, MOUNT MCKINLEY WILL BE IN AFTER TRUMP ORDERS NAME CHANGES However, Yaverbaum cautioned that companies should be careful when wading into political issues. "Generally speaking, I counsel my clients to stay out of politics. You're going to lose half your audience. So if you're going to play, play safely," he said. GET FOX BUSINESS ON THE GO BY CLICKING HERE Trump signed an executive order on Aug. 27 directing the Interior Department to officially rename Lake Ontario "Lake America" within the United States, amid ongoing trade tensions between Washington and Ottawa. MapQuest could not immediately be reached by FOX Business for comment.

entry.title: Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore
entry.body: Antonelli 'walks over water' for win that will go down in F1 folklore - Published Kimi Antonelli's stunning victory in the Italian Grand Prix from 19th on the grid will go down in Formula 1 folklore - and, remarkably, his team boss Toto Wolff said that he had seen it coming on Saturday. After Sunday's race, Wolff said that beforehand he thought that one of his two drivers was going to be standing on the top of the podium. It was an eye-opening statement given they started the race 17 places apart on the grid, George Russell on the front row alongside shock pole winner Pierre Gasly's Alpine; Antonelli on the penultimate row. "I thought one of the two is going to win," Wolff said. "Either George, because he was on the front row, or Kimi because he's going to walk over water, here at Monza. And I felt that yesterday also." Wolff was asked to explain why he felt a performance he was comparing to a miracle was on the cards. "It's been a while that I've seen drivers," he said. "Energy levels, mindset or behavioural pattern. I knew that was his mission today, to win the race. I chatted with his father yesterday. The father also saw that coming. "These are the moments where you can see how a weekend is panning out through the sessions that a special moment can come." - Antonelli takes stunning Monza win from 19th on grid - Published2 hours ago - Antonelli extraordinary as Gasly has superb weekend - driver ratings - Published3 hours ago For the Mercedes drivers, this race was all about the context of the weekend. Antonelli knew coming in that he would be starting at the back because of a grid penalty for using too many engines this year. Russell knew that he had to make the most of this opportunity and cut as much as he could out of his team-mate's 59-point championship lead. Fifth or sixth was the general consensus for what might be realistically possible for Antonelli, who himself said after the race that he had "thought a podium was possible". What changed everything was his remarkable progress in the early laps of the race, which brought to mind another Biblical miracle, the parting of the Red Sea. Antonelli was 14th after a relatively conservative first lap, then 12th at the end of lap two, when Charles Leclerc crashed his Ferrari to bring the race to a temporary halt. "With the red flag, I was already P12," Antonelli said. "And then I knew that I could have a shot at it." A lap after the restart, he was up to eighth, and on the back of the leading group of cars running nose to tail. Seventh a lap later, after dispatching Lando Norris' McLaren. By now, Russell was in the lead, having wasted little time dispensing with Gasly. But the Briton sensed trouble. "A great race from the neutral perspective," Russell said. "As soon as I saw Kimi up to P5 after a handful of laps, I knew he was going to be in the fight with us. That was clearly a very impressive opening few laps." Wolff said: "The differentiator today was the ability to go through the traffic. We've seen it with other great ones in the past. Lewis (Hamilton), who did it in some of the races. That's what he's shown today. When a driver and a car are one, then there's nothing that can stop them." Antonelli in no mood to obey a computer algorithm Briefly, for a few laps, Russell and Max Verstappen threatened to break away in the lead while Antonelli was finding a way past Gasly, the two McLarens and Hamilton's Ferrari. But Russell and Verstappen were fighting at the front, costing each other time, and Antonelli was up to third by lap 13, just 1.8secs off Verstappen in the lead, with Russell between them. Three laps later, the Mercedes drivers were running one-two, and starting to swap places themselves, until, with Russell leading, it was suggested by that team that they give it a rest and try to break away from Verstappen. If Russell could not do so, they said, they would "invert the cars" - put Antonelli into the lead to try himself. But slowly they began to inch clear. At this point, coming up to half-distance, the race victory was still up in the air. There was a virtual safety car (VSC), called when Lance Stroll's Aston Martin broke down at the first corner. Mercedes called Antonelli for new tyres - a decision they had to make as he had switched to the medium compound at the red flag and that would not make it to the end. Russell continued on his hard tyres. "It was the right thing to split the strategies," Wolff said, "because we didn't know what the better one would be. In the morning meeting, we said the hard tyre is going to go forever. You can start on it and finish on it. And you can see with George, it was a forever tyre. "At that stage, the system said that the one-stop comes out ahead, that two-stop was coming close to the end, but didn't catch it. That's what the software said." Antonelli was in no mood to obey a computer algorithm. Rejoining 14.3secs behind Russell, with 24 laps to go and four cars between them, winning was not an easy task. But he made it look like it. Antonelli caught Russell with five laps to go and the win now looked inevitable. There was a hiccup when he ran off the track at turn one with four laps to go after Russell blocked his attack on the inside, and Antonelli lost grip on the loose rubber off line and slid into the gravel trap. That dropped him to 1.7secs off again, but a lap and a half later, he drove past Russell on the straight between the second Lesmo corner and Ascari, and that was that. The home fans, with split loyalties before the race between Antonelli and Ferrari, screamed with delight as he crossed the line, 60 years since the last time an Italian won his home race. "It's one that I will remember forever," Antonelli said. "Definitely the fans gave that little bit extra to push more. The support has been great this weekend. "Definitely seeing the grandstand cheering every lap it gave that little bit of extra to push more and to try and do even better to win it." - Far too late for title fight priority - Hamilton - Published3 hours ago 'Circle closes' after 'everyone doubted' Antonelli in 2024 The win, Wolff said, was "how the circle closed" after Antonelli's difficult introduction to F1, when he crashed in a one-off outing in free practice at this race two years ago, a moment Wolff said was "probably the toughest moment in his career. For himself and his family. A moment where everyone doubted, including himself. "Two years later, it's the biggest glory, the biggest moment of his career (so far). That's probably going to be one of his biggest (ever)." A maiden season in F1 last year followed in which Antonelli showed flashes of promise but little that indicated what has happened this year would follow. "When you talk about the complete driver, there's the aspect of experience that needs to come," Wolff said. "There is also that he has this easiness of a young man that helps to overcome difficult moments. That also helps in managing not getting ahead of himself when having these glorious moments. "There is the fact of is he capable of maturing, of staying the personality that he is, humble, with a lot of introspection, self-criticism, in order to develop. And that only the future is going to show - whether he is like a few drivers before him a complete deal. "But it is still surprising and amazing to see how quickly he develops. For me, it's like an AI agent that continuously self-improves and learns. And there also, his age is for sure beneficial. The ability, cognitively, intellectually, to constantly become better." Russell hurts with title almost a lost cause After the race, Russell tried to put a brave face on it, but it was impossible not to see how much it was hurting him. Speaking in the news conference, sentences ran out of steam, his voice was on the point of breaking at times. Russell gently pointed out, in not quite so many words, that without the VSC he probably would have won - "it would have been very interesting to see how the race would have panned out if there was no VSC". But he was well aware of what Antonelli's stellar performance meant. The strategy, he said, "takes nothing away from Kimi's drive altogether". And the championship, he now knows, is almost a lost cause. Antonelli's win moves him 66 points clear. Russell talked about "taking the positives", about how, after a "very tough run" in the early summer, since the season re-started in the Netherlands two weeks ago, "every lap, every session, I've been sort of in the mix of the top three positions, similar to where I was at the start of the year". But there has not been a hint all year of Russell being able to put together a run of results where he consistently beats Antonelli, which is now his only hope. "It's definitely Kimi's in control of it," Russell said. "And, you know, he's deserving to be in control of it. "For me personally, I'm not even thinking about a fight or a comeback or anything. I'm just focused on taking it race by race and trying to maximise every single weekend. It's going to be exceptionally challenging to overcome that gap. So I'm just sort of accepting that is what it is." Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published19 August - Published6 days ago - Published2 hours ago - Published2 days ago
entry.summary: Kimi Antonelli delivered one of the great F1 drives to win the Italian Grand Prix and leave Mercedes' team-mate George Russell's title hopes almost a lost cause.

entry.title: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach US Open last eight
entry.body: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight - Published Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open. Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4. He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and his quarter-final opponent will be either American eighth seed Ben Shelton or Greece's Stefanos Tsitsipas. A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer. He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18. Asked on court if he is back to "full power", Alcaraz smiled as he replied: "I think so. Except for one year since [his US Open debut in] 2021, I've made the quarter-finals here. That shows how special this place is to me and shows how well I'm playing every time I come here. "I just try to enjoy my time on the court and it doesn't matter that I was out for four and a half months - every time I come here, I play my best." Shelton and Tsitsipas meet in Sunday's night session and seven-time major champion Alcaraz has never previously lost to either player at Tour level, beating Shelton three times and Tsitsipas on six occasions. "If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine." - Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open - Published2 hours ago - How to follow US Open on the BBC - Published1 day ago Alcaraz said after his third-round win that he was happy with the level of fitness he had shown in the early rounds following his lengthy absence, while he demonstrated against Paul that the quality of his shot-making is as good as ever. One sensational cross-court forehand winner early in the second set, which landed in from an almost impossible angle, was measured at 103mph. That came shortly after Alcaraz had broken Paul's serve in the 10th game of a tight, high-quality opening set to take it 6-4. Paul, who was attempting to reach the quarter-finals of his home Grand Slam for the first time, battled hard throughout but Alcaraz proved to be too strong. Paul had two break points when Alcaraz served for the match at 5-4 in the third set, but the two-time US Open champion put together a run of four straight points to seal victory. Former British number one Tim Henman told Sky Sports: "When you haven't played tennis for four weeks, it seems a lot and you can be a bit rusty. This is four and a half months. "If you would have given Alcaraz a blank piece of paper at the beginning of the tournament and asked how he'd want the first four matches to go, he would have scripted it exactly like that. "He's had a few slightly challenging moments but, in the important moments, he's just come up with incredible tennis. That's got to give him so much confidence moving forward." Related topics - Published28 August - Published28 August
entry.summary: Carlos Alcaraz continues his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.

entry.title: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open
entry.body: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open - Published Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulated Serena Williams as she eventually overpowered American Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final. A topsy-turvy contest featured 10 breaks of serve, but Sabalenka recovered from 3-1 down in the second serve to seal a 6-4 6-3 victory with a fifth consecutive game. It was the Belarusian's 18th consecutive win at the tournament, extending her three-year unbeaten streak following back-to-back triumphs in 2024 and 2025. Sabalenka, 28, is the first woman to reach six consecutive singles quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows since American great Williams in 2016. Six-time champion Williams was also the last player to win three US Open titles in a row, and Sabalenka is now three wins from matching that feat. She will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova for a semi-final place, after the Czech sixth seed required six match points to overcome Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in a rollercoaster 7-5 5-7 6-4 win. Despite the straightforward scoreline this was a tricky match which required a resilient display from Sabalenka, who also had the vast majority of the crowd against her. In that context this was an impressive victory for the four-time major winner, who has not always managed to maintain her composure in similarly testing scenarios. "I was just trying to stay focused on myself, not only point by point but ball by ball," Sabalenka said. "I'm happy I was able to turn around the second set, I think it was a key moment." - Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight - Published51 minutes ago - No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive? - Published1 day ago - Williams sisters exit US Open but excite - what does future hold? - Published1 day ago The match began with five successive breaks of serve - mostly due to excellent returning by both players - but it was Sabalenka who finally took charge. Doubles specialist Townsend, who walked out wearing a long, black-feathered outfit, continued to frustrate Sabalenka and forced her to serve out the set at the second opportunity, before making the breakthrough in the second set. But Sabalenka, aware she must lift the trophy to have a chance of retaining her number one ranking, produced an immediate reply as she broke back to love. That signalled the start of Sabalenka's dash to the finish line. The top seed lost just five points across the final five games to end Townsend's challenge in 75 minutes. Sabalenka was full of praise for Townsend, saying: "What an incredible player she is, approaching the net, a great returner, moving well, very brave. "You can see how focused she was. It was really challenging playing her, especially here. "Thank you so much [to the crowd] for being so respectful to me. I knew coming into this match that you guys would be on her side, but you were sometimes cheering for me and I really appreciate that." At home on the US Open hard courts, Sabalenka has not failed to reach the semi-finals here since 2020. But, following a fourth-round exit at Wimbledon, she is aiming to avoid a first season without a major title since 2022. Noskova's sense of relief was cleared as she crouched to the ground after taking her sixth match point about an hour after earning her first. The 21-year-old served for the match in the second set, but missed her first two match points as Kostyuk battled back from 5-3 down to force a decider. The players exchanged breaks of serve in a tense final set, but it was Noskova who emerged, once again, with a 5-3 advantage. Noskova failed to take her next two match points as a couple of misses helped Kostyuk to deuce, and missed her fifth after saving a break point, before finally getting over the line after an emotionally draining two and a half hours on court. "I am more than relieved, this match was so tough, emotionally a bit more than physically," Noskova said. "Today was very close, it could have ended both ways. With all the chances I had in the second set, it was tough to still kind of restart." Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published28 August
entry.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulates Serena Williams by overcoming Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.

entry.title: GB&I make history with first Walker Cup since 2015
entry.body: GB&I make history with first Walker Cup since 2015 - Published Great Britain and Ireland produced the biggest comeback in Walker Cup history to defeat the United States and lift the trophy for the first time since 2015. At Lahinch in Ireland, the USA looked to be on the brink when they swept the morning foursomes to move just three-and-a-half points away from a sixth consecutive victory. But GB&I picked up seven of the 10 points in the singles to clinch victory by 13-and-a-half points to 12-and-a-half and win for the first time in 11 years. Josh Hill had the winning moment as he defeated world number two Tyler Watts on the final hole of the eighth pairing, and that sparked wild celebrations to mark a victory that seemed so unlikely after Sunday morning. For Irish player Stuart Grehan, winning the biennial amateur tournament on home turf meant event more. "I'm close to crying and I'm not an emotional person," Grehan told BBC Sport. "It's unbelievable, it's the best feeling I've ever had on a golf course by a long stretch." Grehan twice defeated world number one Preston Stout in the week, including in Sunday's decisive singles, and he said it was "incredible" to lead the fightback. "With the way the day flowed, everyone on this team is just unbelievable," Grehan added. "It's been an amazing week and to play Preston twice in the singles and get the better of him, I'm really proud of myself and it's amazing." For captain Dean Robertson, the emotions were flowing as he guided GB&I to the Walker Cup for the 10th time. "It's been very emotional and I could not be more proud," he said. "I had full belief in the players, even at lunchtime when we went down 4-0." After Grehan defeated Stout, who battled a bug in the lead-up to the event, in the opening match, that set the tone for the comeback that was to follow. Luke Poulter - son of Ryder Cup legend Ian - delivered a moment of his own to beat Ethan Fang, before US Amateur champion Jack Whaley and star player Tyler Weaver also won their matches for the hosts. Whaley's win, in particular, was impressive as he beat William Jennings by 8&7 - the biggest winning margin ever for a GB&I player. Eliot Baker beat Stewart Hagestad on the final hole to claim his match, and Conor Graham won the last two holes to halve his match with Miles Russell before Hill's decisive moment came in a tight match up with Watts. Even though Ryder Cowan and Josiah Gilbert defeated Ben Bolton and Sam Easterbrook, it came in the ninth and 10th pairings and the comeback was already completed as GB&I won by a single point. When Hill was in the bunker on the 18th, captain Robertson said he thought of his late father and said the shot to get onto the green was reminiscent of Matthew Fitzpatrick's famous bunker shot to help earn his brother, Alex, a tour card at the Zurich Classic in April. "I felt quite calm when Josh was hitting his putt and my thoughts were with my late dad," Scot Robertson added. "To have my mum, brother and all my family here is really special and it's been a really emotional day."
entry.summary: Great Britain and Ireland produce the biggest comeback in Walker Cup history to defeat the United States and lift the trophy for the first time since 2015.

entry.title: Littler beats Humphries to win Czech Open
entry.body: Littler beats Humphries to win Czech Open - Published Luke Littler overcame defending champion Luke Humphries to claim the Czech Open title in Prague. World number one Littler was playing in his first European Tour event since the Belgium Open in March, and beat Krzysztof Ratajski, Danny Noppert as well as Michael van Gerwen on his way to the blockbuster final. He was trailing 4-3 against world number two Humphries, who saw off Andrew Gilding, William O'Connor and Gerwyn Price, before a four-leg burst put the 19-year-old Littler 7-4 in front. Humphries reduced the deficit to 7-6 but failed to level the match as he missed with two darts at double 16 in the 14th leg. Littler capitalised by taking out 39 for a win which secures his place at the European Championship in Dortmund in October. "This is what the fans are in for - me and Luke are back," said Littler. "The two best going at it in a final once again. "It's good to be back and I'm back with a bang. "These long days are worth it, especially lifting the trophy." Littler, who is attempting to complete the calendar sweep of ranking events in 2026, added: "I think I've secured my place in Dortmund - Dortmund is the one I'm chasing." Humphries was aiming to win the Czech Open for a fourth time and third occasion on the trot. "I was going to pull out Thursday, and I made the final, so I can't be too upset with myself because I did really well," he said. "I never give up, especially in finals. I know that Luke is obviously going to throw everything at me. "Hopefully over the next four months, I push him. If he does the clean sweep, he has to do it the hard way."
entry.summary: Luke Littler overcomes defending champion Luke Humphries to claim the Czech Open title on the European Tour.

entry.title: GB's Stevens wins Burghley for first time
entry.body: GB's Stevens wins Burghley for first time - Published Britain's Gemma Stevens won the Burghley Horse Trials for the first time on Sunday, the biggest victory of her career on her 31st attempt at five-star level. The 41-year-old Olympian, riding Chilli Knight, cemented victory in executing a faultless showjumping round to finish on her dressage score of 29.6 - the only rider in the field to do so. Compatriot Katie Magee finished second on Treworra, with USA's Caroline Pamukcu and HSH Blake in third. "It's only taken me 25 years and finally I've managed to win a big B [Burghley or Badminton]. I couldn't be more proud," Stevens said. Stevens, who first competed at the level in 2007, previously rode Chilli Knight's mother, King's Gem. "It's unbelievable, I've known him [Chilli Knight] since the day he was born and this honestly means the absolute world," she said. The win is redemption for Stevens after a disappointing World Championships in Aachen, Germany last month, when she failed to complete the cross-county event for the British team. "Aachen was really tough, but that's sport. You've got to just bounce back and get on with it," she added. Stevens and Chilli Knight previously won the replacement five-star event at Bicton in 2021, after Covid cancelled Burghley.
entry.summary: Britain's Gemma Stevens claims the biggest win of her 25-year career with victory at Burghley Horse Trials.

entry.title: WSL investigating after Palace break substitution rules
entry.body: Image source, Getty Images Image caption, Lexi Lloyd-Smith scored the only goal of the game The Women's Super League says an investigation is under way after Crystal Palace used four substitution windows in their win over Everton. A statement says that Palace "breached" the rules, adding that they only permit a maximum of three substitution opportunities per match. The Eagles made four separate substitutions in the 62nd, 83rd, 90th and 97th minute of Sunday's 1-0 victory at the Borough Sports Ground. The league confirmed the investigation will involve both clubs and referee body Pro Ref. WSL rules do not prescribe an automatic punishment but any breach could be referred to an independent tribunal, which has the power to impose sanctions ranging from a warning or fine to a points deduction or other sporting sanction. Both clubs have been approached for comment. Promoted Crystal Palace beat Everton on WSL return Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed
entry.summary: The Women's Super League says an investigation is underway after Crystal Palace use four substitution windows in their win over Everton.

entry.title: 'I'm only alive thanks to one man' - British driver rescued from car fire in China race
entry.body: 'I'm only alive thanks to one man' - driver rescued from car fire - Published A British racing driver says he is only alive thanks to a rival who pulled him from the burning wreckage of a car. Dutchman Loek Hartog abandoned his own vehicle during the China GT Championship race in Shanghai and doused the flames of Ollie Millroy's Ferrari with a fire extinguisher before dragging him from the vehicle. "I am still alive tonight, entirely thanks to one man," Millroy said in a post on Instagram. "Loek Hartog stopped instantly with no flag marshals or fire crews in sight, and risked his own life to get me out of the car." Organisers said in statement they "will further review and investigate the accident and formulate more comprehensive plans to address shortcomings in competition organisation, support, emergency response, rescue and medical services". Millroy's team, AAI Motorsport, said it "will no longer participate in any races organised by China GT" in a statement that was hugely critical of safety standards at Saturday's race and accused the organisers of negligence. "I don't remember anything between 30 seconds before the crash and one hour after it, but I will remember his incredible act of bravery for the rest of my life," Millroy said. "One day I will tell our three kids this story and Loek will be the biggest superhero in history in their eyes too." Millroy said he suffered five broken ribs, a broken collar bone, broken hand, broken finger and bruised lung in the crash, adding: "It could have been much worse." "Thank you Loek. I owe you my life for your selfless act." Replying to the post, Hartog said: "I am so thankful to have been right at the place I needed to be in space and time." He later wrote in his own post on Instagram: "When I saw a car turning into a huge fireball far ahead, there wasn't really a decision to make. "From what I had seen, I genuinely believed the driver might not be able to get out by himself. I stopped, got out and went towards the car. There was never a moment of doubt. There were moments where I didn't know I would actually be able to get Ollie out. "But this isn't about what I did, and I'm sure many people in the same position would have reacted exactly the same way." AAI Motorsport said Millroy's car "continued to burn for more than a minute" after the accident and that "no timely and effective firefighting and rescue operations were seen". It said: "What might have happened if that driver hadn't stepped up today? "We accept the inherent dangers of motorsports, but we absolutely cannot accept a driver being exposed to avoidable death."
entry.summary: British racing driver Ollie Millroy says he is only alive thanks to a rival who pulled him from the burning wreckage of his car following a crash at the China GT.

entry.title: When Man City call you don't say no - Ndiaye
entry.body: When Man City call you don't say no - Ndiaye - Published Iliman Ndiaye says "you don't say no" when Manchester City come calling, and playing in the Champions League is where he belongs. The 26-year-old could have gone to Tottenham but made a Â£60m move from Everton to City on transfer deadline day and was thrown straight into the starting XI for his new side in a 1-0 Premier League victory over Coventry at the weekend. In the final week of the transfer window, it appeared as though Ndiaye would be moving to Spurs after they agreed a deal with Everton, but they were unable to proceed with the move having failed to sell Richarlison. "There was no stress or panicking," said Ndiaye. "I always say whatever comes, comes. God decides your future - it is already written. "I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing. It was always going to be City. "I wanted Champions League and playing at one of the best teams in the world. I am not saying Tottenham is not, but when Manchester City comes through you don't say no. "It has been a good week for me and topped off with a win." Despite Everton finishing in the bottom half of the table in his two seasons at the club, Ndiaye became a fans' favourite for his skills on the flanks and scoring 17 goals. "When I was speaking with my wife, I was telling her that if I had to leave Everton it would be somewhere where I know I would be playing Champions League," he said. "It was difficult to leave Everton. I created a great connection with the fans and the players there, but we have to move on sometimes and it's how football is." - Fernandez and Ndiaye show signs of promise on Man City debuts - Published1 day ago Ndiaye started his professional career in non-league with Boreham Wood before playing only seven miles away from Etihad Stadium at Hyde United seven years ago. Ndiaye played in the Championship with Sheffield United and had a season at Marseille before joining Everton for Â£15m in 2024. Ndiaye said: "I don't really look back. I just look to the future and work hard. I just look at the next step and this is a big step to join Manchester City. "It is one of the biggest clubs in the world. There are world-class players, world-class stadium and the fans are brilliant. "This is where I think I belong. I have worked hard to get to this point."
entry.summary: New £60m Manchester City signing Iliman Ndiaye says playing in the Champions League is where he belongs.

entry.title: Andy Williams, Every Time I Die Guitarist and Pro Wrestler, Dead at 48
entry.body: Andy Williams, Every Time I Die Guitarist and Pro Wrestler, Dead at 48 Andy Williams, a professional wrestler who was formerly the founding guitarist of metalcore band Every Time I Die, has died at the age of 48. According to reports, Williams — who wrestled under the name “The Butcher” — collapsed at the end of his tag team match Saturday at an Enjoy Wrestling event in Millvale, Pennsylvania. “Our doctors on staff tended to him immediately, administering CPR until the ambulance arrived,” Enjoy Wrestling wrote. Williams ultimately died Saturday night, the Allegheny County Medical Examiner’s Office told TMZ. No cause of death was immediately known. Before he was “The Butcher,” Williams served as founding rhythm guitarist of the Buffalo metalcore band Every Time I Die, serving in that role from their formation in 1998 to their breakup in 2022. During his tenure in ETID, Williams played on all nine of the band’s studio albums, concluding with 2021’s Radical. While with Every Time I Die, Williams began training and then moonlighting as a wrestler in the 2010s, first working the independent circuits before rising to the level of All Elite Wrestling, where he made his debut as “The Butcher” in 2019. “All Elite Wrestling is saddened to learn of the passing of Andy Williams, aka The Butcher,” AEW wrote in a statement Sunday. “A trailblazing musician with ETID and Atomic Rule, Williams made a successful transition into the world of professional wrestling and was incredibly respected by his peers both in and out of the ring. Our condolences go out to Williams’ family, friends and fans.” Williams — who frequently wrestled alongside tag team partner Jesse “The Blade” Guilmette, who was also his partner Saturday at what was Williams’ final match — spent seven years with AEW and its sister circuit Ring of Honor, a run that concluded in June 2026. Following Every Time I Die’s disbandment, Williams joined the group Atomic Rule, which he worked on outside wrestling; in a social media post just hours before his death, Williams told Atomic Rule fans that the band was hard at work on new music.
entry.summary: Founding rhythm guitarist for Buffalo metalcore band successfully segued into wrestling at "The Butcher"

entry.title: Netflix Bets ‘Ink’ and Its Timely Rupert Murdoch Story Can Win Oscars for Danny Boyle and Guy Pearce
entry.body: Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects. Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stage sensation, which opened the 83rd edition in competition before moving through Telluride and Toronto, with the streamer giving it a December theatrical release and a January streaming date. The early temperature is reading warm. “Ink” drew a four-minute standing ovation on opening night in Venice, and the reactions filtering out of Telluride have been buzzing across the mountains, the kind of enthusiasm and respect a Netflix campaign is built to amplify. The subject is an origin myth of modern media: Rupert Murdoch’s 1969 acquisition of a dying tabloid called The Sun and the rapid transformation that followed. Graham, adapting his own Tony-nominated play, approaches the story with the mechanics of a heist. Popular on Variety The central question is not simply how Murdoch built a newspaper. It is how two men helped invent the modern attention economy that shapes all of our lives today. Guy Pearce plays a brash, thirty-something Murdoch, an outsider with a chip on his shoulder and a plan for disrupting Fleet Street. Jack O’Connell plays editor Larry Lamb, the working-class newspaperman Murdoch pushes past every line the establishment believes cannot be crossed. Both actors have obvious awards narratives, but two very different categories to break into. Pearce arrives two years after his first Oscar nomination, a supporting actor bid for “The Brutalist,” which gives him the benefit of recent Academy recognition. And the role could hardly be more of the moment. Murdoch is a figure many hold responsible for the fractured, combustible information environment the U.S. is living through right now and there is a particular charge in watching an actor humanize the young man who lit the fuse. That timeliness is the kind of thing that fuels an Oscar campaign. O’Connell arrives with something different: momentum. Between “Sinners” and the “28 Years Later” films, he is coming off a stretch that has significantly raised his visibility. Being a hot commodity right now, and perhaps even a package deal with Pearce in voters’ minds, could give him a fighting shot in a very crowded best actor field. We have seen roles like Pearce’s cakewalk to nominations before, purely on the nature of the part, even when pundits wrote them off early. Look at the run of real-life figures who landed supporting bids: Jon Voight in “Ali” (2001), Matt Damon in “Invictus” (2009), Kenneth Branagh in “My Week with Marilyn” (2011), Christopher Plummer in “All the Money in the World” (2017), Sam Rockwell in “Vice” (2018), J.K. Simmons in “Being the Ricardos” (2021) and Jeremy Strong in “The Apprentice” (2024). Pearce may not have the most screen time, but he is memorable in every frame. O’Connell has the more obvious breakout narrative and, as the story’s beating heart, the showier dramatic arc. Two performances from one film can coexist comfortably in an awards campaign, but they can also create a strategic problem. The distributor must establish why both actors are essential without letting voters perceive one as stealing oxygen from the other. There is also a screenplay story here, and a recent precedent worth studying. Graham is adapting his own acclaimed play, which puts “Ink” in the adapted screenplay conversation and on a path that “One Night in Miami” walked in 2020. That film, too, launched at Venice and Kemp Powers turned his own stage work into an adapted screenplay nomination while the movie also landed an acting nod for Leslie Odom Jr. A playwright translating his own material, a festival launch and a performance the industry embraces: the template is right there. But Netflix will look to check even more boxes. Beyond the two actors, “Ink” is built to contend in the crafts. Its production design, by Carson McColl and Gareth Pugh, rebuilds a vanished Fleet Street. Fin Oates cuts the film with a fragmented, kinetic energy that recalls the associative style Hank Corwin brought to Adam McKay’s “The Big Short” and “Vice.” Johnnie Burn, the Oscar-winning sound designer of “The Zone of Interest,” lends the film one of the most decorated ears in the business. And composer Daniel Pemberton supplies an original score with the propulsion Boyle’s movies demand, capping a bombastic year that also includes “Project Hail Mary.” Netflix has the resources to make all of those cases. The larger question is whether the company has the bandwidth. Its fall slate is stacked, with “La Bola Negra,” “The Adventures of Cliff Booth,” “Possible Love,” “Gentle Monster” and “The Mosquito Bowl” all angling for the same oxygen. “Ink” will have to compete not only against rival distributors but against Netflix’s own contenders for screeners, headlines, events, Q & As and voter attention. The Venice-Telluride-Toronto sequence helps enormously, giving the movie the sort of early critical footprint that can turn an awards campaign into a sustained conversation. And Boyle’s presence adds another narrative. As the Oscar-winning filmmaker behind “Slumdog Millionaire,” he brings such a distinctive visual and kinetic signature that the fall circuit was an obvious place for the film to bow. The James Graham connection gives “Ink” a larger cultural context. His work has repeatedly mined the intersection of power, institutions and public life, from politics to journalism. “Ink” arrives in a media environment in which the questions surrounding Murdoch’s influence feel less like history than an origin story for the world audiences inhabit now. That resonance is the film’s best weapon, and the campaign will not have to manufacture it. “Ink” argues that we are all still living in the paper they printed.
entry.summary: Netflix wants the “ink” to dry on its Oscar prospects. Danny Boyle made his first trip to Venice with “Ink,” his adaptation of James Graham’s stage sensation, which opened the 83rd edition in competition before moving through Telluride and Toronto, with the streamer giving it a December theatrical release and a January streaming date. entry.title: John Turturro Has Waited 40 Years for an Oscar Nomination. ‘The Only Living Pickpocket in New York’ Makes the Case
entry.body: Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize, an enviable résumé and exactly zero Oscar mornings when his name was read aloud with the words “and the nominees are.” Sony Pictures Classics is determined to end the drought with his work in the acclaimed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York,” which premiered at Sundance last January and made its fall festival bow at Telluride this weekend, where the film and Turturro’s invigorating turn as an aging pickpocket are drawing acclaim. Turturro, 69, has been making the rounds in the Colorado mountains, attending Q&As and a Saturday night dinner hosted by Sony Pictures Classics, where writer-director Noah Segan mingled with press and industry attendees. Popular on Variety Turturro has spent four decades operating in the space reserved for actors everyone recognizes and almost nobody thinks of as an Oscar nominee. He has worked with masters of cinema such as the Coen brothers, Spike Lee and Robert Redford and has appeared opposite everyone from Tom Hanks to Adam Sandler. He’s played gangsters, professors, detectives, eccentrics, husbands, fathers and men who seem to have wandered into the wrong movie and somehow made it better. And yet, the Academy has never invited him to the party. And it’s not like he hasn’t been close. Turturro won best actor at Cannes for the Coen brothers’ “Barton Fink” in 1991. Three years later, his combustible Herbie Stempel in Robert Redford’s “Quiz Show” collected Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations, the kind of precursor support that usually precedes an Oscar bid. But each time, the industry seemed to look elsewhere. The television world has been kinder. His weary defense attorney in “The Night Of,” HBO’s 2016 crime drama, drew Emmy, Golden Globe and SAG Award nominations. His tender, unraveling Irving Bailiff on “Severance,” Apple TV’s dystopian workplace thriller, has since earned him two Emmy nominations, the most recent lost to his own castmate Tramell Tillman in 2025. “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” can change that. In a similar vein to Richard Jenkins’ first career nomination for the 2007 drama “The Visitor,” Turturro can be the overdue veteran to finally see his name in lights. Segan’s Sundance breakout, acquired by SPC for a fall release, gives Turturro something four decades of great supporting performances never could: a movie that he leads, one that lives and dies on him. He plays Harry Lehman, an analog thief operating in a city where the very concept of pickpocketing has become obsolete. Wallets increasingly contain less cash, phones have replaced maps and tickets and two-factor authentication has made the modern world almost aggressively hostile to the old-fashioned criminal. Harry is clinging to a disappearing profession while caring for his ailing wife, Rosie. While that metaphor is hardly subtle, it’s also part of its appeal. Harry is not simply a thief whose trade is dying; he’s a man confronting his own obsolescence. SPC calls it the finest performance of Turturro’s career. Distributor hyperbole is usually best treated as campaign copy. Turturro has never been an actor who needed to announce himself. He slips into other people’s scenes, finds the detail nobody else thought to play and then, almost imperceptibly, becomes the most interesting person in the room. The Academy has rewarded that instinct repeatedly, just not when Turturro has been the person standing at the center of the frame. As an awards campaign, the studio is following a familiar formula: a beloved, never-nominated veteran finally gets a leading role worthy of his gifts. But the strongest version of the pitch is not “Give John Turturro an Oscar.” It is “Look at what John Turturro has been doing all along.” The Academy has historically responded to overdue narratives, particularly when the performance provides a credible reason to act on the sentiment. Turturro has the résumé, the festival pedigree and the late-career showcase that can turn years of admiration into a voting impulse. “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” is a movie about a man whose skills belong to another era, trying to prove they still have value. The meta-text is impossible to miss. Turturro’s awards case makes essentially the same argument about the actor himself. It also helps to have Steve Buscemi in the cast, who could mount his own first awards run for “Wild Horse Nine,” along with the best awards campaigner this side of the sun, Jamie Lee Curtis, who delivers a killer one-scene wonder. Like a lot of SPC films, neither the movie nor Turturro may seem the loudest voice in the room right now and plenty of pundits will write it off early, especially once precursors start rolling in. But as the studio has shown with titles like “The Father,” “Parallel Mothers” and “I’m Still Here,” the ground game and striking when it matters most, is what wins these campaigns. And Turturro may not even be the film’s only awards story. Segan, long a familiar face in front of the camera, wrote and directed “The Only Living Pickpocket in New York” himself and a spare, mournful original like this one is exactly the kind of writer-director calling card the original screenplay race tends to reward. It happens more than voters remember. “Frozen River,” another SPC sleeper, paired Melissa Leo’s lead nomination with a surprise original screenplay nod for writer-director Courtney Hunt and “Nebraska” did the same for Bruce Dern and scribe Bob Nelson. If the film connects with voters, Segan’s script could ride in alongside its star. The best actor field, notably, is shaping up to be incredibly crowded. Heading into the fall festivals, pundits had already penciled in the likes of Matt Damon (“The Odyssey”), Ryan Gosling (“Project Hail Mary”) and Sebastian Stan (“Fjord”), and Venice and Telluride added John Malkovich (“Wild Horse Nine”) and Andrew Scott (“Elsinore”) to the conversation. SPC will have to make noise without overselling a performance whose appeal lies in its subtlety. But if the campaign can persuade voters to see Harry not as a novelty but as the culmination of everything Turturro has spent a career doing, the narrative becomes difficult to ignore. Let’s see if this pickpocket can steal some hearts along the way.
entry.summary: Forty years into a career that has made him one of American cinema’s most recognizable character actors, John Turturro has a Cannes best actor prize, an enviable résumé and exactly zero Oscar mornings when his name was read aloud with the words “and the nominees are.” Sony Pictures Classics is determined to end the drought […]

entry.title: ‘B’Day’ at 20: Behind the Album That Helped Beyoncé Define Her Career
entry.body: ‘B’Day’ at 20: Behind the Album That Helped Beyoncé Define Her Career Just when you thought B’Day couldn’t get any louder, a couple hundred people file onto the dance floor at the Brooklyn venue Baby’s All Right for a 20th anniversary celebration of Beyoncé‘s seminal second album. The space is tiny and tightly packed. When the dance break in “Get Me Bodied” hits, there’s barely any space for people to drop down low and sweep the floor with it. The crowd complies, anyway, clashing against each other as the song instructs them to let their hair touch the floor, wind it back. This was always going to be the legacy of “Get Me Bodied,” a vigorous dance mandate on an album meant to be played loud. Over the past two decades, B’Day has reinforced its longevity. Sure, people can dissect and study the intricacies of Lemonade and Cowboy Carter on a visual and lyrical level, or how she shifted the digital landscape with Beyoncé. These are all records that cemented her as a master of her craft and reinforced her skillset tenfold. But B’Day did it first. It’s the most defining Beyoncé album —— and it came long before it was standard practice to try to define Beyoncé. On the floor at Baby’s, you can feel the bass in your bones when the sirens blare at the start of “Ring the Alarm.” There are 20 lifetimes worth of anger, betrayal, frustration, and disbelief in the way the room screams out each lyric. Their emotions bubble up and boil over as DJ Miss Milan, who helmed the night alongside Byrell the Great, mixed “Ring the Alarm” into “Hold Up,” the Lemonade standout where Beyoncé asks, “What’s worst, lookin’ jealous or crazy? Jealous or crazy?” “Ring the Alarm” has the lyric “the thought of you just touchin’ her is what I hate most” in one verse and “you ain’t never seen a fire like the one I’ma cause” in the next. She’ll take jealous and crazy. The transitions across the first half of the set weave a web between eras. “Naughty Girl” is spliced with teases of “Green Light” for just a moment, before switching into the Beyoncé remix of J Balvin’s “Mi Gente” and dropping fully into “Green Light.” The funk-fueled record was produced by the Neptunes, the now-defunct production duo of Chad Hugo and Pharrell Williams. For B’Day, Beyoncé assembled an army of some of the best producers in pop, hip-hop, and R&B at the time — from Darkchild and Stargate to Swizz Beatz, Sean Garrett, and Rich Harrison. Beyoncé works best when she’s putting everyone else to work, challenging them to challenge themselves. Williams shows up again on “Can I Watch You,” a previously unreleased track that appears on the 20th anniversary extended edition of the album. A few of the added songs were bonus tracks available only on CDs purchased at Best Buy or Circuit City, or versions sold exclusively overseas. After living and growing with the same set of songs for two decades, introducing new material into a remixed and remastered edition should naturally feel slightly disjointed. It’s going to take some work to get used to the new version of “Welcome to Hollywood,” and the disappearance of “World Wide Woman” will likely never be explained. But the blaring “Lost Yo Mind” slides so seamlessly into the track list that it feels both new and nostalgic. But the deluxe release is a true testament to the consistency Beyoncé has established throughout her career. There’s a solid throughline created by her voice and perspective across each new and original track. Beyoncé has never been the kind of artist to lose her way for an era or two and later find her way back with some necessary reset or return to form. Her vision is too distinct, even in instances like I Am… Sasha Fierce and 4, which added about a dozen more classic hits to her catalog without being particularly strong top-to-bottom records. There’s no “Diva,” “Ego,” or “Sweet Dreams” without “Upgrade U,” “Kitty Kat,” and “Freakum Dress.” There’s no “Countdown” without “Get Me Bodied.” There’s no Beyoncé as we know her today without B’Day. The record established and embraced her perspective shift between arrogance and confidence; reveled in the intensity of flustered passion; and in the rare instance that she toned it down for a ballad, contrasted those same feelings with an edge of softness and sensitivity. There would have never been so much pearl-clutching around “Bow Down” or so much inquisition around the events that inspired Lemonade if people had listened more closely to the narrative Beyoncé laid out so clearly on B’Day. B’Day doesn’t make up much of the music Beyoncé performs live these days — the “Déjà Vu” and “Freakum Dress” fakeouts on the Cowboy Carter tour were agonizing teases. This would be a tragedy only if she hadn’t immortalized her tour for the album on The Beyoncé Experience Live, an essential release in the anthology of films Beyoncé has used to archive her decades-long career. It’s a master class in performance built on the strength of songs that were made to define the present moment, but also live far beyond it. B’Day sounds as exciting now as it did 20 years ago, when Beyoncé took over 106 & Park on her 25th birthday in celebration of its release. Earlier this year, Swizz Beatz told Billboard, “Sometimes timing and hype can make albums feel more prolific and sonically epic, but when that fades away, how does that music look when people move on to different things? B’Day has stood the test of time.” So much of what existed during the initial B’Day era is gone now: 106 & Park, the Jay-Z-owned 40/40 club where Beyoncé partied for her birthday, Circuit City, the MTV channels that would play the entirety of the B’Day anthology video album. But the spirit of the album is completely divorced from trends in consumption, or whatever direction pop was heading at the time. B’Day was built to last. It’s why hundreds of people will pack into a sweaty club on a Friday night to celebrate its enduring legacy — not just in New York, but also at parties in Los Angeles, Montréal, Nashville, and more cities across the world. DJ Miss Milan dedicated the second half of the night at Baby’s to running through B’Day from top to bottom. Some of the tracks had already played earlier in the night, but playing them in their intended original order lit a fire in the crowd. “Deja Vu” set the tone, “Get Me Bodied” dialed it up, and by the time the set reached “Check On It,” they were screaming every lyric and ad lib at a decibel so piercing it could rival the first five seconds of “Freakum Dress.” It’s exactly how B’Day is meant to be consumed — as loud as possible for as long as possible.
entry.summary: Hundreds of people packed into sweaty clubs 20 years after its release date to celebrate the legacy of an album meant to be played as loud as possible for as long as possible

entry.title: Macklemore Calls Out ‘Free Palestine’ Onstage, Spurring Petition Demanding He Leave Ed Sheeran Tour
entry.body: Macklemore opened for Ed Sheeran on Friday night in New Jersey at the MetLife Stadium, and during his set the rapper sang out “Free Palestine” before launching into a speech, telling the audience he wanted people in Gaza and the occupied West Bank to know they had not been forgotten. “I believe that every human being walking on this earth deserves exactly the same freedom,” he said. He repeated the remarks during Saturday night’s performance. His politically-themed set sparked a petition from the Israeli American Council, which demanded the rapper be removed from the remaining dates on the Loop tour. Popular on Variety The petition, which does not show how many signatures it has gathered, reads “This was an Ed Sheeran concert – not a political rally, not a protest, and not an activist event. The issue is not whether Macklemore has the right to hold political views. The question is where the line should be drawn when an opening act uses a global concert platform to advance a one-sided political agenda.” Macklemore also called out U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement during his remarks. He released the song “Hind’s Hall,” which criticizes Israel’s actions in Gaza, in 2024 and has directed proceeds from the song to go to humanitarian efforts from the UNRWA. On social media, some concertgoers said they walked out because they had not expected a ‘political rally,” accusing Macklemore of antisemitism. Others applauded his remarks, writing “Music has always been a vital platform for human rights advocacy, not just mindless escape.”

entry.title: ‘Possible Love’ Cast Sobs as Lee Chang-dong’s Epic Embraced at Venice With 6-Minute Standing Ovation
entry.body: Acclaimed South Korean director Lee Chang-dong returned after 24 years to the Venice Film Festival, where he was warmly embraced with a six-minute standing ovation for his sweeping romantic drama “Possible Love.” Directed by Lee and co-written by Oh Jung-mi, “Possible Love” follows the intertwined lives of two married couples — a laid-off factory worker and his spouse, and a wealthy husband and wife who are making a documentary about the injustices facing factory workers — whose lives intersect after a funeral. A meditation on social class and desire, the movie brings together familiar faces from the director’s prior work, including Jeon Do-yeon (“Secret Sunshine”) and Sul Kyung-gu (“Peppermint Candy”), as well as new collaborators in Zo In-sung (“Escape From Mogadishu”) and Cho Yeo-jeong (of “Parasite” fame). As the credits rolled and the lights came up in the Sala Grande theater, the cast started to sob and wiped away tears with napkins. Jeon, Sul, Zo and Cho took turns hugging each other, enthusiastically clapping and giggling at their emotional response to the audience’s enthusiasm for the film. Oh, too, was crying as she basked in the rapturous applause. The claps and cheers would have possibly continued a lot longer, but at the six-minute mark, the actors and director were guided toward the exit and headed out of the Palazzo del Cinema. A major theme of “Possible Love” is the 10th commandment, “thou shalt not covet,” so perhaps the cast and filmmakers were satisfied by the reaction and didn’t need a lengthier standing ovation. Popular on Variety “Possible Love” marks Lee’s first time in competition at Venice in nearly a quarter-century, following his Silver Lion win for “Oasis” in 2002. This is the director’s first feature film in eight years, since 2018’s psychological thriller “Burning.” His other major works include “Green Fish,” “Peppermint Candy,” “Secret Sunshine” and “Poetry.” “I’m not the type of filmmaker who can make movies easily,” Lee said previously of the lengthy gap between projects. “Before I begin a film, I must be certain of what it means — to me, to the audience, and to cinema itself. That is why ‘Possible Love’ took so long to make.” Netflix is releasing “Possible Love,” which is making stops at Toronto and New York film festivals ahead of its theatrical rollout. The movie opens on the big screen in the U.S. 23 before streaming globally on Nov. Netflix opened this year’s Venice Film Festival with director Danny Boyle’s “Ink,” an explosive drama about the rise of Rupert Murdoch’s tabloid empire. Prior to the premiere of “Possible Love,” Lee mused on the film’s title, saying “it asks a question: what is love that is possible?” “When we think about a love story, usually the most typical love story we think about is love that cannot come true,” Lee told Variety. “So to simply put it, you could say that all of these love stories are called impossible love.”

entry.title: Box Office: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day’ Remains No. 1 in Sixth Weekend, Nears ‘Avengers: Endgame’ All-Time Domestic Record
entry.body: “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” was No. 1 at the domestic box office for the sixth consecutive weekend, a rare feat that underscores the movie’s remarkable staying power as well as the lack of competition on cinema marquees. “Brand New Day” earned $18 million over the traditional weekend and is estimated to collect $23.3 million through the Labor Day holiday on Monday. Peter Parker’s latest adventure is enjoying the longest stint at No. 1 since 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water,” which ranked in first place for seven straight weekends. With $923 million to date in North America, “Brand New Day” is primed to soon overtake 2015’s “Star Wars: The Force Awakens” ($936 million, not adjusted for inflation) as the highest-grossing movie of all time at the domestic box office. Meanwhile, Sony’s fourth “Spider-Man” adaptation led by Tom Holland has generated $2.4 billion globally, ranking as the third-biggest release ever behind 2009’s “Avatar” ($2.9 billion) and “Avengers: Endgame” ($2.7 billion) and ahead of 2022’s “Avatar: The Way of Water” ($2.3 billion). This Labor Day weekend closes out the best summer movie season since COVID upended the cinema industry in 2020. Domestic ticket sales between May and early September reached $4.73 billion, according to Rentrak. Those revenues weren’t just strong by post-pandemic standards. They register as the second-largest summer ever, not far behind the season’s high-water mark of $4.755 billion (not adjusted for inflation) set in 2013. Several blockbusters — including major studio offerings like “Spider-Man: Brand New Day,” “The Odyssey,” “Toy Story 5,” “The Devil Wears Prada 2,” as well as indie sleeper hits like “Obsession” and “Backrooms” — were responsible for popcorn season’s outsized success. Those triumphs helped offset some big-budget bombs, including Disney’s live-action “Moana,” Warner Bros. and DC’s “Supergirl” and Amazon MGM’s “Masters of the Universe.” Popular on Variety “This summer could signal a meaningful turning point for movie theaters,” says Rentrak’s Paul Dergarabedian. “More than anything, it serves as a huge reminder of the singular nature of the moviegoing experience and how much fun people have going to theaters.” Unfortunately, summer is ending with a whimper rather than a bang. “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” prevailed over several underwhelming new holiday releases, including Paramount’s R-rated crime thriller “By Any Means,” Lionsgate’s anxiety-inducing sequel “Fall 2: Deadpoint” and A24’s action horror film “Onslaught.” “September and the Labor Day holiday are traditionally sluggish at the box office,” says David A. “We haven’t had a down weekend like this in a long time.” “By Any Means” stumbled in fourth place with $7.4 million from 2,903 North American theaters over the traditional weekend and an estimated $9.1 million through Monday. Audiences seemed to like the R-rated movie more than critics, as evidenced by the “B+” grade on CinemaScore and 52% on Rotten Tomatoes. Directed by Elegance Bratton, “By Any Means” centers around the unlikely partnership between a young Black FBI agent (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II) and a notorious mafia hitman (Mark Wahlberg) as they investigate a wave of brutal killings targeting civil rights leaders. Hammerstone Studios financed “By Any Means” for roughly $30 million, and Paramount is distributing the movie for a fee. “Fall 2: Deadpoint” crash-landed at No. 12 with just $2.3 million from 1,704 venues in its initial weekend of release and a projected $2.9 million through its first four days. Those ticket sales are roughly even with its predecessor, 2022’s survival thriller “Fall,” which opened to $2.5 million. That film managed to climb to $7.2 million domestically and $18 million globally by the end of its run, becoming a modest success against a mere $3 million budget. The sequel follows two friends who travel to Thailand and get trapped at 4,000 feet after a sudden rockslide. “Onslaught” fared even worse, debuting in 13th place on domestic charts with $1.8 million from 1,918 theaters over the weekend and an estimated $2.3 million through Monday’s holiday. What’s concerning is critics and audiences alike rejected the film, which was saddled with a “C” grade on CinemaScore and 54% on Rotten Tomatoes. That doesn’t bode well for box office longevity. Directed by Adam Wingard (“Godzilla vs. Kong”), “Onslaught” stars Adria Arjona as an army sniper who struggles to protect her young daughter from an army of genetically engineered super soldiers. Since the Labor Day newcomers failed to gain much traction, “The Odyssey” easily claimed the No. 2 spot in North America in its eighth weekend of release. The movie brought in $13 million between Friday and Sunday and is estimated to generate a remarkable $17 million through the four-day holiday frame. Christopher Nolan’s blockbuster has remained an epic box office force since mid-July, grossing $584 million in North America and $1.62 billion worldwide to date. Imax has contributed $486 million globally, representing a massive 30% of the film’s total box office tally. Acme” landed in third place with $11.3 million from 3,727 venues in its second weekend, a minuscule 27% decline from its debut. It’s projected to earn $14.5 million through Labor Day. With great reviews and positive audience scores, “Looney Tunes” spinoff has been a hit with $37 million domestically to date. It was originally set at Warner Bros. before the studio shelved the completed film as a $30 million tax write-off. That prompted outrage from the creative community, leading Warner Bros. to allow the filmmaking team to shop “Coyote vs. Acme” around town before selling it to indie distributor Ketchup Entertainment. Also of note, Roadside Attraction’s horror thriller “Buddy” secured seventh place with $5.7 million from 1,771 theaters in its sophomore outing, a rare 5% increase from its debut. It’s estimated to gross $7.2 million through Monday, bringing its domestic tally to $15.7 million. “Buddy,” which premiered at Sundance Film Festival, stars Cristin Milioti, Michael Shannon and Keegan-Michael Key. The gonzo plot follows a group of children who are trapped in a surreal ’90s-style children’s TV series and have to escape the terrifying host (a unicorn, voiced by Key). After a stellar summer, it’s up to fall releases — including “Practical Magic 2” with Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock, Tom Cruise’s comedy “Digger,” a “Resident Evil” reboot from “Weapons” director Zach Cregger and Colleen Hoover’s “Verity” adaptation led by Anne Hathaway and Dakota Johnson — to sustain the momentum. Will the hits keep coming? With tentpoles like “Avengers: Doomsday,” “Dune: Part Three” and “Jumanji 3” slated around Christmastime, North American revenues are primed to surpass $10 billion for the first time since the pandemic. The movies are really, truly back!

entry.title: ‘Woman Unknown’ Review: Some More Problematic Sex — and Its Consequences — by Denmark’s May el-Toukhy
entry.body: Against the rubble gray and stiff mahogany with which director May el-Toukhy washes out her post-Second World War Copenhagen, the pops of crimson in “Woman Unknown” announce a stark symbolism that’s about as subtle as the red swastika eventually smeared on the front door of protagonist Marie (Mathilde Arcel). As obvious as these subliminal scarlet letters may be, they’re not without a certain Hitchcockian power in a film about sexual shame and a kind of violence against women’s bodies that operates from the inside out. But as this is el-Toukhy — whose steely 2019 incest drama “Queen of Hearts” was promptly adapted by French provocatrice Catherine Breillat in “Last Summer” — the film’s feminism, or lack thereof depending on how you take your empowerment, is a prickly matter by design. As with the women played by Emmanuelle Riva in “Hiroshima, Mon Amour” or Charlotte Rampling in “The Night Porter,” a crisis is sparked over Marie’s supposedly soiled sheets, with el-Toukhy basing her story on the many accounts of public punishment received by women from Nazi-occupied countries who had sexual relations with German soldiers during the war. It’s a spicy conceit from the only woman director in Venice’s main competition, and its implications arguably creep out beyond the historical context in question — should our private lives be judged and exposed to real consequences? Not that el-Toukhy has made a particularly open film with this neatly scripted psychodrama, her austere visuals and prim haut-bourgeois setting practically asking to be unraveled. Popular on Variety Marie, a maid and nanny to the twiggy blonde child of her employer Christian (Carsten Bjornlund), a widower and owner of a glove-making factory, carries herself as if permanently bound in a corset: breath held, mouth tight, her eyes shifty as if dreading the next reprimand. It makes sense given her workplace’s exacting standards, in which place settings are arranged according to centimeter-precise measurements and stony head maid Esther (Marina Bouras) is always watching. But early on, when Christian discreetly caresses Marie’s cheek, it’s clear that it’s not just her job that’s at stake should she fall, but her newly gained status as lady of the house. A long shot of a pearly silk dress — a wedding dress — dangling like a carrot in an empty closet doubles as a harbinger of doom when she’s spotted by Karl (Thorbjorn Hedegaard), an old classmate from her hometown who’s much too eager to catch up. It’s through this jittery encounter, and a visit to the doctor where Marie re-ups on the liquid opium she takes to dull the pain of sex with Christian, that we learn she once had a baby boy, and that child caused her to flee her past life. El-Toukhy and Maren Louise Kaehne’s script doesn’t connect the dots for you with explanatory dialogue, but those dots are still awfully close. Scenes of nameless women being knocked around on the streets by gangs of men, who chop off their hair and tear off their clothes before branding them with painted swastikas, make it brutally clear what Marie is hiding from. And what starts out with the echoing, empty rooms of paranoia turns into whispers from the domestic staff after Karl discovers where Marie lives. The building door is marked with Nazi insignia shortly after, leaving Marie desperate to cover the tracks that lead to her. Cinematographer Jasper Spanning’s static, shadowy frames give way to shallow-lensed close-ups as Marie plunges into a panicked spiral that, at one point, sees her consenting to a wad of spit in her mouth. That scene, which begins with a pan over Marie’s naked body as Karl swats her hands away to do as he pleases, rhymes with comparably frigid moments involving the gilded milieu she aspires to join — as when a snooty tailor takes her measurements or when Christian uses her as a hand model to show off a new glove design. This body does not belong to her, and her refusal to cede control of it to her male masters will end in their wrath, a point made repeatedly, albeit with a harrowing range of registers. Marie’s humanity and capacity for tenderness come through in her scenes with children, though these aren’t nearly weighty enough — despite Arcel’s commendably nervy performance — to carry out her concluding crash-out convincingly. Her relationship with the next-door neighbor, a single mother far too liberated to escape scrutiny in midcentury Denmark, gets a few threadbare scenes to prime this spiritual flurry, where red appears one last time in the form of blood on Marie’s hands. Worse than the loogie is the feminine betrayal that weighs on her soul, or at least that’s how it’s supposed to read.
