White commented on E! 4 Instagram post about the new couple with "Sign the papers" and three hands clapping emojis. "Soo much I could say right now because I know what really happened lol," Angelina Pivarnick of Jersey Shore Family Vacation commented on the same post. Thank you to the real trophy for making a beautiful night even better. #Emmys," Parks captioned the photos. "Yasssssss Frack," Porsha Williams commented. She was a faithful contestant on season 4 of The Traitors US. "He made it clear to her he really, really liked her and he fell for her when they were on Traitors," a source told Page Six. "They really do laugh together a lot and their relationship is really sweet," the insider later said. Tamburello posted a video of Parks getting her makeup done on his Instagram story with the words, "…how'd I get so lucky!?" over it. The next video was his "miracle workers" doing his makeup. He showed a short video of the Emmys audience and the announcement that Alan Cumming won for hosting the competition series for The Traitors US. Tamburello hasn't addressed his separation from White recently. entry.title: Witkoff and Kushner, in a first, visit Ukraine for peace talks
entry.body: President Trump's envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner arrived in Kyiv on Sunday for diplomatic talks aimed at resuming negotiations between Russia and Ukraine . Why it matters: Kushner and Witkoff traveled to Kyiv right after talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow. This is Witkoff and Kushner's first trip to Ukraine despite months of negotiating with both sides and multiple trips to Russia. Sunday also marked the highest-level visit by a U.S. official to Ukraine since Trump started his second term. Driving the news: U.S. and Russian officials offered positive assessments of Kushner and Witkoff's three-hour meeting with Putin on Saturday. "Kushner and Witkoff are making an effort, and we are making progress," a Russian official said. A White House official said Witkoff, Kushner and Putin discussed "plans for next steps, which will be announced in the coming weeks." Witkoff, Kushner and their team left Moscow on Saturday night, landed several hours later in Poland, and then traveled by land to Kyiv. Zoom in: Zelensky discussed Ukrainian preparations for continuing the war through the winter, a source familiar with the meetings said. Kushner and Witkoff stressed they want a breakthrough before winter, the source said. Witkoff and Kushner met twice with Zelensky and his senior advisers. National security advisers from the U.K., France and Germany joined a third meeting. After the second meeting with Zelensky, Trump's envoys said they were "encouraged by the substantive discussion" and looked forward to making more progress. What they're saying: A second source who participated in Sunday's talks said the meetings "went well" and that Kushner and Witkoff want to work with the parties on a "refreshed" peace proposal. "Things may move in a good direction if there's a follow-up by all parties involved," the source said. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

entry.title: Dem governors weighing White House face the DeSantis dilemma
entry.body: Top aides for Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis ' failed 2024 presidential campaign have a warning for Democratic governors eyeing a 2028 run: Don't wait too long after November's midterms to jump into the race. Why it matters: In the coming months, Govs. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania, Wes Moore of Maryland, JB Pritzker of Illinois and Andy Beshear of Kentucky will face a dilemma similar to what confronted DeSantis after his 2022 reelection: Do they get in the race early — before their postelection legislative sessions start — and risk not being focused on their constituents? Or do they wait until late spring to rack up policy wins and give their opponents a head start on a White House run? Their allies and some of their teams are already debating which path to take, Democratic sources tell Axios. Driving the news: Many DeSantis aides now regret how they handled the months between DeSantis' commanding reelection victory in November 2022 and his entry into the presidential race in late May 2023, several told Axios. Donald Trump announced his reelection bid in November 2022 and began attacking DeSantis while the governor was scoring state policy wins and promoting a new book — but falling behind in the presidential race. "In this atmosphere, you can't be president by just being a great governor and boasting about your legislative wins," said Ryan Tyson, a Republican pollster and president of the Tyson Group who was a senior adviser to DeSantis. "That's how they did it in the '90s — not anymore. Enough of the voters in these early nomination contests will be driven by emotion more so than logic." A former DeSantis aide added: "There were diminishing returns for DeSantis passing conservative legislation [in Florida's 2023 session] because of his preexisting, extensive record." "I don't think it's very helpful for a Democratic governor waiting to announce for 2028 to use the legislative session to just keep doing more of what they've already been doing," the former DeSantis aide said. "It would have to be new stuff to command media attention or fix a potential political vulnerability." Reality check: The 2028 Democratic primary is different from the 2024 Republican primary. DeSantis was running against a former president who was still extraordinarily popular with the GOP base. The legal indictments against Trump led many Republican voters to rally around him. Trump also made the unorthodox move to go negative against DeSantis in paid and earned media before the Florida governor got in the race. Between the lines: If Democratic governors declare their candidacies before their legislative sessions are over, they could face attacks from rivals in the presidential race in addition to rebellions within their states. Ambitious state legislators could hold up bills and criticize newly elected governors for focusing on national politics just months after winning reelection. Axios asked Shapiro, Moore, Beshear and Pritzker if they had committed to finishing their state legislative sessions before declaring whether they were running for president. None of them directly answered the question. Shapiro spokesperson Manuel Bonder told Axios: "While we appreciate team DeSantis taking a break from banning abortion and rigging our democracy to offer unsolicited advice, I'll repeat what the governor has made clear: The midterms run through Pennsylvania, and the only thing we are focused on is winning up and down the ballot this November."

entry.title: Trump's energy boss wavers on gasoline price path
entry.body: Energy Secretary Chris Wright on Sunday cautiously predicted gasoline price relief is on the way, but stopped short of firm or precise pledges. Why it matters: Pump prices are at their highest Labor Day weekend levels on record, and the midterms loom less than two months away. His appearances on Sunday political shows also comes as diesel prices, which ripple through the economy, are at all-time highs . "I think prices headed downward is — is not an unreasonable expectation," he said on CBS's "Face the Nation." State of play: On that show and others, Wright noted that U.S. gasoline demand typically falls after Labor Day with the end of the traditional summer driving season. He also promoted recent administration moves to ease some environmental requirements for summer gasoline blends. "Gasoline production is about to go up and demand is about to go down. So, if I had to guess, they're more likely to go down than go up," Wright said on CNN's "State of the Union." Catch up quick: U.S. regular gasoline prices averaged $4.15 per gallon Sunday, per AAA data. Data: AAA; Chart: Ben Geman/Axios The intrigue: Wright also pointed to declining prices for gasoline futures contracts in the months ahead. "The marketplace thinks gasoline prices are going to move meaningfully lower. So trust the market, certainly don't trust my predictions.," he said on ABC's "This Week," per a transcript. Yes, but: Futures prices months ahead are volatile, and they're not a crystal ball for what will be happening in retail markets. Pump prices have climbed in recent weeks amid a flare-up in hostilities that has driven crude oil prices higher. Crude oil is already at its highest level in roughly six weeks, with the global benchmark above $96 per barrel at Friday's close, even though more oil appears to have been transiting the Strait of Hormuz recently. What we're watching: Oil prices could see another jump when markets open for the week, following fresh conflicts this weekend.

entry.title: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation
entry.body: Australians will be able to switch off social media algorithms under planned legislation - Published Australians would be able to switch off social media algorithms under draft legislation to be proposed this week. Communications Minister Anika Wells, who last year helmed the government's world-first social media ban for under-16s, said the digital duty of care laws would ensure "some basic safety protections on an industry that hasn't had to observe it". If tech firms such as Meta, Google and TikTok did not give the option to turn off algorithms, they should face "substantial" penalties, she said. Some members of the opposition have criticised the proposal, with Liberal Party leader Angus Taylor saying he was "highly sceptical" and arguing the move could amount to censorship. The government will be taking "expert advice" on whether users would have to opt in or out of the algorithms feeding them content online, Wells said. This means that, as with its social media ban, the government is looking to bring in legislation before fully hammering out the specifics of how it would work. "We want to give Australians more choice over what they see on their social media feeds," Wells told the ABC on Monday. "We know that a lot of Australians appreciate the algorithm both for the enjoyment they get out of it or the utility that they get out of it, seeing local businesses in their suburb. "A lot of Australians will want to choose the algorithm. But we think that big tech should offer them the choice in the first place and they should respect that choice. "Big tech is not a protected species and they should offer their customers basic safety standards." But she admitted that so far no tech firm had been fined for not enforcing the social media ban, despite research consistently showing that the vast majority of under 16s who were on platforms before the ban was introduced last December, still use them. Some members of the opposition have said they support the idea in principle, but others argue it is an attempt to curtail freedom of speech. Taylor told News24 he feared this was "an attempt by the government to censor social media" and that Labor should first try to plug holes in the social media ban. Speaking to Channel Nine's Today show, Wells said: "This isn't about censorship. This is about identifying risks or making big tech identify the risks on their own platform and making big tech mitigate against those risks on their platform." Last week, high-profile consent advocate Chanel Contos gave a speech at Australia's National Press Club calling on the government to seek an opt-in for algorithmic social media feeds, making it harder for tech firms to find a way round any reforms. She argued algorithms were fuelling the prevalence of sexual violence in Australia and exposing young people to misogynistic "manosphere" material. The draft legislation is expected to be introduced in the coming days. As well as addressing algorithms, it is also expected to put an onus on platforms to stop harmful content, such as illegal pornography and videos promoting disordered eating, from being shared. Related topics - Published12 December 2025 - Published8 December 2025 - Published23 January
entry.summary: Firms like Meta, Google and TikTok should face "substantial" penalties if they don't give the option, minister says.

entry.title: Protesters block roads in Portsmouth after 140 migrants rescued
entry.body: Protesters block roads in Portsmouth after 140 migrants rescued - Published Hundreds of protesters gathered in Portsmouth on Sunday night after around 140 migrants in a single dinghy were rescued in the English Channel. In the second major anti-migrant protest of the weekend, police faced off with demonstrators as they blocked roads in an effort to stop the people who had arrived on the small boat from leaving the city. Hampshire Police urged people to avoid the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were brought ashore, and said a dispersal order was in place, meaning anyone failing to comply could be arrested. The government condemned "the intimidating and thuggish behaviour" of the protesters, many of whom were dressed in black and wore masks. Conservative MP for Isle of Wight East Joe Robertson said on X it was "extremely concerning to see an illegal migrant crossing this far west". Protesters said they were trying to stop authorities transporting the migrants to the Manston processing centre in Kent. Police carrying riot shields protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo â an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson â was livestreaming from the scene. "Roads are all blocked, they are never going to be able to leave here," he said. A government spokesperson said: "The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder." "We thank the emergency services who are working to safely manage this situation." Reform UK leader Nigel Farage posted on X: "This week Andy Burnham struck an agreement for 45 more officers on French beaches. Today a boat launched from Baie de Seine, 170 miles from Calais, arriving on the beaches of Hampshire for the very first time. Only Reform will send the boats back." The protest came after a large group of masked men held a demonstration over the small-boat crossings at the Port of Dover on Saturday, causing a major disruption. Days earlier, Prime Minister Andy Burnham and French President Emmanuel Macron met to discuss how to "scale up" efforts to reduce small boat crossings. In August a single small boat carrying a record 230 people successfully crossed the Channel. The latest dinghy launched in Bay of the Seine and was shadowed for around 10 hours by French rescue boats in case it got into difficulty. The French coastguard said it was not safe to attempt to stop the dinghy on water. It reached UK waters at lunchtime and the people on board were met by lifeboats from Bembridge and Yarmouth. French authorities said it was unusual for the migrant boat to depart from the area - 170 miles from where they are commonly launched near Calais - making the crossing to the UK significantly longer. On Saturday, hundreds of protesters, dressed in black and wearing face coverings, blocked roads near the Port of Dover and were heard chanting "stop the boats". A council boss said police were slow to react to the "exceptionally well organised" protest. Kevin Mills, who leads Dover District Council, told the BBC that demonstrators "caught several agencies on the hoof" when they arrived on Saturday. Kent Police is yet to comment, but cabinet minister Jonathan Reynolds said officers "did deal with it swiftly". Last year local officials told the BBC there has been an increase in people trying to depart from Normandy. Earlier on Sunday, a Home Office spokesperson said: "This government is bearing down on dangerous small boat crossings and restoring control at our border. "Joint efforts have seen over 48,000 crossing attempts prevented and 1,100 boats and engines seized since the election." They added: "But we must go further, which is why we have signed a payment-by-results deal with the French to put 40% more boots on the ground on French beaches." A Maritime and Coastguard Agency spokesperson said: "In response to a report on September 6 of a small boat heading towards the Hampshire coast, HM Coastguard sent lifeboats, an HM Coastguard helicopter, an HM Coastguard aeroplane and HM Coastguard Rescue Teams. "Border Force, Border Security Command, Hampshire Police and South Central Ambulance Service were also sent." In bilateral talks on Thursday, Burnham and Macron agreed they were making headway in reducing small boat crossings in the English Channel but now needed to go further. While the number of boat crossings over summer months has dropped to its lowest since 2019, smugglers appear to have started loading more people onto fewer, larger vessels dubbed "mega dinghies". It's thought the people smugglers organising the crossings have been forced to go to much greater lengths to avoid detection following more robust policing in the Calais area. Between 1 January and 1 September 2026, a total of 16, 513 people crossed the English Channel by small boat from France. Downing Street says 45 extra police officers are being deployed to French beaches in a "surge team" to tackle larger dinghies with more people packed onto them. Related topics - Published18 August
entry.summary: The government condemns "thuggish behaviour" in the second major anti-migrant protest of the weekend.

entry.title: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school
entry.body: Austria's Islamic headscarf ban in force as under-14s go back to school - Published As the new school year begins in Austria, a law banning headscarves in schools for girls under 14 has gone into force. The law forbids "traditional Muslim" head coverings, such as hijabs or burkas, in public and private schools across the country. Integration Minister Claudia Bauer, from the conservative People's Party (ÃVP), says the headscarf is "a sign of oppression and a means of controlling girls from the earliest childhood". But critics say the new law is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling in the country and could be unconstitutional. The law was brought in by the conservative-led coalition of three centrist parties, the ÃVP, the Social Democrats (SPÃ) and the liberal Neos. They say the law is a "clear commitment to gender equality" and is intended to protect the rights of young girls. Carla Amina Baghajati, from the official Islamic Community in Austria (IGGÃ), told the BBC that the organisation "firmly opposes the ban". "We believe it unjustifiably restricts the fundamental right to freedom of religion and disproportionately affects Muslim girls," she said. "Rather than protecting children, it singles out a specific religious practice and risks excluding the very children it claims to support." The IGGÃ said it would support legal challenges by girls and their families "who believe that their fundamental rights are being infringed" and who wished to bring their cases before the Constitutional Court. The court struck down a previous ban on headscarves in primary schools in 2020 on the basis that it contravened the principle of Austria's religious neutrality. Teachers are expected to enforce the new ban if they see a child wearing a headscarf by holding a series of talks with the student and their legal guardians. If there are repeated violations, child services must be notified and as a last resort, guardians could face fines of up to â¬800 (Â£685). Some teachers have expressed concerns about having to enforce the ban. The Green Party's Sigi Maurer accused Education Minister Christoph Wiederkehr, from the liberal NEOS, of "creating new conflicts and offloading them onto the teachers". She said teachers were "already under enormous strain" and that Wiederkehr wanted to "foist the role of police officers onto them" on top of their other duties. The opposition far-right Freedom Party (FPÃ) says the current ban doesn't go far enough. It is calling for a general prohibition on headscarves and face coverings in schools for students and teachers alike. The FPÃ's Ricarda Berger said there was "no place for political Islam in Austria, and certainly not in our schools". Austria's Chancellor Christian Stocker, leader of the ÃVP, recently called for a constitutional ban on political Islam, telling Austrian public broadcaster ORF he did not "want to live in an Islamic state". In France there has been a ban on wearing any conspicuous religious symbols, including headscarves, turbans and kippas, in schools for more than 20 years. The Austrian law differs from French legislation in that it specifically targets head coverings worn by Muslim women. Austria, like several other European countries including France, Belgium and Denmark, bans the full face veil (niqabs or burkas) in public. Baghajati said the IGGÃ was concerned about "a troubling trend" across Europe "in which complex social challenges are reduced to symbolic measures aimed at minority groups." "Such approaches may generate political attention, but they rarely solve the underlying problems," she said.
entry.summary: The government says the law is intended to protect the rights of young girls, but critics say it is fuelling anti-Muslim feeling.

entry.title: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority
entry.body: Germany's far-right AfD set for big win in eastern state, just short of majority - Published Germany's Alternative for Germany (AfD) is heading for a dramatic victory in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of its mainstream rivals. Although it is projected to fall short of a majority, the AfD says it has won a mandate to govern. The far-right AfD is on course to win a record 44% of the vote, well ahead of the conservative CDU on 17%, with most interim results counted. Charismatic leader in the state, Ulrich Siegmund, said it was "sensational" and they wanted to start governing as soon as possible. No far-right party has won control of a German state since World War Two, and governing at state level would mean powers over policing, local education and culture. Saxony-Anhalt has a small population of 2.1 million and the AfD in the state is assessed by domestic intelligence as "right-wing extremist", a classification rejected by Siegmund, 35. He along with joint national leaders Alice Weidel and Tino Chrupalla were overjoyed as exit polls revealed they were on track to score more than double the party's result in 2021. Commentators and political opponents spoke of the outcome as a watershed and break with the past. Main TV channel Das Erste cancelled its legendary crime drama Tatort to focus on what the result meant. "This isn't just about Saxony-Anhalt," Siegmund told supporters. "It's a signal for the whole of Germany - a self-confident signal." US President Donald Trump posted a screenshot of the German TV projection on his Truth Social platform, and then Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev took a screengrab of Trump's post and praised a "historic win for the pragmatic AfD". Dmitriev had earlier praised the Russia-friendly AfD as "the party of hope and reason, co-operation truth and hope for Germany". Ahead of Germany's federal election last year, US Vice-President JD Vance endorsed the party, in a move criticised in Germany as political interference. Polish centre-right Prime Minister Donald Tusk saw the result very differently, saying "in Poland only idiots and traitors can rejoice at the triumph of the AfD". Without enough seats to form a majority government, Ulrich Siegmund has so far refused to lead a minority government, even though the party's national leaders see it as a possibility. "If necessary there'll just be new elections, then we'd just get 50 or 55%," said Siegmund, while saying he was prepared to work with individual MPs or a party. For hours it was unclear whether the BSW would reach the 5% threshold needed to enter parliament, although interim results showed it had succeeded. Had it failed, then the AfD would have seen its chances of a majority increase. The AfD is currently heading for 39 seats in the 83-seat state parliament instead of the 42 needed for an outright majority. A crowd of supporters at the AfD election night party HQ erupted in cheers as the projections came up on the screen. A short while later, people burst into singing Germany's national anthem. "We have made history in this state," Siegmund said. His opposite number in the CDU, Sven Schulze, conceded victory as he watched the conservative vote slump by more than half on the previous election. "This was an extremely tough and intensive election campaign," said Schulze, adding that his party would have to deal with the result. Germany's centre-left SPD described the outcome as "truly dramatic" and national leader Lars Klingbeil, whose party is in government nationally with the CDU, described the outcome as a "signal to Berlin" and he was adamant that they would hear it. The anti-migration AfD stands for Alternative fÃ¼r Deutschland. It has not only dominated the election campaign, it is emerging as the dominant force in the result and its supporters believe they are on the march. Turnout in Saxony-Anhalt was particularly high at 76.7%, and AfD supporters in Magdeburg praised Siegmund's success in winning over voters. One man called Ollie said: "This man gives us what no-one else can give." "No matter what government, they all just promise things to get better. This is a party for the working people. It is the alternative for Germany," he told the BBC. Another AfD voter called Bert said people in the east could sense things were not going well: "Things need to improve for us, for my family - I have three children. I'm in fear, I'm really in fear that safety erodes more and more." Other parties refuse to go into coalition with the AfD, operating a Brandmauer or firewall aimed at keeping the far right out of government. In Saxony-Anhalt, the BSW has offered to co-operate with the AfD on some issues if it gets into the state parliament. The AfD leads the opinion polls nationally, ahead of the ruling conservatives of Chancellor Friedrich Merz and the Social Democrats, but their heartland lies in the eastern states. They also won the 2024 state election in neighbouring Thuringia, but failed to secure enough seats to win power. Among the AfD's policies is a highly controversial plan for "remigration", which is widely understood to mean mass deportations of migrants, although the party says it refers to deporting criminals and those in the country illegally. It would not be able to achieve either if it ran the government of one of 16 states. But it would have significant local powers. The party has been particularly critical of the Bauhaus school of design which the Nazis shut down in the city of Dessau in Saxony-Anhalt after they came to power in 1933. The AfD has called it "the dead-end of modernism", prompting some to accuse the party of using similar language to the Nazis. Nikita, a demonstrator at an anti-AfD "Democracy Festival" in Magdeburg on the eve of the vote said Germans had to "learn from our history and not go back. We don't want the dark times any more". Responding to the news from Saxony-Anhalt, the veteran head of the Jewish community in Munich and Bavaria, Charlotte Knobloch, said it frightened her. "On days like this I find it hard to recognise my homeland any more," the 93-year-old Holocaust survivor said, appealing for mainstream parties not to stand by and allow "this decline". One of the AfD's top figures in Saxony-Anhalt, Hans-Thomas Tillschneider, has also been criticised for his approach to Russia. When asked why he had a Russian army mug in his office, he said it was just a souvenir, and "it's not our war".
entry.summary: Germany's AfD hails a "historic result" and is projected to win 44% of the vote in Saxony-Anhalt, far ahead of the conservatives on 17%.

entry.title: Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain
entry.body: Peace talks rich in symbolism but fundamental differences between Russia and Ukraine remain - Published The talks in Kyiv were rich in symbolism. The sight of Donald Trump's envoys setting foot on Ukrainian soil for the first time since Russia's full-scale invasion. The fact they had to travel by train because they could not risk flying and running the gauntlet of Russian drones - weapons launched on the orders of the man at whose table they sat in the Kremlin only hours ago. The symbolism of Ukrainian President Zelensky greeting Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner at Kyiv's Saint Sophia Cathedral, not only an icon of Ukraine's ancient history, but also just a few yards from where Russian drones hit the headquarters of the country's security services on Friday. You did not have to join too many dots to work out the point Zelensky was making. Both sides held talks for several hours; they were later joined by some European national security advisers, including the UK's National Security Adviser Jonathan Powell. And afterwards, all sides spoke warmly of having held substantive discussions. They spoke hopefully of reviving past "trilateral talks" involving both the US and Europe. The US envoys had come hot foot from Moscow where Vladimir Putin had told them Russia was making "tangible advances" on the battlefield. The story they heard from Ukraine was different, in fact the opposite. Ukrainian officials claim that in August they gained more territory than they lost and Russia suffered 42,000 casualties, dead or wounded. Putin had also told the US envoys the root causes of the conflict had to be addressed, shorthand for his longstanding strategic demands that Ukraine cede territory, abandon hopes of joining Nato and reduce the size of its army. After the talks, Zelensky insisted Ukraine would require "strong and clear" security guarantees, including a strong army. Nor did he give any sign of being willing to give up any territory in the eastern Donbas region, an issue he described dryly as "difficult". Witkoff insisted progress had been made and the ingredients for a settlement were there. But he admitted both sides would have to make compromises to narrow the differences between them. And right now, it is hard to see either side doing that. So for now, the expectation in Kyiv is that the fighting will continue and they will face a hard winter ahead. Some diplomats talk of a window of opportunity for a possible settlement next spring. Zelensky thanked the US envoys for their visit because the short-term pause in air strikes agreed by both sides had given the people of Kyiv a brief respite. Few expect it to last for long. - Published30 December 2025 - Published2 days ago
entry.summary: Despite talks between US envoys and both Putin and Zelensky, the expectation in Kyiv is the fighting will continue, writes James Landale.

entry.title: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles
entry.body: Jamaica to bring slavery reparations petition to King Charles - Published The Jamaican government will highlight to King Charles a petition over slavery reparations on Monday, the country's culture minister Olivia Grange has said. It will ask the King, who serves as Jamaica's head of state, to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council, the country's highest court, over the legality of the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica. Grange said it could pave the way for a "long outstanding settlement for the hundreds of years of the most horrific abuse that our African ancestors endured". She will also meet with British Museum officials to discuss the repatriation of artefacts taken during the colonial era. The three questions which the Jamaican government is asking the King to refer to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council (JCPC) are: whether the enslavement of Africans in Jamaica was legal under English law, whether it broke international law, and whether Britain now has a legal duty to provide redress. The petition, which is not a demand for payment, goes to the King who then refers it to the JCPC. King Charles has no personal discretion in deciding whether to make a referral. Grange said: "Once we get the answers, or once we get a response to those questions, then the next steps will be determined." Buckingham Palace has been working closely with the Governor General of Jamaica to ensure the petition is correctly lodged. A Palace spokesperson said: "His Majesty has on many occasions expressed his personal and wholehearted commitment to promoting greater understanding around the issue of slavery and finding ways to address historic wrongs for the benefit of communities today." When slavery was abolished across most of the empire in 1833, the British government paid Â£20m to slave owners in compensation. The loans taken out to raise the money were paid off in 2015. Grange said: "Up to 2015, Britain was paying the slave masters, because we were being considered property. "The question really should be: if in modern times we're still paying back the slave masters for the property that was our people, our ancestors, for property that was because of the abolition of slavery, then why shouldn't we be pursuing some remedy at this time?" Grange will also meet with British Museum officials to "advance discussions on the repatriation of artefacts" taken from Jamaica during the colonial era. She said: "They are priceless, they are significant to the story of Jamaica and we are working to bring them home." In 2015, David Cameron, who was prime minister at the time, ruled out making reparations for Britain's role in the historic slave trade, while visiting Jamaica. Speaking to MPs in Jamaica's parliament, Cameron said slavery was "abhorrent in all its forms". He added that he hoped they could "move on from this painful legacy and continue to build for the future". Related topics - Published26 October 2024
entry.summary: The King will be asked to refer three questions to the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council.

entry.title: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach US Open last eight
entry.body: Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight - Published Carlos Alcaraz continued his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open. Playing just his fourth competitive singles match after an absence of more than four months, the 23-year-old Spaniard produced a masterful performance to beat American 20th seed Paul 6-4 6-3 6-4. He has dropped only one set on his way to the last eight in New York and his quarter-final opponent will be American eighth seed Ben Shelton. A wrist injury caused Alcaraz to miss both the French Open and Wimbledon earlier this summer. He had won the previous two Grand Slams - last year's US Open and this year's Australian Open - meaning the straight-set victory over Paul extended his run of match wins at the majors to 18. Alcaraz is taking a different approach to this year's tournament in New York, putting a greater emphasis on recovery as he looks to keep his wrist injury-free - even if that means giving up his favourite off-court activity on his days off. "I've been really focused on the recovery with my team, with myself, doing the right things off the court trying to be healthy and in a good shape for the next round," he said. "Those days, if I'm practicing or not, I'm trying to be chill and focus on the next round. So golf in this year isn't an option." Alcaraz has won all three of his Tour-level matches against Shelton, who defeated Stefanos Tsitsipas 6-2 6-3 6-4 later on Sunday. "If Shelton were to come through, he is the kind of player that can knock the racquet out of your hand," said American former player Jeff Tarango on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra. "It's going to be a real test to see how Alcaraz's wrist is with a 149mph serve coming to that forehand, but Alcaraz should get through Shelton if his wrist is fine." - Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open - Published30 minutes ago - How to follow US Open on the BBC - Published5 hours ago Alcaraz said after his third-round win that he was happy with the level of fitness he had shown in the early rounds following his lengthy absence, while he demonstrated against Paul that the quality of his shot-making is as good as ever. One sensational cross-court forehand winner early in the second set, which landed in from an almost impossible angle, was measured at 103mph. Former British number one Tim Henman told Sky Sports: "When you haven't played tennis for four weeks, it seems a lot and you can be a bit rusty. This is four and a half months. "If you would have given Alcaraz a blank piece of paper at the beginning of the tournament and asked how he'd want the first four matches to go, he would have scripted it exactly like that. "He's had a few slightly challenging moments but, in the important moments, he's just come up with incredible tennis. That's got to give him so much confidence moving forward." American trio storm into quarter-finals Later on Sunday, Frances Tiafoe, Alex Michelsen and Shelton stormed into the quarter-finals to boost home hopes of a first American men's Grand Slam champion since Andy Roddick won the New York major in 2003. Tiafoe delighted fans in a entertaining victory over 2021 champion Daniil Medvedev, saving a set point in the third-set tie-break before wrapping up a 7-6 (7-1) 6-4 7-6 (8-6) win to maintain his perfect record on Louis Armstrong Stadium. Tiafoe has now won all 10 of his matches on the US Open's secondary show court, while it is just his second win in eight appearances against Russian Medvedev. A two-time semi-finalist in New York, Tiafoe will face Michelsen next after the 22-year-old beat Argentina's Tomas Martin Etcheverry 7-6 (8-6) 6-4 6-4 to reach his first Grand Slam quarter-final. Shelton, meanwhile, surged past Tsitsipas in less than two hours to join his compatriots in the last eight. Former world number three Tsitsipas had been enjoying a resurgence at Flushing Meadows as he defeated Arthur Fils and Jiri Lehecka, the 10th and 18th seeds, en route to his first fourth-round appearance at a Grand Slam in over two years. Tsitsipas' defeat means this is the first year that a player with a one-handed backhand has not reached a major semi-final in men's singles since 1877. In the men's doubles, Britain's Henry Patten and Finnish team-mate Harri Heliovaara, the top seeds, moved into the third round with a 7-5 6-2 win over Matteo Arnaldi of Italy and Germany's Jan-Lennard Struff. British ninth seeds Lloyd Glasspool and Julian Cash won 7-6 (7-2) 6-4 against Czech pair Adam Pavalsek and Patrik Rikl, while Joe Salisbury and American partner Rajeev Ram fought back to beat French duo Theo Arribage and Albano Olivetti 6-7 (2-7) 7-6 (11-9) 6-4. Related topics - Published28 August - Published28 August
entry.summary: Carlos Alcaraz continues his return from long-term injury with a hugely impressive fourth-round win against Tommy Paul at the US Open.

entry.title: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open
entry.body: Sabalenka overcomes tricky Townsend test at US Open - Published Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulated Serena Williams as she eventually overpowered American Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final. A topsy-turvy contest featured 10 breaks of serve, but Sabalenka recovered from 3-1 down in the second set to seal a 6-4 6-3 victory with a fifth consecutive game. It was the Belarusian's 18th consecutive win at the tournament, extending her three-year unbeaten streak following back-to-back triumphs in 2024 and 2025. Sabalenka, 28, is the first woman to reach six consecutive singles quarter-finals at Flushing Meadows since American great Williams in 2016. Six-time champion Williams was also the last player to win three US Open titles in a row, and Sabalenka is now three wins from matching that feat. She will face Wimbledon champion Linda Noskova for a semi-final place, after the Czech sixth seed required six match points to overcome Ukraine's Marta Kostyuk in a rollercoaster 7-5 5-7 6-4 win. Despite the straightforward scoreline this was a tricky match which required a resilient display from Sabalenka, who also had the vast majority of the crowd against her. In that context this was an impressive victory for the four-time major winner, who has not always managed to maintain her composure in similarly testing scenarios. "I was just trying to stay focused on myself, not only point by point but ball by ball," Sabalenka said. "I'm happy I was able to turn around the second set, I think it was a key moment." - Alcaraz delivers statement win to reach last eight - Published4 hours ago - No Brits left in US Open singles - but are there reasons to be positive? - Published1 day ago The match began with five successive breaks of serve - mostly due to excellent returning by both players - but it was Sabalenka who finally took charge. Doubles specialist Townsend, who walked out wearing a long, black-feathered outfit, continued to frustrate Sabalenka and forced her to serve out the set at the second opportunity, before making the breakthrough in the second set. But Sabalenka, aware she must lift the trophy to have a chance of retaining her number one ranking, produced an immediate reply as she broke back to love and dashed to the finish line, wrapping up the victory in 75 minutes. Pegula wins to bring curtain down on Cirstea's Grand Slam career American third seed Jessica Pegula brought the curtain down on Sorana Cirstea's Grand Slam career with a 6-3 6-4 win over the Romanian. Cirstea is set to retire at the end of 2026, despite it being one of the best seasons of her 20-year career. In May, the 36-year-old became the oldest player in rankings history to make her top 20 debut and she is currently ranked at a career-high 17th following a run to the quarter-finals at the French Open. She also reached the third round at the Australian Open and Wimbledon, while she lifted the fourth WTA title of her career at her home tournament in Cluj-Napoca. But Cirstea missed out on a third major quarter-final as Pegula came through a tricky test that saw 11 breaks of serve, securing victory on her third match point. "I just told her I don't know if you're still going to play next year, but you are playing great and I said I have a lot of respect for you," Pegula said when asked what she told Cirstea when they shared an embrace at the net. Pegula, the 2024 runner-up to Sabalenka, will continue her chase for a third straight US Open semi-final when she faces fellow American Emma Navarro, who defeated Russian Anna Kalinskaya 6-4 6-2. - Williams sisters exit US Open but excite - what does future hold? - Published1 day ago - Zheng goes from 5-0 and match point down to victory - Published1 day ago Earlier on Sunday, Noskova's sense of relief was cleared as she crouched to the ground after taking her sixth match point about an hour after earning her first. The 21-year-old served for the match in the second set, but missed her first two match points as Kostyuk battled back from 5-3 down to force a decider. Noskova failed to take her next two match points in the decider, while she missed her fifth match point after saving a break point, before finally getting over the line after an emotionally draining two and a half hours on court. "I am more than relieved, this match was so tough, emotionally a bit more than physically," said Noskova, who missed five championship points before lifting the Wimbledon title this summer. "Today was very close, it could have ended both ways. With all the chances I had in the second set, it was tough to still kind of restart." In the women's doubles, British pair Harriet Dart and Maia Lumsden lost 6-2 6-2 to Spain's Cristina Bucsa and American Nicole Melichar-Martinez, the sixth seeds. Related topics - Published5 hours ago - Published28 August
entry.summary: Two-time defending champion Aryna Sabalenka emulates Serena Williams by overcoming Taylor Townsend to reach a sixth straight US Open quarter-final.

entry.title: Jones shocks Selby to win British Open title
entry.body: Jones shocks Selby to win British Open title - Published Jak Jones claimed the second ranking title of his career by beating four-time world champion Mark Selby 10-6 in the British Open final. The pair were tied at 4-4 after the afternoon session, which included a 139 from Selby. Another century break brought Selby level at 5-5 before Jones, who beat Judd Trump in the semi-final, started to pull away by moving into a two frame lead at 7-5. Breaks of 53 and 62 put Jones one frame from victory and, after England's Selby missed a green on the colours, the Welshman secured victory. "I can't believe it to be honest," Jones, who won his first ranking title with victory at the 2026 Championship League in July, told Channel 5. "I never thought I'd be able to grind Mark Selby down but I've done it today." Jones turned professional at 16 in 2010 and briefly dropped off the World Snooker Tour twice before becoming a mainstay since 2016. He reached the 2024 World Championship final but was beaten by Kyren Wilson. "It's been difficult for the last 15 years - I've been battling away. For my parents, wife and son, it's unbelievable because I haven't really achieved a lot in the game. "This season, to start winning things just feels amazing."
entry.summary: Jak Jones claims the second ranking title of his career by beating four-time world champion Mark Selby 10-6 in the British Open final.

entry.title: Exclusive: Latino leaders push Beshear on Texas' race for governor
entry.body: Dozens of Latino lawmakers and leaders are pressuring Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear , who chairs the Democratic Governors Association, to invest $10 million in the Texas governor's race, according to a letter to Beshear that Axios obtained. Texas state Rep. Gina Hinojosa , who polls suggest is running a strong challenge to Gov. Greg Abbott (R), is trying to become Texas' first Latino governor. Beshear must decide soon how to invest the DGA's cash in the 36 states with governor's races in November. Why it matters: Beshear is considering a presidential run in 2028 . Latino voters are critical in the early primary states of Nevada and New Mexico, and are a key swing vote in general elections. Beshear's decision on where to spend tens of millions in DGA money this fall is an early test of his political instincts — and whether he can carry out an effective campaign strategy without making enemies that could cost him in a 2028 primary. Zoom in: The signees of the letter — which include Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego , a potential rival of Beshear's in the presidential primary — wrote that "not investing in Texas would not only send a message to Latino voters in 2026, but it sends a message to Latino voters heading into 2028." "No other candidate in recent history has come this close to winning the Governor's Mansion in Texas, and we are proud that it is now a Latina that made this a close race, but unfortunately, she has done so without real investment from DGA," the letter says of Hinojosa. There are 36 state governors' races this fall, including several in 2028 swing states such as Wisconsin, Michigan, Nevada and Georgia. And then there's Texas, where a Democrat hasn't won a statewide race in three decades. It's unclear how much money the DGA has for the November elections, but in the last midterm cycle, 2022, the DGA spent about $170 million. Texas is one of the most expensive states to campaign in, and Democratic leaders in Washington have been skeptical about flipping the state blue. Abbott, who is running for a fourth term as governor, has $67 million cash on hand compared with Hinojosa's $3 million, according to the latest finance report in July. The nonpartisan Cook Political Report labels the race "likely" Republican. Even so, most recent polls show Abbott with less than 50% support and Hinojosa within 5 points. What they're saying: "While there will certainly be more investment, announcing a figure would only advantage the [Republican Governors Association] in any counter-investment. I look forward to working with the signees of the letter in supporting Gina," Beshear told Axios in a statement. He said Hinojosa "has proven herself to be a great candidate" and that the DGA is "currently investing by paying expenses and recently providing staff." DGA communications director Sam Newton added: "As the race in Texas becomes increasingly competitive in the final stretch, we will be ready to capitalize on any opportunity to make a real difference." Zoom out: The letter to Beshear is also signed by several members of Congress from Texas, including Rep. Greg Casar, chair of the Congressional Progressive Caucus, and Rep. Joaquin Castro. They argued that an Abbott victory wouldn't affect just Texas but the U.S. House of Representatives. They wrote that Abbott will further gerrymander the state and take away up to 10 more Democratic-held congressional seats over the next four years. "The only way to stop it is to elect Gina Hinojosa as governor of Texas, who has promised to veto illegal maps," they wrote. Between the lines: As the DGA's chair, Beshear would have some advantages if he were to launch a White House run. He's building relationships across the country and glad-handing many potential donors. The potential downside is that the DGA has limited resources and Beshear could wind up creating 2028 foes, depending on which races he invests in and which he doesn't.

entry.title: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested - BBC
entry.body: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested Paraguay's President Santiago Peña has been impeached and placed under house arrest after the collapse of a digital bank with links to his private business interests. Peña was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office due to a widening crisis triggered by the collapse of Ueno Bank earlier this week. He had offered to step down on Thursday. Rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached Peña and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents. Peña, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing. The demise of the digital bank has left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank. An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions prompting widespread protests particularly in the capital, Asunción. The impeachment charges that led to Peña's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. Peña is due to be questioned on Saturday over allegations of breach of trust, influence peddling, and misappropriation of funds, prosecutor Silvia Margarita Gonzalez Vester said. Peña's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. Afterwards, senate president Basilio Núñez said Peña was found guilty of "dereliction of duty". Paraguay's Vice-President Pedro Alliana was then sworn in as interim President. "Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as President until 2028. Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history – a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image." Analysts say Peña is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse. His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic". In an address to the nation on Thursday, Peña said that he was sorry and that "it was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me".
entry.summary: Paraguay's President Santiago Peña impeached and arrested BBC Paraguay president impeached and under house arrest following bank collapse scandal CNN What is ueno bank and how did it trigger Paraguay's political crisis? entry.title: Hegseth calls US-Iran war a 'courageous and historic effort' - Fox News
entry.body: Iran submits nuclear proposal as Hegseth defends war, seeks more money from Congress The Iranian government has submitted a proposal about the future of its nuclear program to the Trump administration. Secretary of War Pete Hegseth is pushing Congress to approve at least $350 billion in defense funding while defending Operation Epic Fury against Tehran. Coverage for this event has ended. Trump declines to confirm US role in reported strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island President Donald Trump declined Friday to say whether the U.S. was responsible for reported missile strikes on Iran's Qeshm Island, while acknowledging that American forces have conducted limited strikes against Iranian air defenses. Asked by a reporter whether the U.S. carried out the reported strikes, Trump responded, "I don't want to talk about it. We do minor strikes, but they knock out. They built a little bit of an anti-aircraft device, and we knocked it out in about 15 minutes, maybe five." Iranian state media reported that two projectiles struck the Suza area of Qeshm Island, according to Reuters. Trump did not specify where the U.S. operation he described took place or whether it was connected to the reported strikes on Qeshm Island. Trump advisers split over renewed Iran strikes as Vance pushes diplomacy: report President Donald Trump's top advisers are divided over whether to resume military strikes against Iran or continue negotiations, according to The Wall Street Journal. Vice President JD Vance and special envoy Steve Witkoff favor diplomacy, while Secretary of War Pete Hegseth and U.S. Brad Cooper support renewed military operations, the newspaper reported, citing U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent reportedly favor maintaining economic pressure through sanctions and the blockade. The disagreements come as Trump weighs further strikes following Republican losses in Tuesday's midterm elections. The president said Friday that Iran wants to reach an agreement with Washington. State Department warns Americans in Middle East of attack threats from Iran-backed Houthis The State Department warned Americans in the Middle East on Friday to remain vigilant amid increased threats of armed attacks by Iranian-backed Houthi militants and potential targeting of U.S. In a security alert posted on X, the department's Bureau of Consular Affairs urged Americans in the region to exercise heightened caution and prepare for possible travel disruptions. The department warned that Iranian-backed Houthis pose an increased threat of armed attacks and that Iran is attempting to target American government officials in the region. citizens were also advised to monitor country-specific security alerts and remain aware of potential flight cancellations and airspace closures. The warning comes as tensions remain high across the Middle East, with President Donald Trump weighing renewed military strikes against Iran while Washington and Tehran continue diplomatic negotiations. Trump says Iran wants deal 'very badly' as nuclear negotiations continue President Donald Trump said Friday that Iran is eager to reach an agreement with the United States, citing economic troubles and damage to Tehran's military capabilities as Washington considers its next steps in the conflict. During a gaggle with reporters, Trump was asked who persuaded him to pursue negotiations after launching military strikes against Iran. "Nobody," Trump responded, defending the strikes and arguing that Iran would have posed a greater threat to Israel and other countries in the region if it had obtained nuclear weapons. "We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," Trump said. The president also pointed to Iran's economic difficulties, asserting that inflation had reached 300% and that its navy had been destroyed. Iran demands concrete US action before nuclear talks can advance Iran is demanding concrete action from Washington before advancing nuclear negotiations, with a senior official saying Friday that Tehran will no longer rely on written U.S. Ali Bagheri, deputy secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, accused Washington of repeatedly violating its commitments over the past 18 months, according to state-run IRNA, as reported by Iran International. “Iran needs to see the US’s practical actions, and [then] the groundwork for opening a new chapter would be prepared,” Bagheri said. The remarks come as Washington reviews a nuclear proposal submitted by Tehran through Qatari intermediaries, while President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran. US offers up to $20 million reward for information on Iran's nuclear program The U.S. is offering a reward of up to $20 million and possible relocation assistance for information about Iran's nuclear program, U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) announced Friday. In a post on X, CENTCOM highlighted the State Department's Rewards for Justice program, which is seeking information about Iran's nuclear facilities, equipment and personnel involved in the program. The reward also covers information about the movement of nuclear-related materials, equipment or personnel, including individuals in the scientific community. The announcement comes as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran while Washington and Tehran continue negotiations over the country's nuclear program. Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military operations targeting Tehran's nuclear facilities. Trump vows Iran will 'never, ever' obtain nuclear weapon during Florida speech President Donald Trump reiterated Friday that Iran would never be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon, pointing to previous U.S. military strikes against Tehran's nuclear facilities. Speaking at the UP Summit at Kennedy Space Center in Cape Canaveral, Florida, Trump credited American B-2 bombers with preventing Iran from developing nuclear weapons. If they did have it, if we didn't go in with those beautiful B-2 bombers a little more than a year ago, if I allowed them to have it today, there would be no Israel. It would have been wiped off the face of the earth, and there would be no Middle East," Trump said. "We will never let that happen. Iran will never, ever have a nuclear weapon. You can rest assured," the president added. Trump's remarks come as his administration considers renewed military operations against Iran while continuing diplomatic negotiations with Tehran over its nuclear program. Qatar denies US-Iran nuclear talks have failed, says negotiations remain ongoing Qatar pushed back Friday against reports suggesting negotiations between the United States and Iran had collapsed, insisting that both countries are continuing efforts to reach an agreement. In a statement, Qatar's International Media Office rejected online reports alleging that Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani had said Washington and Tehran failed to reach a deal. The office accused unnamed parties of misrepresenting the prime minister's comments and spreading misinformation to undermine diplomatic efforts. "His Excellency’s remarks have been deliberately distorted by those who benefit from continued war and instability in our region," the statement read. "Many of these claims are being spread by fake accounts trying to undermine diplomatic efforts and push for further escalation. His Excellency stated today that both sides are continuing to work towards a deal." Qatar said its mediators remain in close contact with both countries as negotiations continue. 3 incoming US lawmakers urge Israel to free Arab journalist detained over interview Three incoming Jewish members of Congress are calling for the release of Arab journalist Abed Abu Shehadeh, who was detained in Israel after interviewing a fugitive former lawmaker. Brad Lander, Steve Weiner and Daniel Biss sent a letter to Israeli Ambassador to the U.S. Yechiel Leiter expressing concern about Abu Shehadeh's detention, according to The Times of Israel. The journalist was arrested Tuesday after interviewing former Israeli lawmaker Azmi Bishara, who fled Israel in 2007 amid suspicions that he aided Hezbollah during the previous year's war in Lebanon. The lawmakers said Israeli authorities detained Abu Shehadeh on suspicion of contact with a foreign agent and that the allegations against him remain sealed. They called for his release, arguing that interviewing controversial political figures is a fundamental part of journalism. Lufthansa reportedly restricts overnight crew stays in Israel amid Iran tensions Lufthansa Group is reportedly changing flight operations to Israel to prevent crew members from staying overnight in the country through Nov. 30 as concerns grow over renewed fighting with Iran. The airline group, which operates Lufthansa, SWISS, Austrian Airlines, Brussels Airlines and ITA Airways, plans to use crew-change stops in Athens and Larnaca, Cyprus, for certain flights, according to Israel's N12 News, as cited by The Jerusalem Post. The adjustments could result in schedule changes or cancellations for some passengers. The reported restrictions come as President Donald Trump considers renewed military strikes against Iran following meetings with his national security team this week. Washington and Tehran are also continuing diplomatic negotiations over Iran's nuclear program. Trump administration sanctions 8 Canadian businesses over alleged Iran ties The Trump administration announced sanctions Friday against eight Canada-based currency exchange businesses accused of helping Iran evade U.S. The Treasury Department said the businesses facilitated transactions involving sanctioned Iranian entities, including cryptocurrency activity linked to Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC). "Canada cannot be a safe haven for illicit financial facilitators that provide sanctions evasion services to the Iranian regime and its proxies," Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said. Several businesses also allegedly helped launder drug proceeds tied to former Olympic snowboarder Ryan Wedding, according to Treasury. The sanctions come as Washington and Tehran continue nuclear negotiations, with Iran demanding relief from U.S. economic restrictions as part of a proposed agreement. Northwestern cancels food festival after backlash over pro-Israel student group A student-run food festival at Northwestern University was canceled after several campus organizations objected to the inclusion of a pro-Israel student group, according to reports. The event, organized by Spoon University Northwestern, faced opposition after Wildcats for Israel was invited to participate. Three student organizations issued a joint statement criticizing the group's involvement, while nearly all participating groups reportedly withdrew from the festival. Organizers subsequently removed Wildcats for Israel from the event and apologized for its inclusion, according to The Times of Israel. The Daily Northwestern reported that the festival was ultimately canceled following the dispute. California Post editor says Americans will be 'grateful' for Trump's Iran war decisions California Post opinion editor Joel Pollak defended President Donald Trump's handling of the Iran war Friday, arguing that Americans will eventually appreciate his decisions despite the political fallout from the midterm elections. Speaking on Fox News' "Life, Liberty & Levin," Pollak said Trump had fulfilled his campaign promises by confronting Iran and securing the U.S. border, even when those decisions carried political consequences. "Trump had a responsibility that he took seriously to do what was in the national interest," Pollak said. "Sometimes being president means you have to make those tough decisions." Pollak argued that previous administrations had avoided confronting Tehran because of the potential political repercussions. "This is why nobody confronted Iran, because it has a political cost. But in the long run, the American people will be grateful for it," he said. Pollak also compared Trump's political challenges to those faced by former President Ronald Reagan, noting that Reagan lost eight Senate seats during his sixth year in office but later became widely respected. "Now, just because you lose Congress doesn't make you a great president. But both Reagan and Trump have done things that were very difficult, sometimes politically unpopular, but absolutely necessary," Pollak said. Trump says US is 'doing very well' with Iran as talks continue amid threat of new strikes President Donald Trump said Friday that the U.S. is continuing talks with Iran and expressed optimism about the negotiations, even as his administration weighs renewed military strikes against Tehran. "We are doing very well with Iran. We're talking to Iran," Trump told reporters during a gaggle Friday. "We have been we haven't lost a soldier in seven months or six months. We have the Hormuz Strait opening, doing more business than they've ever done with oil. And we're doing very well. And we are talking to them," the president added. His remarks come after Iran reportedly submitted a nuclear proposal to Washington through Qatari intermediaries Thursday, outlining demands that include sanctions relief, compensation for war damages and a reduced U.S. military presence in the Middle East. Trump met with his national security team this week to discuss whether to resume military operations against Iran. US reportedly derailed secret Israeli operation in Iran ahead of election A planned Israeli operation inside Iran was reportedly derailed after an Israeli security official inadvertently alerted the U.S. to the mission, prompting Washington to intervene. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and Mossad chief Roman Gofman had reportedly planned the operation ahead of Israel's Oct. 27 election, according to Israel's Channel 12, as cited by The Times of Israel. Senior Israeli security officials opposed the mission over concerns that it could escalate tensions with Tehran and interfere with the election, the report said. The intended target and details of the operation were not disclosed, and the allegations have not been independently verified. The report comes as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military action against Iran following meetings with his national security team this week. Iran reportedly distributes iodine tablets near nuclear sites as Trump weighs new strikes Iranian authorities are reportedly distributing iodine tablets to residents near the country's nuclear facilities amid concerns about a potential attack as President Donald Trump weighs renewed military strikes against Tehran. An Iranian health ministry official told The Times that authorities had sought to distribute the tablets to communities within two to three kilometers of nuclear facilities during each war. The newspaper also reported that an Iranian political journalist was told during a recent briefing that officials were seriously considering the possibility of a U.S. nuclear strike on Pickaxe Mountain, a suspected underground nuclear facility. Iodine tablets can help protect the thyroid gland from radioactive iodine released during certain nuclear incidents, but they do not protect against all forms of radiation exposure. The reported precautions come as Trump considers resuming military operations against Iran following meetings with his national security team at the White House this week. The administration has not publicly indicated that it is considering the use of nuclear weapons. CENTCOM shares image of US attack aircraft preparing for takeoff in Middle East U.S. Central Command (CENTCOM) shared an image Friday showing an A-10 Thunderbolt II attack aircraft preparing for takeoff from a military base in the Middle East. The image shows a U.S. Air Force crew chief directing the aircraft with illuminated signaling wands. CENTCOM did not disclose the base's location or the aircraft's mission. entry.title: Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests - PBS
entry.body: By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Share Copy URL https://www.pbs.org/newshour/science/seeds-and-preserved-hair-in-tomb-point-to-oldest-signs-of-cannabis-high-2800-years-ago-study-suggests Email Facebook Twitter LinkedIn Pinterest Tumblr Share on Facebook Share on Twitter Seeds and preserved hair in tomb point to oldest signs of cannabis high 2,800 years ago, study suggests Science Nov 6, 2026 5:19 PM EST GENEVA (AP) — People may have been getting high off cannabis earlier than previously thought — at least 2,800 years ago, a new study suggests. Archaeologists who led a dig at a monumental tomb in Siberia said they turned up evidence of the earliest known use of cannabis for psychoactive purposes. The findings point to cannabis consumption at least 300 years earlier than previously known use in neighboring China. Please check your inbox to confirm. Ancient drug use has long intrigued scholars. The Greek historian Herodotus wrote about inhabitants of Central Asia smoking cannabis around 440 B.C., and recent archaeologists have found the seeds in tombs across its highlands. The team from Germany, Russia, Sweden and Switzerland said analysis of hair in the royal tomb where cannabis seeds turned up sheds new light on the plant's role in ancient societies. "It's extremely rare that we have both preserved plant parts and human soft tissue with the active compounds in it in the same context," said co-author Gino Caspari, an archaeologist at the University of Bern. It's not clear whether the cannabis was consumed through inhalation or ingestion, he said. The dig took place starting in 2017 at a large burial mound at the Tunnug 1 site in the Uyuk Valley of southern Siberia, home to one of the earliest monumental tombs showing material culture of the Scythians — ancient nomads who migrated from Central Asia to southern Russia and Ukraine. READ MORE: A $28 billion hemp THC industry is fighting to save itself from a looming federal ban The team, deployed "essentially out in the middle of nowhere," lived in tents for months and faced a spring-to-autumn season that variously featured swamps, snowstorms, frosts and swarms of mosquitoes. Herds of horses ran freely across the grassy steppe. Larger artifacts on the site include weapons in the burials, horse gear and animal-style motifs. But the team "struck gold" as it also found tiny black spots that turned out to be cannabis seeds along with preserved human hair, Caspari said. "It's only so often as an archaeologist that you do get to drug test a person that's been dead for almost 3,000 years," he said. Radiocarbon dating on some of the more than 1,000 seeds helped establish the time of origin, and "they are not there by accident" but deposited within the tomb, suggesting that the plant material had significance in the community, he said. Results were published Thursday in the journal Science. Not all independent experts were convinced. A preserved human hair braid dating to about 2,800 years ago at the site of an ancient Scythian burial mound, in the Valley of the Tsars, the Republic of Tyva, south of Siberia, Russia, in this handout image released on Nov. Photo by Frozen Corpses Golden Treasures, T.Wallace & G. Caspari/Handout via Reuters The hair analysis "is scientifically weak" and there's not enough evidence to tell whether cannabis was used, wrote Volker Auwaerter, head of the forensic toxicology section at the University Medical Center in Freiburg, Germany, in an email. "For a central part of the study, the article falls far short of what would have been possible," Auwaerter said. "This matters because the hair data carry the abstract's main claims (cannabis consumption and use for its psychoactive properties)." Today, scholars don't consider ancient accounts trustworthy without corroborating evidence. Because the cannabis plant has other uses — seeds are pressed for oil and fibers used for cloth — their presence alone doesn't confirm drug use. Auwaerter, who was not part of the study, said the data didn't distinguish consumption from external exposure — in other words, the hair could have picked up traces of weed simply by being buried together with it. He said a lab test involving forensic toxicology expertise would have been advisable and easy to arrange. But Elisa Guerra Doce of the University of Valladolid in Spain, who has written about use of consciousness-altering substances in European prehistory, said toxicological hair analysis was not new in archaeology and has been used to identify consumption of psychoactive substances. She was not involved in the study. In an email, she credited the authors for showing, through their methodology, that "cannabis was not merely deposited as a funerary offering but was actually consumed by individuals associated with the burial rite." Jenne reported from Vienna, Austria. A free press is a cornerstone of a healthy democracy. Support trusted journalism and civil dialogue. Donate now By — Jamey Keaten, Associated Press Jamey Keaten, Associated Press By — Philipp Jenne, Associated Press Philipp Jenne, Associated Press
