entry.title: Alcaraz beats Fritz to help Jodar reach ATP finals
entry.body: Alcaraz beats Fritz to help Jodar reach ATP finals - Published Carlos Alcaraz saved two match points to beat Taylor Fritz in the Paris Masters quarter-finals - a result which helped Spanish compatriot Rafael Jodar qualify for the ATP Finals. Alcaraz claimed a 6-7 (10-12) 7-5 6-3 win over Fritz which also ended the American's hopes of reaching the season-ending event in Turin, Italy. Fritz edged a tight opening set, winning the tie-break after both players had chances to take it. He then moved a break ahead in the second set, but Alcaraz rallied to level the match after saving two match points and breaking his opponent twice. The 23-year-old Spaniard dominated the decider after moving 3-1 ahead before closing out the contest with a powerful forehand. "I tried not to let myself down in those difficult moments - to stay strong mentally," said Alcaraz, who will face either Casper Ruud or Nuno Borges in the semi-finals. "We played incredible tennis, both of us, and I used the energy of the people to give them what they wanted to watch. To entertain them." Alcaraz's victory secured 20-year-old Jodar's place at the finals, which will be held at Turin's Inalpi Arena from 15 to 22 November. Earlier, Tommy Paul's hopes were dashed after he suffered a 6-4 4-6 6-3 defeat to fellow American Ben Shelton, which propelled Frances Tiafoe into the finals. American Tiafoe, 28, and Spain's Jodar will both make their debuts at the event, which features the top eight men's singles players in the world. The eight qualifiers are Alexander Zverev, Daniil Medvedev, Flavio Cobolli, Arthur Fils, Alcaraz, Shelton, Tiafoe and Jodar. Who are Jodar & Tiafoe? Jodar only became a full-time professional at the beginning of 2026, but his debut season has drawn major attention and widespread excitement. The Madrid-born youngster won three ATP Challenger titles in 2025 before he claimed his first ATP Tour title in Marrakech in April 2026. Jodar, dubbed the new Rafa Nadal, also reached the quarter-finals of this year's French Open and climbed into the world's top 10 for the first time. At 6ft 3in, he hits heavy, high-speed shots loaded with topspin from the baseline that are designed to force opponents into submission. His serve is several miles per hour faster than the tour average and his attacking style means he is prone to taking risks on big points and in rallies. Tiafoe, meanwhile, is a three-time ATP Tour title winner who reached a career-high ranking of 10th in the world in 2023. He reached the US Open semi-finals in 2022 and 2024, knocking out Nadal en route to the last four in 2022. He won his biggest title to date in Halle in 2026 and also reached the finals in Cincinnati and Acapulco. The Maryland-born player, nicknamed 'Big Foe', is known for his energetic style and passionate celebrations. Related topics - Published6 hours ago - Published17 hours ago
entry.summary: Carlos Alcaraz saves two match points to beat Taylor Fritz in the Paris Masters quarter-finals - a result which helped Spanish compatriot Rafael Jodar qualify for the ATP finals.

entry.title: WTA chair apologises to Pegula for airing of 'diva' comment
entry.body: WTA chair apologises to Pegula for airing of 'diva' comment - Published Women's Tennis Association chair Valerie Camillo has apologised to Jessica Pegula and said the live-streaming of private comments to her coach about fellow player Mirra Andreeva was "regrettable and unacceptable". American Pegula called Andreeva a "diva" in a private conversation with her coach after a practice session for the WTA Tour Finals on Wednesday. However, the comments were aired on a live stream after the WTA failed to tell players there were microphones on practice courts. World number five Pegula called the incident "unfortunate" and said the WTA players' council supported players' calls for more privacy. Camillo said that all audio recording equipment in practice areas had since been removed as "clearly there was a failure in our technical execution and monitoring". "I want to specifically apologise to Jessica Pegula and [coach] Mark Knowles," she added. "What happened was regrettable and unacceptable. Jess is one of the WTA's best advocates and biggest stars. She does not deserve this distraction." - WTA takes responsibility after Pegula 'diva' comment live-streamed - Published1 day ago Pegula was also heard saying French Open champion Andreeva "needs to be humbled" and her coach Conchita Martinez encourages her behaviour. A representative for Pegula said she had been in direct contact with those involved and had been "completely unaware" the conversation could be heard by courtside microphones. None of the players were asked about the incident in the pre-tournament news conference at Indian Wells on Friday, but Pegula did address it in an interview with ESPN. "I think it's something that we have fought a lot over the last couple years as there's a lot more surveillance and audio and access to the players at tournaments than there has been in the past," she said., external "I know for broadcasting that it's great for fans, but I think we've seen a couple incidents now throughout the year, [the] last couple of years really, where it just seems highly unnecessary. "I think [this will] definitely reignite the topic and, hopefully, we can unfortunately use this incident to keep pushing for more player privacy." Pegula's compatriot Coco Gauff called for more privacy after she was captured in the players' area smashing a racquet following a defeat by Elina Svitolina in the Australian Open quarter-finals in January. At the same major, six-time Grand Slam champion Iga Swiatek said players were being watched "like animals in the zoo" by behind-the-scenes cameras. YouTube streams of Wednesday's practice sessions at Indian Wells have since been removed by the WTA, but the footage had already been shared on social media. Referring to the incident in California, where the season-ending WTA Finals are being held, Camillo added: "The WTA is sensitive to player privacy and has policies and procedures in place to balance players' needs for safe spaces with opportunities to bring fans closer to the game. "There was a lack of advanced notice and clear signage to assist players about the recording equipment operating in the area." Related topics - Published6 hours ago - Published17 hours ago
entry.summary: WTA chair Valerie Camillo apologises to Jessica Pegula after her "diva" comment about Mirra Andreeva was live-streamed.

entry.title: Drew Rosenhaus after Brandon Aiyuk’s meeting with 49ers: “To be continued” - NBC Sports
entry.body: It has become abundantly clear that the NFL is delaying the reinstatement of 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk from the reserve/left squad list. It has also become abundantly clear that the 49ers hope to squeeze some cash out of Aiyuk before the league lets him back in. It’s no surprise, then, that Friday’s sit-down between Aiyuk, agent Drew Rosenhaus, and the 49ers did not resolve the situation. “Hey, guys,” Rosenhaus told a group of reporters who had staked out the Friday meeting. We don’t have any further statements right now. But when we do, we’ll let you know.” The situation seems pretty simple. Aiyuk arguably owes the 49ers upwards of $13 million. It’s one thing for the 49ers to have the ability to chase him around for the cash; it’s another for the NFL and the 49ers to delay his reinstatement to the league until he wires the funds. That seems to be precisely where things stand. And the question becomes whether Aiyuk will be willing to strike a deal with the 49ers in order to secure the ability to return to the NFL, with another team.

entry.title: Six tries and a big win - but were Ireland ruthless?
entry.body: Six tries and a big win - but were Ireland ruthless? - Published Before Ireland's Nations Championship game with Argentina, head coach Andy Farrell had been honest about where his side are less than a year out from the World Cup. He admitted his team must improve if they are to challenge in Australia next year - a stark contrast to four years ago when they were riding the crest of a wave before they fell short in the quarter-finals. Despite Mateo Carreras' early try, Ireland had far too much for Los Pumas in Dublin as they ran out 42-12 winners under the Friday night lights. Hugo Keenan stole the headlines with his hat-trick, while Dan Sheehan, Sam Prendergast and Ronan Kelleher also crossed. But despite scoring six tries and winning by a 30-point margin, Farrell was left wanting more. Ireland had 59% territory throughout the game, and also edged possession, but did not score after the 55th minute when Kelleher rounded off a rolling maul. "The scoreline is a good one because not many teams do that to Argentina, they are a dangerous side," Farrell said. "I thought there was outstanding stuff and some clinical stuff, but I think the story of the game is we missed a chance to be ruthless. "Having said that, the opportunities we had in the right end of the field showed the dominance in field position and territory." - Keenan hat-trick as six-try Ireland beat Pumas - Published6 hours ago - Keenan, Baird and Beirne reflect on win over Argentina - Published5 hours ago One concern for Farrell will be an injury list - and a lengthy one at that. Captain Sheehan was forced off in the first half after he failed a head injury assessment, although Farrell said he "seems fine in the dressing room". Wing Robert Baloucoune also went off with a knock, while Sean Jansen sustained a "bang" to his knee and Josh van der Flier and Mack Hansen both have ankle concerns. The injuries to Baloucoune, who departed in the 58th minute, and Hansen, who continued after receiving treatment, will be particularly concerning after the performance of Farrell's back three. They had only played once together before, four years ago against South Africa, and Keenan's first try of the evening came off the back of a flowing move, when Baloucoune powered into space and found Hansen, who in turn set up the full-back to score. That was the catalyst for Ireland's turnaround - and a hat-trick for Keenan in his first home match since the 2025 Six Nations came a year since Hansen's treble against Australia in Dublin. All of Farrell's back three trio have struggled with injuries in the past year, and Friday's win was a glimpse of Ireland's attacking potential if they can stay fit and in form. "I thought the back three were outstanding. Hugo Keenan, 22 months since he played here and didn't remember what side of the pitch we warmed up, which was a bit of an insult. Same with Mack and Rob. They pace they put onto the ball and they were a threat. I'm delighted with the back three." Ireland 'weathered the storm' Beirne said that Argentina "came out firing" in Dublin as they chased a first away win over Ireland, something that came as no surprise to the Irish pack. "We weathered the storm and got into how we wanted to play the game," said Beirne. "What was pleasing about that was some of those tries were proper team tries and everyone was involved with them. That was the biggest takeaway from the game that." But, like Farrell, the second row believes there is more to come at the attacking end of the pitch. "We probably came away a little bit frustrated because we felt we didn't capitalise on a lot of the territory at the end of the game and the chances we had. "That shows how good a performance it was to come away feeling like that." After a bruising opener, Farrell will be forced to assess his squad ahead of Fiji's visit to Dublin on 14 November. After that, world champions South Africa will be a stern test before the finals weekend in London to round out the international window. He had offered Craig Casey a chance to impress at scrum-half as first-choice Jamison Gibson-Park returns to full fitness, and he impressed after a slow start. Ulster back row Nick Timoney also put in a big performance, while Prendergast's showing at fly-half was also largely positive as he put his stamp on the 10 jersey. When asked if the performances gave him food for thought for selections for the rest of the window, Farrell said: "Definitely, 100%. "That's exactly what you are after going into next week. "Having some good competition, we've had it for 10 days in training so how they performed highlights how they have been training. "Whatever side we pick next week, they'll be competing to play the following week."
entry.summary: Despite a six-try and 30-point win over Argentina, Andy Farrell and Tadhg Beirne admit Ireland could have been more ruthless in Friday's win.

entry.title: England 'disappointment' fuels Dewsbury-Hall's Everton heroics
entry.body: England 'disappointment' fuels Dewsbury-Hall's Everton heroics - Published Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall let his performance do all the talking at Hill Dickinson Stadium on Friday night. The Everton midfielder endured a disappointing start to his matchday preparations just hours earlier after learning that, despite his impressive performances in recent weeks, he had been overlooked by England manager Thomas Tuchel for this month's Nations League fixtures. It was a setback for the 28-year-old, who was tipped to earn a place in Tuchel's latest squad but was ultimately left out, with Borussia Dortmund teenager Jobe Bellingham selected instead. By the end of the night, though, Dewsbury-Hall had every reason to smile. The midfielder was celebrating alongside the Everton faithful after his thunderous strike helped the Blues to a comeback victory over Coventry City, securing an impressive 3-1 win and lifting them to fifth in the Premier League table. "It was a disappointing morning, I'm not going to lie. It's a massive dream of mine to play for my country. I know I was close," Dewsbury-Hall told Sky Sports after Everton made it back-to-back Premier League wins. "[I'm] sad, yeah, but really proud of myself and how I have reacted. All I can keep doing is putting in good performances and hopefully one day I get the nod, because I'm never going to give up." 'I'll keep pushing and pushing' The wait until the next international break in March will undoubtedly feel like an eternity for Dewsbury-Hall. But the Everton midfielder is no stranger to taking the long road to success, having experienced plenty of setbacks and detours throughout his career. He did not make his Premier League debut for boyhood club Leicester City until the age of 22, having spent previous seasons gaining valuable experience out on loan in the English Football League with Luton Town and Blackpool. Even when his opportunity to establish himself in the Foxes' first team finally arrived, it came during a turbulent period for the club, which ultimately ended in relegation from the Premier League at the end of the following season. After playing a starring role in Leicester's Championship-winning campaign under Enzo Maresca, the midfielder soon followed the Italian to Stamford Bridge in a deal worth Â£30m. However, Dewsbury-Hall struggled for regular game time during his only season at Chelsea, featuring mainly in cup competitions with limited opportunities in the Premier League. It was only after his move to Everton last summer, at the age of 26, that he appeared to have finally found the right environment to reignite his career and showcase the qualities that made him once such a highly regarded attacking midfielder. Since the start of last season, Dewsbury-Hall has scored 11 goals for Everton in the Premier League and provided seven assists. "I'm really, really enjoying it," said Dewsbury-Hall. "I've got a really good hybrid role in this team, where the gaffer is giving me the freedom to pop up all over the pitch." Tuchel said on Friday afternoon that Dewsbury-Hall had been "very close" to earning a place in his squad, having enjoyed "a very good season" with Everton so far. "I've got the mentality," added Dewsbury-Hall. "I'll keep pushing and pushing and see what happens." Barry draws inspiration from TikTok and Haaland It was not just Dewsbury-Hall who caught the eye against Coventry, with Thierno Barry scoring twice in the space of five minutes at the start of the second half to help Everton come from behind. By taking his tally for the season into double figures across all competitions, the 24-year-old - who struggled for both form and confidence after joining the Blues from Spanish side Villarreal last summer - has already surpassed the eight goals he scored last season. In fact, only Erling Haaland, with 14 goals, has scored more in all competitions than Barry's 10 this campaign for David Moyes' side. Not only is the French forward lighting up Hill Dickinson Stadium with his goals, he is also setting the place alight with his dance moves. Barry has made a habit of celebrating every goal with some kind of viral dance move - and that was certainly the case on Friday night. "I was on TikTok yesterday and I saw an NFL guy do the celebration. I said to Tyrique [George] that if we scored tomorrow, we would do the dance like that, but I think he was shy to do it, so I did the dance alone," Barry told Match of the Day. The former Basel and Villarreal frontman is also drawing inspiration from Haaland as he looks to maintain his impressive goalscoring form. "I'm very happy because I'm a fan of him," said Barry. "I watch a lot of videos of him and try and do the things he does. If I can play with him until the end to get the Golden Boot, I will try." Everton win caps landmark night for Moyes Earlier in the night, Moyes equaled Harry Catterick's record for the most games as Everton manager - with 592 matches each. The late Catterick managed the Toffees from 1961 to 1973. "I am proud," Moyes said in Everton's match programme. "The thought of being the Everton manager who has managed the most games is something I'm very proud of. "Everton has been huge for me and my family. My son David has gone everywhere and my father has lived it with us as well, watching it all.
entry.summary: Kiernan Dewsbury-Hall responds to his England omission by scoring a stunning goal to inspire Everton's 3-1 comeback victory over Coventry City.

entry.title: Lucas: Wofford Rapid Reactions - University of North Carolina Athletics - University of North Carolina Athletics
entry.body: University of North Carolina Athletics November 6, 2026 | Men's Basketball, Featured Writers, Adam Lucas Quick takeaways from Carolina's win over Wofford. Carolina led the entire way in notching a 109-70 win over Wofford to move to 2-0 on the season. The story of that game was the bench. With Carolina building an early lead and sustaining it, Michael Malone was able to give plenty of playing time to the reserves. And they responded, amassing 58 points and nearly outscoring Wofford on their own. Five of the six players who played the most minutes came off the bench. It's hard to pick a standout from the bench, because everyone contributed, but Maximo Adams was excellent. Sean May said Monday night that the Heels needed Adams to be more active on the glass. He took it to heart, collecting his first career double-double with 11 points and 11 rebounds. Jaydon Young also had a great shooting day, hitting four three-pointers and scoring a UNC-high 15 points. After taking over half their field goals from three-point range on Monday, Carolina's offensive approach changed dramatically on Friday. The Heels took just eight 3s out of 32 first half field goals and finished the game having taken just 25 out of 73 shots from distance. The Heels announced on the game's very first possession that this was going to be a different performance than Monday night's win over Western Carolina. Jarin Stevenson took the ball directly to the rim at the first opportunity and slammed through a two-handed dunk through contact. That set the tone for an aggressive, gritty outing. Stevenson had 10 points and three rebounds. It was also the best overall outing (if it's starting to sound like almost everything was good, that's because it was) for Terrence Brown in his very young UNC career. The guard had a team-high 21 points, shot an efficient 7-for-11, and only had one turnover. As a team, Carolina had just eight turnovers as it continues to perform well in an area Malone emphasizes. Carolina's transition game was the best it's been in this young year. The Heels had 24 points in the first eight minutes of the game and finished in Bojangle's territory. That included 20 fast break points. The UNC bench was a big part of that first half performance. Reserves contributed 21 points (Alex Samodurov had nine on his way to 13 for the game) and 14 rebounds (Adams had seven, including two offensive). Angelo Brizzi also added some energy and was +21 for the game. Carolina has now won 20 straight games at the Smith Center. It's the tenth-longest home winning streak in program history. Some people just know how to handle a microphone, and you can put Roger Ayers in that category. When the official was reviewing a bodycheck by Wofford's Cam Lowe in the first half, Ayers completed the review by grabbing the in-arena mic and announcing, "After review, it was an obvious flagrant one foul." You have to appreciate the honesty. The "We want Holbrook" chants started with 3:26 left in the game, and Malone quickly complied. He inserted Holbrook almost immediately and the Hickory native complied with a rebound. The Heels are back in the Smith Center Tuesday night against Wyoming. It will be Carolina's 600th game in the Smith Center. Players Mentioned Saturday, November 07 Friday, November 06 Friday, November 06 Friday, November 06

entry.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Roars Toward Live-Action Foreign-Language Record $30M-$33M Opening At Domestic Box Office - Deadline
entry.body: FRIDAY PM UPDATE: Gkids’ Godzilla Minus Zero looks to be coming in at its opening range of $30 million-$33 million after a $13.5M Friday at 3,254 theaters that includes $6.7M in previews. At that level, that’s not only the biggest-ever opening for distributor Gkids, but it also would be the biggest opening for a live-action foreign-language movie at the domestic box office. It would overtake the 2002 Chinese movie Hero, which bowed to $17.8M. Saturday will dictate if there’s a further expanded audience for the Takashi Yamazki-directed movie. Second place goes to Warner Bros Animation’s The Cat in the Hat with a $5M Friday (including $1M previews) and a three-day total between $17M-$20M at 4,003 theaters. Critics are saying scat to the cat at 48% Rotten on Rotten Tomatoes. Watch on Deadline Angel Studios’ colonial period feature Drummer Boy at 2,850 theaters is third with a $3.8M Friday and $9M opening. A24’s You Can See Everything, booked at 2,473 screens, is seeing a fourth weekend between $8M-$9M in fourth place, -25%, for a running cume of $79.6M not the high end. Sony’s release of Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of the Legend at 1,433 theaters is fifth with $6M over three days, $9M over four days. Outside the top five is Searchlight’s Wild Horse Nine at 1,110 theaters, with $2.3M today and around $5M-$6M. That is around what Wicker debuted at ($5.7M) at 1,471 locations two weeks ago. FRIDAY AM UPDATE: Gkids’ release of Toho’s Godzilla Minus Zero is higher with $6.7M in previews since Tuesday. As we told you that beats a slews of previews, including Legendary’s Godzilla: King of the Monsters, last year’s Predator: Badlands, but also another big Japanese title here, Pokemon: Detective Pikachu at $5.7M. Granted, it was a PG movie to Godzilla Minus Zero‘s R, but that pic posted a $20.5M first day and $54.3M opening back in mid-May 2019. A $30M opening was considered the high end for Godzilla Minus Zero heading into the weekend and now it looks like it’s the low end. The audience score is huge at 96% on Rotten Tomatoes. Sony Pictures’s release of Prime Focus Studios’ Ramayana: Rise of a Legend grossed $3.5 million on Thursday from 1,433 locations (including Wednesday previews), marking the widest North American release for an Indian film. Sony still thinks the movie, which is part of a $420M-$500M two part feature, is bound for a $6M opening. The pic, released in time for Diwali, currently holds a 93% audience score on Rotten Tomatoes’ Popcornmeter. Warner Bros’ The Cat in the Hat came in right where it was at last night with $1M in previews. Searchlight’s previews (both Thursday and early access) for Martin McDonagh’s Wild Horse Nine are at a great $900K. That’s not far from what Paramount/Miramax’s Roofman did last year in previews which was $1M before an $8.1M opening (though that pic was uber wide at 3,362 theaters). Wild Horse Nine is booked in 1,100 theaters. PREVIOUS EXCLUSIVE, Thursday PM: Takashi Yamazaki’s R-rated Godzilla Minus Zero is roaring in the November box office to a great start with what we’re hearing is around $6 million in previews. That includes fan shows from Godzilla Day Tuesday, last night and tonight, the latter being $4M+. Today’s showtimes began at 10AM. It’s very interesting that Godzilla Minus Zero gets an R: There aren’t any lizards who get naked in the movie, nor does any person or monster have a ‘F’ bomb tirade despite massive destruction in Japan as Godzilla and Ghidorah. This is easily a preview record for Godzilla Minus Zero U.S. distributor GKIDs beating their previous high, 2023’s The Boy and the Heron which posted a Thursday and early access previews of $2.39M, and a 3-day of $13M. Early monies here on Godzilla Minus Zero are way above the $2.1M made by Yamazaki’s Godzilla Minus One from its Wednesday and Thursday showtimes which went on to an $11.4M opening. The industry forecast on the high end was $30M+ in North America for Godzilla Minus Zero, which is boosted by Imax and a ton of PLFs, but now it could be way higher when you look at the comps that the sequel is beating. Last year at this time, Disney kicked off November with Predator: Badlands with $4.8M in Wednesday and Thursday previews which yielded a $15.8M Friday and $40M opening. Godzilla Minus Zero in previews is very close to another U.S. Godzilla, Legendary’s 2019 Godzilla: King of the Monsters which posted $6.3M in Thursday previews on its way to a $19.4M Friday and $47.7M opening. Legendary has the rights from Toho to make any English-language version from the Godzilla universe. Godzilla Minus Zero is 91% certified fresh to Godzilla Minus One‘s 99% fresh with critics. That Oscar winning movie landed an A CinemaScore. The only other Godzilla to receive a solid A was Legendary’s Godzilla vs. Kong in 2021 (2024’s Godzilla x King roared an A-). In Japan, Godzilla Minus Zero is up to 1.38 billion yen or $8.7M and that’s through three days. That opening Godzilla Day gross of 910M yen ($5.7M) is indeed a record for a live-action pic in Japan, besting the opening day of Harry Potter and the Chamber of Secrets (840M yen). Warner Bros Pictures Animation’s net $86M production of The Cat in the Hat from filmmakers Alessandro Carloni and Erica Rivinoja is looking like $1M today after previews that began at 2PM. That’s on par with Sony Pictures Animation’s Goat which opened earlier this year and went on to open to $27.7M. Illumination/Universal’s The Grinch posted $2.2M in previews before a $67.5M opening weekend during the second frame of November 2018. Note, Cat in the Hat is one of the few family movies around this holiday season next to Disney’s girl-skewing Hexed which bows on the Wednesday before Thanksgiving.

entry.title: ‘The Remarried Empress’ Becomes Most-Viewed Local Original Premiere Ever on Disney+ and Hulu
entry.body: Korean fantasy romance “The Remarried Empress” has set a new high for Disney+ and Hulu. Based on views across the three days after its Nov. 3 launch, it is the biggest premiere ever for a local original on the platforms worldwide. The series is also the No. 1 Korean title premiere in more than 50 markets. These include the U.S., the U.K., Canada, Mexico, Chile, France, Spain, Germany, Australia and New Zealand. The show had been slated to bow on Nov. Disney+ instead released it a day ahead of schedule as a gesture of gratitude to its fanbase. The show is adapted from the Naver Webtoon series of the same name. It centers on Empress Navier and Emperor Sovieshu, rulers of the Eastern Empire, whose marriage starts to crack as tensions mount across their realm. Things unravel when Sovieshu falls for Rashta, an escaped slave, and goes to extreme lengths to win her over. Navier refuses to give up her dignity. She agrees to what the emperor wants, as long as she is free to wed Heinrey, crown prince of the rival Western Kingdom. The fallout puts the entire empire at risk as Navier fights to take back her power. Shin Mina (“Karma,” “Hometown Cha-Cha-Cha”) plays Navier, with Ju Jihoon (“Light Shop,” “The Trauma Code: Heroes on Call”) as Sovieshu, Lee Jongsuk (“Big Mouth”) as Heinrey and Lee Seyoung (“The Red Sleeve,” “The Crowned Clown”) as Rashta. Cho Suwon (“Still 17,” “Pinocchio”) directs from a screen adaptation by Yeoh Geena and Hyun Choongyeol. Anticipation for the series had been running high. Preview screenings at the Busan International Film Festival sold out, and the payoff trailer racked up 13 million views across YouTube and social platforms within 48 hours. The source webtoon has drawn close to 3 billion views since it first came out. The first four episodes are streaming now. Two more will arrive each Wednesday starting Nov. 11, leading up to the finale on Nov. 25, exclusively on Disney+ and Hulu. Outside the U.S., Hulu operates as an entertainment banner within Disney+.

entry.title: James Bond Shocker: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult Late Contenders for 007 After Auditioning for Denis Villeneuve
entry.body: As James Bond casting rumors heat up, a couple more A-list actors have entered the mix: Robert Pattinson and Nicholas Hoult were among the stars who screen-tested to play the new 007. Both British actors certainly have the acting pedigree to play the suave spy, taking up the mantle after Daniel Craig’s 15-year run. They also have a keen awareness of what it takes to work in major franchise fare: Pattinson stars as Batman for DC Studios and is an alum of both the “Twilight” and “Harry Potter” franchises; meanwhile, Hoult plays Lex Luthor in DC’s Superman movies and starred in the 2010s “X-Men” prequel trilogy. He next stars in the Amazon MGM Studios movie “How to Rob a Bank,” in theaters on Nov. Pattinson also has the Denis Villeneuve factor on his side, after starring in the filmmaker’s upcoming epic “Dune: Part Three.” Last year, Amazon MGM Studios tapped Villeneuve as the franchise’s next director, with “Peaky Blinders” creator Steven Knight hired to write the script. Getting Bond 26 off the ground has been a top priority for the property’s new stewards, producers Amy Pascal and David Heyman. Since then, nearly every 30-something British actor’s name has been bandied about in the U.K. press, with rumored top contenders including Callum Turner, Josh O’Connor and Jack Lowden. Variety has learned that Harry Styles has had discussions about the part, and Theo James, 41, also hasn’t been ruled out. Pierce Brosnan, the Bond of the ’90s, recently gave his stamp of approval to Turner, while Gary Oldman threw his weight behind Lowden, his “Slow Horses” co-star. (Oldman also claimed that the next James Bond has already been picked, but no official casting announcement has been made.) Amazon declined to comment on the casting rumors.

entry.title: Adam Driver Won’t Return for ‘Girls’: ‘I Wish Them the Best of Luck’
entry.body: Adam Driver had a major breakout thanks to his role on “Girls,” but the actor shut down the idea of returning for the reboot of the iconic series in a recent interview. While talking about his role in James Gray’s new movie “Paper Tiger,” Driver was asked by Cinema Blend if he will be returning for the revival. “No, but I wish them the best of luck,” he told the outlet. News of the new “Girls” series broke in mid-October, with creator and star Lena Dunham set to return as Hannah Horvath alongside co-stars Allison Williams as Marnie Michaels, Jemima Kirke as Jessa Johansson and Zosia Mamet as Shoshanna Shapiro. Andrew Rannells also returns to the role of Elijah Krantz. The series will have a limited five-episode run on HBO with production starting in 2027. Driver’s career took off after his run as Hannah’s boyfriend on “Girls.” In addition to his role as Kylo Ren in three “Star Wars” movies, he starred in “Marriage Story” and “The Meyerowitz Stories” for Noah Baumbach; “The Last Duel” and “House of Gucci” for Ridley Scott; “Ferrari” for Michael Mann and this year’s “Misty Green.” He’s also worked with director Jim Jarmusch on “Paterson,” “The Dead Don’t Die” and “Father Mother Sister Brother.” In her recent memoir “Famesick,” Dunham described her tumultuous relationship with Driver, saying, “He could be short-tempered and verbally aggressive, condescending and physically imposing. He could also be protective, loving even,” Dunham writes. After the last episode of “Girls” wrapped, Dunham says Driver told her, “I hope you know I’ll always love you” before he said goodbye.

entry.title: Melania Trump’s Amazon Gravy Train Faces a Brutal New Reality - The Daily Beast
entry.body: Melaniaâs Amazon Gravy Train Faces a Brutal New Reality As Trump grapples with his election humiliation, Melaniaâs latest Amazon payday is coming into focus. Melania Trumpâs latest foray into streaming could come with an unexpected plot twist: congressional scrutiny. Jeff Bezosâ Amazon Prime Video is scheduled to release Melaniaâs two-part docuseries on Nov. 20, just weeks after Americans delivered a scathing repudiation of President Donald Trumpâs second term and expressed concern over corruption within the administration. One episode, titled âFamily & Trust,â will follow Melania as she prepares to become first lady, building on her earlier eponymous documentary. The second episode, titled âPride & Honor,â takes place just after Trumpâs inauguration. On The Daily Beast Podcast, executive editor Hugh Dougherty pointed out the irony of the docuseries announcement coming just after Trumpâs party suffered a humiliating midterm defeat. âHer husband just lost an election in humiliating fashion,â Dougherty told host Joanna Coles. âThe Democrats are going to go after every bit of the grift.â Exit polls showed that Americans are deeply concerned about the economy and cost of living, which has skyrocketed since Trump waged war against Iran. But more than half of voters across the U.S. also said corruption was a âcrucialâ consideration in their voting decisions. Robert Garcia, who is expected to become chairman of the House Oversight Committee, had a brief message for Trump and his âcrime familyâ shortly after Democrats swept the elections: âLawyer up.â âItâs as if theyâve got their hand out for as much cash as they can get, and I wonder if that speeds up... Do they become even greedier now that the clock is ticking?â Coles asked Dougherty, who pointed out that the first couple has already received $10.71 million from the Melania documentary. âThereâs already a serious amount of money thatâs gone to Melania. The Republicans werenât doing any oversight,â he said. âAnd thatâs another aspect of this election: People said, âHold on. Your job is to hold people accountable, to be a check and a balance on power.ââ âNow we have Democrats who are determined,â he continued. âThey have already said some of the targets for subpoenas. Those targets already include Donald Trump Jr., because of his extraordinary business dealings. There is no way that they are not going to go after Amazon, Jeff Bezos, and Melania Trump for thisâIâm going to sayâextraordinary documentary,â Dougherty continued. âWeâve all got questions.â The White House and the Office of the First Lady did not immediately respond to a request for comment on this story. Trump reported a multimillion-dollar licensing fee for Melania on his 2025 financial disclosure report. Amazon, meanwhile, spent $40 million to acquire the documentary and blew another $35 million on marketing. entry.title: Stephen Chow Told Japan to Stop Aping Kung Fu, Says Boss of Film Fund Behind Kore-eda Hirokazu’s ‘Look Back’
entry.body: Hong Kong star-director Stephen Chow once told K2 Pictures founder Kii Muneyuki that Japanese filmmakers should stop imitating kung fu and build action films on their own martial arts instead, Kii said Saturday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. “He said, ‘You have karate, judo, jujitsu and kendo. Only you can turn it into action films, so you should be the ones doing it. Stop aping kung fu,’” recalled Kii, who said he has shared drinks with Chow in Tokyo a few times. He added that he agreed with Chow, pointing to Netflix sumo drama “Sanctuary” as the kind of project that draws on culture unique to Japan. Kii’s K2P Film Fund I, which backed Kore-eda Hirokazu’s “Look Back,” could also open its doors to new investors. The fund closed its $33 million equity round in February. Kii said more companies approached K2 about investing after the close, and that the round could reopen if existing backers agree. He has not yet decided whether to do so. Some 30 companies have invested so far, led by MUFG Bank, Japan’s biggest lender. Other backers include Bandai, Dentsu, the government-backed Development Bank of Japan and property companies Tokyu Land and Mori Trust. Kii serves as the fund’s general partner. TThe equity is being paired with loans that are being added one after another and will ultimately total $67 million, Kii said, for a planned total of $100 million and a target of 50 films over seven years. Kii shared the stage with director Nagata Koto, whose Fukushima-set noir “The Nuke Crab” K2 unveiled at Cannes in May. Kii said he and Nagata are aiming for a hit in Japan and in Eastern Europe, including Poland and Ukraine, where he believes audiences who lived through the Chernobyl accident might connect with it. The project is in development, with a shoot targeted for next year. The film follows those who profited from the huge sums that flowed from across Japan into the radiation clean-up of the Tohoku region. Nagata, whose “Baka’s Identity” competed at Busan last year, described the subject as socially taboo in Japan and the kind of material that productions involving TV networks or major studios would never take on. “When I took it to Kii-san, he immediately said, ‘That sounds interesting, let’s do it,’ and got it started,” Nagata said. Pairing Japan with one other specific market is a strategy K2 calls “Japan plus one.” “What Americans like about Japan, what the French like about Japan, what Taiwanese audiences like about Japan and what Koreans like about Japan are completely different,” Kii said. “The Japan that Japanese people like is different again.” Kii said that while the world knows about the Chernobyl disaster itself, far less is known about how the lives of people in the area changed afterward. Nagata said her goal is to secure international sales early enough that an overseas release can run alongside the Japanese one. She added that shared emotions such as friendship and family can make the unfamiliar feel closer. “I think jealousy and love are the same anywhere in the world, as long as we are human,” she said. K2 Pictures was set up as an alternative to Japan’s production committee system, under which films are made mainly with the local market in mind. Kii, who started out tearing tickets and making popcorn in cinemas before rising to producer at Toei, said the closed nature of that system kept out both foreign and outside investment, which in turn made it hard to share returns with creators. Profits at K2 are calculated title by title, with 70% going to investors and 30% to the creative side. “Producers and the people involved in making the film aren’t putting up money, but the film exists because of their creativity,” Kii said. The company completed six films this year, including “Look Back,” Kore-eda’s live-action adaptation of Fujimoto Tatsuki’s manga, which competed at Venice, and Son Myung-ah’s debut feature “Trophy,” which is due to open in Korea. Kii said the aim is six or seven releases a year, but admitted that a year in, the pace is “pretty tough.” K2 has opened outposts in Taiwan and Korea with the aim of distributing its films directly in both markets. Kii said 99.9% of Japan’s overseas film business consists of licensing deals, which he argued does little to raise the value of Japanese titles abroad. “Japanese people taking Japanese films to that place and promoting them hard there – I think that’s what raises their value,” he said. Greenlighting at K2 rests with its six or seven producers, Kii included, and he said he does not block a project a producer is set on. The only test is whether costs can be balanced against likely revenue. “Nobody can tell whether a film will be a hit,” Kii said. Kii said that applies equally to arthouse and commercial projects. “If it’s only going to bring in JPY50 million ($330,000), make it for JPY20 million ($130,000),” he said later in the session. The same logic applies to first-time directors. Kii said producers can line up pre-sales, streaming rights deals and sponsorships so that a debut cannot lose money, because a big loss makes it hard for a director to get a second film made. “I want to keep launching new directors from K2 Pictures,” Kii said. “And I want them to be grateful for the rest of their lives. Don’t forget us when you make it big.” Kii also wants the law changed. He said a British entertainment lawyer and an American completion bond executive both told him the film business works much like real estate: producers create assets and then turn them into cash. Japan passed an investment trust law around 2000 that lets real estate be securitized, but it does not cover content. Kii said he has been discussing the need for such a law with lawyers and hopes to push for one. The session was moderated by filmmaker Huang Yin-yu Kou of Taiwan’s Moolin Films, who is also the founder of the Cinema at Sea – Okinawa Pan-Pacific International Film Festival.

entry.title: Why ‘Suits’ Japan Swapped Drugs for Cash: NBCUniversal, TBS Format Chiefs on Localizing Hits at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
entry.body: In the pilot of “Suits,” the briefcase that springs open during a job interview is full of marijuana, and it stays that way in the show’s Korean and Mongolian remakes. In Japan, the drugs became money, because drugs can’t be shown on Japanese TV, according to Linfield Ng, VP of format sales and production, Asia at NBCUniversal Formats, which licenses the show. Ng gave the example at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei, where he shared a stage with Fukaya Shunsuke, head of new format sales, Europe at TBS Television, for a session on how formats get adapted market by market. Emily Chang, who heads the financial news team at Taiwan’s Videoland and produces “Shark Tank Taiwan,” moderated. “But the concept is the same. Again, that did not change the DNA of the show,” Ng said. The same thinking applied to “SNL Korea,” which dropped the musical segment because Korea already has a glut of music and countdown shows. Producers there also asked to soften or skip the U.S. show’s politically pointed cold open at sensitive moments, replacing it with topical material. “We just make slight changes to adapt to the local sensitivity and the local landscape,” Ng said. On “Suits,” every legal case is localized while the core story of the man with no law degree stays intact. NBCUniversal has made more than 25 versions of “Top Chef,” and runs a “Top Chef” summit that brings producers from different countries together to trade notes on challenges, shooting styles and what works where. Ng, who joined the company in 2011 after senior stints at BBC Worldwide, Endemol Asia and Warner Bros. Pictures, said his Singapore-based team holds pre-production calls with local partners weeks or months ahead, goes on set with a producer during the shoot and reviews early episodes before they air. Asian versions often add celebrity panels and more behind-the-scenes drama, which he said is agreed well in advance. “So there will never be any surprises where it comes to us, it goes on air, and go like, ‘What is that?’” Ng said. Fukaya, who joined TBS in 2009 and spent 12 years in production before moving into format sales, pointed to “Sasuke,” known internationally as “Ninja Warrior,” TBS’s biggest format hit with local versions in 25 countries. “‘Ninja Warrior’ has a truly universal theme – a human versus giant obstacles – that you can express in one line, and anyone can understand it regardless of country or culture,” Fukaya said. TBS keeps a brand guide for the show, separate from the production bible, that defines it as an Olympics for unknown athletes built on serious sportsmanship. Local changes are measured against that concept. wanted a head-to-head version, TBS built a derivative race format, and Fukaya said every new variation gives the company more ways to sell the brand. Host-driven talk shows, by contrast, rarely work as formats, since what TBS licenses is the framework, rules and game, and the banter between particular hosts can’t be reproduced abroad. Co-development has been a growing part of TBS’s push since the broadcaster declared two years ago that it was starting its first global year. Fukaya made two such shows with U.K. distributor All3Media International, “Lovers or Liars?” in 2024 and “Tono” a year later, serving as business and creative producer on both. In “Lovers or Liars?” four couples take the stage, only one of them genuine, and a panel tries to spot the real pair from clues such as watching them sing or dance together. side proposed ballroom dancing, Fukaya found himself stuck between the two teams, since couples dancing that way isn’t part of Japanese culture. He asked the British creators why they wanted it. The answer was body contact, which helps reveal which couple is real, so the team settled on choreography with plenty of touching. “When cultures clash, I think it’s best for the person standing in the middle to confirm what the creative intent is, and find the point of contact there,” Fukaya said. Asked by Chang whether he ballroom dances himself, he laughed and said he couldn’t. TBS typically airs its co-developed pilots in late-night slots, and Fukaya said ratings in that window matter less than the fact that a show has been produced and broadcast on a terrestrial network rather than pitched on paper. Some of those late-night pilots are now starting to sell well overseas. “I can’t share the details yet, but I think there will be news soon,” he said. Ng said Japan always tests its pilots at midnight. “So how much of a rating you can get at midnight timeslot is actually very challenging,” he said. On the buying side, Ng’s third-party pickups include Korea’s “Hidden Singer” and “Drive Thru-Oke” and Spain’s “Crush.” In 2026 alone, NBCUniversal Formats added three Asian formats: Korea’s “Unboxing the Flavours,” a cooking show that started life on YouTube; TBS’s “Action Arena,” which Ng likened to a studio-based arcade game; and Chukyo TV’s “Save Money” from Japan. He looks for a clear structure, scalability across budgets, a distinct selling point, and formats that are budget- and sponsor-friendly. “Because in the U.S., many a times, it is all funded by the networks, but in Asia, it’s always sponsors first,” Ng said. NBCUniversal Formats has sold more than 40 format brands across Asia, and in 2025 alone had 39 seasons across 17 territories. Ng said rights deals are often split by region: the company may take Asian rights while an owner such as TBS keeps Europe. Some formats don’t cross over at all. Where Are We Going?” and loved it, Ng said, but found it couldn’t work in Europe, where celebrities won’t put their children on TV for privacy and security reasons. Entertainment and game shows account for about 59% of the formats that sell well globally, according to a 2026 K7 report Ng cited, compared with about 40% in Asia. But game shows don’t work in Korea, so his team never pitches them there. Mongolia, meanwhile, buys only what suits its market rather than the biggest U.S. Ng’s advice to Asian creators was to do their research first and know what sets their show apart. “You’ve got to grab them within the first one to two minutes,” he said. Asked by Chang which elevator offers a one-minute pitch with him, Ng said, “You just got to find the right elevator.” Chang put two Taiwanese shows to him. Of Videoland’s night-market competition format, Ng said he enjoyed it but questioned how many countries have a street-food culture big enough to support a local version. He pointed instead to TVBS’s beauty show “Nu Ren Wo Zui Da,” which has been adapted. “Which woman around the whole world doesn’t want to look better?” Ng said. Chang also traced the origins of her own show: “Shark Tank,” licensed by Videoland from Sony Pictures Television, began as Nippon TV’s “Money Tigers” in 2001 before becoming “Dragons’ Den” in the U.K. and “Shark Tank” in the U.S., and has since landed in more than 50 countries. The Taiwan version had to persuade its U.S. partners, with polling and market data, that local viewers needed on-screen captions the original’s clean look doesn’t use. Fukaya, who joined the advisory board of the Format Recognition and Protection Association (FRAPA) in 2026, said the group sets criteria for where a format’s protected idea begins and ends, since proving copying in legal terms is difficult. Building an exact replica of “Ninja Warrior’s” Warped Wall would be a clear violation, he said. Ng said buying an IP means learning from the owner’s mistakes, and that NBCUniversal would never again partner with a company that copies. “No one wants to buy a copy version,” he said. No Reaction” is now under option in over 10 territories across Europe, and Fukaya said buyers are asking TBS above all for comedy game shows, driven by the success of “Documental,” “LOL,” “Freeze” and TBS’s own “Takeshi’s Castle.” “You just have to know your market, and you just have to basically think globally and act locally,” Ng said.

entry.title: ‘Silenced Nights’ and ‘You Are the Film’ to Bookend Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival
entry.body: The 21st Jogja-Netpac Asian Film Festival (JAFF) will open with Lawrence Fajardo’s Filipino drama “Silenced Nights” and close with Ueda Makoto’s Japanese comedy-drama “You Are the Film.” The festival will screen 254 films from 34 countries across its competitive and non-competitive sections. 5 in Yogyakarta, Indonesia, under the theme “Influx.” “Silenced Nights,” which bowed at Toronto, will receive its Indonesian premiere on opening night. “You Are the Film” picked up the White Raven Award at this year’s Brussels International Fantastic Film Festival. “In line with the theme ‘Influx,’ this year JAFF wants to look at how currents of change affect our lives and the way we understand one another. Amid a social climate full of uncertainty and instability, cinema gives us the chance to listen to different experiences and see issues from other perspectives,” said Budi Irawanto, festival president of JAFF. Ten features will vie for the Golden and Silver Hanoman Awards in the main competition, with Dita Gambiro, Riar Rizaldi and Shan Zuolong on the jury. Two of the contenders are first features from women filmmakers. China’s “A Girl Unknown,” directed by Zou Jing, won the Fipresci Prize in Cannes’ Critics’ Week this year. Singapore’s “Ah Girl,” from Priscilla Ang Geck Geck, took the Youth Jury Award at Rotterdam, and its lead actress won the Firebird Award for best actress at the Hong Kong International Film Festival. Also in the main competition are Sompot Chidgasornpongse’s “9 Temples to Heaven,” Jeremias Nyangoen’s “Black Coffee,” Kawajiri Masanao’s “Cherry and Virgin,” Aung Phyoe’s “Fruit Gathering,” Lê Bảo’s “Hearing,” Arvin Belarmino’s “Ria” and Mejbaur Rahman Sumon’s “Roid.” On the local front, 10 Indonesian films will compete in the Indonesian Screen Awards across 10 categories, from best film and director through to original music and poster design. The field includes Eddie Cahyono’s “Ibuku,” which claimed the Busan Award Special Jury Prize at the 31st Busan International Film Festival, and Ravi Bharwani’s “Secrets,” which will world premiere in Yogyakarta. Ferdinand Almi’s “Shattered Vows,” Ariani Darmawan’s “Jani Be Good” and Andrew Kose’s “Mate’s Rate” are also in the running. Sharifah Amani, Tanigaki Kenji and Yoon Ga-eun make up the jury. Shorts are the focus of Light of Asia, where 21 titles compete for the Blencong Awards, while the Netpac Awards consider only debut and sophomore features. Viewers will get a vote of their own through the new Amar Bank Audience Choice Award, which picks a favorite from the Light of Asia selection. Also new this year are the JAFF Awards, which will recognize individuals, communities and institutions that sustain Asian cinema through work ranging from production and financing to archiving, exhibition and knowledge-sharing. “JAFF was born from a community spirit, and over two decades we have seen how a single encounter can open the way for a film’s or a filmmaker’s journey. The JAFF Awards come from the same belief: that Asian cinema grows through the work of many connected people,” said festival director Ifa Isfansyah. Gelanggang Inovasi dan Kreativitas (GIK) UGM serves as venue partner for the awards. Outside competition, the Panorama section gathers 12 features and five shorts from leading Asian directors. They include Hamaguchi Ryusuke’s “All of a Sudden,” Lav Diaz’s “Let Us Through, Dear Ancestors,” Hur Jin-ho’s “The Assassin(s),” Yoon Dan-bi’s “The World Before,” Edmund Yeo’s “The Age of Goodbyes” and John Torres’ “The Remotes.” Asian Perspectives offers 26 features and 28 shorts, and the Indonesian Film Showcase has five local features. The 15-title Rewind strand revisits three Studio Ghibli classics from Miyazaki Hayao: “Spirited Away,” “My Neighbor Totoro” and “Howl’s Moving Castle.” Kurosawa Kiyoshi’s “Cure,” Yeon Sang-ho’s “Train to Busan” and Yasmin Ahmad’s “Mukhsin” are also on the slate, as are a pair of 2000s Indonesian teen romances, Nasri Cheppy’s “Eiffel…I’m in Love” (2003) and Hanny R. “Asian cinema keeps moving forward through new voices, a willingness to experiment with form, and stories that stay close to people’s lives. We put together this year’s program to bring that diversity to audiences, including opening new conversations through films we already know,” said program director Alexander Matius. The Cinematic Concert, back after four previous editions, will see Grrrl Gang perform live against scenes from five shorts screening at the festival. Sponsor partnerships shape several strands. Amar Bank presents Undercurrent, a special screening program of Rafael Manuel’s “Filipiñana” and Kimura Taichi’s “Fujiko,” the latter a winner of Udine’s Golden Mulberry Award and the New York Asian Film Festival’s Uncaged Award for best feature. Cinema XXI returns as main venue partner at Empire XXI Yogyakarta and is backing JAFF Kids and the festival’s Inclusive Screening strand. TikTok Film Circle will pair TikTok creators chosen from Indonesia, Thailand and Vietnam with professional film critics in a film analysis workshop. The Asian Film Awards Academy, meanwhile, is co-presenting five Hong Kong titles in the Hong Kong Film Gala Presentation. On the industry side, JAFF Market runs Nov. 28–30 at the Jogja Expo Center, with six programs: JAFF Future Project, JAFF IP Connection, Talent Day, the Film & Market Conference, Market Screening and Film Lab. JAFF21 is backed by Indonesia’s Ministry of Culture through its Dana Indonesia Raya program. Tickets go on sale via TipTip from Nov.

entry.title: Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils 10 Content Investments, From ‘Gunshot’ to ‘Call of Lobster’
entry.body: Chunghwa Telecom, Taiwan’s largest telecom operator, announced 10 new investments at its “Chunghwa Telecom Content Slate and Partnership Showcase,” spanning film, TV and music projects as well as stakes in two production companies. The company pitched the slate as a way to back Taiwanese original IP and link local creators with partners abroad. The event was held at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF), which Chunghwa has sponsored for five consecutive years. Taiwan’s Minister of Culture Li Yuan attended, alongside Chunghwa chief business officer and senior executive VP Lin Wen-chiyh, consumer business group president Hu Hsueh-hai and representatives from the presenting teams. “Chunghwa Telecom is like a pyramid,” Li said. “I am grateful that, beyond building a strong foundation through its thriving core business, the company is also willing to invest at the very top of the pyramid, supporting film and television professionals as they continue moving forward and creating even better work.” The slate includes four scripted series: police crime drama “Gunshot,” made with PTS Taigi TV, the Taiwanese-language channel of public broadcaster PTS, and S11 Partners; family fantasy “Yesterday’s Daughter, Tomorrow’s Mother,” from producer Phoebe Ma and director Hung Tzu-peng; fantasy adventure “Guides to the World Below,” adapted from a popular Taiwanese comic; and “C’est la Vie,” an urban drama about food and women’s personal growth, with actress Esther Liu as executive producer. Chunghwa has also invested in “Next Z Chef,” billed as Taiwan’s first cooking competition show for young people. Film investments include “Demon of the East: Black Condo,” a horror project tied to a cinematic universe that crosses four Asian countries, and “Call of Lobster,” which won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF’s 2024 pitching sessions and has since been selected for the Culture Ministry’s first international flagship cohort under its Great Voyage Project. The investments also extend to music, including “Speak in Silence,” an Asian tour by Taiwanese indie band Shallow Levée. The tour will run to about 50 shows in Taiwan and eight other countries across Asia. Alongside project financing, Chunghwa and Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative have taken equity positions in DaMou Entertainment and Horiza Creations. DaMou has produced series including “The World Between Us II” and “Wave Makers.” Horiza uses community engagement and crowdfunding to gauge what audiences want. “Chunghwa Telecom is more than just a platform operator; we are also a driving force behind the long-term development of the content industry,” Lin said. “Moving forward, we will continue to connect funding, creative talent, and domestic and international partners, leveraging our group’s resources and industry partnerships to help Taiwanese content reach international markets.” Chunghwa-backed films “Arrested Memory” and “The Photo From 1977” received a combined 12 nominations at the 63rd Golden Horse Awards.

entry.title: Trump replaces chief of staff Susie Wiles with Stephen Miller
entry.body: Angered over his midterm losses, President Trump announced Friday he was replacing Susie Wiles as White House chief of staff with longtime adviser Stephen Miller. Why it matters: Trump is trading one of his few moderating forces with one of the most maximalist champions of his agenda, a striking signal that the president may double down on the hardline policies that helped Republicans lose control of Congress on Tuesday. Driving the news: Wiles submitted her resignation on Thursday night. Sources told Axios her departure was a mutual decision, but driven by Tuesday's election results, for which Trump blamed her. Sources said Trump began expressing discomfort with the scale of the midterm losses and the money his political team spent on Wednesday. Wiles offered to quit for two days before she resigned. Trump accepted her decision on Friday. Trump did not ask for her resignation, said one informed source who spoke with Wiles, "but he couldn't get it out of his head that she was to blame, not him." "Susie could've stuck around, but what's the point?" that person said. "Whether it's right or wrong, Susie knows that serving the president means it's at his pleasure. And if she couldn't change the way he felt, there was no reason to stay." What they're saying: "I am pleased to announce that Mr. Stephen Miller, the current Deputy Chief of Staff of the Trump Administration, and one of my most trusted advisors, will become the Chief of Staff starting Monday, November 9, 2026," Trump wrote on Truth Social, adding that Wiles will move to the Trump Political Operation. Wiles said in a statement posted to X that "[s]erving President Trump in the White House has been the honor of a lifetime. I'm so proud to have been a part of what we've accomplished together." Zoom in: Miller, who served in Trump's first administration, was already a co-equal of Wiles' in some respects. No one in Trump's government knows the levers of power, the operation of the White House and the bold use of the executive branch better than him. An architect of Trump's explosive first hundred days exerting executive authority, Miller has been working on plans to keep operating a muscular White House even in the face of big Democratic majorities. "Trump needs to prepare for war with the Democrats in Congress with all their investigations they're going to launch, and Stephen is a wartime adviser," a Trump adviser explained. Zoom out: Wiles is widely viewed as the most powerful person in the White House outside the president himself, and she achieved something few in his orbit could: earning his trust, influencing his decisions and bringing discipline to an administration defined by historic infighting and upheaval. She was Trump's longest-serving chief of staff, and commanded an extraordinary level of trust from Trump, often serving as the last person he consulted before making major decisions. Her exit also ends the tenure of the first woman ever to hold the powerful position. Her influence stemmed from a relationship with Trump that stretched back to his 2016 campaign when she led his efforts in Florida, and again when she agreed to manage his political comeback following the Jan. 6 riot. Between the lines: Wiles' strength was understanding how to navigate Trump rather than trying to control him. She avoided public confrontations, offered disagreements privately and sought to carry out Trump's priorities rather than restrain them. But her influence had limits. She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller. Friction point: In a grand irony, the very Trump decisions she opposed —the Iran war and the brutality of immigration enforcement — drove Tuesday night's midterm shellacking that led the president to lose confidence in her. Catch up quick: As recently as Oct. 16, Trump emphatically denied reports he was considering replacing Wiles. Trump noted at the time that Wiles would stay as long as she wanted, and he praised her toughness in surviving cancer while serving as his staff chief. Context: Wiles spent decades mastering the art of influencing powerful men while staying out of the spotlight. The daughter of famed NFL broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles has credited growing up with an alcoholic father with teaching her how to handle larger-than-life personalities. In Florida, she became a powerful behind-the-scenes operator for two moderate Republican mayors in Jacksonville, helped elect Rick Scott as governor in 2010, and rescued Ron DeSantis' struggling gubernatorial campaign in 2018. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

She was a critical voice against the war in Iran and repeatedly questioned the hardline immigration tactics championed by Miller. Friction point: In a grand irony, the very Trump decisions she opposed —the Iran war and the brutality of immigration enforcement — drove Tuesday night's midterm shellacking that led the president to lose confidence in her. Catch up quick: As recently as Oct. 16, Trump emphatically denied reports he was considering replacing Wiles. Trump noted at the time that Wiles would stay as long as she wanted, and he praised her toughness in surviving cancer while serving as his staff chief. Context: Wiles spent decades mastering the art of influencing powerful men while staying out of the spotlight. The daughter of famed NFL broadcaster Pat Summerall, Wiles has credited growing up with an alcoholic father with teaching her how to handle larger-than-life personalities. In Florida, she became a powerful behind-the-scenes operator for two moderate Republican mayors in Jacksonville, helped elect Rick Scott as governor in 2010, and rescued Ron DeSantis' struggling gubernatorial campaign in 2018. Editor's note: This is a breaking news story and will be updated.

entry.title: Stephen Miller’s fellow immigration hawks are ‘jubilant’
entry.body: Immigration hardliners and Republican moderates were poised for a wrenching intra-GOP debate after voters rejected supporters of President Donald Trump’s mass deportation campaign. Then Trump named longtime immigration hawk Stephen Miller as his next White House chief of staff — formally placing the mastermind of his crackdown at the center of power in the West Wing. Former and current DHS officials, as well as outside advocates of mass removals of unauthorized immigrants, see Miller’s rise to power as a sign that their side has already won the argument within the administration about how to proceed on immigration enforcement in the last two years of Trump’s term. “He never put a political limitation on it or a carveout saying, ‘Well, we’re only going to go after illegal aliens that have also committed a violent crime or terrorists or gang members,’” said Mark Morgan, who served as Customs and Border Protection commissioner during Trump’s first administration. Morgan argued that some Republicans and administration officials have pushed the president on the idea that his immigration agenda is politically unpopular. He said he hopes Miller will “take this opportunity to try to regroup from the people that the president was listening to on mass deportations — that I think have been giving him some really bad advice.” Following the immigration surge in Minneapolis, which saw immigration agents kill two American citizens in January, Trump softened the tone and tenor of his administration’s immigration crackdown. But while deportation figures remained high, comments from Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin seeming to express openness to a changed approach on immigration prompted deportation proponents to accuse the president of retreating from one of his biggest campaign promises. Now they are “jubilant” about Miller’s promotion and “hope it is an indication of what's to come,” Mike Howell of the Oversight Project, who helped found the Mass Deportation Coalition, told POLITICO. “Miller has spent his entire career basically centered on this issue,” Howell said. “It's been a bad week. So it's nice to go into the weekend with such great news.” Miller, who has been one of the president’s closest advisers on immigration since Trump ran for president in 2016, has been seen as the conductor and architect of the administration’s immigration policies. His role has included setting lofty deportation goals and pushing agencies across the government to devote as many resources as possible to the removal of unauthorized immigrants, even after the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti in Minneapolis. Miller’s views have long made him a boogeyman among Democrats. The longtime Trump adviser has pushed to suspend habeas corpus protections, labeled Good and Pretti “domestic terrorists” and accused unauthorized immigrants of unlawfully voting in U.S. elections with little evidence. Critics have also accused him of embracing theories espoused by white nationalists that refugee resettlement is a ploy to erase American identity. It is unclear how much Miller’s elevation will affect the Department of Homeland Security, which Miller has already closely monitored in his role as deputy chief of staff and the president’s homeland security adviser. While Mullin called Miller “my friend” and “an excellent choice” to be chief of staff in an X post Friday , the two have often disagreed on how to implement Trump’s immigration crackdown. One DHS official — granted anonymity to speak freely about immigration policy dynamics within the administration — said Miller’s elevation is “not great” news for Mullin, who has at times pushed for a more discreet approach to deportations that would prevent immigration enforcement from driving headlines and hurting the president’s political standing. Miller was among those White House aides pushing for a very visible approach to immigration. But Miller’s newfound power comes with limits. While he will be in position to define potential negotiations between the White House and Capitol Hill on immigration, he will also oversee a much vaster policy portfolio than he did until now. Some hardliners acknowledged that his attention will be more divided. In addition, Cabinet secretaries who often relied on Wiles to slow-walk aggressive moves on immigration will still retain their own influence and relationships with the president. Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick and Agriculture Secretary Brooke Rollins have been seen as particularly sensitive to the demands of industry groups reliant on immigrant labor. “Miller being there doesn’t automatically preclude or guarantee that there won’t be a slowdown on immigration enforcement,” argued Mark Krikorian, the head of the pro-enforcement Center for Immigration Studies think tank in Washington. “He’s been very good at surviving and deciding which fights have a good chance of being won. … This is something Miller has been navigating for a decade, the competing tensions within the GOP on immigration.” Still, Miller’s elevation also comes as several of the party’s biggest moderating voices on immigration — including Reps. Mike Lawler (R-N.Y.) and Brian Fitzpatrick (R-Pa.) — have been blown out of power by Tuesday’s election. It’s a combination of events that advocates of mass deportation call ripe for a full deployment of a tactic the administration has not entirely embraced: targeting companies that employ unauthorized immigrants by conducting audits and compliance visits at worksites. Both steps could make a difference in achieving more removals and self-deportations, they believe. “I think you loudly say [to businesses], ‘Get your affairs in order,’” Howell said on what he hopes to see from Miller, “because you know the worksite amnesty is over. We will be at the farms. We will be at the factories. We will be in the industrial hubs. We will be talking to DoorDash and Uber Eats.” Krikorian said Miller’s elevation also provides an opportunity for the administration to marshal bureaucratic resources across the government to verify whether employees’ records match the list of people authorized to work and live in the United States. The administration had previously promised immigration hawks that it would pursue additional audits and reviews of employee authorizations. “That’s the kind of stuff that’ll incentivize compliance and promote self deportation, if they do consistent nationwide paperwork enforcement,” he said. Democrats and some Republicans, meanwhile, believe Trump is making a political mistake. Miller’s promotion comes just days after a brutal wipeout for the GOP in the midterms — in large part driven by a swell of Latino voters swinging Democratic just two years after they helped send Trump to the White House. Among their top concerns were the sweeping immigration enforcement operations that reached a fever pitch earlier this year, which sparked protests across the country. GOP operatives who had already begun privately absorbing the shattering loss of one of the biggest drivers of Trump’s MAGA coalition from 2024 expressed shock at Miller’s new role. “No lessons were learned,” one GOP operative who worked on House races this cycle texted POLITICO. “I guess there’s nothing left to lose.” (The person was granted anonymity to speak freely about the political fallout of Miller’s promotion.) “Voters overwhelmingly rebuke his approach and then he names his most extreme adviser as chief of staff,” said Sarah Pierce, a former DHS official now at the center-left Third Way think tank in Washington.

entry.title: Vance leads behind-the-scenes push for new Iran deal
entry.body: Vice President Vance has spent the past two weeks personally involved in indirect talks with Iran aimed at reaching a new ceasefire and resuming nuclear negotiations, according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: Vance's heavy involvement shows he's taking it upon himself to extract the U.S. from a conflict he blamed for the GOP's staggering losses in this week's election. It also elevates the latest round of indirect talks to the highest levels of the administration. The big picture: U.S. officials and regional sources say that for now Trump is willing to let diplomatic efforts play out and wants to see if any kind of deal is possible. "We're talking to them," Trump told reporters on Friday, when asked what his message to Iran was. But if he changes his mind and orders renewed strikes, the U.S. military is ready to launch strikes on a relatively short timetable. Behind the scenes: Vance has been speaking almost daily to Qatari Prime Minister Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al-Thani, Pakistani Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Asim Munir and other mediators about the negotiations with Iran, sources with direct knowledge said. White House envoy Steve Witkoff and President Trump's adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner are also involved. Vance and Qatari and Pakistani mediators have been discussing the possibility of a working-level technical meeting between the U.S. and Iran in the coming days, but it hasn't materialized yet, the sources said. The vice president's office declined to comment. Catch up quick: Vance was the most skeptical voice in Trump's inner circle about the war before it began at the end of February, advocating instead for a diplomatic solution. He led the U.S. negotiating team to an April summit on Iran in Islamabad, and he was personally involved in talks that led to the U.S.-Iran memorandum of understanding (MOU) in June. Vance then led the U.S. delegation to a round of direct talks with Iran in Switzerland, which ended with an Iranian commitment to invite UN inspectors to visit its nuclear facilities. But shortly after, Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps resumed attacks on ships, leading to the collapse of the MOU. Driving the news: Two weeks ago, Vance sent a letter to the secretary of the Supreme National Security Council in Iran, Mohsen Rezaei, proposing to resume direct negotiations. Rezaei is one of the closest confidants of Iranian Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian officials said Vance's letter created positive momentum toward restarting negotiations. On Wednesday, Vance said the war was the main reason Republicans were repudiated in the election. State of play: Sources involved in the mediation efforts say there has been progress, but it's been very slow. On Friday morning, Trump spoke to Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim al-Thani about Qatar's efforts to bridge the gaps between the U.S. and Iran on a deal. Sheikh Tamim stressed the need to "continue dialogue and pursuing diplomatic means to resolve differences, spare the region further escalation, and ensure freedom of maritime navigation and the security of energy supplies," per a statement from his office.

entry.title: Johnson's meeting request
entry.body: Sen. Ron Johnson is sending a letter Monday requesting a conference meeting to discuss the midterm results and a delay in the leadership election. Johnson has gathered enough signatures to force the meeting under the Senate GOP’s rules and is proposing the gathering for 9 a.m. Tuesday. “Tuesday’s result was a stunning defeat,” Johnson and his backers write in the letter to Conference Chair Tom Cotton (R-Ark.), a copy of which was obtained by POLITICO . “Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice” Republicans still expect their leadership election to be held Tuesday, where Majority Leader John Thune is so far unopposed to lead the party next year in the minority.
