entry.title: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid - The Guardian
entry.body: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused Russia of trying to “plunge Kyiv and the entire country into a blackout”, after a major attack overnight on energy infrastructure in the capital and a bridge over the Dnipro River. Ukraine’s president said Moscow’s preparations for peace talks next week involved pummelling a city of millions with ballistic missiles. Negotiators from Russia, Ukraine and the US are due to meet on Tuesday and Wednesday in Abu Dhabi, the capital of the United Arab Emirates, for talks aimed at ending the war. Zelenskyy appealed to the US Congress – won by the Democrats in the midterm elections – to pay more attention to Ukraine in the face of relentless Russian bombardment. “Ukraine must not be left alone. We are counting on increased bilateral support from the US,” he said. Russia used 172 drones and 36 ballistic missiles in its latest attack on Kyiv and surrounding regions. The city faced serious difficulties with its electricity, water and heat supplies, Zelenskyy said, with five people injured including a 14-year-old girl. The strikes targeted substations in five regions, including one connecting two nuclear power plants to Kyiv. The city’s Northern Bridge, a key transport artery, was closed on Saturday as workers repaired damage to the road’s surface and power lines. The attacks cap a dire week for residents in Kyiv, who have experienced day-long power cuts and interruptions to the water supply. Ukrainian officials say the Kremlin’s goal is to freeze civilians into submission over the brutal winter months, a war crime. They have little confidence that US-backed peace talks will yield concrete results. In an interview with CNN, Zelenskyy described the latest blueprint set out by Jared Kushner, Donald Trump’s son-in-law, as “Yalta 2.0” – a reference to the 1945 summit between Stalin, Roosevelt and Churchill that divided postwar Europe. In a series of social media posts, Kushner said the discussions would include a new security framework for Europe, alongside guarantees for Ukraine. This appears to be a reference to the Kremlin’s longstanding demand that Nato’s expansion across Europe be reversed. Speaking on Friday, Trump said a “big beautiful agreement” could be close, involving “all of Europe”. Shortly before invading Ukraine, the Russian president, Vladimir Putin, demanded that Nato go back to its pre-1997 posture – before the Baltic states and nations in eastern Europe and the Balkans joined. Ukraine and its European partners are deeply sceptical. “The idea of discussing European-Russian security infrastructure is not simple, and it can be dangerous,” Zelenskyy told CNN, emphasising: “We don’t want to be divided by Russia.” Zelenskyy said Moscow had to end its war first, with Ukraine given meaningful security guarantees. After that, “depending on the answers”, wider security architecture could be considered, he said. Western diplomats say agreeing to Russia’s demands would effectively end Nato. Russia’s defence ministry, meanwhile, said its strikes early on Saturday were against energy and transport targets. Since the summer, it has dramatically stepped up air attacks on Ukrainian cities, as its progress on the frontline has stalled. Last month Russia lost 54,000 troops, killed or injured, according to Kyiv – the highest monthly loss in the war.
entry.summary: Blackouts and water shortages in Kyiv after Russia strikes Ukraine’s energy grid The Guardian Drone and missile attacks wound 9 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US AP News Ukraine's power network suffers further damage after fresh Russian strikes BBC Missiles target Kyiv and wound 5 as Ukraine prepares for talks with Russia and the US ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos Zelenskyy accuses Russia of ramping up attacks on Ukraine ahead of U.S. talks CBS News

entry.title: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election
entry.body: No clear winner after tight New Zealand general election - Published There was no clear winner following New Zealand's election on Saturday, as the leaders of its two major parties preparing for negotiations to form a coalition government. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon's centre-right National Party won 42 seats but was 19 short of the simple majority needed to form a government, despite being the largest party, preliminary results show. Combined with their coalition partners ACT and New Zealand First, they would have a slim lead over the left-leaning bloc if a deal could be reached. But opposition leader Chris Hipkins, whose Labour Party won 36 seats, showed no signs of conceding, saying the "shape of the next government" will remain uncertain "for a while". The tight result followed a campaign shaped by the cost of living and unemployment. Projections show the National Party on 42 seats and Labour on 36. The Greens are on 16, with ACT on 13, New Zealand First on 12, the Opportunity Party on 7 and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests, on 5. The electoral commission was not due to announced the official result until 27 November. Luxon congratulated Hipkins on a "very hard-fought race" before addressing party colleagues, saying "whatever the final count, we are incredibly proud of each and everyone for you". He said he would run a caretaker government until the final results were confirmed later in the month, adding: "With those final results there can then be meaningful negotiations." Elsewhere, Labour leader Kipkins said "the people have spoken", adding: "It may take a bit longer to work out what they've said." Hipkins said the results made clear the "next parliament is going to require all of us to compromise, to work together and to find a common ground". More than 99% of votes have been counted in New Zealand, with National and Labour neck-and-neck in terms of vote share. But the preliminary results pointed to historically low support for the two major parties, with a combined vote share of around 60%. They were followed by the Greens, ACT, New Zealand First, centrist party Opportunity and Te PÄti MÄori, which represents MÄori interests. - New Zealand election 2026: What you need to know - Published27 October The Opportunity Party crossed the 5% threshold to enter parliament for the first time, with leader Qiulae Wong saying would work with either side. It has been described as this election's kingmaker as it remains open to working with either major bloc, but its leaders said they would negotiate first with the party that secures the most seats. Speaking at Opportunity's watch party, Wong told supporters: "We believe that we can change the way we do politics to focus on the future, on the next generation, and on finding common ground." Professor Andrew Geddis from the University of Otago, an expert in election law, said "the Opportunity Party as a wildcard player" could "determine which bloc of parties is able to govern". "It will come down to some very fine vote margins not just between the parties, but in individual electorates. We are going to have to wait for the special votes to be processed and counted over the next three weeks," he said. Special votes are votes cast outside a voter's electorate, including overseas. The Greens â who have proposed forcing the country's two main supermarkets to divest stores to create publicly-owned shops â saw their vote rise by a couple of percentage points. Julian McCrann, head of polling at Roy Morgan, told BBC News the cost of living was the main issue for many New Zealanders "Three years ago, Luxon came in saying he'd be making New Zealanders' lives better and solving these economic issues, but he hasn't really delivered," he said. More than half of the country no longer see New Zealand as a land of opportunity, according to an annual social cohesion survey. Record numbers of Kiwis have been leaving the country, with many going to Australia. New Zealand's mixed-member proportional voting system means most governments are coalitions. Each voter makes two choices â for the representative of their constituency in parliament and a political party. Related topics - Published10 hours ago
entry.summary: Weeks of coalition talks could follow after preliminary results pointed to a highly divided national parliament.

entry.title: UK cannot 'cherry pick' EU single market deal, Barnier tells BBC
entry.body: The prime minister has said rejoining the bloc's internal market was among options he could pursue as part of a reshaping of ties since the UK's exit from the EU nearly six years ago. But Michel Barnier told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg that EU members would insist on the UK readopting certain conditions, such as the free movement of people, to gain access. He said there was not a "single market Ã la carte" menu from which the UK could pick and choose what elements it wanted to adopt. Barnier - who led the EU delegation during Brexit talks between 2016 and 2021, and had a three-month spell as French prime minister in 2024 - said the "door is open" within Europe to the UK rejoining as an EU member. But he insisted that any move to rejoin the single market - which allows for goods to be freely traded without border controls - would require the UK to follow the same terms as other members. He added that this included compliance with regulations designed to promote the circulation of goods, services, capital and people, referred to collectively within EU institutions as the "four freedoms". "There will be no possibility to have one freedom and not the other. The four freedoms are clearly the four conditions to be inside a single market." Since becoming prime minister in July, Burnham has suggested he could commit Labour to pursuing a much closer future relationship with Europe, including asking to rejoin the organisation as a full member, though he has ruled out major changes before the next election. His predecessors have struck a series of deals with the EU on different aspects of how the UK and EU interact post-Brexit. Both sides are hoping to use a meeting in Brussels in 10 days' time to unveil deals on food standards, youth visas and re-linking British industry to the EU's carbon trading regime. - Why the prime minister wants to talk about Brexit again - Published13 October Of the four freedoms, the free movement of people - which allows EU citizens to live and work elsewhere in the bloc without a visa - was a key issue during the 2016 Brexit referendum. Burnham's immediate predecessor, Sir Keir Starmer, ruled out re-establishing it for the UK in Labour's 2024 election manifesto and any move to advocate it again would prove a key dividing line with the Conservatives and Reform UK at a future poll. Burnham recently said in an interview that he would not re-establish free movement of people without a referendum, prompting Downing Street to clarify that he was not advocating its return at this point. He has previously said he wanted to lay out "different options" for the relationship with Europe at the Brussels summit later this month, before trying to find a consensus with the British public on a new relationship. Barnier also predicted that EU countries would reject reinstating the British financial rebate, first negotiated in 1985, that lowered UK contributions towards the EU's annual budget while it was a member. The UK's decision to leave the bloc had created "a new situation", he said, meaning a new rebate would be "off the table". 'False promises and lies' Barnier also compared Reform leader Nigel Farage to French politician Marine Le Pen. He said: "We have our own Farage. It is Mrs Le Pen. The same populism, the same lies, the same false promises." Asked by Kuenssberg to clarify what he was referring to with his accusation of lies, Barnier said "for instance, when Mr Farage and Mr Johnson promised the UK people to get back [Â£350] million per week, it was not true, it was not possible. The Vote Leave campaign, of which Boris Johnson became a key figure, has been criticised previously for the slogan on the side of their campaign bus that said Britain sent Â£350m a week to the EU, adding: "Let's fund our NHS instead". Johnson said in 2017 that "once we have settled our accounts, we will take back control of roughly Â£350m per week. It would be a fine thing as many of us have pointed out if a lot of that money went on the NHS". Critics have said that the Â£350m per week was an approximate sum which represents a "gross contribution" and did not take into account the UK's Â£75m-a-week rebate nor the EU's investments in the UK. Johnson has since defended the claim, saying the Â£350m was based on the UK's gross contribution to the EU, and was in fact an underestimate as UK contributions were due to rise. âIn his memoirs published in 2024, Johnson said EU money spent in the UK was not "democratically controlled by the British people", and "even if the net figure was only Â£175m, that was still a hell of a lot of money". Farage, who led Leave UK and was not part of the Vote Leave campaign so not connected to the Â£350m claim, said: "It is the same old Barnier - arrogant, out of touch and a bully. He vindicates our decision to leave every time he opens his mouth." Get in touch What questions do you have?
entry.summary: The former Brexit negotiator says EU countries would reject any British attempts to follow economic rules "a la carte".

entry.title: Italian foreign minister says hackers leaked his personal data
entry.body: Italian foreign minister says hackers leaked his personal data - Published Italy's Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani says he has been targeted by "cyber-criminals" who published his personal data online because of his country's support for Ukraine. "For days now, cyber-criminals have been publishing my personal data on the dark web and seeking further information, effectively exposing me to new threats and intimidation," Tajani wrote on X. He did not specify the nature of the threats, but said the hackers were also targeting his family. The dark web is a hidden part of the internet that is not indexed by common search engines and can only be accessed with specialist software. "Our position on Ukraine is the political reason I have been targeted," Tajani said. "Defending the freedom of a sovereign state, taking a clear stand in support of a nation's democracy and independence, is dangerous in the eyes of these criminal entities." Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni blamed the incident on pro-Russian hackers and offered Tajani her "full solidarity". "The sale of confidential information about institutional representatives is a cause of serious concern and must be tackled with the utmost determination," she said in a statement. Moscow has not publicly responded to the allegations. Meloni also expressed concern about "circulation of false images" which she said were shared by members of Italy's opposition. She did not give details about the content of the images. The Italian government has provided humanitarian and military support to Ukraine in its war against Russia. Tajani, who is also the deputy prime minister, said the government was taking the threats seriously. Related topics Related stories - Published5 days ago
entry.summary: Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has blamed pro-Russian hackers for publishing the details online.

entry.title: Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil
entry.body: Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil - Published Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen will start from the back of the grid at Sunday's Sao Paulo Grand Prix. Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc and Mercedes' George Russell will also have grid penalties, 10 places for Leclerc and five for Russell. Hamilton initially had only a 10-place penalty for exceeding his power-unit allowance for the season, but the new internal combustion engine that was fitted on Saturday morning failed in final practice. That meant Ferrari decided to fit an entire new power-unit to his car, hence the bigger penalty. Verstappen had an all-new engine fitted after Red Bull discovered problems after Friday practice. Leclerc and Russell have both fitted new internal combustion engines. The penalty for Leclerc is bigger than Russell's because it is the first time Ferrari have exceeded the limit of four engines per season on his car, while Russell had already gone beyond that. Verstappen famously won the Sao Paulo Grand Prix from 17th on the grid after an engine penalty in a wet race. Sao Paulo Grand Prix 6-8 November Live commentary on BBC Radio 5 Sports Extra; live text updates on BBC Sport website and app Qualifying is set to be wet, after rain started about an hour before the session, and it is expected to continue overnight, with forecasts saying it could rain at any point on race day. Meanwhile, F1 announced on Saturday that Sao Paulo's Interlagos circuit had extended its contract to host a grand prix until 2035. F1 president and chief executive officer Stefano Domenicali said: "Brazil is an important part of F1's history and our future, and I am delighted that this five-year extension will see us continue racing in Sao Paulo until 2035. "The passion of our Brazilian fans is extraordinary, and every time we return to Interlagos we feel their energy in the grandstands and in the city of Sao Paulo. "The continued success and excitement surrounding the event shows why it holds such a special place on our calendar, and this agreement underlines our long-term commitment to Brazil." Related topics - Published20 hours ago - Published21 hours ago
entry.summary: Red Bull's Max Verstappen and Ferrari drivers Lewis Hamilton and Charles Leclerc will all have grid penalties at the Sao Paulo Grand Prix.

entry.title: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza
entry.body: Tens of thousands of tents flooded after heavy rains in Gaza - Published Heavy rains have flooded tens of thousands of tents where displaced residents have been living in Gaza, with a United Nations official saying almost everyone in the territory needs help. Residents used pots and pans to clear water from their flooded tents, with some saying they were left without shelter. Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, said the "desperate" situation was being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the entry of heavy machinery and supplies such as engine oil. Some 90% of Gaza residents have been displaced by the Israeli war against Hamas, many of them multiple times, with limited access to clean water and sanitation. Aid agencies say the situation is likely to worsen with the start of the rainy season. Speaking to the BBC from Deir Al Balah in central Gaza, Veitch said: "It's just horrific and they're absolutely desperate. "We're providing all the assistance that we can but we're getting stopped on the street as we're driving now because people are begging us for help." The Hamas-run government in Gaza said about 70,000 tents had been flooded. A spokesperson said the "collapse of dozens of cracked walls and roofs" had caused injuries, some of which were critical. Veitch also said there were fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents available in the Gaza strip due to UN budget cuts. "We have to be much more choosy about where we're going to be supporting," he said. "But unfortunately, heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help." Israel has said it restricts the entry of items into Gaza that could be used for military purposes. Maryam Odeh, 34, who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah, told AFP news agency: "We no longer know how to protect our children. "My children ask me where we will sleep tonight, and I have no answer." Khaled al-Najjar, 41, told AFP: "We fear for our children not only from the flooding of the tents, but also from the cold and the widespread diseases." Veitch said aid workers were being "stopped on the street" by Gazans "begging us for help". He continued: "They're absolutely desperate. We saw last year what winter does, and we had deaths from hypothermia last year. "We can expect the same again unless we have very, very urgent action now." A ceasefire came into force in Gaza in October last year, but Israeli air strikes have continued almost every day. Since then, 1,580 people have been killed, according to Gaza's Hamas-run health ministry, whose figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it is targeting Hamas, but often civilians are also killed. Meanwhile, a peace plan for Gaza, brokered by the Trump administration, has stalled. The ceasefire saw thousands of Palestinians held by Israel released in return for all of the 48 remaining hostages held in Gaza, and an agreement to end the war. The conflict was triggered by the Hamas-led attack on Israel on 7 October 2023, when about 1,200 people were killed and 251 taken hostage. Since the war began, 74,594 people have been killed in Gaza, according to the territory's health ministry. - Published6 days ago - Published20 October
entry.summary: Heavy rain has flooded temporary shelters used by Palestinians displaced during Israel's war with Hamas.

entry.title: All Blacks cruise to victory as Scotland fade
entry.body: New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade - Published Nations Championship Scotland (21) 21 Tries: Ashman 3 Cons: Russell 3 New Zealand (24) 43 Tries: Sititi, De Groot, Taylor, Barrett 2, Moorby, Aumua Cons: McKenzie 4 Ruthless New Zealand blew Scotland away in a high-class, seven tries to three Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield. Despite a historic first-half hat-trick from Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman, the All Blacks were mostly magnificent, unrelenting and classy. It was the 34th Test between the nations and New Zealand's tally has yet another win - 32 now, with two draws going back to 1905. Wallace Sititi scored early in a breathless first half. Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor hit back to make it 17-7 at the end of the first quarter. New Zealand's Peter Lakai was binned and Ashman got his second while he was off. The sensational Beauden Barrett scored the first of his double straight after. Then, as the bonkerdom stretched on, Sititi was yellow-carded and Ashman made the All Blacks pay with his hat-trick try. Only three points divided them at the break, but the All Blacks outclassed Scotland thereafter. Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett again and Asafo Aumua struck in the second half. Scotland were beaten out the gate in the end. We hoped for a classic and a classic it was, with bells on. If only for 40 minutes. Beyond that thrilling opening spell it was one-way traffic, a vicious exhibition of All Black class and might. Just like last year, when New Zealand drew first blood, the visitors came roaring out, punishing a penalty given away cheaply with a piece of trickery at a close-range line-out that bamboozled the Scots. A couple of dummy runners broke away and took enough of Scotland's attention with them. Sititi thundered through a gap to score. Kyle Rowe's magnificent 50-22 gave Scotland the field position to strike off a driven line-out - Ashman driving over for the first of his three tries. Unlike his counterpart, Damian McKenzie, Finn Russell converted. New Zealand turned the screw again, forcing Scotland into big defensive set after big defensive set. There's only so much of that you can soak up, though. The visitors looked lethal from all corners. Beauden Barrett's surge downfield, hotly pursued by Matt Fagerson, was the catalyst for their second score. Fagerson was done on the floor, New Zealand went to touch and De Groot went over the line. McKenzie converted; New Zealand by five. And, soon, New Zealand by 10. Another Scotland penalty was punished to the max, the All Blacks executing from the resultant line-out maul. Taylor getting it down this time. This all happened inside the first quarter. Lakai, the terrific openside, was binned for persistent New Zealand offsides. Huw Jones almost scored but got held up. Off a penalty advantage, Ashman blasted through Sititi to score. With Russell's conversion it was a three-point game. Scotland needed to kick on, but instead they got pushed back. The wondrous Beauden Barrett sliced through following huge work from his pack; on the face it simple, but in reality, complex and beautiful. McKenzie restored the 10-point lead, but it didn't last long. Sititi was binned for going off his feet. Scotland had a crack at 13 All Blacks for a brief minute but couldn't break them despite going painfully close through Jones. Lakai returned to make it 15 versus 14 - and that's when Scotland struck. It was that old reliable again, the line-out maul proving devastating. Ashman got on the end of it and over he went for his hat-trick. For a flurry of penalties and back-to-back yellows, New Zealand got what they deserved. Those cards cost them 14 points. Seven first-half tries and three points between them at the break. Now it was time for Test match animals to emerge. When they did, they were wearing New Zealand white rather than Scotland blue. The All Blacks played those key minutes in Scotland's 22, forcing errors and penalties and opportunities. Off a scrum, Jordie Barrett's skip pass found Moorby in space and he sauntered over. More New Zealand heat and more Scotland penalties. Then, a yellow for Sione Tuipulotu. It could have been Ben White just as easily. The pressure the visitors were applying was just suffocating. With the captain off the pitch, New Zealand made it pay - Quinn Tupaea to McKenzie and on to Beauden Barrett for his second of the day. McKenzie's conversion made it 36-21. At 50 minutes, the game was over far too early for Gregor Townsend's side. To rub salt in the wound Aumua finished a gorgeous set-piece to land try number seven; 43-21 and 19-0 in the second half. Scotland had hopes of winning or, at the very least, of taking New Zealand to the wire. The uneasy truth for Townsend and his players is that despite their excellence in the opening half, they were utterly bossed in the second. These All Blacks are far more formidable than the version that appeared at Murrayfield a year ago. Meanwhile, Scotland's long, long wait for glory against the Kiwis carries on and on. Line-ups Scotland: Kyle Rowe; Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones, Sione Tuipulotu (capt), Jamie Dobie; Finn Russell, Ben White; Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman, Zander Fagerson, Gregor Brown, Scott Cummings, Matt Fagerson, Rory Darge, Jack Dempsey. Replacements: Gregor Hiddleston, Pierre Schoeman, Will Hurd, Max Williamson, Josh Baylish, George Horne, Tom Jordan, Blair Kinghorn. New Zealand: Beauden Barrett; Will Jordan, Quinn Tupaea, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby; Damian McKenzie, Cam Roigard; Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (capt), Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi. Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Christian Lio-Willie, Anton Segner, Cortez Ratima, Timoci Tavatavanawai, Rieko Ioane. Related topics - Published5 hours ago
entry.summary: New Zealand canter to a 43-21 Nations Championship win at Murrayfield as Scotland fall away after a thrilling first half.

entry.title: How Democrats used anger over data centers to flip red states - CNN
entry.body: Ken Paxton made it easier to build.” Talarico carried Kaufman County by 1 percentage point as he notched a striking 12-point victory statewide, helping lead Democrats to statewide victory in Texas for the first time since 1994. It was one of many examples where backlash to data centers fueled Democrats’ staggering victories in the midterms. From statewide races to local ballot initiatives, voters demonstrated sweeping support for a tougher stance toward data centers, if not outright opposition to their continued development. About a quarter of voters said AI and data centers were “crucial” to their vote in the midterms, trailing higher priorities such as the cost of living and corruption, according to CNN’s Voter Poll. But when voters were asked about building data centers in their communities, they were overwhelmingly opposed by a roughly 3-to-1 margin. “It was overwhelming, unequivocal, bipartisan backlash from the bottom up that was showing up in every corner of my district,” said Michigan Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, who flipped a Republican-held House seat after centering his campaign early on opposition to data centers.

entry.title: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China
entry.body: Concerns are being raised that neither the Commerce Department nor Nvidia are doing their due diligence when it comes to vetting Chinese firms cleared to handle the company’s H200 AI chips. According to The New York Times, New Matrix is on the list of approved firms, yet its offices are empty, “a hollow gray shell with wires dangling from the ceiling where lights should be.” In fact, the paper could find little evidence that the company exists in any meaningful way: The US let Nvidia sell chips to an empty office in China The government is approving sales of Nvidia’s AI chips to Chinese firms with ties to blacklisted companies. Only scant information can be found online about New Matrix, which was created 17 months ago. At the building that New Matrix lists as its address, a company directory does not include the firm. At the nearby property management agency for the industrial park, a receptionist and a manager both said they had no record of the company. What little information can be found about New Matrix is concerning. Its owners have ties to a Chinese private equity firm that has been blacklisted by the US government since 2024. And according to the Times, this is not a rare lapse in oversight, but a troubling pattern of companies connected to entities with national-security-related trade restrictions being approved to purchase Nvidia chips. Nvidia had been restricted from selling chips to China during the Biden presidency. But the Trump administration relaxed those limits after Nvidia agreed to give the government a 15-percent cut of all sales. The company’s CEO, Jensen Huang, also launched an intense lobbying campaign and was apparently targeted by China’s Ministry of State Security in a spying plot.

entry.title: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests - Phys.org
entry.body: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests Gaby Clark Scientific Editor Robert Egan Senior Editor An alternative model in which the universe is 26.7 billion years old and needs neither dark matter nor dark energy has held up against several major cosmology tests, according to a new University of Ottawa study. The research, titled "A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology," is published in the journal Universe. One model, many observations During 2025 and 2026, Rajendra Gupta, adjunct professor in uOttawa's Department of Physics, and postdoctoral researcher Dr. Nikolaos Samaras tested the CCC+TL model against a range of important astronomical observations. CCC+TL stands for "covarying coupling constants plus tired light." The model suggests that what is usually attributed to dark matter and dark energy could instead come from evolving fundamental constants that govern how forces and particles interact. Scientists have searched for dark matter and dark energy for decades, but neither has been directly detected. The standard cosmological model, known as ΛCDM, also faces questions raised by observations of surprisingly mature galaxies in the early universe. "Most emerging models explain only a limited set of observations," Gupta says. "A new model must not conflict with the pillars of cosmology and astrophysics, and our findings meet that challenge, including the yet-to-be-published cosmic microwave background challenge." CCC+TL changes the Einstein and Friedmann equations, which describe gravity and the expansion of the universe. That meant the researchers couldn't just modify the standard model and existing computer codes. For each test, they developed CCC+TL-compliant equations and code. What the tests found The model's results agreed with several major observations. Its predictions for the amounts of hydrogen, helium and other light elements formed shortly after the Big Bang matched those of the standard model. It also agreed with cosmic-chronometer measurements, which use the ages of galaxies to estimate how fast the universe has expanded over time. In a recent paper published in Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society, the researchers also applied the model to all 175 galaxies in the SPARC database and found it could reproduce their rotation curves without dark matter. A separate study of time dilation in supernova observations also supports the model, although that paper is still under review. The team looked at the Bullet Cluster too. There, the extra gravitational effect the model predicts, rather than the dark matter, tracks the galaxies, not the hot, X-ray-emitting gas. The researchers call this an early proof of concept that needs more study. "Observations attributed to dark matter and dark energy likely originate from covarying coupling constants," adds Gupta, whose paper on the origin of dark matter and dark energy explores the idea. More time for early galaxies to form The model could also help explain why astronomers keep finding large, mature galaxies so early in cosmic history. In the standard model, the universe was about 300 million years old during cosmic dawn. Under CCC+TL, it would have been about 4.6 billion years old at the same observed redshift. That extra time gives galaxies longer to grow and develop. In the researchers' calculations, early galaxies come out about 12 times larger in size and mass than the standard model predicts, as reported in Galaxies. "Impossible early galaxies become predictable galaxies," Gupta explains. "We predict that galaxies exist well beyond the distances the James Webb Space Telescope has reached." That prediction may soon be tested. The James Webb Space Telescope's GLIMPSE program plans to search for galaxies at redshifts that may exceed 50. In the standard model, there may not be enough time for massive galaxies to form that early. CCC+TL has no such limit. "The success should encourage astronomers to take the new model seriously. It is challenging to understand and apply, but we believe it extends the physics of the universe beyond ΛCDM limits," concludes Gupta. Gupta et al., A Big Bang Nucleosynthesis Consistency Test of the CCC+TL Cosmology, Universe (2026). DOI: 10.3390/universe12070193 Journal information: Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society Provided by University of Ottawa
entry.summary: Theory predicting an older universe without dark matter or dark energy passes key cosmological tests Phys.org

entry.title: Earth has a new mini-moon: a 1-metre space rock named 2026 QQ8 was pulled into orbit around our planet in - The Times of India
entry.body: Earth has acquired a temporary companion in space, but it will not stay for long. A small space rock named 2026 QQ8 was pulled into Earth's gravitational grip in April 2026, remained unnoticed for months and was first spotted in August. Now confirmed as a natural object, the roughly 1â2-metre-wide asteroid is expected to remain temporarily bound to our planet until December before escaping and continuing its journey around the Sun in 2027. The discovery was reported by the International Astronomical Union's Minor Planet Center on October 29, after astronomers had gathered enough observations to establish the object's identity and trajectory. Hungarian astronomer KrisztiÃ¡n SÃ¡rneczky first observed it on August 19â20, according to reports by Space.com. Initially, however, scientists were unsure whether the faint object was a natural space rock or human-made debris from an old rocket or satellite. Follow-up observations helped resolve that uncertainty. Astronomers used the University of Hawaii's 2.2-metre telescope and the Lowell Discovery Telescope to study the object. The additional measurements, including how it responded to solar radiation pressure, helped rule out an artificial origin. The Minor Planet Center subsequently classified it as a natural object, most likely a small asteroid, and described it as a temporarily captured object. How Earth captured its new mini-moon The object did not begin orbiting Earth because it was launched towards the planet or deliberately placed there. Instead, it passed close enough for Earth's gravity to temporarily alter its path. Orbital calculations indicate that 2026 QQ8 entered Earth's gravitational sphere of influence in late April. This region is often described using the concept of the Hill sphere, the area around a planet where its gravitational pull can dominate the motion of a smaller passing object against the Sun's influence. When an asteroid passes through this region under the right conditions, it can become temporarily captured. It may then travel around the planet before eventually escaping and returning to an independent orbit around the Sun. Unlike Earth's permanent Moon, however, a mini-moon does not necessarily follow a stable, circular path. Its trajectory can be irregular, and its stay may last only weeks or months. In the case of 2026 QQ8, astronomers expect the temporary capture to last roughly eight to nine months. The asteroid is also not particularly close to Earth by lunar standards. Its closest predicted distance during this temporary stay is about 568,000 kilometres, roughly one-and-a-half times the average distance between Earth and the Moon. It is therefore not expected to pose an impact threat. A visitor that returns to Earth's neighbourhood Although 2026 QQ8 has only recently been recognised as a mini-moon, its path suggests that it has approached Earth before. According to orbital analysis reported by EarthSky, the object comes relatively close to our planet approximately once every decade. It passed near Earth in 1965, but did not come close enough to be captured by its gravity. Its next predicted approach in 2058 is also not expected to result in another temporary capture. Scientists have calculated that 2026 QQ8 takes approximately 359 days to complete one orbit around the Sun, slightly shorter than an Earth year. Its current temporary stay is therefore an interruption in its usual journey around the star, rather than the beginning of a permanent relationship with our planet. The object is expected to remain under Earth's gravitational influence through December. It should then break away, most likely around the end of the year or in early January 2027, and continue along its own solar orbit. Earth may have more than one temporary moon 2026 QQ8 is not the first small object to become a temporary satellite of Earth. Astronomers have previously identified objects such as 2020 CD3 and 2024 PT5, which spent limited periods in Earth's gravitational neighbourhood before moving away. A 2025 study published in the journal Icarus suggested that Earth could have an average of around six lunar-origin mini-moons at any given time. These objects may be fragments blasted off the Moon when asteroids strike its surface. The researchers estimated that such temporary companions could typically remain around Earth for approximately nine months, although the prediction carries considerable uncertainty. Research presented at the Europlanet Science Congress in 2026 also suggested that the largest mini-moon around Earth at any given moment may typically be only about 75 centimetres across. A space rock measuring around three metres could potentially remain captured for 10 to 20 years under suitable conditions. Finding these objects is difficult because they are small, faint and often move rapidly across the sky. Their brief stays also make them challenging targets for astronomers. Improved telescope surveys and follow-up observations are helping scientists identify more of these temporary visitors. The distinction between a mini-moon and a quasi-moon is important, too. A mini-moon is genuinely held temporarily by a planet's gravity. A quasi-moon, by contrast, travels around the Sun on an orbit that makes it appear to accompany Earth, but it is not gravitationally bound to our planet. For now, 2026 QQ8 is a short-lived addition to Earth's neighbourhood. It is too small and distant to be a spectacular sight in the night sky, but its capture offers astronomers another opportunity to study the small objects that move through the region around our planet. By early 2027, the tiny visitor is expected to have slipped free of Earth's gravitational hold and resumed its journey around the Sun.
entry.summary: Earth has a new mini-moon: a 1-metre space rock named 2026 QQ8 was pulled into orbit around our planet in The Times of India Earth has captured a new mini moon — but it won't stick around for long Space A new mini-moon for Earth! Meet 2026 QQ8 EarthSky Asteroid 2026 QQ8, a Likely Temporary Earth "Mini-Moon," Is Ruled a Natural Object XenoSpectrum Earth Traps A Second Moon And It Was Nearly Mistaken For Space Junk HotHardware

entry.title: ‘Brief burst of intense heat’ could give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life - Euronews.com
entry.body: The association is urging EU policymakers to enshrine the ban into formal legislation, arguing it would further accelerate the development of sustainable recycling technologies. Wind turbines undergo flash joule heating Researchers have recently discovered a new way to give hard-to-recycle wind turbine blades a second life – by subjecting them to a “brief burst of intense heat”. The study, published in the science journal Chem Circularity, found so-called ‘flash joule heating’ can transform blades – often made from silica-containing fiberglass and carbon-rich polymer resin – into silicon carbide and graphene, two valuable materials for manufacturing. Blades were heated to about 2,000°C in seconds; at such high temperatures, carbon can react with silica to form silicon carbide, a hard, heat-resistant material. Carbon can also reorganise into graphene under these conditions, a material known for its strength and ability to conduct heat and electricity. The research team found that adding the broken-down blades to other materials before heating made the new material more useful for creating new rotor blades.

entry.title: Sequoia shutting down its Scouts program marks the end of an era
entry.body: Sequoia this week announced a broad overhaul in a memo posted to X, a move that includes closing its London office and shutting down its scout program. Observers warn that it would be a mistake to read too much into the London closure, since the British capital has a thriving AI scene. On the other hand, the decision to end scouts says more about where venture investing is headed. That’s partly because 17 years ago, Sequoia pioneered the scouts model, in which select founders and operators write checks on the firm’s behalf. Amid increased competition for deal flow, many VC firms followed suit. But a consensus now seems to be emerging that the model has reached its limits in its current form. Not everyone was sold on the model in the first place. “They pioneered the scout program but [to be honest] it never made sense to me!” VC Sheel Mohnot wrote on X this week. “The scouts themselves don’t really care that much about the investments, you can still miss (like they did with Uber), not sure what it gets you. I suspect other firms will shutter theirs too,” he added. To be clear, Sequoia didn’t make a case against scouts in the memo. Instead, it framed its decision as part of a broader need for more focus. But its goal of “putting more energy behind fewer people and things” is likely to resonate with others who’ve questioned the ‘spray and pray’ approach to scouting. Rival firm Andreessen Horowitz (a16z), for instance, rolled out a global scout network aimed at spotting opportunities in the U.S. and also in smaller European hubs. But a16z partner Gabriel Vasquez told TechCrunch earlier this year that the firm had revamped its program to double down “on the best people.” Under this new approach, Vasquez explained, scouts get more resources but are also expected to be more active, such as by co-hosting dinners with the firm. “They get more budget, but we have reduced the number,” he said. This also seems to indicate that it is VC firms that have been driving an overhaul of the model. For founders, being a scout is attractive: it brings them closer to firms they may want checks from someday, or even a partner role with, and being seen as someone who can write a check can raise their standing among other founders. Some scouts will undoubtedly mourn the end of Sequoia’s program. Among them is Station F boss Roxanne Varza, who wrote on LinkedIn that she was “sad” to hear that the program was getting cut off, and “hope[d] that other funds [w]on’t follow suit.” Varza, a former Sequoia scout from 2020 to 2025, told TechCrunch that she had no information beyond what has been shared publicly, but observed that becoming a scout had often been a stepping stone for aspiring investment managers. “I cannot name all of the incredible scouts that have gone on to join or build funds, but there are quite a few. And the scout programs may have helped them get there — allowed them to build an investment track record, allowed them to build relationships with various funds directly, and more,” she wrote to TechCrunch. According to Varza, the program’s impact went beyond the individual level, instead helping the entire ecosystem become more mature. “I believe they have helped to foster the investment culture and early-stage investment landscape that we now see in Europe, for example,” Varza said. While others may agree with Varza about the role these programs have played, they may still have run their course for two reasons. First, seasoned operators may get more financial upside as angels. When it’s their own money, they get to keep the returns, too. Second, leading VC firms are now big and well-known enough that the best founders tend to come to them, so they worry less about missing deals, except at the very earliest stages or in niches and geographies where they have less reach. Still, the pull of those early and niche deals is why scouts programs are much more likely to get revamped than to disappear entirely. “While Sequoia may be cutting the program, venture partner-style deals are likely to continue,” said Varza in her email to TechCrunch. “Scouts was just a way to scale the format. I don’t imagine Sequoia would end all forms of venture partners, but they are full of surprises.”
entry.summary: Sequoia pioneered the scouts model and many VC firms followed suit, but a consensus now seems to be forming that the model has reached limits in its current form.

entry.title: World of Warcraft: Forever is the biggest launch in WoW history, beating Wrath itself - Windows Central
entry.body: Blizzard confirms: World of Warcraft Forever is the biggest launch in WoW history, beating Wrath of the Lich King — is WoW: Retail cooked? Blizzard confirmed that World of Warcraft Forever is absolutely huge, and potentially represents a headache for World of Warcraft's retail arm. World of Warcraft is the game that absolutely refuses to die, and in fact, it's potentially now bigger than ever. Confirmed today on the official Warcraft social media channels, Blizzard said that World of Warcraft Forever represents its biggest launch in history by peak players, beating even the likes of Wrath of the Lich King from WoW's previous height almost two decades ago. "Congratulations, you made HISTORY!" the post reads, "WoW: Forever has achieved the biggest launch in WoW history by peak concurrent players," and also confirmed that it has "the highest number of returning WoW players in history" as well. For those who don't know, World of Warcraft is an MMORPG where thousands of players pile into single servers to create a persistent, online living world. Microsoft and Xbox acquired the game a few years ago along with Activision, Blizzard, and King, and it has already been teasing a World of Warcraft port to Xbox consoles for some time. The game is presently only available on PC and cloud streaming services like NVIDIA GeForce Now. The retail version of World of Warcraft has strayed intensely from the game's original vision in recent years, leading to players leaving the game and potentially even the genre en masse. World of Warcraft Forever is essentially a remix and polish of the original vision for World of Warcraft, with minimal handholding, a boosted sense of risk and reward, a reduction in "convenience" features that reduce in-game social interaction, atop a boost in visual quality. WoW:F also has thousands of new quests and stories, taking place in an "alternative timeline" of sorts that exists a year or so before World of Warcraft's original base game. It remains to be seen if WoW:F can maintain the momentum it has seen, but the whole ordeal leaves World of Warcraft's main arm, currently dubbed Midnight, with a bit of a headache in my view. The only game that could kill WoW was, in fact, WoW itself Many games have tried to kill World of Warcraft over the years, but none have truly succeeded. WoW and Final Fantasy 14 remain the only large, populated purely subscription-based MMORPGs at least in the West as of writing, with incumbents relying on free-to-play business models to entice players. World of Warcraft's subscription model ensures it can pump out huge amounts of content at a rapid clip, although in recent years, many have been wondering if it has become too rapid. World of Warcraft's main "retail" arm has seen a huge decline in quality, with players asking the firm to slow down to focus on the details and polish. Blizzard so far has ignored those calls. WoW:F represents a complete reversal on what WoW retail has become in essence. World of Warcraft retail has abandoned all forms of immersion, friction, world building, and outdoor levelling gameplay for a focus on arcade-style endgame content which, while admittedly still fun, is frankly quite exhausting. World of Warcraft's story writing has been dismal for years, and bugs have been more prevalent than ever before. RELATED: World of Warcraft's Ion Hazzikostas promises Retail won't get abandoned The WoW:F team exists separately from the WoW: Retail team, and the divergence in philosophies are stark. WoW:F's focus on social systems, in-game immersion, understated and environmental storytelling, and slower, more methodical gameplay seems far more inline with what lapsed WoW players actually want. I feel World of Warcraft's retail arm has focused on "data telemetry" over good human design instincts and it has led to the game's hollowing out. Hopefully, World of Warcraft: Forever can give Blizzard a hard lesson in listening to players directly — something I feel the retail team no longer does. Join us on Reddit at r/WindowsCentral to share your insights and discuss our latest news, reviews, and more. Jez Corden is the Executive Editor at Windows Central, focusing primarily on all things Xbox and gaming. Jez is known for breaking exclusive news and analysis as relates to the Microsoft ecosystem — while being powered by tea. Follow on X.com/JezCorden and tune in to the XB2 Podcast, all about, you guessed it, Xbox! entry.title: British soldier ignored order to pull his SIM card, then got blackmailed
entry.body: An Estonian newspaper recently revealed that a British soldier disobeyed a direct order to remove the SIM card from his cellphone before being deployed to a part of Estonia, approximately 90 miles west of the Russian border. As a result of his refusal to engage in this element of operational security (opsec), the soldier, Daniel Barton-Kennedy, had his phone hacked, and nude photos of himself were stolen and used as blackmail against him. Eventually, Barton-Kennedy was court-martialed for disobeying a lawful command, pled guilty, was reduced in rank, and ordered to serve 10 months in detention. According to a 21-page British appeals court document shared with Ars Technica by Eesti Ekspress, the Estonian newspaper that first reported on this saga, the story begins in January 2026. At the time, Barton-Kennedy was a corporal, with over seven years of service, serving in the 1st Battalion of the Duke of Lancaster Regiment of the British Army. His unit was deployed to participate in “Exercise Eastern Warrior” in Tapa, Estonia, roughly halfway between Tallinn, the capital city, and the Estonia-Russia border. While in the United Kingdom, on January 7, Barton-Kennedy, along with other members of his unit, were briefed on their orders and given specific instructions to “remove SIM cards and switch off location settings and to use a trusted virtual private network on all personal electronic devices.” Once the unit arrived in Estonia, days later, they were given further briefings and reminders of this policy. Despite this, Barton-Kennedy ignored the instruction.

entry.title: Rare opening-week title game rematch doubles as a familiar warning: UConn is yet again a national title threat - CBS Sports
entry.body: BOSTON — Having a national title game rematch in the opening week of the college basketball season is about as common as a comet. Thankfully, we got it Friday night when No. 4 Connecticut squared up against the reigning champs/16th-ranked Michigan at TD Garden, with the Huskies winning 85-77. The matchup marked the earliest tilt between the previous season's men's title game participants since Duke and UConn played just days into the season at Madison Square Garden in November 1999. Friday's contest was only the second time in the past 17 seasons that men's college basketball replayed the natty the ensuing season. It also featured the teams responsible for three of the past four NCAA trophies. The two big questions surrounding one of the biggest games of November: 1. How would Michigan look without Dusty May, who took the Dallas Mavericks job more than a third of the way through the offseason? Could Dan Hurley really have another national title contender again? The majority of this column will deal with a resounding answer to No. 2, so let's address No. 1 in short order first. The game was a whistle-plagued, foul-infested affair that tallied 59 free throws on 48 hacks and took nearly two and a half hours to play. It wasn't a cosmetic masterpiece, just like the last time these two played at Lucas Oil Stadium (when the teams combined to shoot 34.1%, the second-worst accuracy in a national title game since 1950). And though Michigan was clearly the inferior squad, it's not hard to see how it could play its way to top-four status in the Big Ten. U-M should have one of the nation's best sophomores (Trey McKenney, who scored all of his team-high 22 points in the second half) and figures more likely than not to author a respectable follow-up season to one of the greatest championship struts in the modern era. "This team isn't defending a national championship," Wolverines coach Mike Boynton said following the loss. "They're trying to establish their own legacy." The crowd split felt 80/20 in favor of UConn, which is hardly a shock given the drivability for Huskies fans from around New England. "Today was a road game for us," Michigan fifth-year wing Roddy Gayle said. Michigan's loss meant that, for the first time since 2000-01, the Wolverines failed to begin a season 2-0. What's more, UConn was Michigan's first ranked opponent this early into a season since 1993. Boynton's team has a lot of opportunities to validate itself this month, starting with Marquette next Wednesday, then Villanova on the road Nov. 21, followed by the 16-team Players Era field in Las Vegas the week of Thanksgiving. Much more to come on the fellas in Maize and Blue soon enough. Let's pivot to Hurley's Huskies, who again seem to have all the pieces to make another Final Four. Hurley has a way of dropping hints about the confidence level in his teams. When the two-time national champion says the following after a 41.8% shooting night that included inducing 13 fouls to three of Michigan's starters, it's a promising sign of what's to come. "I think we're one of the best teams in the country, kind of a game that you should win by 15 and you win by eight," He said. "We're great at that." Sardonic Hurley portends many good days ahead. The Huskies won by keeping Michigan at arm's length thanks to shooting nearly as well from 3 (40.9% on 9-of-22 shooting) as they did from the field (41.8%; 23-of-55). Sinking 30 out of 36 free throws wound up being significant — as was Michigan's 7-for-28 showing from beyond the arc. The story on Friday night in Boston was the guard play, though. UConn's backcourt of Silas Demary Jr. and Braylon Mullins look ready to quickly stake a verifiable claim as the best 1-2 backcourt duo in the sport. After both struggled mightily in the national championship game — Demary due to a severely sprained ankle — they combined for 44 points, 11 rebounds and three steals here. The shooting wasn't efficient, but the tandem outplayed Elliott Cadeau and McKenney, the former of which was a shell of the player we saw win Final Four MOP in Indy. (Nineteen points back in April, but just eight points, plus five turnovers and a foul-out in the follow-up.) "It was gonna be a game where the guys that can go make plays off the dribble were gonna have to do that vs. that particular defense, and he's the best guy that we got doing that," Hurley said of Demary. UConn's rugged senior point guard didn't watch clips of the title game — and Hurley didn't let him watch. Had Demary not been what he said was at 50% effectiveness seven months ago, maybe things would go differently. Demary told CBS Sports he couldn't plant his foot with any kind of conviction due to the nature of the sprain. The taping around his ankle and all the painkillers administered didn't have a positive impact on his effectiveness. He scored just two points and fouled out. No point in living in the past and no point in even watching that kind of failure. So he's got no interest in ever watching it. "It's hard to see you get that close to your end goal and come up that short," Demary told CBS Sports. "You don't want to relive those same moments that you went through in the moment. I had this game circled since we lost." The preseason pick for Big East Player of the Year, Demary said he needs to be the vocal leader that Alex Karaban and Tarris Reed Jr. "I've had enough experience to be around the right guys and be around the right people to know how to lead a team," he told CBS Sports. "I have one of the, if not the best, leaders in the country that knows how to do it. He's helped me along the way. Coach Kimani (Young) has helped me along the way, and I think I've taken on that responsibility of being a guy that everybody goes to, no matter what the game presents. I feel like I got to lead this team in every huddle, talking them through each and everything, seeing what I'm seeing and trying to communicate as much as I can." Mullins is off to a nice start as well. After sinking the winning 3 to get UConn over top-seeded Duke in the East Regional final, the power of that shot vaulted his profile to a national level, making him one of the most recognizable players in the game. He's had back-to-back games of 20-plus points. His 23 on Friday led all others. But Demary is the dude. He's at 12 assists and zero turnovers through two games, and Mullins told CBS Sports everything on this deep UConn team flows from Demary at the top. "He's gonna do big things this year, and we need him for every single game," Mullins said. "I'm gonna try to be up to his standard as much as I can, but I mean he does a lot for us." Then there's Colben Landrew, the next NBA-level talent to pick Hurley's program as his launching pad to the pros. "You can see just the talent and the different things he could do, driving the ball, making a 3, getting on the offensive glass," Hurley said of Landrew. "The guy's just, he's a stud. I mean, 22 minutes, eight rebounds, six defensive and his level of physicality from freshmen is, it's a different level." We're almost a week into the season. Duke has looked ridiculous and might win 20 games this season by 20-plus points. 1 Florida absolutely looks the part, as does No. 3 Illinois, which is averaging 116 points through two games and down two of its six best players. Connecticut is in the top tier with those teams as well. An obvious win against a ranked team was necessary, just to be sure. Hurley called the win "a confidence builder" for a non-con slate that ranks among the best you'll find. (Ohio State, Arizona and Duke await later this month.) "There was an enormous amount of pressure on us to win this game today, not because of what happened in April," he said. "There's no get-backs on that. It was just, with what we got coming up with our schedule, like, we really needed to win this game today." Winning these types of games has become the expectation. Connecticut's now at 10 straight regular-season, neutral-site victories over ranked opponents. Hurley has the reputation of this program hovering over the sport, with potentially the best backcourt in college basketball — and reinforcements on the way. Before the game, veteran shooting guard Solo Ball was active in warmups. His broken wrist was initially supposed to keep him out this season. Instead, a return in the next month or so appears likely. So here we are again with UConn owning prominent real estate atop the sport and ready to map out another route to another Final Four.
entry.summary: Rare opening-week title game rematch doubles as a familiar warning: UConn is yet again a national title threat CBS Sports UConn's Demary, Mullins exact revenge against Michigan in title game rematch ESPN Silas Demary Jr. can do it all. His UConn team looked capable of winning it all against Michigan The New York Times Outside shooting freezes out Michigan basketball in UConn rematch Detroit Free Press No. 4 UConn beats No. 16 Michigan in rematch of NCAA title game at TD Garden The Boston Globe

entry.title: New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade at Murrayfield - BBC
entry.body: New Zealand cruise to victory as Scotland fade - Published Nations Championship Scotland (21) 21 Tries: Ashman 3 Cons: Russell 3 New Zealand (24) 43 Tries: Sititi, De Groot, Taylor, Barrett 2, Moorby, Aumua Cons: McKenzie 4 Ruthless New Zealand blew Scotland away in a high-class, seven tries to three Nations Championship victory at Murrayfield. Despite a historic first-half hat-trick from Scotland hooker Ewan Ashman, the All Blacks were mostly magnificent, unrelenting and classy. It was the 34th Test between the nations and New Zealand's tally has yet another win - 32 now, with two draws going back to 1905. Wallace Sititi scored early in a breathless first half. Ethan de Groot and Codie Taylor hit back to make it 17-7 at the end of the first quarter. New Zealand's Peter Lakai was binned and Ashman got his second while he was off. The sensational Beauden Barrett scored the first of his double straight after. Then, as the bonkerdom stretched on, Sititi was yellow-carded and Ashman made the All Blacks pay with his hat-trick try. Only three points divided them at the break, but the All Blacks outclassed Scotland thereafter. Josh Moorby, Beauden Barrett again and Asafo Aumua struck in the second half. Scotland were beaten out the gate in the end. We hoped for a classic and a classic it was, with bells on. If only for 40 minutes. Beyond that thrilling opening spell it was one-way traffic, a vicious exhibition of All Black class and might. Just like last year, when New Zealand drew first blood, the visitors came roaring out, punishing a penalty given away cheaply with a piece of trickery at a close-range line-out that bamboozled the Scots. A couple of dummy runners broke away and took enough of Scotland's attention with them. Sititi thundered through a gap to score. Kyle Rowe's magnificent 50-22 gave Scotland the field position to strike off a driven line-out - Ashman driving over for the first of his three tries. Unlike his counterpart, Damian McKenzie, Finn Russell converted. New Zealand turned the screw again, forcing Scotland into big defensive set after big defensive set. There's only so much of that you can soak up, though. The visitors looked lethal from all corners. Beauden Barrett's surge downfield, hotly pursued by Matt Fagerson, was the catalyst for their second score. Fagerson was done on the floor, New Zealand went to touch and De Groot went over the line. McKenzie converted; New Zealand by five. And, soon, New Zealand by 10. Another Scotland penalty was punished to the max, the All Blacks executing from the resultant line-out maul. Taylor getting it down this time. This all happened inside the first quarter. Lakai, the terrific openside, was binned for persistent New Zealand offsides. Huw Jones almost scored but got held up. Off a penalty advantage, Ashman blasted through Sititi to score. With Russell's conversion it was a three-point game. Scotland needed to kick on, but instead they got pushed back. The wondrous Beauden Barrett sliced through following huge work from his pack; on the face it simple, but in reality, complex and beautiful. McKenzie restored the 10-point lead, but it didn't last long. Sititi was binned for going off his feet. Scotland had a crack at 13 All Blacks for a brief minute but couldn't break them despite going painfully close through Jones. Lakai returned to make it 15 versus 14 - and that's when Scotland struck. It was that old reliable again, the line-out maul proving devastating. Ashman got on the end of it and over he went for his hat-trick. For a flurry of penalties and back-to-back yellows, New Zealand got what they deserved. Those cards cost them 14 points. Seven first-half tries and three points between them at the break. Now it was time for Test match animals to emerge. When they did, they were wearing New Zealand white rather than Scotland blue. The All Blacks played those key minutes in Scotland's 22, forcing errors and penalties and opportunities. Off a scrum, Jordie Barrett's skip pass found Moorby in space and he sauntered over. More New Zealand heat and more Scotland penalties. Then, a yellow for Sione Tuipulotu. It could have been Ben White just as easily. The pressure the visitors were applying was just suffocating. With the captain off the pitch, New Zealand made it pay - Quinn Tupaea to McKenzie and on to Beauden Barrett for his second of the day. McKenzie's conversion made it 36-21. At 50 minutes, the game was over far too early for Gregor Townsend's side. To rub salt in the wound Aumua finished a gorgeous set-piece to land try number seven; 43-21 and 19-0 in the second half. Scotland had hopes of winning or, at the very least, of taking New Zealand to the wire. The uneasy truth for Townsend and his players is that despite their excellence in the opening half, they were utterly bossed in the second. These All Blacks are far more formidable than the version that appeared at Murrayfield a year ago. Meanwhile, Scotland's long, long wait for glory against the Kiwis carries on and on. Line-ups Scotland: Kyle Rowe; Kyle Steyn, Huw Jones, Sione Tuipulotu (capt), Jamie Dobie; Finn Russell, Ben White; Rory Sutherland, Ewan Ashman, Zander Fagerson, Gregor Brown, Scott Cummings, Matt Fagerson, Rory Darge, Jack Dempsey. Replacements: Gregor Hiddleston, Pierre Schoeman, Will Hurd, Max Williamson, Josh Baylish, George Horne, Tom Jordan, Blair Kinghorn. New Zealand: Beauden Barrett; Will Jordan, Quinn Tupaea, Jordie Barrett, Josh Moorby; Damian McKenzie, Cam Roigard; Ethan de Groot, Codie Taylor (capt), Fletcher Newell, Scott Barrett, Fabian Holland, Tupou Vaa'i, Peter Lakai, Wallace Sititi. Replacements: Asafo Aumua, George Bower, Pasilio Tosi, Christian Lio-Willie, Anton Segner, Cortez Ratima, Timoci Tavatavanawai, Rieko Ioane. Related topics - Published5 hours ago

entry.title: Kiwis reap rewards of gamble on 'freak of nature' Ponga
entry.body: Kiwis reap rewards of gamble on 'freak of nature' Ponga - Published "He's a tough character and he was so adamant he was playing." Kalyn Ponga, in the words of his head coach Stacey Jones, was never going to miss New Zealand's Rugby League World Cup semi-final. But it was a remarkable return to action for a player whose tournament turned from dream to nightmare just over three weeks ago. In the World Cup opener against Australia in Sydney on 15 October, Ponga seemed to be enjoying a perfect New Zealand debut. Then it all went wrong. The 28-year-old scored two second-half tries but was forced off late in the game - having played for 20 minutes with a broken left forearm sustained in a tackle with Cameron Munster. The Kiwis went on to lose 24-22; Ponga required surgery. Just 23 days later, their talismanic full-back â initially named as a reserve, and then on the interchange bench â made a shock return to the starting 13 and delivered a starring performance as New Zealand overpowered Tonga 34-10 to reach their first Men's Rugby League World Cup final for 13 years. "Where sports science is these days â I saw what he had in his arm, the rod or plate was covering his whole arm," Jones said. "We didn't know until after our second-to-last training that he was going to be all right â he ticked all the boxes. Just a tough person." - Ponga-inspired New Zealand reach World Cup final - Published5 hours ago - New Zealand sweep aside Samoa to reach Women's World Cup final - Published8 hours ago Playing with black protective bandaging taped to his left forearm, Ponga was directly involved in four of New Zealand's six tries. His fancy footwork and slick handling setting up scores for Briton Nikora, Casey McLean and Xavier Willison. He largely dominated the contest with opposite number Lehi Hopoate, notably clearing out the full-back as he fumbled a grubber kick in Tonga's in-goal area for New Zealand's second try, scored by Dane Gagai. In defence, a bruising try-saving block on Demitric Vaimauga indicated no cause for concern about his wounded wing. "Obviously a freak of a player," said Kiwis captain James Fisher-Harris. "The defensive mindset he had tonight, he saved a couple of tries. That's what I love about KP. "He's a freak of nature. His leadership skills are underrated. He's really good for us, our spine especially." But while it was undoubtedly the Ponga show at the home of his NRL side Newcastle Knights, New Zealand are not just a one-man band. Gagai sparked the counter-attack for McLean's try by forcing a knock-on around halfway. Jahrome Hughes added directness with his carries and when putting boot to ball. Dead-eye kicker Jamayne Isaako mastered fierce winds to kick five out of six conversions, curling two over from the left touchline, to take his tally for the tournament to 36 from 38 attempts. Asked if this was New Zealand's best shot at adding a second title to their 2008 triumph, Fisher-Harris paused before replying: "Yes." "We're just trying to chase history," he added. "We've only done it once but we've been building with this squad, this generation, for the past six or seven years." 'Missed opportunity' but Tonga not blaming weather For 48 minutes, New Zealand and Tonga played with the intensity and fever of two sides seemingly locked on course for the drama of a golden-point extra-time finish. Then the Kiwis' relentless pressure told, with two tries in five minutes extending their lead to 14 points and turning a contest into a procession. The weather in Newcastle impacted the match from kick-off but deteriorated dramatically in the second half, with Tonga toiling in the face of howling wind and rain â conditions best encapsulated by a restart blowing back into their own half. But head coach Kristian Woolf did not use this an excuse for his side's defeat by New Zealand, stating his team "didn't handle the conditions as well as they did". Unbeaten through the group stage, Tonga lacked direction in attack, were guilty of poor decision-making at the end of sets, and looked vulnerable defending a bouncing ball. "It was a disappointing way to finish. Whoever was against the wind in the second half was going to find it tough and we just had to handle it better," said Woolf. "It's a bit of a missed opportunity with what the group's been able to do, how talented the group is, some of the footy we've played, but we just couldn't get it done tonight." Putting the result into perspective, with Tonga playing in the semi-finals for just the second time, Woolf added: "Once upon a time, we were just happy to be in the finals and be competitive. Now, we see ourselves as real players and believe we can win it. "We thought we could do that tonight. We certainly think we've got a team that is capable of doing that. Tongan rugby league can be really confident going forward." New Zealand women 'hungry' for success The last time New Zealand had teams in both the men's and women's finals on Australian soil, they walked away with two trophies. For the men, it was a maiden title; for the women, a third consecutive crown. Neither side has lifted the trophy since then, losing a combined four finals. In Brisbane next Sunday, a nation will be hoping history repeats itself. New Zealand women maintained their 100% record of reaching the trophy match with a controlled 32-0 win over Samoa, spearheaded by a hat-trick for dual-code international Stacey Waaka. But although yet to lose in the tournament, and having conceded just 24 points across four matches, New Zealand know they will face a stiff challenge from either three-time defending champions Australia or Fiji in the final. "The tournament has been around building. How we started [an 18-12 win over Fiji] wasn't how we wanted to start â we got tested early, faced some adversity and challenges which will help us next week," said captain Georgia Hale. "It's a challenge we are hungry for. The focus will be really internal, it's around our pack, our threat, what we can control, what we believe in. It will be a huge task but one we've been working towards for four years."
entry.summary: Kalyn Ponga's return to Rugby League World Cup action, just 23 days after breaking his arm, was a risk. But New Zealand head coach Stacey Jones felt it was a risk worth taking - and was proved right.

entry.title: Rahm edges ahead of Hatton & McIlroy in Abu Dhabi
entry.body: Rahm edges ahead of Hatton & McIlroy in Abu Dhabi - Published Abu Dhabi Championship third-round leaderboard -18 J Rahm (Spa); -17 T Hatton (Eng), F Laporta (Ita); -16 R McIlroy (NI); -15 A Scott (Aus); -14 M Jordan (Eng), D Puig (Spa) Selected others: -12 S Bairstow (Eng), N Kimsey (Eng); -11 T Fleetwood (Eng), E Ferguson (Sco), A Sullivan (Eng); -9 A Rai (Eng); -8 E Chacarra (Spa), M Wallace (Eng); -1 P Reed (US) Jon Rahm has a one-shot lead going into the final round of the Abu Dhabi Championship but Ryder Cup team-mates Tyrrell Hatton and Rory McIlroy are in close contention. The 31-year-old Spaniard shared the overnight lead with Italy's Francesco Laporta and fellow former LIV player Hatton, but moved clear of them both with a six-under-par 66 at Yas Links on Saturday. Hatton and Laporta both carded a 67, as did McIlroy, who goes into the final round in fourth place on 16 under. Rahm, who said recently that he does not know what 2027 holds after quitting the LIV tour, is aiming for a first solo tournament triumph since winning the Masters in 2023. Reigning Masters champion McIlroy remains in hot pursuit, however, after bouncing back in spectacular fashion since being given a two-shot penalty in the opening round for improving his lie before taking a chip shot. The six-time major winner hit 11 birdies in a second-round 63 and another eight in his third round, but a double bogey six at the par-four 10th - and another dropped shot at the 17th - left McIlroy two shots off the lead. And he acknowledges that it will take something special on the final day to reel in Rahm and co. "There are low ones [scores] out there and I am going to have to shoot a low one - something in the mid to low 60s - to get it done tomorrow and that will be the goal," said McIlroy. Hatton, meanwhile, is looking forward to going head-to-head again with Rahm after playing alongside the two-time major champion, and Laporta, in Saturday's final group. All three will play together once again on Sunday. "Obviously final group tomorrow there's a lot to play for," said Hatton, who briefly moved level with Rahm at the top of the leaderboard in the third round after holing his seventh birdie of the day on the 14th. "Naturally we are going to want to beat each other. Hopefully I can get off to a good start and put him under some pressure." Rahm, who is chasing his first win in the Abu Dhabi Championship, responded well after being put under pressure by Hatton on Saturday. He reclaimed the outright lead on the 15th with a superb, curling 20-foot birdie putt and came close to extending his advantage at the last, just coming up short with another birdie chance as he finished without a single dropped shot. Laporta also produced a bogey-free round to keep pace with the field's big hitters as the 36-year-old, who shot 10 under par to claim a first-round lead, bids for a first title on the DP World Tour. Elsewhere, Australian Adam Scott remained bogey-free for the tournament after three rounds and moved up to fifth place on 15 under with a 66. And Englishman Matthew Jordan is a shot further back, alongside Spain's David Puig, after a third-round 69. Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago
entry.summary: Jon Rahm leads Tyrrell Hatton and Francesca Laporta by one shot, and Rory McIlroy by two, after the third round of the Abu Dhabi Championship.
