entry.title: Tongue ruled out of Australia tour as Rashid stars in warm-up
entry.body: Tongue ruled out of Australia tour as Rashid stars in warm-up - Published England fast bowler Josh Tongue has been ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of Australia with a toe injury. The 28-year-old suffered the injury in Pakistan last month and didn't take part in the final two games of that tri-series. He will now return to the UK for further assessment and miss the one-day and T20 matches in Australia, which start with an ODI in Perth on 13 November. Tongue, who has taken 46 wickets in 17 matches this year, is likely to be back for the three-match Test series in South Africa in December, with the squad set to be named next week. The white-ball tour of Australia will mark the first time England have played down under since the 2025-26 Ashes demolition. Coach Brendon McCullum had previously said he wanted a strong team for the ODI leg of the trip to Australia in the build-up to the World Cup in southern Africa next year. The New Zealander also conceded he would have to rotate his squad for the T20 leg, given England's schedule in a busy winter of five separate overseas tours. Rashid stars in warm-up win Adil Rashid took four wickets as England beat Western Australia by 92 runs in their one-day warm-up match in Perth. The 38-year-old was left out of the final three matches of the October tour of Pakistan and Sri Lanka but highlighted his importance down under, taking 4-35. Fast bowler Jofra Archer chipped in with 3-34 as England ultimately cruised to victory. It wasn't all straightforward though as a sloppy batting display saw England bowled out for 251. Ben Duckett top scored with 49 while Liam Dawson was unbeaten for 44. The hosts had England in trouble as they reached 60-1 before Rashid took a flurry of wickets, including Jayden Goodwin and Ashton Turner in successive deliveries. Archer finished off the Western Australia tail, bowling them out for 159 and securing the win. Related topics - Published17 hours ago - Published28 August
entry.summary: England fast bowler Josh Tongue is ruled out of the upcoming white-ball tour of Australia with a toe injury.

entry.title: F1 Brazil GP long runs: Kimi Antonelli dominates as Ferrari endures a nightmare Friday - Motorsport.com
entry.body: F1 Brazil GP long runs: Kimi Antonelli dominates as Ferrari endures a nightmare Friday The newly crowned world champion set the pace in both qualifying and race simulations at Interlagos, with Mercedes emerging as the team to beat while Ferrari struggled with balance and tyre degradation Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Steven Tee / LAT Images via Getty Images Kimi Antonelli has been the benchmark throughout the Formula 1 weekend in Sao Paulo so far. The newly crowned world champion was not only the fastest driver over a single lap in Free Practice 2, but also made a strong statement in the long-run simulations. Mercedes therefore appears to be in the strongest position heading into the remainder of the weekend. Ferrari, by contrast, endured an extremely difficult Friday. In the qualifying simulations, Antonelli was 0.253 seconds faster than Lando Norris in the McLaren and 0.259 seconds clear of Max Verstappen in the Red Bull. However, it was the race simulations towards the end of the session that offered a more meaningful indication of Sunday's prospects. Different stint lengths and tyre compounds need to be taken into account when analysing the data. Tyre degradation is particularly high in Brazil, meaning that even a difference of just a few laps can have a noticeable impact on average lap times. Once the figures had been adjusted accordingly, Antonelli also emerged as the fastest driver over a long run. The Mercedes driver completed a particularly impressive 20-lap stint on the soft tyre. His team-mate George Russell was the second-fastest driver, although his adjusted average was already 0.311 seconds per lap slower. Max Verstappen followed in third, 0.474 seconds per lap behind Antonelli. Antonelli sees room for improvement, but Mercedes remain optimistic Antonelli himself was satisfied with the session but acknowledged that there was still room for improvement in the race simulations. "It wasn't bad," he said. "I felt good with the car over a single lap. There is still a little bit of work to do on the long run. Overall, though, I feel good and I'm looking forward to tomorrow." Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images Mercedes deputy team principal Bradley Lord echoed the positive assessment. The team had made a strong start to the weekend with its car, although both drivers were still struggling with understeer – an issue that had largely disappeared following the upgrade package introduced in Malaysia. Nevertheless, Lord believes Mercedes' long-run pace is on a par with Norris and Verstappen. He currently places Ferrari half a step behind, although he expects the Scuderia to make progress when temperatures rise on Saturday. Mercedes particularly strong in the second and third sectors A closer look at the sector times reveals where Mercedes is gaining its advantage. In the first sector, the Silver Arrows were comparatively slow. Ferrari, in particular, initially set a strong pace through this section. The picture changed considerably in the second and third sectors, however. The second sector is the more technical, twisty part of the circuit, while the third is largely about top speed along the straights. Mercedes was exceptionally strong in both sections. This suggests a well-balanced car that performs convincingly not only on the straights but also through the corners. George Russell, Mercedes, Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Alastair Staley / LAT Images via Getty Images Verstappen, by contrast, consistently lost time to Mercedes across all three sectors. There is therefore no single area that can be identified as the Red Bull's main weakness. McLaren showed a similar pattern, with Norris also unable to attribute his deficit to one particular section of the circuit. The McLaren driver acknowledged that Mercedes had looked stronger in the second session. "FP1 was certainly a surprise – a pleasant one. In FP2, we struggled a little more compared to Mercedes. Basically, we were two tenths of a second off on every lap," Norris said. At the same time, he was encouraged by the team's latest upgrades. Although he had initially run only some of the new components on his car during the practice sessions, they had already delivered the desired effect. McLaren plans to bring the complete package together on Saturday. Ferrari in trouble: More than a second off the pace The biggest surprise of Friday, however, was Ferrari's disappointing performance. Even in the qualifying simulations, Lewis Hamilton was 0.45 seconds off the pace. On the relatively short Sao Paulo circuit, that represents a considerable deficit. The race pace looked even more concerning. Charles Leclerc's adjusted long-run average was 1.072 seconds per lap slower than Antonelli's. Hamilton was almost identical, losing 1.090 seconds per lap. In this respect, Ferrari is no longer anywhere near the leading group and instead finds itself firmly in the fight with the upper midfield. Dino Beganovic, Ferrari Photo by: Guido De Bortoli / LAT Images via Getty Images The sector breakdown is particularly revealing. Ferrari can still keep pace in the first sector and even looks competitive there. However, the Scuderia loses significant ground in the second sector, which is dominated by corners. There is another problem on the straights: in the third sector, Ferrari is sometimes only matching Aston Martin's pace. Team principal Frederic Vasseur confirmed after the session that the team was struggling with both car balance and energy deployment. "We had a few issues with energy deployment during the laps. We still need to fine-tune everything. On his fastest lap, he lost a few tenths on the straight. I would say it's not a disaster," he explained. From Vasseur's perspective, the more important issue is that Ferrari has yet to find the underlying feel it wants from the car. "We know that we still have a lot of work to do on the balance. The balance wasn't good, it wasn't great. I think the asphalt is the complete opposite of what we had a week ago. That creates a lot of work and makes things very different compared to last week." Racing Bulls, Audi, and Alpine set for a close midfield battle Further down the order, an intriguing three-way fight is emerging between Racing Bulls, Audi and Alpine. The three teams are closely matched in the long-run analysis, meaning that even relatively small differences could decide several positions on Saturday and Sunday. Arvid Lindblad, Racing Bulls Photo by: Colin McMaster / LAT Images via Getty Images Gabriel Bortoleto was classified as the fastest driver outside the leading group in FP2. Competing in front of his home crowd, the Brazilian also impressed over the longer runs in his Audi, recording an adjusted average deficit of 0.933 seconds per lap to Antonelli. Liam Lawson was marginally quicker in the Racing Bulls, finishing 0.925 seconds behind. Pierre Gasly also kept Alpine firmly in contention with a deficit of 1.041 seconds. The battle between these three teams is therefore likely to be particularly close over the remainder of the weekend. Haas, Williams, Cadillac and Aston Martin further adrift A more substantial gap opens up behind that midfield battle. Oliver Bearman was the next driver in the order, losing 1.618 seconds per lap in the Haas. Alexander Albon followed in the Williams, 1.770 seconds off the pace. Cadillac is not completely out of contention at the back of the field. Sergio Perez recorded a deficit of 1.919 seconds per lap, putting him ahead of Carlos Sainz in the second Williams and both Aston Martin drivers. Rookie Rafael Camara was also unable to get ahead of the Cadillac. Aston Martin, meanwhile, endured a difficult Friday. The expected disadvantage in top speed through the third sector was not compensated for in the other sections of the circuit. Overall, the team was 2.321 seconds per lap slower than Antonelli over the long runs. High tyre degradation points towards another two-stop race Tyres will be one of the decisive factors on Sunday. Pirelli has opted for compounds one step softer than those used last year. In 2025, the C2 to C4 compounds were selected for the Brazilian Grand Prix. This year, the range moves up to C3 through C5. As a result, last year's soft tyre is equivalent to this year's medium. Andrea Kimi Antonelli, Mercedes Photo by: Sam Bloxham / LAT Images via Getty Images Tyre degradation was already particularly noticeable during the long-run simulations, averaging around 0.15 seconds per lap. This is especially significant at Interlagos, where the high demands placed on the tyres have historically made the Brazilian Grand Prix a two-stop race. Antonelli's 20-lap stint on the soft tyre is therefore particularly impressive given the high levels of degradation. Nevertheless, no compound should be ruled out for the race at this stage. Instead, all three tyre options could play a role on Sunday. From Formula 1 to MotoGP we report straight from the paddock because we love our sport, just like you. In order to keep delivering our expert journalism, our website uses advertising. Still, we want to give you the opportunity to enjoy an ad-free and tracker-free website and to continue using your adblocker.

entry.title: Richard Lloyd, Television’s Virtuoso Guitarist, Dead at 75
entry.body: Richard Lloyd, Television’s Virtuoso Guitarist, Dead at 75 Richard Lloyd, the Television co-founder and guitarist who helped bring a deft virtuosity to punk’s stripped-down fury, has died at the age of 75. Lloyd’s family said in a statement that the guitarist died Saturday morning at his home in Chattanooga, Tennessee. “His loving wife Sheila and his dog Willie Mays were with him at the end,” his family said in a statement to Rolling Stone, adding that Lloyd died from Cholangiocarcinoma, a bile duct cancer. Lloyd was diagnosed with bile duct cancer in March 2026. According to a GoFundMe set up to help Lloyd cover medical expenses and other costs, the guitarist developed tumors in his liver, including one that was so close to a major blood vessels, his doctors were unable to operate and remove it. Television were one of the most innovative bands of punk’s first wave, thanks largely to the twin guitar attack of Lloyd and frontman Tom Verlaine. While many of their peers perfected a loud, fast pummel of power chords, Lloyd and Verlaine (who died in 2023) developed an intricate interplay of riffs and licks, and never shied from spiraling into headier realms inspired by jazz, art-rock, and even jam bands. Lloyd and Verlaine’s stellar guitar work anchored Television’s seminal debut, Marquee Moon, which was released in 1977. That album cemented Television’s place in the punk pantheon, even though their output otherwise consisted of just two more albums, 1978’s Adventure and 1992’s Television. 25, 1951 in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania and raised largely in New York City. His first instrument was the drums, but he was fascinated by the guitar and decided to switch after a “hallucinatory experience.” “My drums lost all their color — like in the Wizard of Oz in Kansas — and everything became grayscale,” Lloyd wrote in his 2017 memoir, Everything Is Combustible. “The drums didn’t sound good anymore, and I heard a voice — an auditory hallucination that told me, ‘You need to play a melody instrument.’” One of Lloyd’s first guitar partners was Velvert Turner, a musician from Brooklyn, who himself was developing his guitar skills under the tutelage of Jimi Hendrix. After dropping out of high school, Lloyd moved to Boston, where he played with blues legend John Lee Hooker. He also spent some time traveling and living in Los Angeles, but eventually moved back to New York City and embedded himself in the proto-punk scene there. Television formed not long after Lloyd returned to NYC in 1973. His friend, the manager Terry Ork, took him to see Verlaine play at a club, and Lloyd knew instantly they would make a great musical pair. As he put it to The Stranger in 2015, “I saw Tom play and I thought, ‘He’s got it.’ And I knew I had it. But I was missing something and so was he. What he was missing, I could supply. And vice versa.” Explaining what he had that Verlaine didn’t, Lloyd continued, “The fleshing out of all the songs. All the filigrees and arabesques on Marquee Moon are all mine. Even though the solos are maybe different, during the verses, when Tom’s singing, I’m playing all the melody. I brought a rock & roll heart.” Joining Lloyd and Verlaine in the first iteration of Television was Richard Hell on bass and Billy Fica on drums. Hell eventually left and was replaced by Fred Smith, who’d been playing with Blondie. The band soon became a fixture at legendary punk clubs like CBGB and Max’s Kansas City. They released a debut single, “Little Johnny Jewel,” in 1975, before signing with Elektra Records, which released Marquee Moon two years later. One of Lloyd’s most impressive contributions to Marquee Moon was his idea to double track some of his most intricate guitar parts. As he wrote in Everything Is Combustible, he thought it was “sad and pathetic” to go into a recording studio and come out with a record that just sounded like a band playing live in a room. Wanting to give the record something extra, he insisted to Verlaine and co-producer Andy Johns that he could replicate the part he’d laid down for “Venus” note-for-note to give the song more depth. “When I came back into the room they were saying they couldn’t believe it, but it sounded perfect,” Lloyd wrote. “Tom wanted me to do it on everything, but I knew that it was a kind of ear candy that should come in and out of the various songs to make it a real record. So, I refused to do it in some instances, and in others I did double or more.” For example, on “Guiding Light,” he laid down eight different guitar tracks “which is why it sounds powerful and thick. I did my very best to make it a record — not a live document.” Despite having the backing of a major label like Elektra, Marquee Moon failed to make a commercial dent, and the band’s opening tour slot for Peter Gabriel scarcely created more fans. Not long after the release of Adventure in April 1978, the band broke up. The following year, Lloyd released a solo album, Alchemy, which earned some positive reviews, but also went nowhere commercially. During this time, Lloyd’s drug use was spiraling out of control. In his memoir, the guitarist admitted to overdosing on numerous occasions, and compared his experiences in the early Eighties to the Great Depression. “I could hardly draw people to gigs and I was thoroughly addicted to heroin,” he wrote. It wasn’t until 1984 that Lloyd got sober, and two years later he released a second solo album, Field of Fire. Lloyd would release seven more albums over the course of his career, including a live record, 1987’s Real Time; a collection of unreleased material, 2010’s Lodestones; and what would be his final solo album, 2018’s The Countdown. He also toured regularly, worked as a session musician — including gigs with Matthew Sweet and X’s John Doe — and gave guitar lessons. While Lloyd was part of Television’s reunion in 1992 and rejoined the band again for a stint in the early 2000s, he left ahead of a 2007 tour commemorating the 30th anniversary of Marquee Moon. In that interview with The Stranger, Lloyd expressed frustration that the band wasn’t focused on doing new things; he said that, after the release of their 1992 self-titled album, the band wrote and demoed eight songs, but nothing would likely come of them because Verlaine had “run out of lyrics.” Lloyd evinced a complicated relationship with Verlaine during his latter years. On the one hand, he would insist he loved Verlaine and wouldn’t have spent 35 years in a band with him if he didn’t, but also characterized him as difficult to work. Lloyd also remained upset that Verlaine took all of Television’s publishing, even though Lloyd said he contributed significantly to the band’s songwriting. Though unafraid to voice these opinions, Lloyd insisted he wasn’t bitter. As he told The Stranger, “I didn’t get into this for the money. I got into it to become a renowned guitarist who’s made an irrevocable impact on rock & roll history.”
entry.summary: Guitarist, who was diagnosed with bile duct cancer in March 2026, died Saturday from Cholangiocarcinoma, his family announced

entry.title: ‘Godzilla Minus Zero’ Director Takashi Yamazaki Dreamed of Seeing His Hometown Destroyed by King Ghidorah. He Finally Made It Happen.
entry.body: It’s been just over two years since “Godzilla Minus One” collected the Oscar in visual effects. Writer, director and VFX supervisor Takashi Yamazaki became the first helmer to receive a VFX trophy since Stanley Kubrick for 1968’s “2001: A Space Odyssey.” Reflecting on that historic night, Yamazaki, speaking through a translator, said, “It was just such a shock to us. I never thought that would happen in a million years because here we are on the other side of the planet making movies for our domestic market.” He continued, “That people in Hollywood even saw the movie, let alone give it a nomination and responded to that, shows how open-minded the Academy is to different types of films.” He said the win opened up “doors, options and possibilities for my career.” One of those doors opening is “Godzilla Minus Zero.” Now in theaters, the sequel picks up in 1949, two years after the tumultuous events of “Godzilla Minus One,” and continues the story of the Shikishima family as they face “an all-new calamity.” It is the 38th film in the Godzilla franchise and the 34th produced by Toho, the Japanese entertainment company that originally created the franchise. Yamazaki returns to both the director’s chair and as VFX supervisor. The sequel stars Kamiki Ryunosuke and Hamabe Minami and marks the first time a Japanese feature has been shot for Imax screens. Yamazaki discussed the film and why bringing one of his favorite kaiju, King Ghidorah, to the big screen in this installment fulfills a childhood dream. How did you balance telling this story with the biggest, loudest action sequences, but at the core, keep it deeply emotional? I wanted to make sure that what’s happening on the human layer and what was happening on the kaiju and Godzilla layer were not separate from each other. It was important that the actions taken by humans affect the actions that the kaiju take, and vice versa. How the kaiju responds then causes the humans to act in a certain way. So the two are intertwined. It was important for the engagement and the immersion that all aspects of the story are affecting each other. How did you come up with the title ‘Godzilla Minus Zero,’ and what does “zero” mean in the context of this film? Zero represents this idea of neutrality. Our characters have an ordinary life, which, given the period and what’s happening in the film, is hard to attain. After “Godzilla Minus One,” I felt that this family attained that only to be faced with a new tragedy that’s pulling all of these humans apart from each other. In certain disciplines of math, there is a difference between putting the negative sign in front of zero and what it represents is this idea of approaching zero. That’s exactly what the characters in this film are doing. They’re trying to claw their way back to what feels neutral — an ordinary life — after being thrown into this massive tragedy. There are so many great sequences in the film. One key moment is when Godzilla emerges for the first time and rises out of the water as the seaplane is taking off. I read that it took 2 billion water particle visual effects shots. Can you discuss what it took from page to screen to pull that off? The screenplay says something along the lines of “Godzilla emerges from the ocean and chases the seaplane.” But I also do the storyboarding for the film myself. When I was trying to compose the shot, I opted for a long-lens type of visual effect shot because Godzilla in this film is 50.1 meters tall (164 feet). If you line up the different Godzilla movies, Godzilla is on the smaller side. By compressing the depth of field with a long lens, we could create the illusion of Godzilla’s size. The seaplane is trying to take off, headed toward the camera. So there’s a lot of forward movement. We get to see the waves behind the seaplane, and the waves are Godzilla emerging from the ocean, trying to mount the plane. If it does, it’s over for everyone. The long lens certainly helped create and amplify that drama. The shot turned out even better than I had imagined thanks to the wonderful team that we have doing VFX. This particular scene was important to me because it’s the first time we see a full frontal view of Godzilla emerging from the ocean. It took a lot of time to render all those particles. It was important that we spent a lot of our resources, time, and rendering power on this shot because of how crucial it is for the audience to feel that threat. King Ghidorah is a big part of the Godzilla lore, and it was fantastic seeing your vision of this character. What was it like for you to bring this character to life in your film? When Ghidorah made its silver screen debut in “Ghidorah, the Three-Headed Monster,” it was the first kaiju to appear in Matsumoto City, the same city where I was born and raised. I was very excited to go to the movie theater and see Ghidorah smash up my hometown. But when I got to the theater and saw the film, Ghidorah flies over Matsumoto Castle, and that was it. With “Godzilla Minus One,” I was able to make the movie I wanted to see as a child. King Ghidorah appears in Matsumoto City, which is the same city where I set that scene, and it smashes it up. It’s really a dream come true for me. At the same time, I really love King Ghidorah as a kaiju because the design is amazing. There’s an emotional sequence with the young child Akiko crying that involves her parents. What was it like shooting that and getting the actress to cry for so long in the way that she did? We shot “Godzilla Minus One,” and Akiko (Sae Nagatani) was 2 years old. Every time she was about to cry and get cranky, that’s when we would run in with the cameras and the actors and begin shooting. She’s 5 years old now, and if we explain scenes, she has a very good understanding of what we are trying to do and gives us the type of reactions we’re looking for. Without too much explanation on my part, she was able to give us the performance. Given you did all the storyboards, what was the most satisfying scene or sequence for you to pull off? You see it in the trailer: there’s a mother and a baby in the house, and they’ve been levitated by Ghidorah’s gravity beam, and then they fall. This shot came out brilliantly. At first, I was struggling, trying to figure out how we would shoot this. We built the set, and this piece had a little bit of a tilt to it. We used drones to shoot around it, so we had our visuals, which we fleshed out with VFX. It’s a very scary and violent scene, and it tells us a lot about King Ghidorah’s power. It also serves as an indirect expression of how much terror and fear it can incite within people. Do you have another Godzilla movie in you? Let’s all stay excited for the third installment of this franchise … This interview has been edited for length and clarity.

entry.title: Dolly Parton's manager drops lawsuit against her nephew - BBC
entry.body: Dolly Parton's manager drops lawsuit against her nephew The manager of the late country music star Dolly Parton has dropped a lawsuit against her nephew. The civil case was filed by the company that manages Parton's business interests less than a month after her death. It included allegations of threats, intimidation and coercion against Bryan Seaver, the relative who publicly confirmed Parton had died in August. A temporary restraining order was also sought. Seaver, who previously served as Parton's head of security, denied the allegations. In a statement to the BBC's US partner, CBS News, Seaver's attorneys said he was "grateful to put this misunderstanding behind him so that the family can grieve peacefully". Seaver, the son of Parton's sister Cassie, owns the security firm Squadron Augmented Protection Services (SAPS). It provided security to Parton, who died of cancer aged 80, for the final 20 years of her life. Weeks after Seaver confirmed her death, both he and his company were dismissed by She's Alive, which manages Parton's estate. Danny Nozell, Parton's longtime manager and the head of She's Alive, filed for a temporary restraining order against Seaver and his company, which was granted by a judge. In court filings, he accused Seaver of "an obscene, deliberate and escalating campaign of threats", after demanding payment from the estate. The documents included messages in which he allegedly threatened to damage Parton's brand and business interests if his demands were not met. The filings also alleged that Seaver used his experience as a military contractor to intimidate employees. Seaver denied threatening the estate and in a statement published by TMZ at the time, he said he was a "career soldier and military contractor" but insisted he had simply been "talking frankly in a private way with Danny who I thought was my friend".

entry.title: Deep Purple’s Ian Gillan Undergoes ‘Successful’ Surgery After Medical Emergency
entry.body: Deep Purple’s Ian Gillan Undergoes ‘Successful’ Surgery After Medical Emergency Deep Purple singer Ian Gillan offered a health update Saturday, a week after a “medical emergency” forced the band to postpone their European tour. Gillan returned to social media Saturday to tell fans that he recently underwent surgery, which would be followed by a period of rest and recovery. “I had a procedure yesterday which was successful,” Gillan wrote. “I now have to rest, in order to make a complete recovery and ensure that I’m as fit as can be before getting back to work, thanks everybody for your patience and understanding. I really do appreciate it and apologize for all the inconvenience.” The group postponed a pair of Germany shows last weekend — and subsequently nixed the remainder of their tour — after announcing that Gillan was hospitalized with an unspecified health issue. A few days later, Gillan updated fans, saying he “had a medical problem whilst in Leipzig which required urgent attention at the hospital.” However, “I was hoping that I would get the all clear to hang on until the end of the tour, but there are very serious risks involved in me doing so.” Deep Purple’s postponed European tour was scheduled to run through November 25. As of now, the band’s Latin America tour — scheduled to begin December 5 in Sao Paulo, Brazil and conclude December 19 in Mexico City — is still on the schedule.
entry.summary: "I now have to rest, in order to make a complete recovery and ensure that I’m as fit as can be before getting back to work," singer writes

entry.title: Alanis Morissette comes out as pansexual - Page Six
entry.body: Alanis Morissette comes out as pansexual See more of our coverage in your search results. Alanis Morissette came out as pansexual during the Nov. 3 episode of the “Handsome” podcast, co-hosted by Tig Notaro, Fortune Feimster, and Mae Martin. Towards the end of the segment, Feimster told the singer, “I’m sorry for the men that hurt you, but I’m not sorry for the songs that came from it,” adding, “Did it make you want to be a lesbian at any point?” Morissette answered, “I’m pansexual, so, yeah.” To this, Notaro interjected, “Wait, you’re not really pansexual, are you?” “I am,” clarified Morissette. When the hosts joked that she should have started the podcast with this news, Morissette joked, “I like to leave it for the epilogue.” Pansexuality can be defined as a sexual, romantic, or emotional attraction to people regardless of their gender identity or sex. Want more celebrity and pop culture news? Start your day with Page Six Daily. Morissette recently made a remark about her “amazing” moment in 2000 kissing Sarah Jessica Parker during an episode of the “Call Her Daddy” podcast in September, saying that the idea for a same-sex smooch for her guest appearance on the show came direclty from her. “I reached out to them and I said, ‘Might it be a nice time for Carrie to experience a lesbian moment?’ And they said, ‘Why, yes. We were thinking the same thing.’” “I do recall kissing her — it was very pleasant,” she noted, calling the experience “easy” and “buoyant.” The Canadian singer-songwriter has been married to husband Mario “Souleye” Treadway since 2010. They are parents to Ever, 15, Onyx, 10, and Winter, 7. Morissette has been weathering more troublesome headlines of late, having taken legal action against her former tour manager in September, accusing her of blackmail by trying to frame her for drug trafficking. The Canadian singer’s lawsuit in Los Angeles court called ex-tour manager Keren Urinov a “disgruntled” ex-employee and described how she allegedly attempted to extort her boss after she had been caught with drugs in her luggage while on tour in Europe, which then threatened to pin it on Morissette. Morisette found fame in 1995 with her album “Jagged Little Pill” — which became one of the defining and biggest selling records of the decade. It was adapted into a Broadway music in 2019, for which she won two Tony Awards. This year, Morissette was inducted into the Songwriters Hall of Fame. Discussions are moderated for civility.
entry.summary: Alanis Morissette comes out as pansexual Page Six See more headlines & perspectives on Google News

entry.title: Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult Screen-Tested for James Bond Role: Reports
entry.body: Robert Pattinson, Nicholas Hoult Screen-Tested for James Bond Role: Reports Robert Pattinson and Nicolas Hoult are among the latest actors to screen test for the role of James Bond, according to multiple sources, joining a widening field of hopefuls vying to play 007. Both Variety and The Hollywood Reporter revealed Friday that Pattinson — already the star of The Batman series, and veteran of the Harry Potter and Twilight franchises — auditioned for the Bond role for director Denis Villeneuve in late-October; Pattinson and Villeneuve, who will shepherd the upcoming Bond films, recently worked together on Dune: Part Three. Hoult, who reportedly finished runner-up to Pattinson to play Bruce Wayne/Batman in that superhero reboot, also screen-tested to take over for Daniel Craig in the much-desired 007 role. Hoult, who has featured in the Superman and X-Men franchises, next appears in Amazon MGM Studios’ How to Rob a Bank, the same studio that will produce the new Bond films. Variety adds that Harry Styles “had discussions” about playing Bond, but it’s unclear whether he actually audition for the role. Amazon MGM Studios did not comment on the reports of the new screen tests, and have remained largely silent throughout the audition process, which began in May 2026. “The search for the next James Bond is underway,” the studio said at the time. Pattinson and Hoult join previously reported hopefuls Callum Turner, Jack Lowden, and Josh O’Connor, the three actors who were considered the favorites to play 007 before Pattinson and Hoult leapt into the race; the Bond buzz around Jacob Elordi, once considered the favorite to play 007, has quieted in recent weeks. Last year, the studio announced that Denis Villeneuve would direct the next Bond film, a follow-up to 2021’s No Time to Die, Craig’s final outing as the spy. The Dune filmmaker will serve as executive producer alongside Tanya Lapointe, while Amy Pascal and David Heyman will produce the upcoming project. The film is being written by Steven Knight, best known as the creator of Peaky Blinders. “I’m a die-hard Bond fan,” Villeneuve said when the announcement was made. “To me, he’s sacred territory. I intend to honor the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honor. Amy, David, and I are absolutely thrilled to bring him back to the screen. Thank you to Amazon MGM Studios for their trust.”
entry.summary: Harry Styles also "had discussions" about playing 007 as audition process expands beyond the three actors considered the favorites to take over for Daniel Craig

entry.title: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades
entry.body: Monty Don bids 'final goodbye' to Gardeners' World after two decades - Published TV horticulturalist Monty Don thanked viewers and his furry friend Ned the dog while presenting his final episode of Gardeners' World, after more than two decades on air. The head gardener on the long-running BBC TV series signed off from Longmeadow garden, where the show has been based for 16 years, on Friday. "From myself, Ned, and Longmeadow it's the final goodbye," he said on the programme, adding it had been "a privilege and pleasure" to share his garden experiences with so many people. During the episode, Don, 71, confirmed he would remain part of the presenting line-up for next year's Royal Horticultural Society (RHS) Chelsea Flower Show. He added he will feature in two winter specials, expected to air between now and Christmas. One celebratory episode will see him reflect on his years presenting the series and the changes he has seen at Longmeadow, external, which is also the garden of his private home, which he and his wife Sarah bought in 1991. 'Good luck with your own gardens' Don replaced Alan Titchmarsh on the show in 2003, at his predecessor's request. "I first began presenting Gardeners' World 23 years ago at Berryfields, and we came here to Longmeadow 16 years ago - in that time, things have changed," he recalled, on Friday's farewell. "The garden has grown, Nigel has been and gone, and Nellie and Patty [his previous dogs], but there has been one constant factor, and that has been the incredible privilege and pleasure of sharing my garden and my gardening life with you here, as well as working with so many superb people. Thank you for coming on that journey with me and good luck with your own gardens in the future. So, for the last time... goodbye." Details of the next series of Gardeners' World will be announced at a later date, the BBC noted in a statement ahead of Don's farewell. His successor has not yet been named. Bookmakers and viewers have pointed to regular co-presenters like Frances Tophill and Adam Frost as top contenders, though Tophill has played down expectations of stepping directly into his shoes. Prior to fronting Gardeners' World, Don hosted other shows including Tomorrow's World, Holiday and - a preview of coming attractions - a gardening segment on This Morning. He took a three-year break from the programme after suffering a minor stroke in 2008. In September this year, Don announced that the current series would be his last. In a statement, he said working on the show had been a "deeply rewarding experience", but added that "now is the right time for a change". The BBC said at the time that Don had "inspired and guided millions of viewers with his warmth, wisdom and passion for gardening" since joining the programme in 2003. Don was made an OBE by Queen Elizabeth, in 2018, for services to horticulture, broadcasting and charity. And he also received the RHS Victoria Medal of Honour - highest honour in horticulture. His final episode of Gardeners' World is available to stream now on BBC iPlayer. entry.title: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed
entry.body: Relief, tears and sadness: Married at First Sight UK cast react to show being axed - Published "I'm delighted and so relieved no-one else will have to go through the same again." That's what one woman - who alleged she was raped on Married at First Sight UK - texted to me, as the news broke that the show was being cancelled. Another woman, who also says her on-screen husband raped her, was in tears at the news. She told us she felt "great, consuming relief", but added she was "astounded" it had taken an external review for Channel 4 to finally pull the plug on the show. Commenting on the review, she said: "Suggesting the programme could reasonably continue with the implementation of a 'safe word', 'panic button' or 'lockable bathroom with an extra bolt inside' is absolute insanity to me." The Channel 4 show was plunged into crisis in May this year, after BBC Panorama revealed rape allegations from two female cast members on the show, while a third woman - Shona Manderson, the only woman who was identified - alleged a non-consensual sex act. The men involved have denied all the allegations against them. As the news emerged on Thursday morning that Married at First Sight UK - better known as MAFS UK - was being axed, my colleagues and I reached out to the three women who had contributed to our investigation. None of them had been informed in advance of the decision to cancel the show, they said, although two had contributed to the review. Shona Manderson told me by telephone her main feeling was relief that their voices had been heard. "Speaking out wasn't easy, but knowing that our voices have helped bring about change makes it all worthwhile," she said. Over the day, more MAFS UK cast members were in touch with us. Several were pleased by the decision to scrap the series, but others said it did not go far enough and called for more accountability. One cast member, who asked to remain anonymous, said people watching at home do not always appreciate this "isn't simply a television show" for those taking part. "These are real people, real emotions." Others we spoke to felt the show should have been taken off-air sooner. They include April Banbury, who took part in the 2022 series and whose on-screen husband was subsequently arrested on suspicion of controlling and coercive behaviour. The police investigation against him was later dropped, and her partner called the allegations against him "false". "I'm glad MAFS has been cancelled. It should have happened years ago," Banbury told us. "We want answers, we want those responsible to be held accountable, and we want to know how this was allowed to happen in the first place,â added another cast member, who asked to remain anonymous. He was echoed by Lia Perin, Partner at Taylor Hampton and lawyer for a number of MAFS UK participants. âCancelling the show may prevent future harm, but it does not resolve questions about the treatment of previous contestants,â she told the BBC. "Channel 4 owes them answers, not simply assurances that lessons have been learned." Others writing on social media said their experiences had been more positive, and that they were sad to see it go. Jay Howard, from the 2023 series, external, said the show had brought her friendships and opportunities, while Marilyse Corrigan, a 2021 bride, external, said it was a chapter of her life she looked back on "with fond memories". A number of cast members we spoke to also expressed concern for staff who had been working on the show, as well as sorrow for fans. Lara Eyre, who appeared on the 2022 series, told me she felt we were now "on the edge of a curb on how we treat reality TV stars and safeguarding", adding it was a "real shame" for those who filmed this year's series, which will never be aired, as well as a shame for fans of the show. "I know a lot of people loved it, I loved it," she said. âYes, I know it was traumatic, for sure, and there was a lot of bad things that went with the good. But it was a big part of a lot of people's lives, so it's sad it's not going to be on any more, but I also think this could've been avoided." Where does this go from here? As the dust settles, there are still many questions. Only "a summary of findings" from Channel 4âs review has been released, rather than the full report. We still do not know what the broadcaster did when it was first warned about the serious allegations by the production company. Why did it take them so long to investigate? And why did they only do so once BBC Panorama raised the alarm? We put some of these questions to Channel 4's boss Priya Dogra on Thursday. She said the broadcaster's handling of incidents as they arose was appropriate, and that the review had borne that out. In a statement to BBC News on Friday, Channel 4 said its review âdid not seek to adjudicate on the serious allegations of wrongdoing against a small number of past contributors highlighted by Panorama, as those allegations remain a matter for the relevant authoritiesâ. The Dark Side of Married at First Sight Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm. Watch on iPlayer now It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcomâs broadcasting code. Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front of the Digital, Culture, Media and Sport committee on 17 November, so we may hear more then. Either way, this is not the end of the story. There is an ongoing Ofcom investigation into the show - and in June, a male cast member was arrested on suspicion of rape. The decision to scrap MAFS UK will also inevitably raise questions about what happens with the wider Married at First Sight format. If one broadcaster says the show has ârun its course,â then those global versions may also come under the spotlight. Channel 4 has already said it will not be showing international editions like MAFS Australia again. And for the TV industry more broadly, questions will once again be asked about reality TV - and whether shows like this can ever keep their contributors safe. If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk Get in touch What is your reaction to the cancellation of MAFS UK? entry.summary: The show was cancelled after a BBC Panorama investigation heard allegations from three former cast members.

entry.title: Trump's "war-time consigliere" and the Miller Doctrine
entry.body: Stephen Miller is no Susie Wiles: He believes in almost limitless presidential power, considers the Democratic Party an extremist organization, and dreams of ruthless crackdowns on immigration and foreign adversaries. Why it matters: Miller, the new White House chief of staff, isn't just unlike anyone who's had the job under Trump — he's unlike any to occupy the powerful position in the modern era. He puts the hard in hard-liner and understands how to pull the levers of power to get his way and make the U.S. government a MAGA machine. Miller's appointment sets the stage for two years of partisan warfare with the new Democratic-led Congress, which is likely to launch investigations of Trump's administration, political committees and allies. "Stephen is Trump's wartime consigliere," Roger Stone, one of the president's oldest friends and advisers, told Axios. The big picture: Despite his post-midterm comments about finding ways to work with Democrats, Trump's choice of Miller signals that he's not looking for truces. He's prepping for war, and sees Miller as a brass-knuckle general and tactical expert impervious to criticism or traditional restraints. Trump's MAGA brain for a decade, the 41-year-old has detailed his Miller Doctrine in speeches, policies and press conferences: Presidential power is "very substantial and will not be questioned." Miller said those words about Trump's Muslim travel ban in 2017 on CBS's "Face the Nation," but to him they broadly apply to other areas of the executive's authority. Court authority is limited. In May 2025, when courts blocked aspects of Trump's deportation policies, Miller said the rulings were the work of "radical rogue judges" who were "at war" with the executive and legislative branches. The political opposition is a threat to America. "The Democrat Party is not a political party. It is a domestic extremist organization," Miller told Sean Hannity in August 2025. He also warned that if Democrats won Congress, "it's game over." They just won it. Homeland security is the nation's spine. A key architect of the administration's hard-line immigration policies, Miller said in a March speech: "Our national security, our homeland security, the safety and well-being of our people begins at home, begins in our neighborhood, begins in our home region." America should use "hard power" in the Western Hemisphere. "The cartels that operate in this hemisphere are the ISIS and the al-Qaeda of the Western Hemisphere, and should be treated just as brutally and just as ruthlessly as we treat those organizations," Miller said in the same speech, to foreign leaders at the Shield of the Americas conference. Behind the scenes: Miller's Shield of the Americas speech indicated the depth of his involvement in Trump's Latin America policy. He has a keen interest in Mexico and was a driving force in the military action leading up to and including the deposing of Venezuela's Nicolás Maduro. Miller has a close working relationship with Secretary of State and National Security Adviser Marco Rubio, and he has friendly relations with El Salvador leader Nayib Bukele, a crucial Trump ally in extending U.S. power. "Stephen makes Marco more aggressive on policy, in a good way. When Stephen isn't around, Marco defaults back to being more of the politician," said one White House official who worked with the two. "If people thought regime change in Cuba was going to fall by the wayside, Stephen Miller should make them think twice," the source said. "Today is a bad day for the Cuban regime." Go deeper: Trump advisers see Miller's elevation as a way to reenergize the president's populist base, which failed to turn out in sufficient numbers for the midterms — and in some cases voted for Democrats. Advisers point to Trump's handling of the Epstein files and his decision to attack Iran — which in turn escalated fuel prices — as reasons he lost support among those voters. Without winning them back, Republicans say, they'll have no chance in the 2028 elections. Critics also fault the harsh immigration enforcement championed by Miller, as well as voters' perceptions of corruption in Trump's administration, as additional drags on Republicans. Miller's allies dismiss questions about his management experience, noting that he has overseen the Department of Homeland Security and regularly runs morning meetings with the White House staff focused on immigration policy. They also point to the size of his White House policy team, one of the administration's largest. With Trump's legislative agenda effectively stalled, Miller's allies argue he is particularly well suited to a White House that will increasingly rely on executive orders and legal battles — areas in which Miller has extensive experience. Yes, but: Some critics worry that Miller's elevation could mean Trump turns Miller's hard-line immigration agenda into a centerpiece of his final two years in office — something that could continue to alienate independent and moderate voters, as it appeared to do in the midterms. Trump's administration and supporters expect the criticism and are unfazed. "It's Miller Time," said another Trump adviser. "Buckle up."
