entry.title: What we know so far after Krakow gun attack
entry.body: What we know so far after Krakow gun attack - Published At least six people were killed and several others injured when a gunman suspected to have ties to the far-right opened fire in central Krakow, the second largest city in Poland. Three bodies were found at his home when it was searched by police. Here's everything we know so far. How did the attack unfold? The attack began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in Krakow's Main Market Square, the bustling central point of the city. Police said a man drove into the square before beginning to fire "at random people from his car". Footage from the scene shows scenes of panic as people fled, with the sound of gunfire clearly heard. A passing tram was shot at during the apparently random attack, shattering windows but no passengers were injured. Armed officers raced to the scene and engaged in a gunfight with the attacker, who was shot within three minutes of the attack beginning, preventing a further massacre, officials said. The gunman was shot but is alive and has been arrested. Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify shows the moment a police officer confronts the suspect on the ground before firing his weapon several times. The officer then falls to the ground, apparently having been injured himself. Shop windows in the square have signs of damage, seemingly from bullets, with glass shards scattered along the floor. City officials have urged people who live in the city and tourists to stay away from the area while an investigation continues. The suspect's car, found at the intersection of Dietla and Stradomska streets, was checked for possible explosive devices, police said, but none were found. Residents of nearby buildings had been evacuated while the operation was under way. How many people have died and been injured? Six people - four women and two men - are confirmed to have been killed, including a British national. Three victims are Polish and two have not been identified. Sixteen people, including five foreigners and the attacker, were taken to hospital. Among those being treated are two police officers who were shot while detaining the attacker. The interior ministry later said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal. Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk later named the injured officers as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur MoraÅski. Tusk said three bodies - two women and one man - were found at the gunman's house when it was searched after the attack. One of the police officers was described as being in a "very critical condition" by a Polish government minister after being shot three times while arresting the attacker. The officer is undergoing surgery, he added. Polish authorities have not confirmed the names and ages of the other victims. What do we know about the suspect and motive? Police have identified the attacker as a 25-year-old Polish man but have not confirmed his name. The suspect was wearing "military-style attire" and had a military-grade weapon, according to a police spokesperson. However, authorities have confirmed the attacker was not a soldier. "Many pieces of weapons and ammunition were found in his vehicle", the spokesperson added. Polish media has reported the suspect had a firearms permit and may have obtained the weapons from his family home. A minister has said early investigations indicate he was inspired by "far-right ideologies". The minister also described him as an "ultra-nationalist" without giving further details. His home is being searched with support from counter-terrorism police. How did witnesses describe the attack? The shooting happened in one of the largest medieval squares in Europe, a busy location which is also a popular tourist destination. Jonathan Balshaw from Ipswich was there with his Polish girlfriend Dominika. The couple were outside St Mary's Basilica, in the corner of the square, when the shooting started. Jonathan said: "We ran down the side of the church and through the side door and hid with several other people until the gunfire died down. "A lot of shots were fired, more than 20 with it sounding like multiple different firearms - there were two distinctly different noises." Caitlin Shasby from Newcastle arrived in Krakow yesterday with her friend Jon for a long weekend. She said they heard shots from their hotel room but were not sure what was happening until their hotel rang them and told them to "stay in our rooms until further notice". What has the reaction been in Poland and internationally? After travelling to Krakow, Prime Minister Donald Tusk said : "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism...that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow." Krakow Mayor Åukasz GibaÅa has signed an order declaring a period of mourning in the city which will last until Wednesday, 11 November. US ambassador to Poland Tom Rose described it as a "savage and murderous attack". The EU's top diplomat, Kaja Kallas, said the shooting was "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland".
entry.summary: Six people were killed in a random shooting in the city's main square, and three bodies were later found at his home.

entry.title: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government - Al Jazeera
entry.body: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government Former army chief has 28 days to build a coalition that would end Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure as prime minister. Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, passing over the former army chief’s rival, Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog told Eisenkot of his decision on Saturday evening and will formally hand him the mandate at a ceremony on Sunday, the president’s spokesperson said. Herzog held consultations with political parties this week to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority in the October 27 general election. Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu, the current prime minister. Eisenkot will have 28 days – with a possible 14-day extension – to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, the minimum threshold for a government. In the October election, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats. Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats. He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote. Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank on Herzog’s decision, said the president “took the predictable route” in selecting Eisenkot, as he had the highest number of recommendations. “The hard work will begin now for Eisenkot to put together a government that can pass a vote of confidence at the Knesset that: one, will not break too many of the promises he made on the campaign trail; and two, that can survive the opposition of the right-wing bloc led by Netanyahu,” Odeh said. If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the allotted time, Herzog will nominate another candidate. If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, who will be granted a final 14 days. If, once again, no government is formed, a new election will be called within 90 days, with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister. United against Netanyahu government Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List – a coalition of Arab-led parties that holds 11 seats – told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Herzog’s decision was “expected”. “We were concerned that the president would move towards a national unity government,” he said, referring to a proposed power-sharing agreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu. Instead, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate, granting him a “considerable margin”. Tibi said he believes Eisenkot is headed for a minority government “with external support from the Arab parties”. While this would not be a “dream government” for Arab-led parties, Tibi prioritised bringing down “the government of Netanyahu, [Itamar] Ben-Gvir and [Bezalel] Smotrich”. Hours before Herzog’s decision, Netanyahu had warned that a government formed by the opposition bloc with support from Arab-led parties would lead to Israel’s collapse. “Such a government, dependent on Islamists, will dismantle the state of Israel from within, as is happening in European countries, and far worse than that,” Netanyahu said in a prerecorded video speech, echoing the language of far-right politicians who falsely claim parts of Europe have come under Islamic law. Netanyahu “described us as supporters of terrorists and terrorism”, Tibi said. “My response to him is this: Netanyahu is the biggest terrorist in Israel and the region, and the foremost supporter of terrorism, particularly Jewish terrorism in the West Bank and the Palestinian territories.” Al Jazeera’s Odeh noted that although Eisenkot has expressly said he does not wish to form a government with Arab-led parties, “they both share quite compelling reasons to get rid of Netanyahu”.
entry.summary: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government Al Jazeera In setback to Netanyahu, rival Eisenkot to be tasked with forming next Israeli government. But the path remains complicated CNN World in Brief: Israel’s Eisenkot gets first crack at forming government; gunman kills six in Krakow The Economist Israel’s president picks Yashar leader Gadi Eisenkot to form government The Guardian Eisenkot Seeks to Oust Netanyahu as Prime Minister. Here’s How. The New York Times

entry.title: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse
entry.body: Paraguay's former president charged after bank collapse - Published Prosecutors in Paraguay have charged former president Santiago PeÃ±a over his alleged role in a banking scandal that led to his impeachment. He has been accused of breach of trust and administration for personal gain. PeÃ±a, who denies any wrongdoing, was forced from office after a bank collapse triggered a crisis that left more than half of the country's population without access to their accounts. He was arrested on Friday minutes after lawmakers, including from his own party, unanimously voted to remove him from office following the collapse of Ueno Bank, which has links to his private business interests. He had offered to step down but rather than accept his resignation, senators impeached PeÃ±a and charged him with misconduct, meaning he has been stripped of the immunity usually granted to ex-presidents. PeÃ±a, who until last year held shares in the company that owned the bank, has denied any wrongdoing. The impeachment charges that led to PeÃ±a's removal alleged he had conflicts of interest, manipulated regulatory oversight, diverted pension funds, and participated in an institutional cover-up involving the central bank. PeÃ±a's deputy, Pedro Alliana, has been sworn in as the new interim president and promised not to "abandon" the millions of people affected by the scandal. "Compatriots who are now going through a difficult time as a result of the financial collapse will be fully compensated," said Alliana, who will serve as president until 2028. The demise of the digital bank left more than half of Paraguay's population without access to their savings after it was seized by Paraguay's central bank. Long lines of people trying to withdraw money from Ueno branches snaked down the streets of the capital Asuncion on Tuesday and Wednesday. An estimated three million depositors remain unable to access their savings and pensions, prompting public outrage particularly in the capital, AsunciÃ³n. Protests erupted across the country in response, with thousands taking to the streets on Thursday to demand their money. Earlier demonstrations featured clashes with the police, who used tear gas and water cannons on the crowd. PeÃ±a's impeachment passed with 44 out of 45 senators voting in favour of it. "It was never my intention to betray the trust you placed in me," PeÃ±a said in a video posted on X announcing his resignation, adding his priority was "the peace of mind of Paraguayans who entrusted their savings to our financial system". Afterwards, senate president Basilio NÃºÃ±ez said PeÃ±a was found guilty of "dereliction of duty". Senator Rafael Filizzola said: "We are facing the biggest corruption scandal in our democratic history â a tremendous blow to the state, to private citizens, and to the country's credibility and image." Analysts say PeÃ±a is likely to now be prosecuted over the bank's collapse. His defence lawyer Ricardo Preda described the allegations as a "reckless accusation" that was "irresponsible and opportunistic".
entry.summary: Santiago Peña was ousted due to a banking crisis which left millions of people unable to access their money.

entry.title: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme
entry.body: US offers $20m reward for information about Iran's nuclear programme - Published The US has announced a reward of up to $20 million for information about Iran's nuclear programme. The State Department's Rewards for Justice is also offering to potentially relocate the person who provides such details. President Donald Trump claimed last year that Iran's nuclear facilities had been "completely and totally obliterated" following a bombing campaign by the US and Israel. Iran insists its nuclear programme is peaceful and that it has no intention of developing a nuclear weapon. Meanwhile, the US military says it is setting up a task force to enhance Washington's efforts to restrict Iran's movement of weapons and sanctioned material across its borders. The US military's Central Command (Centcom) said Task Force Iron Gate would operate from Tampa, Florida, and would work with other US government agencies. As well as the movement of weapons, it will also focus on dual-use and illegal revenue streams. Centcom estimates that its naval blockade of Iran's ports has prevented the country from exporting more than $25bn in crude oil. A US State Department statement about its multi-million dollar reward said it was offering the money for information about the Iranian programme, including "facilities, equipment and associated personnel". It said Iran's "lack of compliance with the IAEA [the International Atomic Energy Agency] on safeguards obligations has led to the agency's loss of 'continuity of knowledge' regarding Iran's production and inventory of key components like [nuclear] centrifuges". Centrifuges are needed to produce enriched uranium, which can be used to make reactor fuel for civilian use but also for nuclear weapons if enriched to around 90% purity or higher. There had been mounting speculation that the US might resume significant strikes in Iran after the midterm elections, though Trump told reporters, prior to the polls, that he was in "no rush" to do so. In an interview with Fox News on the eve of the midterms, the president also said the US "might need to go after Pickaxe [Mountain]", an underground site linked to Iran's nuclear programme. This was "not a big deal" and could be done in "one hour", Trump said. The president has repeatedly threatened to bomb the suspected underground site on previous occasions. However, both Trump and Vice-President JD Vance have said public opposition to the war on Iran fuelled heavy losses for their Republican Party in this week's midterm elections, which has led to speculation the White House may no longer seek an escalation in the conflict. On Friday, Trump insisted that Iran was keen to end the eight-month conflict with the US, stressing the damage to Tehran's economy and military. "We're dealing with them now. They want to make a deal very badly," he said. Qatar's foreign ministry spokesman said on Tuesday that both sides were "reviewing the ideas and proposals we have presented" and that it remained hopeful of a deal being agreed. Iranian negotiators had discussed with mediators a proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz within two days once the US met its seven conditions. The US and Iran reached a preliminary agreement to end the war and reopen the strait in June, but it collapsed within weeks after Iranian attacks on shipping resumed and the US reinstated its blockade. Related topics - Published4 days ago - Published22 June 2025
entry.summary: Donald Trump has repeatedly raised the prospect of renewing strikes against Iran's nuclear facilities.

entry.title: Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE to be released from custody - CBS News
entry.body: Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE to be released from custody A Wisconsin state trooper originally from South Africa was released from custody late Friday night after he was detained by Immigration and Customs Enforcement officials Thursday at an airport while trying to visit his parents. Carel Aaron Van Der Merwe entered the country in 2019 at 14 years old and attended high school in New Mexico, according to his attorney. According to Attorney Mark Christopher, Van Der Merwe's parents applied for asylum, and he was granted work authorization because the process can take years. Van Der Merwe attended the New Mexico Military Institute for college and wanted to serve in the U.S. military, but was not permitted because of his immigration status. Van Der Merwe started working as a Wisconsin state trooper in July 2025. He is authorized to work in the country, according to Christopher. The Department of Homeland Security said in a statement that Van Der Merwe had legal permission to stay in the country until September 2019 but "in defiance of our nation's laws ... overstayed his admission." WKBT in La Crosse, Wisconsin, said Friday afternoon that Van Der Merwe had a conversation with Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin and will be released. "It's one of the more egregious and ridiculous cases I've ever come across," said Christopher. "I can't think of any public utility or benefit of detaining him." Christopher says that Van Der Merwe's release came with conditions — he is under an "order of supervision" with the specifics to be ironed out within the next two weeks.
entry.summary: Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE to be released from custody CBS News Wisconsin state patrol trooper detained by ICE released from custody The Guardian ICE arrests Wisconsin state patrol trooper with pending asylum case at airport, attorneys say NBC News UPDATE: Wisconsin State Trooper released from ICE custody, according to attorney news8000.com Wisconsin state trooper detained by ICE ABC News - Breaking News, Latest News and Videos

entry.title: Briton among six killed in 'far-right' shooting in Krakow
entry.body: Six killed in Krakow 'far-right' shooting, as three more bodies found in attacker's home - Published A gunman believed to have been inspired by far-right ideology has killed six people and injured more than a dozen others in an attack in the busy centre of Poland's second largest city. Police said the attacker drove onto Main Market Square in Krakow, a popular tourist attraction, on Saturday afternoon and began randomly firing at people. The attacker, who was equipped with military-style weapons and attire, was injured in a gunfight with police, one of whom was critically injured in the process. The 25-year-old Polish man - described by one minister as "ultra-nationalist" - has been taken to hospital for surgery. Poland's Prime Minister Donald Tusk said another three bodies were found during a search of the suspect's home around 125 miles (200km) away from Krakow. Tusk said there were "strong indications" the two women and one man were the suspect's immediate family members. He said: "Until now in Poland we haven't had such drastic cases of terrorism... that's what we have to call this cruel attack on people's lives here in Krakow." Four women and two men were killed in the square. Three were Polish, one was British and two have not been identified, officials said. UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham said: "I'm shocked and saddened by the appalling shooting in KrakÃ³w today." "My thoughts are with the families of those who have lost their lives, everyone injured and all those affected by this senseless violence. The United Kingdom stands in solidarity with the people of Poland," he added. The rampage began shortly before 15:00 local time (14:00 GMT) in the historic centre of Krakow, an ornate square which has long been a draw for tourists. Footage showed the attacker's vehicle speeding through the centre of the city, and people fleeing as the sound of gunfire rang out. The glass front of shops were shattered by bullets and a tram was shot at during the attack, which police say lasted for around three minutes. Images from the scene showed overturned tables and scattered belongings left behind as people ran for their lives. Armed police officers pursued the attacker's car until it crashed, at which point they engaged him in a firefight. Distressing footage authenticated by BBC Verify captured the moment a police officer confronted the suspect as he lay on the ground. The officer, who is visibly injured, can then be seen falling to the ground. A Polish minister later said one police officer was fighting for his life and a second was expected to recover from a less serious injury. Tusk later named them as Senior Constable Jakub Kulik and Senior Constable Artur MoraÅski - he said they "saved many lives" and called them "true heroes". The gunman wore full military tactical gear during the attack and was described as having a military-grade weapon - but the government said he was not a member of the Polish armed forces. More weapons and ammunition were found in a car belonging to the suspect, whose name has not been confirmed. Poland's Interior Minister Marcin KierwiÅski said "everything suggests that he was fascinated by far-right ideologies" and held "ultra-nationalist views". Tusk vowed that any "possible supporters of the perpetrator" would be detained and appealed to the public for information. A massive armed police presence was deployed across Krakow on Saturday evening, as security measures were ramped up in the capital Warsaw and elsewhere. Of the 15 injured, two were police officers and five were foreign nationals - the interior ministry said they were from Britain, Austria, Russia, Germany and Portugal. European foreign policy chief Kaja â Kallas called it "a tragedy that will be felt far beyond Poland." British foreign secretary Ed Miliband said on social media the UK government "deeply mourns" those who died in the "appalling attack". "All of my deepest condolences go to the families of the victims," he added. The Foreign Office updated its advice, external after the attack and said people in the area should follow the advice of local authorities. Witnesses who were close to the attack described panic and confusion around the square as it unfolded. Cezary, a 24-year-old Polish university student in Krakow, said he did not realise the loud bangs he heard were gunshots until he saw four bodies lying on the street. "We were still hearing gunshots, a lot of people were screaming," he said, adding that he saw someone trying to resuscitate a person covered in blood on the ground. Caitlin Shasby, from Newcastle in the UK, said she heard shooting from her hotel room and was told to take shelter inside as police "barricaded" the street outside. Another witness told Polish news website Inertia: "I saw shots being fired from the driver's side window and smoke was coming out. "I ran to the police station in the main market square - when I burst inside, it was full of people hiding on the floor." A period of mourning has been declared in Krakow until 11 November. Related topics - Published2 hours ago
entry.summary: Police in the Polish city say the attacker randomly fired at people after driving on to Main Market Square.

entry.title: Ambika Mod says the 'glass ceiling is always getting higher' for South Asian actors
entry.body: Ambika Mod says the 'glass ceiling is always getting higher' for South Asian actors - Published An overworked junior doctor, an aspiring writer and now a ruthless assassin. Ambika Mod's TV credits are becoming as diverse as the roles are complex. The actress broke through as the overwhelmed Shruti in BBC medical drama This Is Going To Hurt in 2022, and gained wide recognition for her starring role as Emma Morley in Netflix's miniseries adaptation of David Nicholls' bestselling novel One Day. Mod, who joins the cast of Black Doves for the second season of the streamer's spy thriller, tells BBC Newsbeat she is careful about the roles she takes on. As the daughter of Indian immigrants the 31-year-old, from Hatfield, says a "central tenet" of her work is to "change how South Asian women are seen on-screen and the characters that we are seen in". She has previously spoken about not having access to the same "privilege", external some of her fellow actors do when it comes to roles. Fans have questioned why she hasn't gone on to appear in as many roles as her One Day co-star Leo Woodall, who's since appeared in major films including Bridget Jones: Mad About the Boy and A24's Anthony Bourdain biopic, Tony. Addressing this remark, Mod tells Newsbeat she thinks "there's definitely an issue in this industry with systemic racism". "I think it is really hard for South Asian actors to really push through. "I feel like the glass ceiling is always getting higher and higher and higher." A report from the Creative Diversity Network, external suggested that representation of minority ethnic groups on and off-screen dropped slightly last year, after a few years of improvement. And similar research from media watchdog Ofcom , externalfound people from certain backgrounds are less well-represented across the UK broadcasting industry. It said "people from minority ethnic groups (across the industry as a whole) only account for 11% of those in senior management roles". It also found under-representation in creative, production and on-screen roles. Mod says she doesn't know if on-screen representation is changing, but says she "won't engage" with a role if she thinks its tokenistic or stereotypical. "I've been very, very lucky in my career so far from very early on to play really complex, meaty roles and to have changed the narrative in many ways," she says. "And I'm not looking to regress." And when it comes to considering what to take on next, she says she tries to follow advice Dame Emma Thompson once gave her: "There's no such thing as a career, there's only what you do next." "I'm always just trying to focus on what the new challenging thing is going to be, or cool people that I want to work with," she says. "And also what's going to be fun, as well." Her latest role as Laila, a lawless agent of the covert Black Doves, attracted her as it subverted a lot of espionage genre tropes. The character is introduced in season two to assist Keira Knightley's agent Helen on a mission as the stakes get even higher for those working with the secretive organisation. Mod says it was "such a good time" working alongside Knightley and getting to do some extreme stunt sequences together. "Honestly, the main reason I wanted to do it was because of all the stunts," she says. "Really badass but it was so much fun. "It was just so fun to take down an absolutely staggering number of men in every single episode." The thriller also has a dark humour to it, which aligns well with Mod who often brings a dry wit to her characters. Her comedic career goes back to when she was about 18, and while studying at Durham University she was part of its sketch comedy group. Despite having not done stand-up for about five years, she says she would "love" to do more comedy in the future. "I do sometimes think about going back to it," she reveals. "I have a lot of stories to tell." Related topics - Published9 February 2024 - Published8 September 2025
entry.summary: The actress joins the cast of Black Doves for the second season of Netflix's spy thriller.

entry.title: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rain
entry.body: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rain - Published Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday. It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it. Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme. Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning. "When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it. "It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with. "I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high." The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year. Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row. Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year. Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage. Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect. - Norris takes pole in rain-delayed qualifying - Published4 hours ago - Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil - Published3 hours ago Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions. "We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace. "We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it. "I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly. "These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well. "It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake. "But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding." Russell reminds himself 'I haven't forgotten how to drive' For Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them. Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history. Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector. The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened. He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second. It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest. But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second. "Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying." He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there. "In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet." Alonso back at the sharp end The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created. With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light. This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it. Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again. "We took some risks in Q1, in Q2, where the conditions were a little bit unknown for everybody and we made it through and then our first Q3 of the year, so obviously pleased with that," Alonso said. "Then in Q3 I was expecting maybe a little bit more. I was first on the queue. But the tyres were ice cold in Q3, so I had no grip. "But yeah, I look at the times now, I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me. So yeah, it's way too much, you know, in front to really dream about any higher positions. "There is less time full throttle (in the wet), because there is no grip. So obviously they cannot exploit the extra power. "But still the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners. We still have a little bit of an issue there. "But no, I think these conditions is more about the level of risk you want to take. There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there." Alonso joins Norris and Russell in hoping for a wet race, feeling that if it's dry he will inevitably sink back to Aston Martin's natural level, especially with the long pit straight where Honda's lack of power will render him defenceless. Hamilton and Leclerc 'moving on' after talks The race promises much with Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all aiming to make progress from the back, even if the drivers feel that overtaking at Interlagos will be harder in this year's new-style cars than before. For Ferrari, it has been a difficult weekend, that started with clear-the-air talks between Leclerc and Hamilton after their first-lap battle cost them victory in Mexico last weekend. Both took new internal combustion engines, which gave them 10-place grid penalties, and then Hamilton's brand new one broke in final practice. So Ferrari gave him another one, leaving him at the back with Verstappen. The two multiple champions will be in competition to see who can make progress faster, and perhaps Ferrari are not so unhappy that Hamilton and Leclerc are separated by six places on the grid. Both drivers said all was well after their chat on Thursday evening. Leclerc - who returned to Europe between the two races to be at the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca - said: "It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long. "At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and it will be important to look ahead. "I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away. Of course, there is tension. Of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those then helps a whole lot." Hamilton added: "Me and Charles sat and spoke and we squashed it, and we're moving on. "We still have a huge amount of respect for each other and I'm glad we had a chat and now we move on. "We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes in those scenarios it takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side. "It's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other." Sao Paulo starting grid after penalties 1. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) 4. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) 6. Fernando Alonso (Aston Martin) 9. Arvid Lindblad (Racing Bulls) 13. Lance Stroll (Aston Martin) 18. Max Verstappen (Red Bull) 22. Sergio Perez (Cadillac) Related topics - Published3 hours ago - Published1 day ago - Published1 day ago
entry.summary: Polesitter Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven.

entry.title: Hutchinson beats Buatsi to win WBC light-heavyweight title
entry.body: Hutchinson beats Buatsi to win WBC light-heavyweight title - Published Willy Hutchinson was crowned the WBC light-heavyweight champion after he produced the performance of his career to beat Joshua Buatsi in Manchester. Hutchinson, 28, edged the tense rematch with the judges scoring it 117-112, 115-113, 115-113 to avenge his defeat by Buatsi in 2024. Saturday's contest was initially for the interim title but was upgraded when American David Benavidez gave up the WBC gold to move up to cruiserweight. It was a childhood dream come true for Scotland's Hutchinson, who said before the fight he wrote about his dreams of becoming a WBC champion at the age of 13. An emotional Hutchinson said after his win was confirmed: "I want to tell the story one more time. My dad was working in Sweden. I signed it in a book, I said I will become a world champion. "Can I say thank you to my coach because I'll you one thing, without him I don't think I'll be here today let alone boxing. This man dug me out of a hole that I never thought that I would get out of, so this is all a bonus baby." Ticket sales were modest for a world title fight as it was clear that it did not capture the attention of the British public. But those inside made the atmosphere as raucous as possible, with the Manchester crowd favouring Hutchinson. And they were delighted when the result was read out and Hutchinson became the eighth British light-heavyweight champion - the first since Nathan Cleverly in 2017. Hutchinson improved his record to 21 victories with two defeats, while it is the second time Londoner Buatsi has lost in 22 professional fights. Hutchinson shows class to join British elite Fight week was dominated by predictions that Buatsi, five years Hutchinson's senior, is over the hill. And the Londoner did nothing to prove otherwise as Hutchinson often toyed with his opponent in the centre of the ring. The first fight in 2024 had Buatsi walking to the ring as a comfortable favourite, and he backed that up with crushing body shots to send Hutchinson tumbling twice. But this time around, Hutchinson was a different fighter. In his own words, he had "matured" after picking up two wins since last facing Buatsi. Hutchinson clearly had the crowd on his side as he made the walk to cheers, while Buatsi was met by a chorus of boos as he paraded around the ring before the bell. For Buatsi, the strategy was very much the same as the first encounter - whip shots into the body - but Hutchinson now had answers. The AO Arena is famous for its boxing nights with the city's favourite boxing son, Ricky Hatton, becoming world champion here for the first time in June 2005 in a thriller against Kostya Tszyu. This did not reach those heights, as the upper tier was closed off because of a lack of ticket sales - and fans of Manchester's Jack Rafferty departed after he won the co-main event. This did not deter Hutchinson from advancing in the latter rounds and landing rapid triple jabs, while also switching stances. As Manchester royalty Bez, of the Happy Mondays, watched on from ringside, Hutchinson's corner told him "three rounds and you're a world champion" after the ninth. Despite Buatsi's advances late on, Hutchinson held out to become world champion for the first time. The world is now Hutchinson's oyster. Being world champion means Hutchinson will be a wanted man in the light-heavyweight division. Former world title challenger Anthony Yarde was perched ringside and that is a fight that could thrill British boxing fans - now with gold involved, could it happen? Hutchinson addressed Yarde, who stepped into the ring and said "he's no walkover but let's go. Him next." But if Hutchinson v Yarde does not come to fruition, then there is the small matter of Dmitry Bivol v Callum Smith for the other three light-heavyweight titles on 12 December. Whoever wins that could be Hutchinson's next opponent in what would be a huge undisputed bout in 2027. Domestic rival in Ben Whittaker, who is ranked third with the WBC and holds the silver title, could also emerge as a potential option. entry.summary: Willy Hutchinson is crowned WBC light-heavyweight champion as he produces the performance of his career against Joshua Buatsi in Manchester.

entry.title: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government
entry.body: Israel's president tasks opposition leader Eisenkot with forming government - Published Israel's president says he will task opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot with forming a new coalition government. Isaac Herzog has been holding talks with political parties after neither Eisenkot's bloc nor that of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu secured a majority in Israel's parliament, known as the Knesset, following last week's election. Eisenkot will now have 28 days to try to form a new administration, with a potential 14-day extension. "Now is the time to form a national emergency government. I will do everything to ensure we are worthy," the former military chief wrote on X. No political party in Israel has ever won an outright majority, meaning all governments have been coalitions. Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies won 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset, while Eisenkot's centrist Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc won 48. Two Arab-led alliances, the United Arab List and the Joint List, together won an unprecedented 19 seats following a surge in turnout among Arab voters. That positions them as potential kingmakers. However, all but one of the Jewish parties pledged before the polls not to work with them to form a government. Herzog said that, after consulting all parties during the week, he would give Eisenkot the first chance to form a government. A statement from the president's office said he had informed both Eisenkot and Netanyahu of the decision. Following consultations with delegations from the incoming Knesset members, Eisenkot received 67 recommendations for the premiership and Netanyahu 46, the statement said. The president has broad discretion to pick someone they believe has the best chance of building a coalition and does not have to choose the leader of the party with the most seats. The election results had implied three possible options for the formation of a government: a national unity administration involving both Netanyahu and Eisenkot, a right-wing coalition involving Netanyahu and defectors from Eisenkot's bloc, or an Eisenkot-led government supported by the Arab parties. Eisenkot and every member of his bloc bar one has previously refused to enter government with Arab parties, but there has been speculation that an agreement could be reached. He could also attempt to reach a deal with ultra-Orthodox parties, but that too would be difficult. There is precedent for a unity government. In 2020, following three deadlocked elections, Netanyahu and his centrist rival Benny Gantz agreed a power-sharing deal in which the leadership rotated between the two. During his consultations with the parties, Herzog had said that to prevent another round of elections and to build a stable government, he expected "factions and their representatives to understand that, in the current reality, not every commitment and promise can be fulfilled". In the period 2019 to 2022, one of the most politically fractured in Israeli politics, there were five separate elections as Netanyahu and his rivals struggled time and again to co-operate. Related topics - Published3 days ago - Published29 October
entry.summary: Neither PM Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc nor that of his rival secured a majority in last week's election.

entry.title: How midterm elections sent Wall Street from celebration to mayhem in just 24 hours / this week - Yahoo Finance
entry.body: Wall Street's tumultuous midterm election week kicked off with a celebration among investors. On Wednesday, stocks soared after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress. The Dow (^DJI) surged more than 1,500 points. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rallied nearly 2%. And in less than 24 hours, stocks reversed course, plunging Thursday as Wall Street and Main Street investors alike ditched artificial intelligence winners and chip stocks, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) into correction territory. The extraordinary reversal marked just the latest whipsaw in a year of wild swings, with the market's best expectation of future volatility, the VIX (^VIX), spiking to its highest level since President Trump extended the deadline for the Iran war in late March. As the election results rolled in, Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, was glued to his television, flipping between CNN, Fox, MSNBC, and Bloomberg while watching stock futures slip. When Sosnick went to bed, futures were still down roughly 1%. Democrats had won control of both the House and Senate, resolving one major source of uncertainty for markets, while introducing a specific complication to the country's artificial intelligence investment boom. States where newly elected governors have promised to stop or pause data center construction account for an estimated 45% of planned US data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. In Texas, where more than half of the country's data center capacity is planned for construction, stakes were especially high. Democrat Gina Hinojosa had just won the race to become governor after promising a moratorium on new data center approvals. The shift caught the attention of one of the world's most prominent business titans. "Data centers in space look pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X early Wednesday. By Wednesday morning, Wall Street was seeing silver linings in the blue wave. The Dow jumped 3%, its best day in months. The S&P 500 rose 1.6%, and the Nasdaq gained 1.4%. Investors appeared to welcome the prospect of a divided government, potentially limiting some of President Trump's agenda. Oil prices (CL=F, BZ=F) also plunged, helping ease inflation concerns. And the removal of election uncertainty ushered in a sharp drop in the VIX. That drop may have encouraged volatility-sensitive trading strategies to buy stocks, adding more upward pressure to the rally, according to Sosnick. As prices climbed, more investors piled in. But beneath the rally, trouble was brewing.

entry.title: Musk Says SpaceX Could Buy a Legacy Telco and Use Its Spectrum 10 Times Better - 24/7 Wall St.
entry.body: Musk Says SpaceX Could Buy a Legacy Telco and Use Its Spectrum 10 Times Better Musk hinted at a telecom takeover without naming a target, while a rival CEO put a staggering price on SpaceX's ambitions. Debt, regulators, and a spectrum gap stand between the boast and a real deal. This post may contain links from our sponsors and affiliates, and Flywheel Publishing may receive compensation for actions taken through them. Elon Musk told investors on November 6, 2026, that SpaceX (NASDAQ:SPCX | SPCX Price Prediction) could buy a legacy telecom carrier and use its airwaves “ten times more effectively.” He made the comment by video with Ron Baron at the annual Baron Investment Conference in New York. Musk also said SpaceX could go far with the spectrum it already has, and he named no target. He made any purchase conditional on SpaceX using spectrum better than the incumbent does. Verizon (NYSE:VZ) and AT&T (NYSE:T) each slipped 0.89%. SpaceX rose 8.62% to $134.27, but Musk also gave his revenue outlook in the same conversation, and the stock had lost 19.89% over the prior month during a post-election Nasdaq rout. What SpaceX Already Owns in the Airwaves Spectrum means licensed radio frequencies. A phone can connect to a satellite or a tower only on airwaves the operator has the legal right to use, so those licenses determine whether direct-to-phone service can work at scale. SpaceX bought AWS-4 and H-block licenses from EchoStar on September 8, 2025, for roughly $17 billion. It paid $8.5 billion in cash and $8.5 billion in SpaceX stock. It has also agreed to buy nationwide 800 MHz licenses, with closing expected in the first half of 2027. There are also reports of talks over Boost Mobile, but nothing has been confirmed. Why Deutsche Telekom Puts the Entry Price Near $220 Billion On Deutsche Telekom’s November 5 earnings call, CEO Tim Hoettges said SpaceX would need at least EUR 200 billion, or about $220 billion, to compete with the established US carriers. His company controls T-Mobile, so he has a reason to make entry look expensive. He put SpaceX’s spectrum at 76 MHz, compared with roughly 400 MHz for T-Mobile. He said leasing tower space alone would cost $20 billion to $30 billion, but he still said his company has to assume SpaceX will enter the market. Debt and Regulators Come With Any Carrier At the close, the three carriers were worth about $507 billion combined. SpaceX was worth roughly $1.77 trillion, so a deal paid partly in stock is possible on paper. A buyer would also take on debt, including Verizon’s $166.2 billion or AT&T’s $159.6 billion, along with labor unions, retail stores and landline networks. Antitrust regulators and the FCC would both have to approve it. How Each Stock Took the Remark T-Mobile is down 18.46% year to date, and its third-quarter report pointed to worry over SpaceX’s fourth-carrier ambitions. Verizon closed at $45.71 and AT&T at $21.63. No one linked their small moves to Musk. Viasat (NASDAQ:VSAT) rose 7.7% to $63.95 after its results. That is a drop of 83%, which shows Starlink is already pulling customers from older satellite providers. What SpaceX Investors Need to Weigh Before the 800 MHz Closing At $134.27, SpaceX’s price likely already assumes Starlink Mobile succeeds. Turning Musk’s comment into a carrier business would bring debt, regulators, and a bill that Hoettges puts at $220 billion or more. T-Mobile’s recent results give a useful point of comparison. It raised its 2026 Core Adjusted EBITDA guidance to $37.35 billion to $37.45 billion and raised its dividend 15% to $1.17 a share, and its stock price already reflects the fear of SpaceX. Keep an eye on the 800 MHz closing in the first half of 2027. If no SpaceX filing with the FCC or SEC names a US carrier by then, the comment is still just a hypothetical, and T-Mobile’s discount should narrow. entry.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo - TechCrunch
entry.body: A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports. The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed. An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers. A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm. The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”

entry.title: AI broke the cybersecurity world. What’s next?
entry.body: Today, I’m talking with Alex Stamos, chief security officer at Cognition and longtime cybersecurity expert, about what a mess cybersecurity is right now. AI broke the cybersecurity world. Going inside the security ‘dark ages’ with Alex Stamos. This episode is part one of a special series looking at AI in real life. I’ve always enjoyed talking to Alex because he’s so direct, and you’re going to hear him say that the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry as we’ve known it is essentially overdue to the unrelenting, AI-boosted waves of hacks, breaches, and attacks — and this is only the beginning of how much AI is changing security. Both private actors and also state actors, like Russia or North Korea, are breaking into systems all over thanks to AI helping them both detect and exploit vulnerabilities all at the same time. It’s got a real frontier feel to it, Alex notes, just like the ’90s, when the whole idea of an always-online world was brand-new. That much disruption means a lot of places where bad guys can get in while everyone else is left scrambling. Alex isn’t a doomer in the long run, but he does think we’re in for a “dark age” while we try to figure out how on earth to adapt to the new era. There’s a lot going on here — we even got all the way to how AI-powered misinformation and slop might be managed on our social networks. Okay: Alex Stamos on how AI is upending cybersecurity. This interview has been lightly edited for length and clarity. Alex Stamos, you’re the chief security officer at Cognition. You’re also a lecturer at Stanford University Cyber Policy Center. Hey, thanks for having me, man. I’m excited to talk to you. It’s been a long time since you and I chatted in what you might call the “content moderation era” of internet policy discourse. I feel like you and I talked a lot about how all that was working, about election security, all those sorts of things. We’re in a new era of big problems on the internet, particularly around cyber defense, cybersecurity. You’ve been thinking about this stuff a lot. You referred to the past few weeks as “security awareness month.” Tell me what’s going on. Just give me the lay of land right now. October is traditionally security awareness month. Lots of companies run events and deal both internally and then tell people, “Change your password, use multiple passwords, use a password manager.” What has happened over the last month is we’ve had a couple of these big bugs, PHP, Node and such. What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached. You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry. A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November. I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin. Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time. The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. That’s- That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ‘90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster. I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now. It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible. You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties. You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now. Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s. That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that. There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing. All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable exploit code. It’s not quite there yet to be automatic. You still have to have a bunch of skills, but we’re really, really close. What’s really concerning, and what you see with the ARTEX stuff, is you can now kind of let loose on the operational side. It was all a fantasy. These vulnerabilities have always existed. These companies have never been safe. And that is what we’ve seen over the last decade is these mostly Russian ransomware actors nailing the mid-size companies that most people have never heard of that are actually really important, like some midsize industrial company that makes some widget that we all depend upon. I once did work for the largest distributor of medical and dental supplies in the country, and they got really hit badly by a Russian ransomware actor and then dental offices across the country were canceling appointments. Didn’t even make the news, but it was because they couldn’t get gloves, because they couldn’t get supplies. It’s because a company like that’s got one security guy and a 10 person, 12 person IT team and they’re going up against a 20 person Russian ransomware team, they’re toast. But it’s just because there’s only a handful of Russian teams that could do that. Now two or three Russian kids can have a whole bank of Macs or, if they have the money, they can buy Nvidia H-100s and they can run a ton of agents who do this all day and that is what is changing. I’m sorry, you asked who was doing this. For Binance, it’s North Koreans and they have an entire team where all they do is steal Bitcoin. Other people have gotten out of it because it’s really hard to compete against a foreign intelligence agency that recruits their smartest kids and all they do is steal Bitcoin. They’re extremely good at it. And for the Binance hack, we could talk about it. There’s probably some AI component, but mostly that was actually human intelligence and very, very smart social engineering and the North Koreans are... I mean, you have to give it to them. They’re very, very good at that. But for the other stuff, it looks like for the people who are breaking into the AI companies is what’s called the Chinese cottage access industry, which are small Chinese contractors who break into companies and then sell
