What’s been less discussed is a huge number of companies have been breached. You have a series of AI-related companies, the neoclouds that have been breached in succession. You have the Binance hack, which is the largest heist of anything in human history. You have the Cursor incident where one of the things that’s going on here is these hacks are being chained together. From what we know right now, one of the companies that was broken into was Fireworks, which is a prominent provider of AI services to a number of companies. From the Fireworks hack, API keys were stolen that allowed people to break into Cursor. Once they got into Cursor, they then pushed a bad plugin, which went to 5,000 more companies and that caused 5,000 potential breaches. It’s just this kind of permanent continuous breach that is going on throughout the tech industry. A CISO friend of mine said to a bunch of us, “Is anybody else tired?” And everybody said yes, because effectively we have been at DEFCON 2 for all of October and now going into November. I’m going to ask you some really dumb questions here. Who is behind all these attacks? Is it Russia? Is it North Korea? Do we know? It’s a variety of different groups. It is not just because adversaries have decided, but what has happened is, from my perspective, we are at the start of the takeoff of adversary capability enabled by AI, that the open-weight models have now gotten to the point at which you can automate most of the kill chain. This “kill chain” term is something we stole from the military. In the military, they mean to actually kill something. They’re the steps you do to blow something up. In cyber, the kill chain is the things you do to have an effect on a target. So to steal information, to turn something off, to steal money, to steal Bitcoin. Traditionally, you do research upfront, you look at a piece of software, you find a vulnerability, you write exploits, and you do that all way ahead of time. And then you have a human being go and take that stuff you built and deploy it against either one target — because maybe you’re a government and you’re going against Lockheed Martin or you’re going against another government or you’re a ransomware actor — and you take all that work you did and you deploy it against hundreds or thousands of targets really fast. Now with AI, what’s happening is this kill chain has inverted where you can run an AI system that just goes hog wild and it looks at the targets and it finds the bugs in real time and it writes the exploits in real time and it breaks into these companies. One of the things that’s happening is that these systems are going and they’re so good at finding bugs that they are finding the bugs in real time and writing the exploits in real time. The system that everybody’s talking about is not the only one, but the system we’re talking about is a thing called ARTEX, which is a Chinese open-source tool that anybody can go look at. There’s an English translation on GitHub that you can check out. And if you power it on the back end by something like an obliterated GLM-5.3, it will let you break into a shocking number of organizations. This started with three South Korean banks. This week, about 200 more companies have been hit. I’ve been helping a couple of companies. Cognition is not an incident response company, but we do go in and help people fix their bugs afterwards by using our tools. It is shocking the companies that are getting hit by something you could just download. It has been a long time since you’ve been able to go and just download an open-source tool and break into multi-billion dollar companies. It’s like the ‘90s. That’s- That’s what I was thinking about. I think about Windows in the late ’90s, early 2000s when it was a security disaster. I started saying this actually in the beginning of this year, that it’s an incredibly exciting and terrifying time, because the last time it felt like this was when I was a much younger man and I would go to the very early DEFCONs. DEFCON these days is like 40,000–60,000 people. Back then [in the 1990s] it was a couple hundred people and it was one track and you’d go in and somebody would give a talk and you’d leave the room and you’d think, “Every company in the world is vulnerable to this attack.” The difference was that the entire world didn’t run on the internet. You could go do bad things, but you couldn’t ruin the world and you certainly couldn’t automate it in the way you can now. It’s back to those days where tools you could just get and build yourself could do crazy things. It’s back to the Wild West days. Back in those days, there were a couple hundred people who had those skills and we were all in one room in Las Vegas and most of them were actually good guys. They didn’t want to be criminals. And now you have a much larger ecosystem of people, many of whom live in places where the law enforcement can’t touch and who have a big economic incentive and have access to these tools. The other big thing is they no longer have to use frontier models that have protections, that have logs that are available to law enforcement. My M5 Mac Ultra Studio finally showed up and I’ve been running a quantized obliterated GLM-5.3 and oh my God, what you can do is incredible. You mentioned the economics of frontier models. The economy of cyber is one of those things that has gotten sophisticated over the years. One of the things that our systems got safer is you could pay the number of people at DEF CON a whole bunch of money to protect all the systems and it was economically smart to pay them to be defenders instead of attackers. I’m just rewinding my own brain through this history. There was a long conversation in our industry about security through obscurity by hiding all the bugs and hiding all the code versus open source and being really transparent. There was an etiquette that developed about how to reveal the bugs and when to give people notification. There were transparency reports and bug bounties. You could call it an etiquette, you could call it an economy. We built a culture around cybersecurity and cyber defense and how the attackers and defenders would operate. What you are describing changes it all for a whole number of reasons, but the one that sticks out to me is the economics of it. I can go buy a Mac Studio, I can get an open-weight model and I can just start and that does not place me inside of the culture. There’s not going to be some old man, an Obi-Wan Kenobi saying, “Here’s how you act like a cybersecurity Jedi.” I’m just going to start doing stuff. Tell me how that’s changing right now. Effectively, the last era of security from my perspective started with the Microsoft, the Bill Gates “trustworthy computing” memo in the early 2000s. And that is when we started designing how we do software security and these big companies, Microsoft and Oracle and then later Amazon and Salesforce and these folks, started hiring ex-hackers. I was part of that generation of the ex-hackers who were at DEF CON and Black Hat and got hired by the companies to go break their stuff. We started coming up with responsible disclosure, bug bounties, consulting companies, so the Foundstone and @stake and then Mandiant and CrowdStrike, these companies grow up and we get this huge industry that is now RSA and Black Hat. This multi-billion dollar security industry grew up in the 2000s and 2010s. That era is over, like you said, because it was based upon a couple of assumptions. One was that there was a hierarchy of skillsets of people who could do this stuff. You had the script kiddies who could download tools to do things and then the next level up of the people who could write those tools and that was a more rarefied skill set. There were the vulnerability researchers and then there were the gods, and that god tier was in the hundreds of people and those are the people who could do the really, really good vulnerability research, who could write the really, really good shell code, who could reverse engineer patches from Microsoft or somebody like that. There was also the assumption that there were a limited number of people who could be operational in an attack. If you wanted to build an attack team, then you have a small R&D component and then you have a much larger operational component. If you were a professional attack team at U.S. Cyber Command, at Russia SVR, at Chinese MSS, that you build the structure of your R&D team of elite people and then your less elite operational people, and that was copied then by the Russian ransomware actors. You have to have a conspiracy of people to do this stuff. A lot of this stuff also fell apart with the invention of Bitcoin because one of the assumptions was that you had to have people who could launder money and Bitcoin meant that nerds could launder money. So that started to change the economics of the entire thing. All this stuff is falling apart because of AI, because the skillset issue is that now script kiddies have a bunch of the skillset of the Dave Vitales and the other cyber gods who could do these things, such that with this Mac that’s sitting on my desktop, I can reverse engineer a Microsoft patch and walk through and then write stable

entry.title: After the midterms, things are looking rocky for Elon Musk and data centers
entry.body: Democrats’ historic victory in this week’s midterm elections could also have a dramatic effect on the tech industry. In dozens of local ballot measures, voters rejected data centers. And even when they weren’t voting on the issue directly, they were electing politicians — like Texas’ new governor-elect Gina Hinojosa — who campaigned on the promise of restricting data centers. On the latest episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, Kirsten Korosec, Sean O’Kane, and I discussed what the midterms mean for the tech industry. Sean kicked it off by noting that Elon Musk “seems to have basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars” to Republicans, while his companies are now headquartered “in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn.” And Kirsten said that while data centers probably weren’t the main cause of the “blue wave,” they’ve become an “an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about” getting their projects approved. And now, “we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, ‘Actually, we can change our policies.’” Keep reading for a preview of our conversation, edited for length and clarity. Sean O’Kane: First off, let’s talk about the fact that one of the biggest data center builders was also the largest donor to the Republican Party. Elon Musk seems to have gotten basically nothing out of donating half a billion dollars — maybe even more, by the time we see the final count — and in fact is now sitting there with all of his businesses in a state that has, remarkably, turned about as blue as it could possibly turn for the first time in a very long time, if ever. That, I think, is the biggest thing hanging above a lot of this discussion. But, there were also a bunch of ballot measures up around the country that would have paved the way for data centers to get built faster. Almost all of them got shot down, or voted against. [Actually, many of the ballot measures would have imposed restrictions or moratoriums on data centers, and almost all of those measures passed.] With [Democrats] in power, there is a consensus view, at least in the tech world, that this is going to mean we have a lot of roadblocks ahead for data centers, especially in places like Texas, where [you have] folks like the governor-elect [Gina] Hinojosa, who has spoken pretty openly about this being a campaign promise and something that she wants to focus on once she takes power, now that she’s beaten Greg Abbott. It’s the thing that I think the tech world is maybe a little too focused on. I’m curious what you guys think about that. Anthony Ha: I don’t necessarily think that they’re too focused on it, but I understand why it would feel a little bit disproportionate — the data center ballot measures, certainly there were a number of them, but it wasn’t something that was on the ballot everywhere. And in different races, the dynamic might have been a bit different, but there was this undercurrent and sense that it seems to be an issue that reaches across the country, that is bipartisan in a lot of ways, but that the Democrats seem to have been more effective at harnessing that energy. And of course, there’s all kinds of reasons why the Democrats did so well on Tuesday, but it does seem like anti-AI and especially anti-data center sentiment was a big part of it. That seems like a pretty potent political force. The next two years, [and] potentially beyond that, are going to be more difficult for tech companies in general, and hyperscalers, data center companies in particular. I also imagine that they have to be a little bit worried about: Is this going to continue to be an issue, not just with the people who got elected this year, but potentially in 2028 and beyond? I don’t think that the data center issue is what brought everyone to the polls and led to the quote-unquote “blue wave.” However, I will say that data centers have been an increasingly grassroots issue, in part because of how hyperscalers and companies have gone about getting these data centers [approved] — very secretive, oftentimes requiring NDAs of a elected officials or appointed officials, not sharing information about the scale of a project in very environmentally sensitive areas, including in the Southwest, where there’s very much a water scarcity issue. So I think that a lot of folks — Republicans, independents, and Democrats — all saw this as wrong. They were motivated by it, but I don’t think it was a singular issue. Now, here’s the interesting thing. There was a lot of waving of hands about how [AI companies] can’t possibly operate under any other circumstances. And we’re already seeing companies like OpenAI all of a sudden go, “Actually, we can change our policies.” They just released what they call a compute campus policy blueprint. They’re not going to require NDAs anymore. They’re going to share their plans and supposedly operate in less secrecy. I think what this shows is that when you put up either a regulatory certainty in the marketplace, or at least signals of going in that direction, then corporations will respond. If you don’t do that, they will not necessarily do the thing that we hope that they will do. Anthony: One thing I want to emphasize is that they’re calling it this [their] “compute campus policy.” And part of what that’s doing, beyond laying out these policy changes, is also an attempt to rebrand data centers, because they have become such a toxic phrase. So they’re not data centers anymore, they are compute campuses, and I’m curious, whether either of you think that’ll take. Sean: I mean, this is ridiculous. It’s not going to change anything. It’s going to cause them more effort. For a company that likes to say that it’s no longer focused on side quests, OpenAI still loves to go in different directions a lot. And this is just the latest kind of thing where it’s just like: Why are you spending time on this at all? It doesn’t really seem like it’s going to move the needle. Kirsten: I have a great idea for OpenAI. Because in the spirit of making threatening things seem cute, they should 100% create a compute campuses avatar, [a] cutesy thing, and then just present that instead of a power-, energy-sucking, water-sucking data center. Anthony: And if these are just lovely compute campuses, they should just build their own offices there or work next door, see how that works out for them. Something else that I’m wondering about is, to what extent the election is maybe the second part of a one-two punch. [We’ve just seen] a big shift in how Wall Street is reacting to a lot of these hyperscalers and AI companies and this sense that [investors] are not excited about the idea that they should be spending all this money building new data centers, spending all this money on compute. And so there’s a financial incentive not to build all these data centers. I’m very curious how that’s going to play out. [From a regulatory standpoint,] it’s probably going to be harder to build data centers. Wall Street is probably not going to reward you for building data centers. But at the same time, to get to the scale that they want to get to, they are probably going to need to build data centers somewhere.
entry.summary: On Equity, we unpacked what the midterms mean for the tech industry.

entry.title: Megaspeed exec was recruited to spy on Nvidia CEO, according to US intelligence memo
entry.body: A memo circulated earlier this year claimed that technology executive Alice Huang was recruited by China’s Ministry of State Security to spy on Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang, according to multiple media reports. The New York Times, which had previously said Nvidia’s chief executive had been the target of Chinese intelligence, was the first to report on the memo, which was reportedly based on U.S. The Financial Times subsequently reported that the memo also claimed Jensen Huang had a romantic relationship with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singapore-based company called Megaspeed. An Nvidia spokesperson told the NYT that Jensen Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang were “not unusual,” and that the company does not share classified information with its customers. A separate NYT report examined New Matrix, a Chinese company authorized by the U.S. Commerce Department to buy advanced Nvidia chips. But at the office address listed by New Matrix, reporters only found “a hollow gray shell,” raising concerns that it could be a front for a blacklisted private equity firm. The Nvidia spokesperson said the company sells “the first, best and most of our technology in America.”
entry.summary: A memo circulated earlier this year reportedly claimed that China’s Ministry of State Security recruited a female technology executive to spy on Nvidia's CEO.

entry.title: Binance CFO is leaving to ‘pursue a new venture’ after $6.3 billion hack
entry.body: Binance’s chief financial officer Kaiser Ng is leaving the cryptocurrency exchange. According to Bloomberg, co-CEO Yi He said in a statement that Ng’s departure will allow him to “pursue a new venture after more than five years at Binance,” and that a transition plan has been “implemented over the last half year.” The announcement comes barely more than a week after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance users. The company froze withdrawals for several days; after accounts were unfrozen, users withdrew a net $3.6 billion in the first few hours. Binance and the FBI blamed a North Korean group called TraderTraitor for the hack. The company also said that it would cover all losses, promising, “Binance will bear the financial impact of the stolen funds. These losses will not be passed on to users.” Ng will be replaced as CFO by Justin Yek.
entry.summary: The announcement comes barely more than a week after hackers stole $6.3 billion worth of cryptocurrency from Binance users.

entry.title: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished - Business Examiner
entry.body: John Langford, a partner researcher manager at Microsoft Research New York, has left Microsoft. He declared the AI Frontiers group over, according to Digg, which summarised a post on his blog, Machine Learning (Theory). Langford announced the post on social media on Nov. The group had about 50 people. It was moved out of Microsoft Research and into Microsoft AI in early September. Langford wrote that he found places for his team members as well as he could before leaving, Digg reported. His account does not detail the group's formal status or where remaining staff were assigned. What AI Frontiers Built Langford wrote that he and colleagues created AI Frontiers inside Microsoft Research in 2023. They wanted more organized research after the release of ChatGPT. Much of the group's work centred on making AI agents function reliably. Projects he named include Autogen, a framework for coordinating agents. Another is Fara, an agent that operates a computer to carry out tasks. Shunyatax also described some researchers in the group as exploring ways to improve models without simply making them larger. Scaling Versus Research Langford described the leadership philosophy in Microsoft AI as focused on scaling rather than research, Digg reported. He said the environment focused mainly on getting, making and refining data. He conceded the business logic. In his assessment, returns to scale are more predictable than returns to research. Still, he called a scaling-only approach misdirected and unenjoyable, Digg reported. They concern the unit his group joined, not company-wide policy. Shunyatax reported that Langford's position was not that scaling should stop. It said he argued scaling and fundamental research should run side by side. No Route to Use Langford wrote that he could not get innovations used, or even seriously considered, while in Microsoft AI. A return to Microsoft Research held little appeal. He doubted research could reach use from there either. Langford wrote, in a post Digg summarised, that he is not comfortable being at a company where his research has no path to real use. He added that there will be no internships with the group in the coming year. He wished well to the colleagues he is leaving behind, according to Digg. His profile on the research platform alphaxiv lists him as a founding member of Microsoft Research New York. It also names him a co-creator of the Vowpal Wabbit machine-learning library. A 2023 Test of Time Award at The Web Conference recognised his contextual-bandit paper on personalised news recommendation. The paper describes algorithms that learn which article to show a reader. Other Microsoft Departures Shunyatax placed the AI Frontiers news alongside other senior changes at Microsoft. It cited the planned departure of former LinkedIn chief executive Ryan Roslansky from his later responsibilities over the Office and Teams divisions. It also cited the move of former AI platform head Eric Boyd to Anthropic. Shunyatax said the material does not establish that those changes stemmed from disagreements over research strategy, or that they are linked to Langford's exit.
entry.summary: Microsoft Researcher John Langford Exits as AI Frontiers Group Is Declared Finished Business Examiner Microsoft Ended Personalizer 10.2 Years After Langford Paper FourWeekMBA Major AI Research Rift at Microsoft: AI Frontiers Head John Langford Quits, Declares Research Group Over The 420.in Microsoft AI research clash: John Langford quits, declares AI Frontiers over India Today Langford Exits Microsoft: Its 50-Person AI Frontiers Is Over FourWeekMBA

entry.title: Scientists Discover Two Enormous Tears in a Tectonic Plate Beneath Iran - ScienceAlert
entry.body: On the scale of human generations, the tectonic plates that form Earth's crust and upper mantle are moving incredibly slowly. They are constantly moving, though, and across millions of years, that movement leads to some globally significant shifts in the landscape. Researchers led by a team from the Chinese Academy of Sciences have now found extensive evidence of two giant tears in a tectonic plate called the Arabian Plate, underneath southeastern Iran. The tears are being caused by different rock densities. One part of the plate is what's known as an oceanic slab and was once part of the ancient Neo-Tethys Ocean. The basalt rock here is heavier and thinner and is being pushed under a neighboring plate (the process of subduction). Meanwhile, the other part of the plate is continental rock – thicker in size but less dense in composition, with lighter ingredients that make it granite-like. This rock doesn't like to be pushed underground, and instead forms mountains when it hits resistance. That mismatch is what's causing the ruptures. In a new study published in Nature Geoscience, the researchers have detailed their findings, explaining how the discoveries give us a new perspective on how oceans disappear and continents collide as tectonic plates shift. What's more, there's a good chance these tears will eventually meet. "The coexistence of these two tearing modes provides a rare snapshot of the short-lived early transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision," write the researchers in their published paper. To measure geological activity deep underground, the researchers used a network of 69 different seismic monitoring stations to detect the vibrations coming from distant earthquakes. As these vibrations change speed based on rock temperature and density, a picture of tectonic plate activity can be put together. The recordings, taken between March 2017 and September 2018, revealed the two tears: one horizontal (where the Zagros collision zone meets the Makran subduction zone), and a smaller vertical one, closer to the surface (by the Makran Trench). "We show that in the Makran subduction zone, the oceanic lithosphere has continuously subducted to depths of at least 450 km, whereas in the Zagros collision zone to the west, the continental lithosphere has subducted no deeper than 300 km, resulting in east–southward slab tearing and detachment," write the researchers. "We further identify another slab tear that probably initiated at the junction between the Makran Trench and the transform boundary and has propagated southward as the continental plate advances northward." That second tear is more due to the movement of the plates than the differences between the oceanic and continental rock, the researchers suggest – but seeing them both at the same time in the same region is very unusual for geologists. These rips in the plates have been progressing for several million years, according to the study models, and those same models indicate that it's likely that they'll eventually meet each other. "While the two tears initiate independently, the intervening continental-oceanic boundary segment is progressively consumed as tearing advances," write the researchers. "This progressive linkage is expected to eventually drive coalescence of the two tears." The next question is how the tears, and their possible merging, might go on to affect volcanic activity in the region. It appears that hot magma is already filling some of the gaps caused by the ruptures. We might have left planet Earth by the time the tears do combine, but for geologists today it's a rare look at these forces in action, particularly the final stages of the Neo-Tethys ocean – part of the Wilson Cycle that describes how oceans are made, expand, and then gradually vanish as tectonic plates move around. "The transition from oceanic subduction to continental collision is a key stage in the Wilson Cycle," write the researchers. "Yet, key processes governing this transition remain unclear owing to sparse observations of structure at depth." The research has been published in Nature Geoscience. This article was fact-checked by Peter Dockrill and edited by Peter Dockrill. While we pride ourselves on our process, we are only human. If you spot a mistake, please let us know.
entry.summary: Scientists Discover Two Enormous Tears in a Tectonic Plate Beneath Iran ScienceAlert Seismic evidence for double slab tears at the Neo-Tethyan subduction–collision transition Nature Two tears in the Arabian Plate discovered beneath southeastern Iran — ScienceAlert UA.NEWS

entry.title: Parents want safer phones for kids. These companies are answering the call.
entry.body: As parents become increasingly concerned about the potential dangers of unrestricted smartphone access for children, a growing number of companies are developing devices specifically designed for kids. Today’s kid-friendly phones typically feature touchscreens, cameras, and communication capabilities similar to regular smartphones. However, the software on these devices is heavily modified to remove or restrict access to web browsers, social media, app stores, and other distractions. Parents can usually manage these devices through a companion app, allowing them to approve contacts, monitor locations, set screen time limits, select available apps, and, in some cases, receive alerts regarding cyberbullying, explicit content, or online predators. In addition to these modified devices, some companies offer a more minimalist approach, creating devices that focus solely on calling and texting. There are also home phones designed specifically for children, like Tin Can and the recently launched Pinwheel Home. Here’s a look at the major players shaping the kid-phone market. The Bark Phone The Bark Phone is probably one of the most popular kid-specific smartphones on the market. Built on Samsung Galaxy hardware and powered by Bark’s monitoring software, it only allows calls and texts with approved contacts. Bark continuously scans texts, emails, photos, and supported apps for signs of cyberbullying, grooming, suicidal ideation, sexual content, and other potential concerns, then sends alerts to parents. A big standout feature is that parents can gradually unlock web browsing, apps, and other features as their child matures. The phone also includes GPS tracking and screen-time management. Current pricing for the standard model is $240, plus a required wireless plan beginning at $29/month. Higher-tier plans add internet access and unlimited texting. Gabb Gabb is a well-known name in the kid-friendly phone category. Unlike Bark, however, Gabb focuses less on monitoring content and more on eliminating online risks altogether. Its phones don’t include social media, a browser, or an app store. Instead, children get calling, texting, and a carefully curated selection of preloaded apps, including a camera, calendar, and calculator. The company also touts its “worry-free” music streaming library with millions of songs. Additionally, parents can view location and manage certain device settings, while optional services such as “Gabb Guard” help block spam calls and unwanted texts. Current phone pricing starts around $159.99, with cellular service starting around $24.99 per month. Pinwheel With Pinwheel, parents approve every app, control contacts, schedule screen time, create custom routines, and monitor location history. One standout feature is the ability to create different “modes” throughout the day. For example, limiting the phone to calling and navigation during school hours before unlocking additional features after homework. Pinwheel phones start around $119, while the Caregiver Portal subscription begins at $14.99 per month without cell service. (Cellular service can be purchased separately through participating carriers.) The company recently launched two landline phones for $68 and $79. It also offers a smartwatch at $160. Teracube Thrive Launched in 2022, Teracube offers a tailored version of Android known as Thrive OS. This enables parents to approve every app download, filter web browsing, set app-specific and overall screen-time limits, monitor location, and create customized routines for school or bedtime. However, because it has more traditional smartphone features, it’s often recommended for older children. Thrive currently sells for $99, with plans starting at $35 per month. Ooma MyPhone Unlike the other products in this roundup, Ooma MyPhone isn’t a mobile phone at all. This kid-focused home phone is designed as a modern replacement for the traditional household landline. The service allows calls only between approved contacts through its Trusted Circle feature, offers scheduled Quiet Hours, provides address-based 911 service, sends emergency alerts when 911 is dialed, and lets parents review call logs through an online portal. There are no apps, internet browsing, texting, or social media. The phone costs $99.99, while service starts at $7.99 per month. Tin Can For $100, Tin Can resembles a landline phone with a distinctive tin can design, which is the inspiration behind its name. This device does not require a traditional phone jack, but connects via Wi-Fi. Only approved contacts can make calls, effectively preventing spam or unauthorized communications. Parents can easily manage contacts through a user-friendly companion app. Tin Can offers a free plan for calling other Tin Can users, as well as a $9.99 per month plan that allows calls to all approved contacts. Waffle A newer entrant in the space, Waffle recently opened preorders for its screen-free devices: Waffle Home ($119), a landline phone, and Waffle Go ($169), which looks like a portable walkie-talkie or kids’ toy with three simple buttons that can only make voice calls and listen to voice notes. Parents can approve contacts via the companion app, as well as see location and control when devices can call. The new phones will ship on November 23. TextNow, the Canadian telecommunications company, recently launched its new mobile phone for kids. and while it looks like a normal touchscreen smartphone, it doesn’t have an app store, social media, or unrestricted web access. Parents can see their kids’ location and battery life, as well as control things like the games they play and who they have in their contacts. costs $149.99 upfront, with a $19.99 per month plan.
entry.summary: As parents look for alternatives to unrestricted smartphones, a growing number of companies are building phones designed specifically for kids, from feature-limited mobile devices to minimalist home phones.

entry.title: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission - Space
entry.body: Send your name to Saturn's moon Titan with NASA's upcoming Dragonfly mission NASA is asking the public to send their names to Titan for an ambitious mission that will see a flying craft explore the Saturn moon in 2034, if all goes according to plan. We still may be some time away from sending humans to distant reaches of the solar system, but you can send your name to Saturn's moon Titan, which has the ingredients of life on its surface thanks to NASA's Dragonfly mission. Dragonfly is an SUV-sized nuclear-powered rotorcraft that NASA aims to launch towards Titan in 2028. The agency opened a special events page in late October to allow members of the public to put their name on the spacecraft. The names will be put upon a chip on Dragonfly during the spacecraft's assembly, and all names must be submitted before Jan. The agency says that the mission has no "ordinary itinerary," as Dragonfly aims to between areas miles (or kilometers) apart after arriving on the surface in 2034. "Nearly a billion miles away, an extraordinary destination awaits. Titan has an atmosphere, rivers and lakes, seasons, sweeping dunes and a landscape rich in organic material," NASA officials wrote in the event page. "Upon arrival in 2034, Dragonfly will fly from place to place on this intriguing world to uncover clues about this remarkable moon, and the chemistry that could help us understand the ingredients for life." Dragonfly will be one of just a few flying crafts on another world, with the first being NASA's plucky Ingenuity mini-helicopter that arrived on Mars along with the still-running Perseverance rover in 2021. Ingenuity was only designed to make five flights, but made it to 72 until its blades were damaged during a landing on Jan. NASA is now planning a SkyFall mission on Mars that would use three helicopters, and which may launch as soon as late 2028 for the Red Planet. Dragonfly, however, is not the first mission to Titan: that would be Huygens, which operated for just a few hours on Jan. 14, 2005 after deploying from the Cassini spacecraft. Huygens was the first lander on an outer solar system world, and measured Titan's atmosphere and took data from the surface. For its part, Cassini flew by Titan more than 100 times before the mission concluded in September 2017, providing valuable long-term data about the moon from above. Dragonfly aims to show the moon from up close for about 3.3 Earth years. Its destinations will include dunes and a young impact crater called Selk, according to NASA. "Dragonfly is expected to make one flight every one to two Titan days, which is called a Tsol and lasts about 16 Earth days," NASA officials added of the mission. Dragonfly will stop at a variety of geologic sites, where it will collect samples of surface material for analysis inside the rotorcraft by a suite of scientific instruments." Dragonfly's goals include learning more about prebiotic chemistry, or the conditions prior to life arising in a location; figuring out if Titan had habitable conditions in the past; and looking for "chemical indicators" of life based on water or hydrocarbons. Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams. entry.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Now Boots on Jailbroken PS5 and iPhone 17 Pro Max - TechPowerUp
entry.body: Saturday, November 7th 2026 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Now Boots on Jailbroken PS5 and iPhone 17 Pro Max Nintendo's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on November 5, and it is already running on a jailbroken PlayStation 5 and an iPhone. On PS5, Vampinity posted results in the GitHub repository for EglantinePS5, a PS5 port of a Switch emulator based on Eden. On firmware 12.40, the game loads a save, and Link can walk out of his house into Kokiri Forest at roughly 15 to 20 FPS. However, it runs out of memory a couple of minutes in, with heavy white fog and missing geometry in the forest. Vampinity calls it "nowhere near playable" and says Claude wrote the patches. Apparently, much of the shader work was borrowed from forks of Lichii, the emulator that got the remake running on PC on launch day. The iPhone port comes from developer Joe Jiang, who showed Kokiri Forest running on an iPhone 17 Pro Max. According to Jiang, memory was the hardest part, since the game wants about 9 GB while a single iPhone app is capped at 8,192 MB. He claims his approach keeps quality intact and peaks at just 3.4 GB when loading scenes. Apparently, the method isn't specific to Ocarina, and Jiang says it could bring any Switch or Switch 2 game to iOS, iPadOS, Apple TV, Android, and HarmonyOS. He hasn't released it yet, but it isn't the first Switch 2 game on iPhone. Mario Kart World booted on one shortly after the console's first jailbreak went public. The PS5 port, meanwhile, needs the Relapse jailbreak, which covers firmware 7.00 through 13.60. Neither is a practical way to play the game yet, but I'm sure Nintendo isn't too happy about the remake breaking containment this quickly. Sources: Vampinity on GitHub, Joe Jiang on X

entry.title: Billam-Smith stopped as Clarke repeats amateur win
entry.body: Billam-Smith stopped as Clarke repeats amateur win - Published Former cruiserweight world champion Chris Billam-Smith was knocked down and stopped for the first time in his career as Chev Clarke won their all-British non-title fight on Saturday. Londoner Clarke landed a big right hand at the start of the seventh round and although Billam-Smith beat the count, he was down again moments later after a barrage of punches. The contest was allowed to continue but the Bournemouth fighter looked unsteady on his legs and when Clarke connected with two more blows, the referee stepped in. Billam-Smith immediately protested against the decision, while Clarke stood in the middle of the ring shrugging his shoulders. Clarke moves to 13 wins with two defeats and inflicts the third professional defeat for Billam-Smith who also lost to Gilberto Ramirez in 2024 and Richard Riakporhe in 2019. "I do what champions do," said Clarke, who also beat Billam-Smith when they met in the amateur ranks a decade ago. Arsenal won and I won. My training camp was good and you saw that in the ring. I'll take all-comers going forward." The likes of heavyweight Johnny Fisher, Traitors star King Kenny and strongman Eddie Hall were all spotted watching on from ringside in a Copper Box arena that was far from full, with just the lower tier of seats open for fans. After a slow start to the contest with lots of holding, Clarke looked the sharper man as he landed some clean shots on the former world champion. In the second round, the Londoner landed a big overhand right to the side of Billam-Smith's head. Clarke also connected in the third round with a big uppercut and an overhand right that snapped back Billam-Smith's head. The former world champion, struggling to find his rhythm, was caught by another uppercut before Billam-Smith responded with a short right hook that made Clarke stumble back to his corner. But in the seventh round Clarke broke Billam-Smith down, scoring two quick knockdowns before the referee intervened. Fight promoter Dana White said after the fight that he felt the decision to stop the fight might have been a little premature. Bentley beats bloodied Mosley Jr and calls out Benn In the main support bout, Britain's Denzel Bentley beat a bloodied and brave Shane Mosley Jr, out-classing the American to win via a unanimous points decision. Bentley scored a big knockdown in the second round, landing a straight right hand that made Mosley stagger backwards before following up with another right hand that dropped him to the canvas. Mosley survived the count and the rest of the round but was routinely tagged by Bentley throughout the contest. The Londonder landed sharp shots off the back foot and in the fifth round drew blood over the right eye of Mosley. Bentley ended the fight strongly, boxing at times with his hands down and moving round his opponent as he landed eye-catching shots that attracted applause from the fans. After 10 rounds the scorecards read 96-94 96-93 95-94 in Bentley's favour, with the 31-year-old then pointing at Conor Benn in the audience and suggesting a potential future match-up between the two. Bentley was stripped of his WBO middleweight title in late October having agreed to fight Mosley instead of face his mandatory challenger. His interim title was previously elevated to a full world championship belt following Janibek Alimkhanuly's decision to move up to super-middleweight. entry.title: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Lando Norris and George Russell hoping for more rain in race after wet qualifying - BBC
entry.body: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rain - Published Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday. It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it. Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme. Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning. "When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it. "It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with. "I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high." The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year. Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row. Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year. Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage. Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect. - Norris takes pole in rain-delayed qualifying - Published4 hours ago - Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil - Published3 hours ago Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions. "We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace. "We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it. "I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly. "These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well. "It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake. "But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding." Russell reminds himself 'I haven't forgotten how to drive' For Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them. Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history. Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector. The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened. He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second. It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest. But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second. "Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying." He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there. "In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet." Alonso back at the sharp end The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created. With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light. This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it. Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again. "We took some risks in Q1, in Q2, where the conditions were a little bit unknown for everybody and we made it through and then our first Q3 of the year, so obviously pleased with that," Alonso said. "Then in Q3 I was expecting maybe a little bit more. I was first on the queue. But the tyres were ice cold in Q3, so I had no grip. "But yeah, I look at the times now, I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me. So yeah, it's way too much, you know, in front to really dream about any higher positions. "There is less time full throttle (in the wet), because there is no grip. So obviously they cannot exploit the extra power. "But still the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners. We still have a little bit of an issue there. "But no, I think these conditions is more about the level of risk you want to take. There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there." Alonso joins Norris and Russell in hoping for a wet race, feeling that if it's dry he will inevitably sink back to Aston Martin's natural level, especially with the long pit straight where Honda's lack of power will render him defenceless. Hamilton and Leclerc 'moving on' after talks The race promises much with Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all aiming to make progress from the back, even if the drivers feel that overtaking at Interlagos will be harder in this year's new-style cars than before. For Ferrari, it has been a difficult weekend, that started with clear-the-air talks between Leclerc and Hamilton after their first-lap battle cost them victory in Mexico last weekend. Both took new internal combustion engines, which gave them 10-place grid penalties, and then Hamilton's brand new one broke in final practice. So Ferrari gave him another one, leaving him at the back with Verstappen. The two multiple champions will be in competition to see who can make progress faster, and perhaps Ferrari are not so unhappy that Hamilton and Leclerc are separated by six places on the grid. Both drivers said all was well after their chat on Thursday evening. Leclerc - who returned to Europe between the two races to be at the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca - said: "It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long. "At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and it will be important to look ahead. "I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away. Of course, there is tension. Of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those then helps a whole lot." Hamilton added: "Me and Charles sat and spoke and we squashed it, and we're moving on. "We still have a huge amount of respect for each other and I'm glad we had a chat and now we move on. "We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes in those scenarios it takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side. "It's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other." Sao Paulo starting grid after penalties 1. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) 4. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) 6. entry.title: Vikings could end up with both Daniel Jones and Jonathan Taylor - NBC Sports
entry.body: Before Week 8, the Vikings had been linked to Colts running back Jonathan Taylor. After Week 8, Colts quarterback Daniel Jones became a potentially more attractive target for the Vikings. With the trade deadline less than three days away, why not both? The performance of quarterback Kyler Murray in the 19-15 loss to the Lions made the passing game a front-burner issue for the Vikings. But the running game remains not good enough. In Detroit, running back Jordan Mason had eight carries for 20 yards. Running back Aaron Jones had five carries for 22 yards. A package deal could allow the Colts to get the first-round pick they won’t get by trading Taylor alone. And perhaps the Colts could get another pick or two, perhaps contingent on the playing time and/or performance of either or both players. Regardless, with Minnesota previously linked to Taylor and currently linked to Jones, the Colts trading both to the same team could get Indianapolis something they won’t get by trading Taylor and Jones to two different teams — a first-round pick.

entry.title: 'The worst conditions in my 35-year career' - commentating in the FA Cup fog
entry.body: 'The worst conditions in my 35-year career' - commentating in the FA Cup fog - Published One of the most important attributes for a commentator is to be able to see the action you are trying to describe but that became a luxury for BBC Sport's Steve Bower when Altrincham hosted Notts County in an FA Cup tie on Saturday. As thick fog enveloped the Moss Lane ground, he could barely see what was going on in a first-round game being televised live on BBC Two. "One of the more challenging of my long career, that's about 35 years now," said Bower about the experience. "I was reminded by a colleague - maybe I'm a jinx - that we had a similar thing on the BBC about three years ago when we did York against Wigan in the first round and the fog came in. From where we were, opposite the dugouts, once the play went to the centre circle and beyond, we couldn't see a thing. "We couldn't see which team had the ball, let alone which player had the ball after about the 60th minute. Bearing in mind it went to extra-time, it was challenging. "I just kept looking down at my phone and it was text message after text message from people saying, 'You're sounding great, but I can't see a thing'. In the end, you have to roll with it and do the best you can." 'It's like a spot-the-ball competition' National League Altrincham were on for an upset when they took a 2-1 lead against the League One side but a late Callum Roberts equaliser for County took the game to extra-time before the visiting side won on penalties. "The frustrating thing is that for an hour it was a really good FA Cup tie, it had everything," said Bower. "It was on for another giant-killing script but then the frustrating thing is that it becomes a non-event because, without stating the obvious, people can't see half of it. "Also, it's not then about the tactics, or the shape of it, or the aggression, or the effort because you just can't see it. As a spectacle in trying to describe a game like you normally would, it's impossible." Bower's radio colleagues were not faring much better as they tried to work out what was going on. "I can just about see the bright white numbers on their shirts, but I am struggling to see what is happening on the far side of the pitch," said BBC Radio Nottingham commentator Adam Hassell. Former Notts County striker Mark Stallard, who was also speaking on BBC Radio Nottingham, said: "We're looking around, and here in the press box no-one knows where the ball is! It's like a spot-the-ball competition. "I played in the Notts County cup side against Wimbledon when it was abandoned - they equalised in the second half and I didn't see any of it!" Stallard later said: "We genuinely cannot see the linesman or the players on the far side. It's slightly farcical having to commentate for radio listeners." 'A very unique evening all around' The managers of both teams were on the touchline but even they were struggling as tactics went out of the window. "[Notts County boss] Martin Paterson said credit to Altrincham, they were the better team in the first half and, as for the second, I couldn't see it. He was laughing," said Bower. "Neil Gibson, the Altrincham manager, was saying, 'We were trying to get down to pitchside to look tactically at what they had done after those four substitutions. Is it a back four? Have they gone to a box midfield? But we just couldn't see'. "So even from a tactical point of view, the players had to stop playing long diagonal passes and things like that because they couldn't see, they were just having to play short five, 10 yard passes so the game changed in that sense as well. "It was very, very close to getting called off." Bower said some of the players told him they couldn't see both goals or the corner flags from the centre circle. "It will live long in the memory, that's for sure," said Bower. "Even on the penalties, you were having to rely on the crowd's reaction before committing to the tale. "You couldn't see the goalkeeper's save, for instance, until the first replay came in." The penalties took place in front of Altrincham fans and, while Bower had replays to call on, the Notts County fans "couldn't have seen anything" from the other end as they had to go on "crowd reaction". "Obviously, the Altrincham fans all had their phones on with the lights trying to put the Notts County players off as well in the fog. A unique evening all around." entry.summary: BBC Sport commentator Steve Bower gives an insight into trying to commentate when thick fog engulfs a stadium and you can barely see the action.

entry.title: 'Curtains for Robinson' or can floundering Aberdeen boss survive?
entry.body: 'Curtains for Robinson' or can floundering Aberdeen boss survive? - Published Stephen Robinson has vowed to "keep fighting until told otherwise" as his Aberdeen future hangs by a thread following the "unacceptable" 4-0 defeat by Hibernian. The Pittodrie manager, who was already under intense pressure, had labelled the visit of Marink Reedijk's side - bottom of the table going into the game - as a must-win. But his bedraggled team were no match for Hibs, and home fans began streaming for the exit at 2-0 down. By the bitter end of the four-goal mauling, chants of "You're getting sacked in the morning" rang out and those that had stayed vented their ire at a miserable-looking Robinson as he made a beeline for the tunnel. "Stephen Robinson looks beleaguered down there, a man lost," said Aberdeen legend Willie Miller on BBC Sportsound. The television cameras then panned to Adrian Bevington, the chief executive appointed in September. A month and a half into the job, he has a big decision to make. Aberdeen now occupy the relegation play-off place, above only Kilmarnock, after a fourth Scottish Premiership defeat in five. "I don't know [what the implications may be], I don't make that decision," Robinson said post-match. "I'm Aberdeen manager until told otherwise, I'll keep fighting until told otherwise. "The performance isn't acceptable, the result isn't acceptable. "It's the story of the season - if you don't take chances, you lose matches. They had five opportunities, scored four of them. That's the difference." Former Celtic striker Chris Sutton says it feels like "the club is too big for him, the job is too big for him" and suggested the 51-year-old should "do the honourable thing and walk away", but is "probably going to end up getting the sack". Poor recruitment & 'major issues' Pre-match, the Aberdeen head coach had insisted his players knew the "magnitude" of the situation in front of them. It didn't seem that way, as they went on to turn in an insipid performance, spurning a few decent opportunities before completely capitulating in the second half. "It's utterly embarrassing," said Miller. "They look ashen-faced down there. Robinson was depressed after the Falkirk result [1-0 home defeat] and this one is 10 times worse than that, so I don't know how he'll cope with it." Robinson, appointed in March, has won just six of 21 league games, losing 11. He steadied the ship last season and steered the club clear of relegation worries, but the trap door has already started to loom. "He has now made sweeping changes in personnel," Miller said. Fifteen players were signed in the summer. Few have made a positive impact. "Recruitment is vital and when you look at the performances, the recruitment is poor. The players aren't up to scratch, not up to playing at this level and dealing with high-ish expectations," added Miller. "I'm not talking about trophies, I'm talking about being in the top six and they're nowhere near that. There's major issues that have to be confronted." Should Aberdeen dispense with Robinson, it would be their sixth managerial change since Derek McInnes left in 2021. "I don't know [if he can survive this]," Miller added. "He had an opportunity to get to a cup final. They lost that and then get beat 4-0 by a team at the bottom of the table. Put all that together and there's major decisions to be made over this weekend." Robinson 'not the right fit' for Aberdeen Aberdeen have now lost four consecutive games in all competitions. At home, they've won two of seven in the league. They've scored three goals in their past six league outings at Pittodrie, and they all came in the 3-1 win over St Mirren. The Dons are the joint lowest scorers in the league, alongside the Buddies, on 12 goals. "You do get that feeling it could now be curtains for Robinson," former Scotland midfielder Michael Stewart said on Premier Sports. "You get a sense sometimes with the nature of a result, it can be what finally pushes something to the point of no return." His colleagues Alan Hutton and Charlie Mulgrew, a former Aberdeen defender, concurred. "I felt like [the players] gave up towards the end," Hutton added, with Hibs scoring twice in the last six minutes. "The reaction of the fans, to boo the team and manager, doesn't look great coming into an international break. "I've watched Aberdeen this season and I don't see an identity from them, I don't see a clear plan moving forward. There's been so much change in terms of personnel and formation. I just don't see it in the pitch, it's as if they're hoping for something to happen." Northern Irishman Robinson earned the move to Pittodrie on the back of three successive top-six finishes and a League Cup triumph with St Mirren, but he wasn't a popular choice among some Aberdeen fans. "I don't think Robinson seems to be the right fit for Aberdeen," Mulgrew said. "His style with his St Mirren team, it's not what the fans at Pittodrie like to see on the pitch. They tried to go with wingers today but there was no end product, they huffed and puffed. "Chances fell to [Kevin] Nisbet but he looked like he had no confidence. I think that'll be the end for Robinson." What are the fans saying? Colin: We're a relegation waiting to happen. I wasn't thrilled to see Robinson to take over but I expected him at least to make us hard working and organised. But I can't believe how sloppy and passive we were. And, apart from Ayoub Mouloua, there's no pace, creativity or goal threat from anywhere. Bill: Robinson was a panic purchase at the time. He has been always well out of his depth and he must go but the problem is higher than him, which needs to be acknowledged by the board. Mikey: Changing so many players at once was a mistake. Brought too much risk and placed too much trust in a manager just in the door who was stepping up a level. He looks like doesn't want to be there any more. Greig: Time is up, it's clearly not working. Zero improvement in the playing squad/performances this season. It runs deeper than Robinson, six managers, likely seven since Dave Cormack took over and McInnes left the club. Serious questions have to be asked about the club's direction from the top down. Sandy: Robinson says he will keep on fighting I see no signs of fighting. I sincerely hope Dave Cormack has someone on the backburner or it's Championship for us next season. Related topics - Published18 June 2023
entry.summary: Will the "unacceptable" 4-0 home defeat to fellow strugglers Hibernian signal the end of Stephen Robinson's Aberdeen tenure?

entry.title: Sylvester Stallone Says His 20-Year Rivalry With Arnold Schwarzenegger Only Ended When He Ran for Governor and Wasn’t ‘Doing Movies Anymore’
entry.body: Sylvester Stallone is reminiscing about his now-infamous rivalry with fellow action star Arnold Schwarzenegger through the 1980s and 1990s — and why they only laid down the hatchet when the latter ran for governor of California. In a recent interview on “The Rest Is Entertainment” podcast, the “Rocky” actor answered whether he felt the competition between the two actors shaped his career and led him to take risks. “Yeah, it did,” said Stallone. “You know, we were very confrontational.” He continued: “Because you have two people arriving at the beginning of a different genre and we both want to be in charge of that genre. I never wanted to be an action guy, but I did ‘First Blood’ and I said, ‘This is interesting because action films, if done right, are modern mythology. It’s like what they used to do, you know, ‘The Iliad’ and ‘The Odyssey’ and Hercules and Achilles.’” “So, I see this guy, and I could tell right away he’s going to be a problem,” Stallone said, referring to Schwarzenegger. “You know, we were at the Golden Globe Awards, and he’s sitting there and he’s eyeballing me, and — we call that stink eye — I said, ‘Okay, all right. I got it, pal.’ And then he wins.” The two continued to vie for the title of top action star, with both actors liking “to challenge” one another, said Stallone. “We’re both physical, and now, who’s going to be the vanguard, the leader in that genre? So I do ‘Rambo,’ he does ‘Commando,’ and it went back and forth, back and forth, on and off screen. It was very contentious, trust me. Which I enjoyed.” The two later partnered on the movie-themed chain restaurant Planet Hollywood in 1991, but Stallone noted that they wouldn’t even get on stage together to give a speech. Their rivalry “wasn’t put to bed until 20 years later,” said Stallone, when Schwarzenegger decided to run for governor. “We went to the same cigar place. I said, ‘Enough of this. We’re not in competition anymore.’ He’s not doing movies anymore. Thank you very much for waking me up and lighting a fire under me. And he felt the same way.” To this day, they remain friendly — “We’re always going to be competitive… That’s the nature of the beast, and I enjoy it. But we’re not as financially competitive anymore,” Stallone concluded.

entry.title: AI Could Make Filmmaking Costlier Than the 35mm Era, Korean Pioneers Warn at Taiwan Creative Content Fest
entry.body: AI is already slashing the cost of commercials, but runaway token fees and piecemeal revisions could leave feature producers paying more than in the days of 35mm film, a Korean AI production pioneer told Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Kim Kwang-jib, founder and CEO of AI content studio Studio Meta-K, said that with the most expensive commercial tools, the token bill alone for a 100-minute film can top KRW500 million ($366,000). AI companies are all losing money, he said, and are keeping prices low as a marketing play. “If they raise token costs roughly tenfold, it could go above what the films we’re shooting now cost,” Kim said. “KRW500 million could become KRW5 billion ($3.66 million).” Hollywood, with KRW200 billion ($146.6 million) budgets, could absorb that and still make very cheap AI films, Kim said. Korean, Taiwanese and other Asian features typically shoot live action and VFX for KRW3 billion-KRW5 billion ($2.2 million-$3.66 million), and a tenfold jump would force them to ask whether AI is efficient at all. He drew a line back to celluloid. Preproduction was meticulous when every take burned through film stock, then digital let crews shoot and cut freely without extra cost. With AI, every re-render is paid for again. If a client sends 10 changes at once, Kim said, Studio Meta-K can make them all and re-render a single time, paying for just one extra pass. If the same 10 changes arrive one a day over 10 days, the studio has to re-render 10 times and pay 10 times over. The final budget, he said, comes down to how few rounds of revisions there are. “Unless the preproduction stage is made solid, I think AI could end up spending even more money than in the 35mm film era,” he said. Lee Sang-wook, head of the AI Content Lab at MBC C&I, a subsidiary of Korean broadcaster MBC, said budgeting is harder still because the tools keep moving. His lab’s 139-minute feature “Raphael” took around a year and four months to make, and new tools and updates arrive weekly. “If you apply technology from a year ago, the scenes look very old,” Lee said. He added that a single shot on “Raphael” sometimes tied up around 10 artists for an entire day. The film was made with emerging directors discovered by the lab, who raised investment and set up their own studio, and the lab’s work drew backing from Korea’s Ministry of Culture, Sports and Tourism and the Korea Creative Content Agency. “Raphael” will open in Korean cinemas on Nov. The lab began experimenting with generative AI shorts in 2024, before packaging AI content as a genre strand, “The Prompt: Next Drama,” on Korean streamer Wavve. “When we made AI short films in 2024, the market reaction was very cold, in Korea as well,” Lee said. He wanted to face audiences directly, he said, and a cinema release can move to streaming later while the reverse order is hard. He also wanted to show that AI studios, many of which work on an outsourcing model, can take commercial bets through IP development. On commercials, Kim cited a Pizza Hut spot that aired on TV last year, which took about eight months and roughly KRW2 billion ($1.4 million) to produce. A version Studio Meta-K made in-house took about two weeks and around KRW30 million ($22,000), or about 2% of the cost. In advertising, he said, production costs can fall by more than 90%. Drama is a harder sell. Kim does not think audiences will yet pay to watch fully AI films or series, so he favors a hybrid model with star actors. A scene requiring more than 500 extras, with costumes, hair and makeup to match, could be generated with AI, leaving only the close-ups of the leads to shoot live. The company is producing war scenes with AI for KBS program “History Special.” His larger pitch was to reverse the pipeline. Rather than calling in AI after a shoot and edit have already eaten the budget, Studio Meta-K is testing building an entire 100-minute film at film-like quality in preproduction, then reshooting only the parts that feel off, such as emotional bust shots. For now perhaps 50 of those 100 minutes would need to be reshot in live action, Kim said, but he expects that eventually nothing will need shooting at all. Kim founded Studio Meta-K in 2022 as a K-drama and film company alongside well-known drama directors and writers. Its stated aim is to use AI to cut production costs and own IP rather than take outsourced work, and it has completed more than 100 commercial projects. This year the company was selected for two government R&D projects worth about KRW15 billion ($11 million) combined to build SaaS-based platforms, leading a consortium that includes an MBC subsidiary, KBS and MBN. Studio Meta-K raised around KRW3 billion ($2.2 million) in a Series A last year and around KRW10 billion ($7.3 million) this month, and is preparing for an IPO next year. The company is also turning Im Kwon-taek’s 1993 classic “Seopyeonje” into an animated feature, re-editing the original footage and converting it into animation with AI for a theatrical release next summer. The project, a collaboration with Busan’s Dongseo University, has the director’s involvement. Studio Meta-K has several animated features in production simultaneously. The two companies split on open-source tools. Kim said free open-source models have improved sharply, and on one animated project Studio Meta-K builds easy shots with open-source tools and reserves paid commercial tools for difficult ones. Lee said MBC C&I steers away from open-source because it cannot verify the transparency of the training data, noting that no AI model yet meets EU AI Act guidelines. The company has also joined C2PA. Lee said delivery to streamers is tougher than meeting cinema DCP specs, since platforms analyze files mechanically rather than by eye, and AI output still struggles with requirements such as bitrate and color grading. Kim expects issues like color depth and bitrate to be solved soon. On jobs, Kim said crews of hundreds on a single scene will grow rarer, and roles such as drone operators and set work could largely disappear. Some companies are already keeping preproduction staff and laying off production crews in favor of co-producing with Studio Meta-K, he said. “I don’t see AI replacing that workforce,” Kim said. “I personally think workers who have learned AI will replace workers who haven’t.” Lee compared the shift to the arrival of sound, which cost theater musicians their jobs, and the move from film to digital cameras, which raised the editor’s importance. He predicted new roles including previsualization artists who break down scripts into previs, and continuity supervisors charged with keeping locations and characters consistent. One studio in Korea already has more than 50 AI artists working together, he said, and technical directors will matter more as the technology advances. Spatial consistency, he added, is harder to achieve than character consistency. Actors, Lee said, have warmed to AI. On a daily drama, previs of a dangerous accident scene turned cast skepticism into approval once performers saw AI would handle shots that could injure them. He does not believe AI can ultimately replace actors’ emotional detail. “If the ones consuming my content were AI, I don’t know, but the viewers and audiences who consume it are still people,” Lee said. Archin Yen, director and VFX supervisor at WWWIND Studio, moderated the session. Asked how directors can keep AI from flattening their vision, Kim said AI tools can be learned in a few months, while film grammar such as the 180-degree rule, lenses and editing can take years. Most AI videos he sees default to eye-level, front-on bust shots that film and TV rarely use, he said. “Every VFX company in the world uses the same tools, but I think it differs depending on who uses them,” he said. “In the end, I think that human 5% decides the quality.”
