entry.title: ‘Pokemon’ Anime Studio OLM Trains AI Coloring Tool on Just Three Frames in Japan Government-Backed Project
entry.body: OLM, the Japanese animation group behind the “Pokemon” anime series and films, has developed an AI coloring tool that picks up a show’s look from just three hand-painted frames, OLM Digital board director Yotsukura Tatsuo said at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. The tool came out of ANIMINS, a 15-month research project Yotsukura led under GENIAC, a generative AI program overseen by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry. The project, which looked at how anime creators could put AI to use, wrapped in February. Because AI models usually need vast amounts of training data that studios struggle to assemble, OLM took the opposite approach. An artist colors three frames by hand, and the system learns that show’s line shapes and color palette on the spot in about 90 seconds, then colors each remaining frame in around 15 seconds. The more frames an artist paints by hand, the more accurate it becomes. “Strictly speaking, it isn’t generative AI,” Yotsukura said. Training only on a production’s own frames means no other works are harmed, he added, and the tool can adapt immediately when a new character or creature, such as a dragon, appears. The point OLM most wanted to stress, he said, is that it fits into existing anime workflows without disrupting them. At proof-of-concept stage, Yotsukura estimated it has cut painting workload by around 30%, though the checkers who review every colored frame have somewhat more to do. Toon Boom Animation, the Canadian maker of animation software Harmony and Storyboard Pro, is tackling the same bottleneck. Product marketing director Harry Ravelomanantsoa said the beta of the coloring tool in Ember, the company’s AI suite, is wrapping up, and in-betweening is expected to enter beta within a couple of weeks. One Manila studio that tested the coloring tool cut the painting time on a scene of 90 seconds to two minutes from 15 hours to two or three. OLM employs around 600 staff across Japan, Malaysia, Thailand and the U.S. “As you probably saw passing through the first floor, we make the ‘Pokemon’ anime – not the games – including the TV series and the theatrical films,” Yotsukura said, referring to the 2026-27 Pokemon Asia Championship Series: Taiwan Premier Ball League, held Nov. 7–8 on a lower floor of the Taipei Nangang Exhibition Center, where TCCF is running Nov. The group’s slate also includes kids’ titles “Beyblade” and “Hanakappa” and the adult-skewing “The Apothecary Diaries.” Yotsukura, who also serves as CTO for the group’s Malaysian and Thai arms, noted that an in-house R&D division is unusual for a Japanese animation company. The group is experimenting with AI for in-betweening as well. But Yotsukura said the bigger gains may come from indirect uses across productions that involve more than 100 staff. With a startup partner from the GENIAC project, OLM is exploring anime-specific AI agents that could help new directors or production managers joining a series that has run for a decade or more, for instance by recalling what a director intended for a given cut. Agents could also speed up approvals and license management for secondary uses of its titles, which Yotsukura called the most revenue-critical part of the business. Because those areas are sensitive, OLM is proceeding with care, he said. Yotsukura likened the gap between AI demos and production reality to gacha, the Japanese capsule-toy machines where each JPY500 ($3.30) turn may or may not yield the prize you want – roughly what an AI generation credit costs, he said. AI gets close enough to 80% to raise expectations. “Raising it from there to 90 or 100% turns into work so hard it can make you heartsick.” Hobbyists may be happy with 80%, he said, but professional animators need tools that return their direction 100% of the time and let them make corrections. Anime is also highly sensitive to color, and AI tools that edit an image can shift its RGB values even when the result looks fine. “The creative stays with the artist, and the mechanical time goes to AI, to Ember,” Ravelomanantsoa said. Yotsukura said he agreed almost entirely with that split. “AI can only do what it has learned,” he said, adding that the kind of images that move audiences in cinemas, and the never-before-seen ideas behind hit anime, still have to come from people. He compared AI’s arrival to that of 3DCG, which took around 20 years to be accepted in anime. “Twenty years ago, I kept rejecting it, saying, ‘How could this ever be used in anime?’ Now it’s unthinkable for anime not to have 3DCG,” he said. AI will move far faster, Yotsukura said, because its quality is already high from the start. Charles Beirnaert, chief creative officer of Blue Spirit, the French studio behind Netflix’s “Blue Eye Samurai,” said the studio uses no AI at all on that series. “We’re not allowed to use AI for the Netflix projects,” he said. Blue Spirit asks every time at what stage AI might be permitted, he added, and the answer is always no – though he acknowledged the rule may not apply to every Netflix partner. On an Amazon series, the studio may use AI only to pre-visualize characters and robots, with none of it reaching the final image. Netflix’s published guidelines for production partners, issued in August 2025, require them to disclose any intended use of generative AI, with written approval needed for certain uses, including generative AI material in the final product. Away from those shows, Beirnaert’s team is testing AI on a series it is greenlighting as a conventional CG show, with a shorter YouTube version under consideration. A team of around 20 spent roughly three months on the traditional pilot. Using AI, one person recreated that work, covering everything from modeling and layout to animation, within days. The animation fell short of the original, Beirnaert said, but the backgrounds came out better. “For me, AI is not meant to replace animators. The day every animator is replaced, I will change job and do something else,” Beirnaert said. The two diverged when an audience member asked how much money AI could save. Beirnaert offered what he called a random estimate of €1 million on an €8 million budget, and said AI may help projects that stall at 80%–90% financed find the rest. Yotsukura said OLM is in a different position: it is brought in only after a budget is fixed, and sees AI as a way to gain more creative freedom within that budget rather than to shrink it. A year or two ago, the question was how many staff AI could replace, he said. Now it is shifting toward new shots that AI tools made possible. Moderator Kao Chieh, a lecturer at Shih Chien University, put the split down to a difference between Eastern and Western animation companies. Japanese anime already has creativity in abundance, Yotsukura said, but technology could play a bigger part, with the two driving the industry forward like a pair of wheels. “I think ‘not using AI’ is probably no longer an option from here on,” he said.

entry.title: Chomet Denies AI Use In Dior Ad, Cites 'Automated Interpolation' - Cartoon Brew
entry.body: Four-time Oscar-nominated French director Sylvain Chomet has responded to questions about the potential use of generative AI in a new ad campaign he helmed for luxury fashion brand Dior, which had been explicitly promoted as hand-drawn in the original materials released with the short, including a behind-the-scenes video. Speaking exclusively with Variety, Chomet and his producer Aton Soumache unequivocally rejected viral speculation that many of the frames of the short were generated using artificial intelligence. According to Soumache, the ad was created over seven months by a team of 20 artists, six of them animators. While denying claims of AI use, Soumache did tell Variety: “We used an automated interpolation system for a very small part of the process, but the film itself is traditional 2D animation.” It’s an interesting distinction that deserves a bit of scrutiny. First, the original ad was presented as hand-drawn by Dior in its exclusive announcement with WWD (Women’s Wear Daily): “The film we’ve created together for Dior is all hand-drawn using techniques that go back to the 1940s,” Dior’s creative director Jonathan Anderson said in the piece. That description, however, leaves out a major detail about the production process, according to the filmmakers’ own explanation. Automated interpolation is not necessarily the same thing as generative AI, and encompasses a range of different technologies, including but not limited to AI-powered tools capable of synthesizing new frames. Neither filmmaker identified the software used or explained precisely how the process worked. Soumache characterizes the interpolation as a “very small part of the process,” which also leaves considerable room for interpretation. Is he referencing a small percentage of the finished frames, the number of shots, or maybe a limited portion of the production schedule? Without knowing what he’s referring to, or even which technology was used, it’s impossible to a concrete conclusion regarding the extent of automation in the finished film. Of the extra fingers, blurry tree stars, morphing dog collar, and uncanny bee tailors that fueled the original speculation, Chomet offered a more conventional explanation: that his team employed established animation techniques in which exaggerated or overlapping shapes convey movement. Unlike the unspecified interpolation system, these techniques have existed for generations in animation production. They’re foundational to the craft of hand-drawn animation. Whether they explain every instance identified by viewers online is another question, and one that cannot be settled by a general explanation of the technique. None of this proves that generative AI was used. Nor does the employment of artists over a seven-month production necessarily rule it out. And that’s been the main problem since the beginning of this ordeal. The language from primary sources was explicit in describing the film as hand-drawn. Now, the filmmaker and producer have acknowledged that intermediate frames were generated through interpolation. But they have not provided sufficient evidence to remove doubt about the potential use of AI. Until they or Dior provide more specific information about their interpolation tools and workflow, their statements have done little to assuage suspicions. Given Dior’s status in the fashion industry and its emphasis on the short as a celebration of traditional craftsmanship, greater transparency would go a long way toward resolving the questions surrounding its production.

entry.title: Papua New Guinea’s Most Expensive Film, ‘Mussau: The First Song,’ Wraps Shoot, Unveils First Looks (EXCLUSIVE)
entry.body: Papua New Guinea’s most expensive film to date, the $4.5 million historical drama “Mussau: The First Song,” has wrapped principal photography after a 40-day shoot across two provinces. Filming took place on Mussau Island in New Ireland Province and in Goroka, in Eastern Highlands Province. PNG-based producer NAFA Productions celebrated the wrap at a Thanksgiving event in Port Moresby on Saturday. Government figures at the event included Belden Norman Namah, Minister for Arts, Culture and Tourism; Chief Secretary Ivan Pomaleu; and Chief Censor Jim Abani. Indian director Bijukumar Damodaran, a three-time Indian National Film Award winner, is at the helm. Parul Agrawal produces, and Noelene Taula Wunum is executive producer. Inspired by a true story and set in the 1930s, the film centers on Taula Livovoa, a young islander who walks away from tribal violence and takes up a faith that is new to him. His choice sets off a sweeping social change that the producers rank among the South Pacific’s most remarkable. The dialogue is in six languages: Mussau, Emirau, Agarabi, Gadsup, Tok Pisin and English. Some of them are indigenous languages with small numbers of speakers that are at risk of dying out. The producers present the film as a way to protect the country’s linguistic and cultural heritage and bring it to a global audience. Much of the cast was drawn from the local community, and many are acting on screen for the first time. Some had never watched a film before. Several roles are played by great-grandchildren of the real people whose lives inspired the story. Two British actors round out the ensemble. Mussau Island has little infrastructure and patchy communications, which made the shoot hard to pull off. The 120-person crew, 20 of them technicians from India, spent 30 hours at sea crossing the Pacific to reach the island. Temporary lodging and facilities were set up there. Islanders helped throughout, including on sequences shot in the sea at high tide. The unit then moved on to Goroka to finish filming. “This has been one of the most challenging and rewarding journeys of my filmmaking career,” Damodaran said. “The people of Mussau welcomed us into their lives, their culture and their history, and their contribution has been invaluable. Having descendants of the original historical figures portray some of these characters, alongside community members who had never seen a film before, made this journey even more profound.” Hilda Tanimia wrote the story. The screenplay is by Jennifer Litau, who also served as translator, along with Joses Imona and Damodaran. The cinematographer is Yedhu Radhakrishnan and the editor is Davis Palakal Manuel. Arnold Laena handled production design and Gladice John designed the costumes. The music comes from Music Masters of PNG and the Murat Choir. The cast includes Freddy Sutchiff, Candy Ali, Daniel Lee Hird, Kevin Jackson, Jamie Napo, Calvin, Alan Balalua, Frank Eke and Dolvin Aite. NAFA Productions wants the film to bow at a top-tier international festival in 2027. It also hopes the film will be Papua New Guinea’s official entry for best international feature at the 100th Academy Awards. Damodaran has made that run once before. His earlier PNG–India co-production “Papa Buka” was the first film Papua New Guinea ever submitted to the Oscars’ international feature race.

entry.title: Meet the Rising Stars Competing for Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys
entry.body: Meet the Rising Stars Competing for Best New Artist at the Latin Grammys One of the most anticipated categories at the Latin Grammys is Best New Artist. In the past, the once-in-a-lifetime award has gone to people who have gone on to become major stars: Puerto Rican disruptors Calle 13, Colombian superstar Karol G, and Mexican singer-songwriter Silvana Estrada. Recent winners include Venezuelan prodigy Joaquina, Bogotá-based pop girl Ela Taubert, and Mexico City’s alt-star Paloma Morphy. For the 2026 ceremony, which takes place on Nov. 12 in Las Vegas, 11 upstarts from Latin America, the U.S., and Spain are hoping to take the honor next. With 11 nominees this year instead of the usual 10, Rolling Stone caught up with four of the promising nominees ahead of the biggest night in Latin music. We spoke to Aria Vega, who is bringing the sound of Colombia’s Caribbean coast to the mainstream; rising Mexican-American singer Delilah, who has been blending genres with ease; Fabian, the son of Peruvian icon Gian Marco, who is blazing his own trail; and Mexican-Swedish maverick Sofia Monroy. Aria Vega What does the nomination for Best New Artist mean to you? It means a lot because it represents more than just me. It represents my family, my people, my team, Barranquilla, and everybody who’s believed in me along the way. It also feels like an invitation to bring my world to a bigger audience. I’m still at the beginning of my journey, and having this kind of recognition gives me even more motivation to keep creating, experimenting, and showing people what I’m capable of. I’ve worked so hard to get here, and to have the music and everything we’ve been building recognized in this way is incredibly special. I’m grateful, excited and honestly just hungry for everything that’s still ahead. How do you feel about representing Barranquilla and the culture of Colombia’s Caribbean coast?It’s a huge responsibility, but also something I do very naturally because it’s who I am. I don’t have to pretend to be from the coast or try to represent it in a certain way. It’s already in my accent, my humor, my music, my personality, and the way I see the world. I love showing people a different perspective of Barranquilla and the Caribbean coast. There’s so much creativity, beauty, character, and culture there. I want people to see us beyond the stereotypes and experience the coast through my eyes. If I can make somebody curious about where I’m from, or make someone from back home feel proud to see themselves reflected in what I do, that means everything to me. You recently met Shakira during her residency in Madrid. Meeting Shakira was incredibly special. She’s someone who has represented Colombia and Latin culture on a global level for so many years, so being able to share that moment with her was surreal. She’s opened doors for so many Colombian artists and I have so much respect for what she’s built. Of course I’d love to work with her one day! Imagine two Barranquilleras in the studio together. That would be something very special. I think we’d have a lot of fun! What can we expect from your debut album that you’re working on? My album Costeñita Core is my baby. It’s a project where I’m putting together all the different pieces of who I am and the world I’ve been building. It’s very personal, but it’s also playful, colorful, feminine, a little chaotic, and full of personality. Musically, I want people to discover different sides of me. I’m exploring sounds, emotions, and ideas while staying connected to my Caribbean roots. Visually, I’m also putting a lot of myself into the project. I want people to feel like they’re stepping into my world when they listen to it. It’s my universe, my perspective, and my way of showing people what “Costeñita Core” really means. I’m so excited for everyone to finally experience it. Delilah How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist? It’s honestly a dream come true. It’s one of those things you hope and dream about as an artist, but you never really know if or when it’s going to happen. To be recognized by my peers, fellow musicians, and members of the Latin Recording Academy is such a huge honor. It means that the music I’m putting out into the world is being heard, and that means everything to me. It’s also a reminder of how far I’ve come and all the people who have believed in me and supported me along the way. I know there is still so much I want to do and so much I want to explore as an artist. This nomination makes me even more excited to keep creating, growing, and sharing my music with the world. What does it mean for you to represent women in música mexicana in this category? It’s a huge honor and something I take very seriously. I want to do the category justice and make sure my voice and my sound are heard and heard well. I want to represent my music, my fans, and everyone who has supported me in a way that makes them proud. Música mexicana has such a rich history. I feel incredibly lucky to be part of a generation that gets to bring new ideas and sounds into the genre while still honoring its roots. I hope I can contribute something meaningful to that. This is especially meaningful to me as a young woman, but also as a big sister. I take that responsibility seriously because I know how important it is for young girls to see women being themselves, having a voice, and making their own choices. I hope I can show other young women that they don’t have to fit into a certain mold to belong in this industry. They can be themselves and do things their own way. How would you say that being both Mexican and American influences the way that you make music? It influences my music in so many ways, sometimes in ways I don’t even think about consciously. Growing up in a bilingual household, both cultures have always been part of my everyday life. You can hear it in the way I mix English and Spanish, in different touches throughout my songs, and even in the way I express myself. My background, the music I grew up listening to, and the different influences around me are all incorporated into what I create. I don’t feel like I have to separate those parts of myself. They’re both who I am and I think that combination is a big part of my sound. What was the experience like opening for Natanael Cano’s concerts at the Estadio GNP Seguros in Mexico City? It has been an incredible experience both times. Mexico City has such an amazing energy, and being able to perform there and share my music with those audiences, especially opening for an artist like Natanael Cano, is something I’ll always remember and those experiences hold a really special place in my heart. It’s also meaningful to be the only woman to have had that opportunity. I feel proud to represent women in that space and show that I can be myself and do things my own way. I don’t feel like I have to change who I am or fit into a certain expectation to belong on that stage. Being able to connect with those audiences while staying true to myself has made both experiences even more meaningful. Fabian What does it mean for you to be nominated for Best New Artist? It still feels pretty surreal. I think it’ll really hit me once I get to Vegas. It’s something I’ve dreamt about for a long time, especially because it’s one of those things you only get to experience once in your career. I’m mostly excited about the opportunity to represent Peru and show people just how much talent and how many new, interesting proposals are coming out of our country. I feel really proud to be part of that. Your sister Nicole was previously nominated for Best New Artist in 2022. How do you feel about following in your family’s legacy? My family was incredibly excited [about the nomination]. They’ve seen all the work and love that’s gone into this since day one. Nicole actually cried when I called her, which was really sweet. I can only imagine what it’s like to see your little brother experience something you’ve experienced yourself. I’m especially excited that my first Grammy experience is something I get to share with her, especially since she’s also nominated twice this year. It’ll definitely make the whole thing even more special. I’ve always thought that sharing music with my family is one of the biggest blessings. It’s pretty much all we’ve ever known at home. Growing up, I was always taught to approach this career with a lot of respect, love, and appreciation for what it means to make music. I think those values have stuck with me from the beginning. At the same time, I want to find my own way of doing things and build something that feels very much like me. How are you carving out your own space in Latin pop music? When I moved from Lima to Los Angeles at nine, I was suddenly exposed to so many different kinds of music. I would go to festivals, discover new artists every week, and find myself getting really excited about all these new sounds and proposals. A lot of what I was hearing resonated with me, but when I tried to find something with a similar approach in Spanish, I couldn’t really find it. I think that’s where the idea for my project started. I wanted to bring some of those Anglo-inspired sounds into Spanish-language music, without losing the way I naturally write and express myself. I guess I’m trying to create the kind of music I wish I had more of when I was growing up. What can we expect from you next? I’m currently wrapping up everything for my debut album, which is coming out next year. It’s been an insane process. I started writing the first demos back in July 2025, so the fact that I’m now finishing everything in November 2026 feels pretty crazy. I’ve always been an album person. I think there’s something really special about creating a complete project, and I hope we never lose that culture of making albums. Sofia Monroy How do you feel about being nominated for Best New Artist? It means a lot, especially because it feels like recognition of a journey that hasn’t necessarily been linear. I’ve spent years figuring out who I am as an artist, experimenting, making mistakes, and finding my own voice. I think being nominated is a beautiful reminder that there’s space for different perspectives and ways of making music. But more than anything, I see it as a confirmation that you should always trust your intuition and follow your own path, even when it doesn’t necessarily make sense to anyone else at the time. Sometimes you just have to trust that little voice in your head. Would you say that being both Mexican and Swedish influences the way that you make music? I think growing up between two cultures has shaped almost everything about the way I see the world, and naturally, that translates into my music. I’ve always felt like I exist somewhere in between, never entirely one thing or the other. But I’ve also come to realize that I don’t necessarily have to choose. I think I’m a walking contradiction in many ways. I’m made up of two cultures, two languages, two very different ways of seeing the world, and sometimes those things coexist beautifully, and sometimes they clash. I think that’s something that has become a big part of my artistic identity. I’ve stopped trying to make all those different parts of myself fit together into one coherent picture. You’re nominated for your Best New Artist for your album Morena. What do you want people to take away from that album? I want people to feel something. Morena was born out of a personal search, an attempt to make sense of a lot of things I was experiencing at the time: identity, belonging, grief, love, my roots, and my relationship with life and death. It was also a way for me to reconnect with my father, who passed away when I was young. I think Morena exists somewhere in between all these things. She’s a reflection of different parts of me, but also something that exists beyond me. I guess the album became a way of navigating all these different versions of myself and understanding where I come from. There’s a quote I really like about how we’re not just one thing, but little pieces of everyone and everything we’ve encountered. I think that’s very much what Morena is about: accepting that you can be many things at once, that you don’t necessarily have to choose, and that all these seemingly contradictory parts can coexist within you. What do you want to achieve with your music? I want to build a world that people can enter and feel connected to. I want to make music that challenges me creatively, that allows me to experiment and evolve, and that doesn’t necessarily sound or look the same from one project to another. Of course, I have ambitions. I want to reach more people internationally, perform on bigger stages, collaborate with artists I admire, and continue growing my career. But I think one of the most beautiful things about making music is being able to connect with people through emotions. To share something so personal and have someone on the other side of the world recognize a piece of themselves in it. I think that’s quite extraordinary.
entry.summary: Aria Vega, Delilah, Fabian, and Sofia Monroy are among this year's contenders for one of the ceremony's most coveted awards

entry.title: Meet the Vigodas: Conan O’Brien Plays Out His Teenage Dream With L.A. Cover Band
entry.body: Meet the Vigodas: Conan O’Brien Plays Out His Teenage Dream With L.A. Cover Band When Conan O’Brien takes the stage at the Teragram Ballroom in downtown Los Angeles on Friday night, he’s wearing tight black jeans, a custom black jacket sporting the band’s name, and a wide smile. He greets the crowd by asking how many people had seen his cover band, the Vigodas. A few shout that they had, but the vast majority were there to see him for the first time. And despite his fame, that makes sense. Though he’s probably one of the most recognizable and beloved people in Hollywood, at this point, the band has only done about 10 shows around Southern California since premiering in August. They draw a wide range of fans. Some know him from his days hosting Late Night, while others seem to be dedicated listeners to his long-running interview podcast, Conan O’Brien Needs a Friend —a smattering appear young enough to have only seen clips of him during his network heyday. The band run through more than a dozen covers — from Elvis Presley and Elvis Costello to Bo Diddley and John Lennon — an eclectic mix of rock & roll spanning the 1950s through the 1980s that is probably best described as the music that won’t get out of O’Brien’s head. “When I was in college, when everyone else was starting to listen to U2 and Oingo Boingo, I was into hardcore rockabilly,” O’Brien, 63, tells Rolling Stone backstage before the show, running his fingers through the front of his ginger mane, which leaves it in a four-inch wave above his head. “I had the hair for it.” He loved the raucous sounds of Jerry Lee Lewis and early Elvis Presley. “Over the years, I would pick up these songs that were like adrenaline,” he says. “One of them is Ronnie Hawkins’ version of ‘40 Days,’” which they play later during their set. Though the crowd never seems to break a sweat, they’re engaged through the hour-plus set, occasionally singing along and doing little solo swing dances in place. (There are also a surprising number of couples making out.) But the best part of the night is the overwhelming joy on O’Brien’s face as he jams onstage with four other guys 20 years his junior, whom he only met a few months ago but became fast friends. O’Brien is probably still best known for his decades as a talk-show host, but it was the podcast that launched the band, he says, when he had singer Norah Jones on in May 2023. “I’ve known Norah over the years, and she always remembered me having a guitar whenever she would come do the late-night show,” O’Brien says. “She said, ‘How’s the guitar going?’ And I said, ‘You know, it’s kind of sad because I don’t really have anyone to play with, and I need someone to kind of kick my ass and help my game.’ She said, ‘I know a guy.’” The guy was guitarist Jason Roberts, who’d played in Jones’ band for half a decade. He started giving O’Brien lessons, and they would nerd out about their shared love of the Beatles. “We text about the Beatles a lot,” Roberts says later. “We just both love the Beatles so much.” About six months ago, O’Brien asked Roberts if he’d be down to take their lessons to the next level. “He was just like, ‘Can you help me put a band together?’” Roberts remembers. “And I said, “I know the exact guys for this.” O’Brien tells the same story. “A week later, we’re in Hollywood, and we’re playing,” he says. “I’m just floating, so happy.” They named themselves after the late actor Abe Vigoda — another towering figure with an expressive face, best known for his roles in The Godfather and Barney Miller. “Abe was a fixture on my old late show, he did hundreds of bits for us, and he was a sweet and hilarious man. I always knew his iconic mug was the face of our band,” says O’Brien. He had never played in a band as a teenager, but always wanted to. “For years and years and years, you could argue that the only reason I wanted a late-night show was so I could have a band,” he says. Back when he was working with the Max Weinberg 7, and later Jimmy Vivino and the Basic Cable Band, he would join them to jam every time they had rehearsal. “I’d put on a guitar and I would play with them and sing songs,” he says. “We had a good repertoire. And then when I went through my Tonight Show madness” — referring to the six months he spent behind the desk of the NBC institution from 2009 to 2010 — “we went out on the road and we did a comedy show, but also it had a lot of music in it too, and that was my happy place.” O’Brien seems comfortable as a cover man, satisfied to reinterpret the music he loves — often by speeding them up. A few years ago, he ran into Beverly D’Angelo at a party, and she commented to him at just how fast his version of “40 Days” was when she heard it on tour. Earlier this year, when the Rolling Stones asked him to introduce them and their new album at a concert in Brooklyn, he ran into Keith Richards backstage. “Keith said to me, he said, ‘I heard your ‘Monkey Business,’” O’Brien says, referring to the Chuck Berry cover he recorded with Jack White for 2010’s Live at Third Man. O’Brien was surprised he knew who he was, much less had heard his 16-year-old record. “[Keith] went, ‘You sound like a fucking auctioneer.’” O’Brien laughs. “He’s not wrong.” Part of the joy of the band is the excuse to tour different venues in Los Angeles. Their first show was at Permanent Records Roadhouse, a tiny club in East L.A. where they played as a surprise guest after Fred Armison’s regularly scheduled set. Since then, they’ve had a tour of Los Angeles’ finest small stages, from the Troubadour to the Lodge Room to the Moroccan Lounge. “I’m a connoisseur of kooky backstages,” he says, remembering a time he hung out with his friend and idol Bob Newhart backstage at the Chicago Theatre. “I had a goofy dressing room, and Bob Newhart said, ‘Conan, no matter what you achieve in show business, whenever you get to the theater and they show you your dressing room, there’s always a piece of dead brown lettuce on the floor. That’s just the way it is.” He smiles at the thought. “It’s very humbling.” Aside from getting to see the bowels of these Art Deco monuments, the other point of the band, O’Brien says, is to be able to share the stage with other musicians whose work he loves. There are the folks in his outfit, sure — Roberts the guitarist, Erik Kertes on bass, Ben Alleman on keys, and Josh Adams on drums (Rob Jensen filled in on Friday for Adams, who is on tour with the Fruit Bats). But there are all the openers, too, like Malena Cadiz tonight — an Americana singer-songwriter with a lush voice — or Sam Evian, who opened for them at Pappy and Harriet’s out in Joshua Tree a few weeks ago. Each night, he asks those openers to join them for a song or two. “I want it to be a hootenanny,” O’Brien says. “I want it to be something where we roll along and other people jump in. Because I have no future in the music business, but I can be like a small part of it.” The Vigodas’ Teragram Ballroom Set List “7 Nights to Rock” – Nick Lowe “No Action/Radio Radio” – Elvis Costello “Baby Let’s Play House” – Elvis Presley “You Can Have the Crown” – Sturgill Simpson “Werewolves of London” – Warren Zevon “Jump into the Fire” – Harry Nilsson “Hello Mary Lou” – Ricky Nelson (with Malena Cadiz) “Twenty Flight Rock” – Eddie Cochran “Forty Days” – Ronnie Hawkins “I’m So Tired” – John Lennon “Victoria” – The Kinks (with Gaby Moreno) “Proud Mary” – Ike and Tina Turner (with Gaby Moreno) “Who Do You Love” – Bo Diddley “Not Fade Away” – Buddy Holly (partial song) “Polk Salad Annie” – Elvis Presley “Up on Cripple Creek” – The Band
entry.summary: Late-night legend and prolific podcaster talks rockabilly, kooky backstages, and a lifelong dream come true

entry.title: Zohran Mamdani and Puerto Rican Band Chuwi Discuss Gentrification, Music, and Making Change
entry.body: Zohran Mamdani and Puerto Rican Band Chuwi Discuss Gentrification, Music, and Making Change The Puerto Rican band Chuwi, made up of siblings Lorén, Willy, and Wester and their best friend Adrián, has spent the last couple years achieving international fame through a major collab with Bad Bunny, also ending up as his opening act on tour. But they’ve also used their platform to speak out about Puerto Rico — their debut album, Libertad, from last month, tackles government corruption, the economic and social effects of colonialist policies, and more — and on Friday, they joined Mayor Zohran Mamdani in San Juan for a conversation about issues central to the islands’ future. As part of a visit engaging local organizations and community leaders, Mamdani sat down with the musicians to hear more about their perspective. “I look forward to listening to Puerto Ricans to hear about what the struggles are that they’re facing and how New York City can be a partner in fighting for working people wherever they may call home,” the mayor told Rolling Stone. The meeting was part of the annual Somos Conference, where New York State lawmakers meet with Latino advocates over four days in Puerto Rico. The conference’s goal is to create a space where attendees can speak directly with those in positions of power about what’s most important to their communities. This year marks the 40th anniversary of the event, and it is customary for the mayor of New York City to attend. Last year, Mamdani flew down just days after he was elected. This year, he returned, 10 months into his first term, and seemed clear-eyed about what he wanted to talk about during his 72 hours in town. His central focus is bridging the gap between the archipelago and the nearly 600,000 Puerto Ricans who call New York City home, with Mayor Mamdani targeting issues that matter to both. “What I’ve heard from Puerto Rican New Yorkers is a concern about displacement and gentrification, not only in the neighborhoods that they’ve helped to build in New York City, but also right here in Puerto Rico,” he says. The mayor met with various coalitions and activist groups, such as Defend Cabo Rojo, FURIA, La Tejedora, and PR No Se Vende (“Puerto Rico Is Not for Sale”) that have dedicated themselves to combatting those challenges. But before those meetings, he scheduled an equally important sit-down with Chuwi, given their mission to spread the word about Puerto Rico’s struggles through their music. Chuwi became a household name after they collaborated on the song “WELTiTA” off Bad Bunny’s Grammy-winning DeBÍ TiRAR MáS FOToS. They went on to be the opening act of his 59-date world tour. On Libertad, the band went back to their protest music roots and leaned more than ever into the politics. They’ve addressed some of these themes on the album since their earliest EPs, but never as directly as the LP. Lorén initiated the conversation with Mamdani by describing how she was in New York City the week before the 2025 election. She told him she was impressed by the enthusiasm she saw for his campaign, saying that she found it very inspiring as a Puerto Rican. “What you guys are doing is inspiring,” Mamdani said, complimenting how they use their music to spread important messages without compromising the artistic side. “When you’re not at a desk, it’s easier to tell the truth,” he said. He noted that as artists, they have the unique privilege of being able to speak out and that their music is a connection to home for many fans. Indeed, even Bad Bunny himself said last year that listening to Chuwi during his time living in Los Angeles pre-DtMF made him homesick. Willy took the opportunity to ask Mayor Mamdani about how he’s been able to achieve so much in his term so far: “Why is it you can do these policies that other mayors couldn’t?” “When you get elected you get disconnected,” Mamdani said. He explained that leaders can become cut off from the people they serve, and that the environment can turn into tinted SUVs and private hotel rooms. He gave examples of things he does “intentionally” to stay connected, like biking around the city. “Institutions change slower than people,” and too much patience sometimes inadvertently leads to complacency. “The more you stay with the people the more you stay impatient. You have to keep [them] around you,” he says. Chuwi pointed out how skeptical many citizens are about politicians, and how cynicism has become the prevalent feeling, especially in a Puerto Rico that has been suffering economically for almost two decades, even before Hurricane María dealt a blow to its infrastructure in 2017. Mamdani acknowledged that feeling, and said Puerto Ricans might be skeptical because “they know about history.” He said he’s aware of the gap between what politicians promise and what citizens actually expect them to deliver on. “How do you collapse that separation?” he said, sharing that he feels “inspiration” is a stronger force than “disillusionment” and that he tries to wake up every day “ready to fight” and to “use pressure in a productive way.” Aware of how heated things can get in politics, and having been on the receiving end of a fair share of criticism, Willy asked how the mayor deals with mud-slinging and negative rhetoric in politics. Mamdani said that treating people who disagree with him harshly or with judgment leads to both sides feeling like there has to be a winner or loser in the debate. He stressed the importance of speaking to people who aren’t just “those who feel comfortable with you.” Mamdani then pivoted to asking Chuwi about their future plans. The band said that they’ll be returning to cities they visited over the summer, hinting at a big tour of their own. Mamdani playfully reminded them he used to be an artist as well — as an indie rapper going by the alias Mr. Cardamom — and reminisced about how rough it was the first few years. “I was the opener to the opener to the opener,” he joked. “I once performed at 5 p.m. for a band that was playing at 9 p.m. I was singing to the seat savers.” He said he was delighted by the possibility of Chuwi going to different countries with their music, because as he put it, “through that, others will hear and see their own struggles.” Lorén thanked the mayor for meeting with them, sharing that their grandparents were one of the families that moved to New York City during the post-WWII migration wave, and in fact got married in the city. Mamdani stressed the importance of Puerto Ricans in the history of New York, especially in organized labor movements. Lorén shared that her grandfather worked at a textile factory in the city. Willy capped off the meeting by thanking Mayor Mamdani for meeting with the organizations working on the ground in P.R. He stressed how important their goals were when it came to pushing for the abolition of Puerto Rico’s tax haven status, protecting the coastal maritime-terrestrial zone, and trying to stop large developments that threaten Puerto Rico’s habitats like Esencia in Cabo Rojo and Moncayo in Fajardo, among other causes. “Politicians [in Puerto Rico] won’t meet with them unless it’s in a court room or public hearings,” he said. Afterwards, Chuwi told Rolling Stone they felt inspired by the mayor’s words. “Being that he’s the mayor of New York, and New York has significant importance in Puerto Rico, it was super important to be able to discuss these matters with him,” says Wester. They also pushed back on critics who might accuse Mayor Mamdani of wading into issues outside his jurisdiction. “My counterargument is that we’re a colony of the United States, and New York is — and has always been — extremely important in Puerto Rico. “The rest of the world is watching what’s happening here on the island, yet our own politicians aren’t addressing it. I think it’s fair game.” “It’s important to understand that this isn’t like the Financial Oversight Board. Just because people from outside — rather than locals — are addressing these issues, it doesn’t mean they’re coming here to exert control or anything like that,” Adrián says. “People hear ‘the United States is coming here to do things in Puerto Rico’ and immediately think, ‘Oh, Junta de Control Fiscal.’ No, it’s not [necessarily] that. It’s about creating a dialogue between the two sides.” As the meeting wrapped up and Chuwi said their goodbyes, the mayor snuck in one last question: are they doing a show in New York in the near future? Chuwi let Mayor Mamdani know they’ll be seeing each other again soon.
entry.summary: The New York mayor sat down with one of the island's most outspoken new acts for a conversation about Puerto Rico's future

entry.title: "Congress will investigate": Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang faces probe over alleged Chinese spy ties
entry.body: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang is facing increasing congressional scrutiny after multiple reports Friday night suggested he had a romantic relationship with a purported Chinese spy. Why it matters: Huang is arguably the world's most powerful CEO, the man who runs one of the world's largest companies and whose products are central to the world's most important technology. The mere suggestion that he was in some way compromised by a Chinese intelligence agent could quickly become a major, bipartisan focus of the incoming Congress. What they're saying : Sen. Chris Coons (D-Del.) promised a probe of the latest Times report and Huang's relationships. "The more I learn about the insane relationship between the Trump Administration, Chinese spies, and AI billionaires, the more I'm convinced there is nothing this administration does that isn't corrupt. Congress will investigate and get answers," Coons posted to X, linking in another post to the Times' story. Catch up quick: A series of reports over the last 10 days has raised concerns about an allegedly illicit relationship with an undercurrent of espionage. Oct. 29 : The New York Times reported that Jensen Huang and a tech executive named Alice Huang had a "close relationship," that U.S. authorities had concerns about her intelligence connections with China, and that President Trump had been briefed on the situation. Oct. 31 : The Wall Street Journal reported that intelligence authorities in the U.S., Singapore and Taiwan all had reason to believe that Alice Huang might be a Chinese spy. Nov. 5: A group of House Republican committee chairs asked Jensen Huang to give them a briefing on his relationship with Alice Huang and Nvidia's controls over sensitive information, saying they need to determine "the extent to which U.S. national security has been placed at risk." Nov. 6: Both the New York Times and Financial Times reported that Alice Huang was in fact a Chinese spy, recruited by top intelligence officials specifically to spy on Jensen Huang. Her purported goal: to convince him to lobby U.S. officials to allow chip exports to China. The FT also reported that Jensen Huang and Alice Huang had a romantic relationship. For the record: Nvidia has repeatedly and firmly denied that Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang was anything but a typical business contact, and insisted that no sensitive information would have been shared with her or anyone else. The company did not respond to Axios's request for comment on Saturday. The Chinese government has also publicly denied engaging with Alice Huang to spy on Jensen Huang. The big picture: President Trump and his administration have staked the country's future on beating China in the race to develop and control advanced AI. Nvidia's chips are central to that vision, and Jensen Huang has been close to Trump throughout this term. There've been back-and-forth fights over whether Nvidia's chips can be sold to China or not, but also extensive reporting that those chips are making their way to Chinese companies regardless. What's next: The Republican chairmen who requested a briefing from Jensen Huang gave him a Nov. 11 deadline to set a date for their meeting.

entry.title: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government - Al Jazeera
entry.body: Israel’s president picks Eisenkot over Netanyahu to form next government Former army chief has 28 days to build a coalition that would end Benjamin Netanyahu’s long tenure as prime minister. Israel’s President Isaac Herzog has tasked Gadi Eisenkot with forming the country’s next government, passing over the former army chief’s rival, Benjamin Netanyahu. Herzog told Eisenkot of his decision on Saturday evening and will formally hand him the mandate at a ceremony on Sunday, the president’s spokesperson said. Herzog held consultations with political parties this week to decide who he would appoint to form a government after neither side secured a majority in the October 27 general election. Some 67 lawmakers, including from Arab-led parties, endorsed Eisenkot, leader of the Yashar party, to form the next government, while only 46 backed Netanyahu, the current prime minister. Eisenkot will have 28 days – with a possible 14-day extension – to build a coalition of at least 61 of the Knesset’s 120 seats, the minimum threshold for a government. In the October election, Eisenkot’s four-party alliance won 48 seats, while Netanyahu’s right-wing and religious bloc secured 53, leaving both short of the 61 needed for a parliamentary majority. Arab-led parties, representing Palestinian citizens of Israel, won a record 19 seats. Eisenkot has ruled out forming a government with the Arab-led parties, which would give him a 67-seat bloc. Winning over the two ultra-Orthodox parties, United Torah Judaism and Shas, would give him exactly 61 seats. He could also form a government with fewer than 61 seats if he wins a parliamentary confidence vote. Al Jazeera’s Nour Odeh, reporting from Ramallah in the occupied West Bank on Herzog’s decision, said the president “took the predictable route” in selecting Eisenkot, as he had the highest number of recommendations. “The hard work will begin now for Eisenkot to put together a government that can pass a vote of confidence at the Knesset that: one, will not break too many of the promises he made on the campaign trail; and two, that can survive the opposition of the right-wing bloc led by Netanyahu,” Odeh said. If Eisenkot fails to form a government within the allotted time, Herzog will nominate another candidate. If the second nominee fails, a parliament majority can back a third candidate, who will be granted a final 14 days. If, once again, no government is formed, a new election will be called within 90 days, with Netanyahu staying on as a caretaker prime minister. United against Netanyahu government Eisenkot led Israel’s military from 2015 to 2019 and sat as an observer in Netanyahu’s war cabinet for the first eight months of Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza, which began in October 2023. Ahmad Tibi, a senior member of the Joint List – a coalition of Arab-led parties that holds 11 seats – told Al Jazeera on Saturday that Herzog’s decision was “expected”. “We were concerned that the president would move towards a national unity government,” he said, referring to a proposed power-sharing agreement between Eisenkot and Netanyahu. Instead, Arab-led parties endorsed Eisenkot for the mandate, granting him a “considerable margin”. Tibi said he believes Eisenkot is headed for a minority government “with external support from the Arab parties”. While this would not be a “dream government” for Arab-led parties, Tibi prioritised bringing down “the government of Netanyahu, [Itamar] Ben-Gvir and [Bezalel] Smotrich”. Hours before Herzog’s decision, Netanyahu had warned that a government formed by the opposition bloc with support from Arab-led parties would lead to Israel’s collapse. “Such a government, dependent on Islamists, will dismantle the state of Israel from within, as is happening in European countries, and far worse than that,” Netanyahu said in a prerecorded video speech, echoing the language of far-right politicians who falsely claim parts of Europe have come under Islamic law. Netanyahu “described us as supporters of terrorists and terrorism”, Tibi said. “My response to him is this: Netanyahu is the biggest terrorist in Israel and the region, and the foremost supporter of terrorism, particularly Jewish terrorism in the West Bank and the Palestinian territories.” Al Jazeera’s Odeh noted that although Eisenkot has expressly said he does not wish to form a government with Arab-led parties, “they both share quite compelling reasons to get rid of Netanyahu”.

entry.title: How midterm elections sent Wall Street from celebration to mayhem in just 24 hours / this week - Yahoo Finance
entry.body: Wall Street's tumultuous midterm election week kicked off with a celebration among investors. On Wednesday, stocks soared after Democrats swept both chambers of Congress. The Dow (^DJI) surged more than 1,500 points. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) rallied nearly 2%. And in less than 24 hours, stocks reversed course, plunging Thursday as Wall Street and Main Street investors alike ditched artificial intelligence winners and chip stocks, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite (^IXIC) into correction territory. The extraordinary reversal marked just the latest whipsaw in a year of wild swings, with the market's best expectation of future volatility, the VIX (^VIX), spiking to its highest level since President Trump extended the deadline for the Iran war in late March. As the election results rolled in, Steve Sosnick, chief strategist at Interactive Brokers, was glued to his television, flipping between CNN, Fox, MSNBC, and Bloomberg while watching stock futures slip. When Sosnick went to bed, futures were still down roughly 1%. Democrats had won control of both the House and Senate, resolving one major source of uncertainty for markets, while introducing a specific complication to the country's artificial intelligence investment boom. States where newly elected governors have promised to stop or pause data center construction account for an estimated 45% of planned US data center capacity, according to Goldman Sachs. In Texas, where more than half of the country's data center capacity is planned for construction, stakes were especially high. Democrat Gina Hinojosa had just won the race to become governor after promising a moratorium on new data center approvals. The shift caught the attention of one of the world's most prominent business titans. "Data centers in space look pretty appealing right now," Elon Musk posted on X early Wednesday. By Wednesday morning, Wall Street was seeing silver linings in the blue wave. The Dow jumped 3%, its best day in months. The S&P 500 rose 1.6%, and the Nasdaq gained 1.4%. Investors appeared to welcome the prospect of a divided government, potentially limiting some of President Trump's agenda. Oil prices (CL=F, BZ=F) also plunged, helping ease inflation concerns. And the removal of election uncertainty ushered in a sharp drop in the VIX. That drop may have encouraged volatility-sensitive trading strategies to buy stocks, adding more upward pressure to the rally, according to Sosnick. As prices climbed, more investors piled in. But beneath the rally, trouble was brewing.

entry.title: Tech stocks are now cheaper than the S&P 500 for the first time since 2017 — here's what history says comes next: Chart of the Day - Yahoo Finance
entry.body: Tech stocks are now cheaper than the S&P 500 for the first time since 2017 — here's what history says comes next: Chart of the Day Wall Street partied the day after the midterms and woke up Thursday to tech's worst day since the 2020 COVID crash. Strip out the AI trade, though, and most stocks barely noticed. The equal-weight S&P 500 (RSP), a stand-in for the typical stock, closed at a record Wednesday and ended the week within about 1% of where it started. The headline indexes weren't so lucky. The S&P 500 (^GSPC) and Nasdaq (^IXIC) each fell about 3% for a fourth straight losing week, capping a week of whiplash that ended with a Friday bounce in chip stocks. The selling did something few investors would have bet on a year ago. It made tech cheaper than the broader market. Tech stocks in the S&P 500 (XLK) traded at about 17 times expected earnings this week, below the broader index's 18 times for the first time since 2017, Truist Wealth chief investment officer Keith Lerner wrote in a note Thursday. At the October 2025 peak, the sector fetched 32 times. "At a 32.0x P/E last year, the market had baked in a lot of good news," Lerner wrote. "Arguably, at almost half that level, the market is already pricing in a lot of bad news." Chips took the brunt of it. The PHLX Semiconductor Index (^SOX) fell for a fifth straight week and lost nearly 30% over that stretch, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. Micron (MU) and Sandisk (SNDK) each lost more than 20% this week alone. Lerner sees "something of a buyers' strike in tech," and he told Yahoo Finance Friday that chips are the first to feel any slowdown in data-center building, a risk that hung over the midterms. But a slower build-out could ease the cash drain on the biggest AI spenders. "If this forces a little bit of a slowdown and maybe a little bit of positive in cash flow, I think that could actually elongate the cycle," he said. Truist's advice is to stay overweight US large caps and add small caps "as a partial hedge against periodic sharp rotations away from megacap tech." The firm also notes that stocks have risen in the year after every midterm since 1946. History favors patience, mostly The S&P 500 has had 33 streaks of four or more losing weeks since 1990. Three months later, it was higher about 80% of the time, with a median gain of 6%, according to Yahoo Finance calculations. That's better than the typical three-month return of about 3% after any week. The exceptions came during the dot-com bust and the 2008 financial crisis, when the S&P 500 kept falling for another year. Michael Martin, founder of TraderMindset.com, isn't buying the dip. "It's a time to harvest cash right now," Martin, who runs a commodity futures strategy with Victor "Trader Vic" Sperandeo, told Yahoo Finance. "I don't think these are buying opportunities.

entry.title: CPU-Z Data Shows 16 GB RAM Gaining Ground While 32 GB and 64 GB RAM Shares Shrink - TechPowerUp
entry.body: Saturday, November 7th 2026 CPU-Z Data Shows 16 GB RAM Gaining Ground While 32 GB and 64 GB RAM Shares Shrink PCs with 32 GB and 64 GB of RAM are becoming less common, at least in the latest CPU-Z Validator statistics. According to Doc TB, one of the developers behind CPU-Z, this is the first time RAM capacity on PCs has declined year over year. 32 GB is still the most popular configuration at 37.2% of validations, though its share is down 2.5% compared to a year ago. 64 GB took a much bigger hit, falling 18% to 7.3%. Lower capacities are moving the other way, with 16 GB up 12.9% to 33.0% and 8 GB up 5.5% to 11.0%, while 96 GB and 128 GB setups dropped by more than 26% each. Memory type tells a similar story, with DDR4 now making up 54.5% of validations, up 6.0%, while DDR5 slipped 2.9% to 32.9%. Of course, these figures only cover systems that users actually submit to the validator over the last three months, so they aren't a full picture of the PC market. Steam's September survey, for example, showed 32 GB overtaking 16 GB as the most common configuration among gamers, but that promptly flipped with the October survey. Still, the timing makes sense. Memory prices have climbed sharply this year, and Team Group expects the worst of the shortage to land between Q4 2026 and Q2 2027. DDR4 platforms may also get a second wind, with DDR4 motherboards getting released for unannounced LGA1700 processors expected in early 2027. It looks like plenty of people are sticking with older DDR4 systems or settling for 16 GB instead of paying current prices. Sources: CPU-Z Validator, Doc TB on X, via Videocardz

entry.title: Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Now Boots on Jailbroken PS5 and iPhone 17 Pro Max - TechPowerUp
entry.body: Saturday, November 7th 2026 Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake Now Boots on Jailbroken PS5 and iPhone 17 Pro Max Nintendo's Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake launched on Switch 2 on November 5, and it is already running on a jailbroken PlayStation 5 and an iPhone. On PS5, Vampinity posted results in the GitHub repository for EglantinePS5, a PS5 port of a Switch emulator based on Eden. On firmware 12.40, the game loads a save, and Link can walk out of his house into Kokiri Forest at roughly 15 to 20 FPS. However, it runs out of memory a couple of minutes in, with heavy white fog and missing geometry in the forest. Vampinity calls it "nowhere near playable" and says Claude wrote the patches. Apparently, much of the shader work was borrowed from forks of Lichii, the emulator that got the remake running on PC on launch day. The iPhone port comes from developer Joe Jiang, who showed Kokiri Forest running on an iPhone 17 Pro Max. According to Jiang, memory was the hardest part, since the game wants about 9 GB while a single iPhone app is capped at 8,192 MB. He claims his approach keeps quality intact and peaks at just 3.4 GB when loading scenes. Apparently, the method isn't specific to Ocarina, and Jiang says it could bring any Switch or Switch 2 game to iOS, iPadOS, Apple TV, Android, and HarmonyOS. He hasn't released it yet, but it isn't the first Switch 2 game on iPhone. Mario Kart World booted on one shortly after the console's first jailbreak went public. The PS5 port, meanwhile, needs the Relapse jailbreak, which covers firmware 7.00 through 13.60. Neither is a practical way to play the game yet, but I'm sure Nintendo isn't too happy about the remake breaking containment this quickly. Sources: Vampinity on GitHub, Joe Jiang on X

It is the first time Ohio State has had three or more losses by Nov. 7 since 2011, when interim coach Luke Fickell had to step in for Jim Tressel. What started as a 14-0 Ohio State lead completely flipped after a successful Oregon fake punt while backed up deep in its own territory. It was the most unanswered points Ohio State had given up in a game since 1999, when Wisconsin scored 39 straight on the Buckeyes. With the offense sputtering after taking that early lead, the Ohio State defense failed to hold up against Dylan Raiola and the Ducks' passing attack. Raiola -- who has endured some low moments during his first season in Eugene -- completed 25 of his 40 passing attempts for 257 yards and two touchdowns. Conversely, Ohio State quarterback Luke Fahey looked like the freshman he is. After that hot start, Fahey struggled to get in a rhythm. He missed several throws, and his lack of connection with star wideout Jeremiah Smith was apparent. Smith did pad his stats and his Heisman Trophy resume with a garbage-time touchdown reception, but it was far too little, too late. entry.title: Player Personnel Handbook implies that the NFL can delay (or deny) Brandon Aiyuk's reinstatement - NBC Sports
entry.body: Until very recently, people throughout the league believed that the procedure for returning from the reserve/left squad list was administrative, and essentially automatic. The Brandon Aiyuk case shows that, in the NFL’s view, it definitely is not. The Collective Bargaining Agreement is silent on the topic of the reserve/left squad list. The relevant language regarding placement (and eventual reinstatement) from the reserve/left squad list appears in the NFL’s Player Personnel Handbook. In the year when the player is placed on reserve/left squad, he can’t play for his current team or any other team. His season is basically over. The window for reinstatement opens the next year. Here’s the key language from the Player Personnel Handbook regarding reinstatement: “A player on Reserve/Left Squad must apply to the Commissioner for reinstatement to his club’s Active List. No player on Reserve/Left Squad shall be reinstated in the same season in which he is placed on Reserve. A player applying for reinstatement in a season subsequent to the season in which he is placed on Reserve/Left Squad is prohibited from being reinstated in the last 30 days of the regular season or thereafter during the postseason, and no such player will be reinstated during the period between the trading deadline of a subsequent season and the 30-day deadline unless the club initiates the reinstatement request and the Commissioner approves it.” While the provision doesn’t say it expressly, the language implies that the Commissioner has apparently unlimited discretion when it comes to approving the application to reinstate the player. In Aiyuk’s case, the Commissioner has dragged his feet since October 27, setting the stage for an apparent effort by the 49ers to leverage Aiyuk’s desire to be reinstated to his willingness to reimburse up to $13 million in previously-paid bonus money. The NFL Players Association has remained silent throughout the process, and perhaps for good reason. The absence of any provision in the CBA regarding the mechanics of the reserve/left squad list arguably means that the situation falls within the NFL’s “management rights” clause, which allows the various teams “to manage and direct their operations in any manner whatsoever, except as specifically limited by the provisions of this Agreement.” With no limitations in the CBA as to the operation of the reserve/left squad list (or reinstatement from it), the NFLPA may be without options. Precedent becomes relevant to the overall analysis. How has the league handled past requests for reinstatement from the reserve/left squad list? If the league has previously not delayed reinstatement (for whatever reason), there’s an argument to be made that it should not be delayed as to Aiyuk. Regardless, it’s becoming increasingly obvious that the NFL and the 49ers are working together to tie Aiyuk’s reinstatement to his satisfaction of the debt that the 49ers believe Aiyuk has incurred through his prior default under his contract. It should be two separate issues, with the 49ers having the ability to pursue the recovery of bonus money from Aiyuk and Aiyuk having the ability to be reinstated. By tying the two together, the 49ers have found a way to condition Aiyuk’s reinstatement on his willingness to wire a significant payment to the 49ers. Can the NFL and the 49ers do that? The question is whether Aiyuk and/or the NFLPA can come up with a legal argument against the obvious effort to block Aiyuk’s return until he returns millions to the 49ers. If Aiyuk wants to be reinstated quickly, his best (and perhaps only) play will be to return millions to the 49ers, with the ensuing goal of earning it back as his career continues elsewhere.

entry.title: Sao Paulo Grand Prix: Lando Norris and George Russell hoping for more rain in race after wet qualifying - BBC
entry.body: Qualifying conditions borderline - but Norris and Russell hoping for more rain - Published Lando Norris says qualifying for the Sao Paulo Grand Prix brought "some of the wettest conditions" in which he had ever driven - and he is hoping for more rain in the race on Sunday. It was the third consecutive year in which Norris has taken pole in Brazil, and it came in a session that was stopped for nearly an hour and a half because conditions were too dangerous to continue when officials initially tried to start it. Many drivers agreed that conditions were borderline in the extreme. Mercedes driver George Russell, who qualified second to Norris and was miffed about a team miscommunication that he felt robbed him of pole, said: "Q1 was extremely challenging. The visibility was zero down the straight into Turn Four. I was wheel-spinning in fifth gear, over 200km/h (120mph), aquaplaning. "When you're aquaplaning on the straight and you can't see in front of you, it's... I'm not even sure what the word is to describe it. "It does seem a bit crazy. I guess that's what we have to deal with. "I love driving in the rain. I love driving in the rain here, but at some point, if that was a race, there was no way we should be driving in that because the chances of seeing a really, really horrific incident are very, very high." The rain - combined with grid penalties for four of the usual front-runners, including Russell - has produced an unfamiliar grid with several drivers exploiting the opportunity of the weather to produce their best results of the year. Racing Bulls' Liam Lawson - who still does not know whether he has a seat next year - and Audi's Nico Hulkenberg occupy the second row. Haas driver Oliver Bearman is sixth, and Aston Martin's Fernando Alonso and Williams' Alex Albon in eighth and ninth both made it into the top 10 for the first time in 2026. Ferrari's Lewis Hamilton and Red Bull's Max Verstappen, who won this race in the wet two years ago from 17th on the grid, start 20th and 21st after replacing their engines and exceeding their allowance for the year. Hamilton's team-mate Charles Leclerc, who qualified fourth, has a 10-place penalty, also for engine usage. Sunday's forecast is for light rain, and the unpredictability of the weather at the Interlagos track, which is famous for it, means the teams and drivers will be open-minded about what to expect. - Norris takes pole in rain-delayed qualifying - Published5 hours ago - Hamilton & Verstappen to start from back in Brazil - Published3 hours ago Norris had not taken pole since the Spanish Grand Prix in September, and although his McLaren has upgrades on it, which he acknowledged had improved the car, he felt he owed it to the conditions. "We're lucky it's wet, because if it was dry, I wouldn't be sitting here," said Norris. "In the dry, we definitely didn't have the pace. "We've looked better this weekend but we still had some small issues, and we've not been up to the pace of the Mercedes. The wet kind of gave me an opportunity and I made the most of it. "I'm hoping for a wet race. There's a good likelihood it'll be wet. There's a bit of rain, I think, tomorrow at times, and it'll still be damp through the day, so we could just have an exciting race with a little bit of everything, honestly. "These are conditions where you feel like you can make a little bit more of a difference at times, for sure. And I feel like I'm against good guys who also have the capabilities of going for pole, and today we managed to do it because I put two good laps together and I had a good gap, and we managed things well. "It was tense when you want to push so much. You need to kind of learn about the conditions, but you also need to not make a single mistake. "But actually, I felt pretty confident through the whole of qualifying. Q3 was definitely the trickiest because it was also difficult to see, because of the light, where were the dry bits, the wet bits and puddles, things like that. So, more rewarding." Russell reminds himself 'I haven't forgotten how to drive' For Russell, there was another disappointment in a season that has been full of them. Last weekend, he had to watch team-mate Kimi Antonelli clinch the world title and become the youngest champion in history. Here, he felt pole was his had he not been told to back off on what he felt would have been his fastest lap after he came across Albon in the twisty middle sector. The team felt the imminent heavier rain would hold off long enough for him to do another lap. They were wrong, and Russell swore over the radio asking what had happened. He was reminded by team boss Toto Wolff that he was still P2, to which he responded, short-tempered, that he was not there to be second. It might have seemed a loss of perspective, given his five-place grid penalty meant he would not have been on pole even if he had been fastest. But for Russell his feelings were rooted in self-validation after a difficult year, and it was not related to the fact that it promoted Antonelli to second. "Gives me the confidence and reminds me again that I haven't forgotten how to drive," he said. "That's important in circumstances like these and it would have meant a lot to me to clinch the pole with a great performance like we showed in qualifying." He added: "I felt really confident in the rain. I think my pace, along with Lando's, was by far the best out there. "In the rain here, it's always a challenge. I hope it is wet tomorrow. I feel I've got a greater chance if it's wet." Alonso back at the sharp end The wet conditions provided Alonso with a chance to demonstrate the waste of talent that this year's uncompetitive Aston Martin-Honda car has created. With its down-on-power and difficult engine, Alonso has been struggling all year. There have been few chinks of light. This was a rare opportunity to shine, and he took it. Up at the sharp end throughout, he dropped away - if only relatively - in the final session when he could not get temperature in his tyres. It may have been because he was first in the queue in the pit lane in his eagerness to get in a lap time before the rain worsened again. "We took some risks in Q1, in Q2, where the conditions were a little bit unknown for everybody and we made it through and then our first Q3 of the year, so obviously pleased with that," Alonso said. "Then in Q3 I was expecting maybe a little bit more. I was first on the queue. But the tyres were ice cold in Q3, so I had no grip. "But yeah, I look at the times now, I think P6 is 1.8 seconds in front of me. So yeah, it's way too much, you know, in front to really dream about any higher positions. "There is less time full throttle (in the wet), because there is no grip. So obviously they cannot exploit the extra power. "But still the engine is very important in terms of drivability and the way it behaves in the corners. We still have a little bit of an issue there. "But no, I think these conditions is more about the level of risk you want to take. There is a little bit of aquaplaning here and there." Alonso joins Norris and Russell in hoping for a wet race, feeling that if it's dry he will inevitably sink back to Aston Martin's natural level, especially with the long pit straight where Honda's lack of power will render him defenceless. Hamilton and Leclerc 'moving on' after talks The race promises much with Leclerc, Hamilton and Verstappen all aiming to make progress from the back, even if the drivers feel that overtaking at Interlagos will be harder in this year's new-style cars than before. For Ferrari, it has been a difficult weekend, that started with clear-the-air talks between Leclerc and Hamilton after their first-lap battle cost them victory in Mexico last weekend. Both took new internal combustion engines, which gave them 10-place grid penalties, and then Hamilton's brand new one broke in final practice. So Ferrari gave him another one, leaving him at the back with Verstappen. The two multiple champions will be in competition to see who can make progress faster, and perhaps Ferrari are not so unhappy that Hamilton and Leclerc are separated by six places on the grid. Both drivers said all was well after their chat on Thursday evening. Leclerc - who returned to Europe between the two races to be at the birth of his first child, a daughter named Bianca - said: "It was good to speak. This is always needed after a moment like this. It took proportions that are way too big, but it has been around also for way too long. "At the same time, it was a very special week for me, so I couldn't really have those discussions before. And it was important to have those discussions, but now I consider that a closed chapter, and it will be important to look ahead. "I really believe that when we speak, things are much better straight away. Of course, there is tension. Of course, we want to finish ahead of each other, and sometimes we are not going to do things right. And it's OK sometimes to disagree on the way you see things, but at the same time, discussing about those then helps a whole lot." Hamilton added: "Me and Charles sat and spoke and we squashed it, and we're moving on. "We still have a huge amount of respect for each other and I'm glad we had a chat and now we move on. "We've been getting along just fine as normal. Sometimes in those scenarios it takes having a conversation and there's been no demands from either side. "It's both just giving our points and areas we can do better and support each other." Sao Paulo starting grid after penalties 1. Liam Lawson (Racing Bulls) 4. Isack Hadjar (Red Bull) 6. entry.title: Rob Gronkowski's Patriots Hall of Fame celebration takes awkward turn with teammate's story about adult toys - Fox News
entry.body: It's safe to say that former New England Patriots linebacker Niko Koutouvides won't be getting another speaking invitation from the team anytime soon. Rob Gronkowski's induction into the New England Patriots Hall of Fame took an awkward turn on Saturday outside Gillette Stadium. Koutouvides recalled a story about how Gronkowski brought adult toys to training camp in 2011 and discussed them with Aaron Hernandez. The story didn't sit well with social media users. "I'm going to ask all children here, whatever you hear, do not ask any questions after this, OK?" Koutouvides said to begin his story. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE When you have to tell children not to ask questions about what you are about to say, you probably shouldn't say it at all. But alas, Koutouvides plowed ahead. "So Rob goes, 'I just got the Jenna Jameson adult toy', and for those who don't know, Jenna Jameson, she was like an Oscar-winning actress, OK. 'And this thing was awful, I got ripped off,'" Koutouvides said. Jameson is an adult film actress, and Gronkowski put his head in his hands, appearing uncomfortable as Koutouvides started telling the story. "So hold on, it gets a lot better than this guys. So then Aaron (Hernandez) rebuttals, 'Oh, I got a whole package in college,' and started to go through the description of each procedure you needed to take in order to be successful," Koutouvides continued. "And it included microwaves and oils and all types of stuff. So I'm going into my eighth year in the league, they're just getting off their two phenomenal rookie seasons, they're going into Year Two. Remember, this is his phenomenal second year." Koutouvides questioned why Gronkowski had brought the adult toy to training camp, where players would spend two and a half weeks. Outside that door when we get out in two and a half weeks, is everything we want outside that door!'" "And they both look at me and they go 'you've got a good explanation Niko but, more importantly, those two and a half weeks feel like three and a half years. And I said 'we're gonna have a great experience, the three of us', and the rest is history from there." Gronkowski quickly made sure Koutouvides' speech was history once he concluded. "Thank you very much, you're done," Gronkowski said. Social media took issue with Koutouvides' story. "A player that nobody knows goes up there and talks about Aaron Hernandez and an adult film star while being completely disjointed in telling an uninteresting story. Why was he speaking?" one user wrote on X. Another fan called it "horrendous," while other fans questioned why Koutouvides was even speaking.
