entry.title: Walsh-inspired Australia crush irate Samoa to reach World Cup final
entry.body: Walsh-inspired Australia crush irate Samoa to reach World Cup final - Published Australia (26) 44 Tries: Dearden, Preston, Trbojevic, Walsh 3, Best, Bostock Goals: Munster 6 Samoa (2) 12 Tries: Crichton, Tago Goals: Crichton 2 Before kick-off, Samoa's ceremonial war dance - the Siva Tau - turned into an intense confrontation, with their players getting right into the faces of their Australian opponents, and a couple even going forehead to forehead. It turned out to be the closest Samoa got to Australia all evening. Australia dominated at Sydney Football Stadium, triumphing 44-12 to reach a 16th successive men's Rugby League World Cup final. In a repeat of the previous World Cup final, a worked-up Samoa side lost their way with errors and ill-discipline, allowing Australia to run in eight tries, including a Reece Walsh hat-trick. Australia - who have won the past three world titles in a row - will face New Zealand in Brisbane next Sunday, with kick-off at 08:35 GMT. Samoa had taken the lead after three minutes when Stephen Crichton â whose golden-point drop goal beat England in the 2022 semi-final â landed a penalty in front of the posts. But Australia led soon after when Tom Dearden picked up from a scrum and blasted through the non-existent line to score. Australia's next two tries came after they got six again thanks to poor Samoa discipline. Jacob Preston burst under the posts on 15 minutes; 10 minutes later, Tom Trbojevic - joint-leading try scorer at this Men's World Cup - got his eighth try of the tournament, benefiting after Crichton reached into the ruck. Walsh got in on the party - celebrating with a backflip - and the scoring was topped before half-time when Bradman Best bounced off tackles and into the corner. Both sides were fired up by regional rivalry, as the Siva Tau showed pre-match. Samoa's Brian To'o leaned his forehead into the face of Tino Fa'asuamaleaui, the Australia prop who played for Samoa in 2019. But Samoa's passion dissolved into frustration as the game got away - not helped by some questionable refereeing decisions. The most egregious came on the half-hour, when Crichton appeared to have grounded to close the score to 16-6 after Francis Manuleleua had beaten Walsh to a high ball. But a slow-motion replay led to the debatable conclusion Manuleleua had knocked on. It was the final straw for some Samoa players - Spencer Leniu was sin-binned for speaking out of turn to referee Adam Gee just before the break. Crichton did get his try in the second half after Walsh dropped a bomb, and Izack Tago scored in the corner with 18 minutes left. But Walsh quickly responded after both Samoan scores, keeping them at arm's length while scoring his first international hat-trick. Bostock added gloss with eight to go. The damage was done - mostly by Samoa to themselves. Matt's player of the match: Jacob Preston I loved the industry and punch of Jacob Preston's work for Australia on the left edge. He tirelessly hung on the shoulder of his half- and full-back and it was a genuine weapon to unpick Samoa. He scored a try with a typical battering ram line to blow Samoa open, showed timing and hands to put Bradman Best away out wide and consistently challenged the Samoans' own formidable back rowers to match his energy and finesse. Harry Grant was another candidate with his probing from hooker, and Reece Walsh caught the eye with a hat-trick, and from Samoa's perspective captain Stephen Crichton led with quality and effort. Preston though edges it - work-rate and contribution in tandem for the Kangaroos.
entry.summary: Reece Walsh scores a hat-trick as Australia reach the Men's Rugby League World Cup final by overwhelming a Samoa side left fuming by a series of refereeing calls against them.

entry.title: Messi makes history with MLS Golden Boot
entry.body: Messi makes history with MLS Golden Boot - Published Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi has become the first player in MLS history to win the Golden Boot in consecutive seasons. The eight-time Ballon d'Or winner scored 26 goals in 31 appearances, four clear of FC Dallas striker Peter Musa and five more than Nashville's English forward Sam Surridge. Messi becomes only the sixth player to land the award twice, joining a list that includes former Charlton Athletic and Southampton striker Bradley Wright-Phillips. In addition to his goals, the 39-year-old notched 17 assists over the course of the MLS season, ensuring his 43 goal contributions was also a league best for the second year in a row. And the World Cup winner could soon make more history as he bids to become the first three-time Landon Donovan MLS MVP winner. The former Argentina forward landed the award in 2024 as Inter Miami won the Supporters' Shield title and also in 2025 as they won the MLS Cup. Despite Messi's magic, Miami weren't able to land top spot in the MLS Eastern Conference, with the team finishing 17 points behind Surridge's Nashville. They will now face Columbus Crew over three games in the first round of the MLS Cup play-offs which begin later this month. Related topics - Published6 October - Published2 days ago
entry.summary: Inter Miami forward Lionel Messi becomes the first player in MLS history to win the Golden Boot in consecutive seasons.

entry.title: I haven't thrown anyone under the bus - Khawaja
entry.body: I haven't thrown anyone under the bus - Khawaja - Published Usman Khawaja said he has "not thrown anyone under the bus" with revelations about the sandpaper scandal that engulfed the Australia team in 2018. In his autobiography - Sabr - and in an interview with the Sydney Morning Herald, Khawaja claimed the entire team should take responsibility for the plot to use sandpaper on the ball in the third Test against South Africa eight years ago. At the time, the only players punished were captain Steve Smith, vice-captain David Warner and opener Cameron Bancroft. Speaking in videos posted on Instagram on Sunday to clarify his comments, Khawaja said: "You would have seen when I mentioned it was all of us, that's implying that whether we like it or not, we are all responsible for what happened together. "As a team, we need to take that collectively. "But now that everyone's talking, am I going to deny that everyone knew? Nah, I won't deny that, either. But I never speak on behalf of anyone else in my book, contrary to what the headlines in clickbait media would have you think." Other players involved in the Cape Town controversy have repeatedly denied involvement or knowledge of the plot to alter the condition of the ball by rubbing it with sandpaper. Four bowlers who played for Australia in that Test - Pat Cummins, Mitchell Starc, Josh Hazlewood and Nathan Lyon - remain part of the team. Cummins has been Test captain since 2021. In 2021, the quartet released a joint statement which said they "did not know a foreign substance was taken on to the field". On Saturday, Darren Lehmann, the Australia coach who resigned in the wake of the ball-tampering scandal, also denied Khawaja's claims when he told ABC: "I don't think everyone would have known." Khawaja retired from international cricket in January. He scored 6,229 runs in 88 Tests for Australia. In October, it was revealed that Khawaja had met with Cummins to discuss the contents of the upcoming autobiography. That meeting took place before Australia's recent Test series in South Africa, which the Proteas won 2-1. In the videos on Instagram, 39-year-old Khawaja explained that blame for the plot should have been shared among the entire set-up, not only Smith, Warner and Bancroft. "I waited till the [South Africa] series was over. I haven't thrown anyone under the bus," Khawaja said. "The guys that are currently in the team right now and the other people that were there on the South African tour, including me, we're not the victims. "These three guys took the blame for all of us, and they're the victims. Yes, it was tough for everyone, including me. I had sleepless nights, too." Khawaja also defended not revealing his version of the sandpaper saga at the time, or following the bowlers' statement in 2021, and instead waiting for his autobiography. "You ask why didn't I say anything in those four years after that while I was still playing? I never wanted to be the first guy to chat about this," he said. "Call me a chicken or whatever you want, I didn't know how to do it because I was still on the team. How was I ever supposed to bring this up when I knew some of my team-mates didn't want to talk about it?" Cricket Australia is yet to indicate a desire to re-open the investigation into the events at Newlands in 2018. A statement from the governing body said: "There has been a great deal of speculation in the eight years since the 2018 Cape Town Test, including extensive media coverage throughout last month's series in South Africa. "During this time there has been the ongoing opportunity to present any relevant information, and this remains the case. All relevant information presented to CA to date has been properly considered and we remain comfortable with the findings of our integrity process." - Published7 October - Published1 day ago - Published22 hours ago - Published28 August
entry.summary: Usman Khawaja says he has "not thrown anyone under the bus" with revelations about the sandpaper scandal that engulfed the Australia team in 2018.

entry.title: I want to face Baumgardner, it will be boxing's next great rivalry - Dubois
entry.body: I want to face Baumgardner, it will be boxing's next great rivalry - Dubois - Published Alycia Baumgardner challenges Elif Nur Turhan for the IBF lightweight world title on Sunday, 8 November. In her BBC Sport column, Britain's unified lightweight world champion Caroline Dubois explains how she sees the fight unfolding and why she wants the winner in 2027. Women's boxing is crying out for its next great rivalry and I genuinely believe Alycia Baumgardner and I could deliver one of the biggest fights the sport has ever seen. We've had Katie Taylor against Amanda Serrano and Claressa Shields against Savannah Marshall. Those were massive occasions that took women's boxing to another level. But we're entering a transitional period. We've had some incredible champions and unforgettable nights, yet the sport needs its next big fight and its next big star. I believe Baumgardner and I could provide both. I'm the WBC and WBO lightweight world champion, she's one of the biggest names in women's boxing and there's already plenty of bad blood between us. I respect what she's achieved, but I also know that when I beat her - and I believe I'll knock her out - I will be the biggest name in women's boxing. To be the best, you've got to fight the best. I need Baumgardner as much as she needs me. But first she has to get past Turhan. I'll be ringside to watch it all unfold and I'll be ready to call out the winner. 'Baumgardner knows I'm her most dangerous opponent' Baumgardner called me a puppy when we exchanged words in Miami last year. I don't think she's underestimating me - I think it's all talk. In fact, I believe she's frightened of what happens when she gets in the ring with me. She knows I'm her hardest fight, her biggest fight and her most dangerous fight. In my opinion, that's why it hasn't happened yet. But I do respect Baumgardner enormously. We don't always get the money, attention or promotion we deserve and she's worked hard to build her name. I've looked at how she and Shields have promoted themselves and taken inspiration from that. I'm only 25 and still have plenty to learn. And I understand why Baumgardner wants to get paid properly for fighting me. I want exactly the same thing. It's a high-risk, high-reward fight for both of us, so it needs to happen on the biggest possible stage, with the biggest possible prize. My dream is for the fight to headline the O2 Arena in London â not far from where I grew up. I fought on the undercard when Shields beat Marshall there in 2022, and the atmosphere was unbelievable. I remember the crowd going wild when those two women walked out. Imagine Baumgardner and me as top billing with all four world titles on the line. I genuinely believe it could be even bigger than Shields-Marshall. 'I want to become undisputed in 2027' My goal has always been to become undisputed world champion, ever since I first laced a pair of gloves. We're working towards a fight with WBA champion Stephanie Han and then I'd want the winner of Baumgardner-Turhan for the final belt. Women's boxing is different from the men's game. Sometimes it feels like being a world champion isn't enough. You have to become undisputed and then people expect you to move up and do it again before you get the recognition you deserve. Look at Taylor, Shields and Gabriela Fundora. But as important as the belts are, boxing ultimately thrives on big fights, rivalries and moments that capture people's imagination. That's what Baumgardner and I could create. I believe the winner of our fight could become the next face of women's boxing, and I'm determined that person will be me. Why Turhan could shock Baumgardner If Baumgardner loses to Turhan, it doesn't mean our rivalry is finished before it even really started. Sugar Ray Leonard, Roberto Duran and Thomas Hearns all suffered defeats. Mikaela Mayer is another fighter I admire because she's lost, rebuilt and continued challenging herself against the best. But my priority is becoming undisputed, so if Turhan wins, she's the woman I'll be chasing. Turhan exploded on to the scene when she stopped Beatriz Ferreira. It was a sensational performance, although I don't think she's looked quite as impressive since. She is heavy-handed, aggressive and dangerous, particularly early in fights. If Turhan catches Baumgardner early, I think she has the power to knock her out. But if Baumgardner gets behind her jab, makes her miss and keeps turning her, it could become a very difficult night for Turhan. They're fighting three-minute rounds, something Turhan hasn't experienced before and I can see her tiring if Baumgardner makes her work. Baumgardner is technically the better boxer, and if she survives those early rounds, I expect her to take control. If Baumgardner calls me out afterwards, I'll stand up to her. I'm not somebody who scripts these moments. If I feel like getting in the ring and telling her exactly what I think, that's what I'll do. But first she has to win and I've got my own job to do against Han. Get those fights out of the way and we could create something really special. Caroline Dubois was speaking to BBC Sport boxing journalist Kal Sajad. Related topics - Published1 day ago - Published12 hours ago - Published8 October More boxing from the BBC - Published28 August
entry.summary: In her BBC Sport column, Caroline Dubois believes a fight with Alycia Baumgardner could redefine women's boxing.

entry.title: Is there something missing despite Rangers' impressive form?
entry.body: Is there something missing despite Rangers' impressive form? - Published Rangers are unbeaten in their past 12 matches in all competitions, winning 10 of them, and moved to within a point of the Scottish Premiership summit after Saturday's 2-0 win away to St Mirren. They thoroughly deserved their victory. They have the best defensive record in the top flight and the third best attacking record, but it feels as though they are not playing to their full potential. In Paisley, Derek McInnes' side never quite put the game to bed despite a host of chances and St Mirren should really have pulled one back in the closing stages. "There's still not that element of control," former Celtic striker Chris Sutton said on Sky Sports. "That killer instinct is really important, but they don't control games the way they should. That will be the worry. Eventually that will bite Rangers in the backside." Sutton's sparring partner on Sky - former Rangers and Scotland striker Kris Boyd - agreed. "They are a good team, but with Rangers teams of the past, that would have been three or four," he said. "There is something missing." Ryan Naderi - who put Rangers in front from the penalty spot and has scored six in his past eight league matches - should have scored before he did. Strike partner Kevin Kelsy missed a host of chances at the start of the second half before midfielder Dan Neil's deflected shot nestled in the bottom corner to make it 2-0. Rangers' expected goals in their 12 league matches this season is 29.8. They have scored just 21. Key striking duo Youssef Chermiti and Lawrence Shankland are both out injured and that goes some way to explaining their profligacy in front of goal, but it doesn't tell the full story. Naderi and Kelsy have performed admirably this season - there have only been two matches since August in which neither man has scored. It is the players behind them who have not fully stepped up to the plate. South Korean winger Kim Min-su is yet to score or assist in Rangers colours since signing from Girona in the summer, although he created more chances than any other player on Saturday, while Badredine Bouanani has shown undoubted quality without regularly delivering end product. Against St Mirren, there were plenty of promising attacking positions that did not result in a shot as players took the wrong option and allowed the home defence to recover. As McInnes pointed out: "Loads of chances. It's quite ironic we scored from a penalty and a deflected shot, but some of our work was really clean up until the last part. "What becomes a good chance could be a brilliant chance if we just take care with the weight of pass and make the right decision. "There are umpteen examples in that game today and it's something we need to improve on. We've got to take ownership that we can do better in these moments. "The top players make these decisions at breakneck speed and pick the right pass." It is obviously something McInnes has impressed on his players and Neil referenced the need to be more ruthless. "We speak all the time about being more clinical and there were a couple of chances we could have done better with," the former Sunderland midfielder said. McInnes - who fell agonisingly short of winning the title with Heart of Midlothian last season - was open about how he wants and expects more from his players moving forwards, despite their impressive form. "It's not been perfect," he said of the past two and a half months. "We've had the draw with Hearts and the draw at Dundee. "Our fight is with ourselves to keep improving. If we can keep winning and getting those improvements as we go along, there's hopefully more to come from us." If those improvements do come, Sutton believes Rangers could be hard to stop. "They seem like a team that have another gear or two and that will be a worry for the other teams in the league," he added. Related topics - Published18 June 2023
entry.summary: Rangers made it 12 games without defeat in all competitions with a 2-0 win at St Mirren on Saturday, but Ibrox legend Kris Boyd believes there is "something missing".

entry.title: James Talarico Crashes ‘SNL’ Cold Open: ‘I’m the Guy Who’s Been Texting You Every Day Asking for $5’
entry.body: James Talarico crashed this week’s “Saturday Night Live” cold open in order to ask the question on everyone’s mind: How many more of these “Donald-Trump-freezes-the-action-to-ramble” cold opens is “SNL” going to do? Responded “Donald Trump” (James Austin Johnson): “Infinity!” Talarico popped up near the end of the cold open to cheers from the “SNL” audience. “I’m the guy who’s been texting you every day asking for $5,” he said, introducing himself. (“In this economy, who can blame you?” said Trump.) “But I think, Mr. President, if we can work together, we can make life better for everyday Americans. It’s clear people want something new. I’m talking, of course, about SNL’s cold opens. How many of these Trump freezers are they going to do?” “Saturday Night Live” opened its first episode post-midterm election with Sarah Sherman as Chuck Schumer and Kenan Thompson as Hakeem Jeffries celebrating this week’s “blue tsunami” while refusing to admit that with young Democrats energized, perhaps it’s time for them to step aside and pass the torch to the next generation. But then, of course, Donald Trump (James Austin Johnson) freezed the frame and gave his take on the election. “The Democrats never would have won without this horrible economy and terrible war,” he said. “So, in the words of Moana’s big fat friend, ‘You’re welcome.’” Trump then noted that “They’re saying the era of Trump is over” — leading “JD Vance” to pop in: “and the era of Vance has just begun!” Responded Trump: “No, no way… Who the hell was that?” Trump then pointed out that “the other day we lost, and I didn’t even say it was rigged. I accepted the results, which is almost scarier in a way. It’s like, ‘What the hell is he planning?’ I’ll tell you what I’m planning: ballroom. That’s all I care about. Look at that beam, big beam over there. Look at that, and marble. The likes of which you’ve never seen. The next two years are going to be awful. I don’t want to work with these people. It’s not that they’re Democrats; it’s that they’re millennials.” “Trump” then went on a long discourse about the millennial fave TV show “New Girl”: “You know that was a show where Jess was the new girl, but really it was about ensemble, right? You know I said you got to figure out Winston. They didn’t have Winston figured out the first time. When they gave him the cat, that’s when they unlocked a lot of stories for Winston.” Then came Pete Hesgeth (Colin Jost): “You think some election is going to stop me? Do I look like a person who gets less crazy when backed into a corner? I live a YOLO lifestyle. You only lose often, so I’m gonna keep losing for you, sir, unless Congress impeaches me. But you won’t let that happen, right… Now, if you’ll excuse me, I have to go weigh the female soldiers. Peace out, war in.” Talarico’s appearance came just days after he won the Texas senate race with 55.09% of the vote, beating Ken Paxton and flipping the seat Democrat — the first time there’s been a blue senator in Texas since 1988. Talarico’s win was part of the “blue tsunami” that gave the Democrats control of the House and the Senate, as well as a majority of governorships. Saturday’s episode came with a bit of history: Comedian Druski was host, making him the first online content creator to host the sketch show. Druski, whose real name is Drew Desbordes, was joined by musical guest The Strokes. This season’s guest hosts have so far included New York Knicks superstar player Jalen Brunson (Sept. 26), “Verity” actress Dakota Johnson (Oct. 3), comedian Shane Gillis (Oct. 10) and “Obsession” star Inde Navarrette (Oct. 31), while the music guests have included Katseye, Turnstile, Rosalía and Gracie Abrams. The Halloween episode hosted by Navarrette averaged 5.2 million viewers, making it the biggest audience of the season so far. Next up, comedian John Mulaney is set to host the Nov. 14 episode, while Phoebe Bridgers will be the musical guest.

entry.title: ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Drags Trump Over Midterm Drubbing, Stephen Miller Promotion
entry.body: ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Drags Trump Over Midterm Drubbing, Stephen Miller Promotion Saturday Night Live‘s Weekend Update rubbed in the GOP’s midterm losses and knocked Donald Trump‘s promotion of Stephen Miller as his next chief of staff. Tuesday’s midterms will leave Trump without Republican majorities in either chamber of Congress for the next two years. The president, reacting to his party’s disastrous showing, told reporters this week that he “tried hard” and “left it all on the field.” “And to continue the football analogy: failed concussion protocol,” Colin Jost joked. Trump has tried to avoid taking responsibility for the midterm results, instead blaming candidate quality. “And I’m surprised that Trump couldn’t find any new, young talent, because he used to have a guy for that,” Jost joked while showing a photo of him and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. Jost added that Trump, who has been adding more and more gold to the Oval Office and has taken much more of an interest in interior decorating compared to his first term, can spend his lame duck period “doing what he does best: bejazzling the White House.” Co-anchor Michael Che then turned how Speaker of the House Mike Johnson has said he will not look to be the GOP leader in the new Congress. Jost, addressing how Trump on Friday replaced Susie Wiles with Miller as chief of staff, was critical. “Things are going to get out of hand real quick,” he predicted. “Going from Wiles to Miller is like trying to get through a dinner party by switching from wine to meth.” Also on Weekend Update, Elon Musk (Jeremy Culhane) stopped by to explain how he felt about blowing hundreds of millions of dollars on Republican candidates who lost, how the stock prices of SpaceX and Tesla dropped, and the discontinuation of the cybertruck due to low sales.
entry.summary: "Going from Wiles to Miller is like trying to get through a dinner party by switching from wine to meth," Colin Jost jokes

entry.title: ‘SNL’ Weekend Update Brutally Roasts Elon Musk Over ‘Epic’ Midterms Defeat
entry.body: An unhinged “Elon Musk” hit the “Saturday Night Live” Weekend Update desk this week to address the outcome of Tuesday’s midterm elections — and Musk, as played by “SNL” featured player Jeremy Culhane, didn’t quite know how to address it. The real Musk, of course, spent nearly $500 million on Republican candidates, especially in his home state of Texas — which then saw most of its statewide races turn Democratic. “Weekend Update” anchor Colin Jost attempted to get “Elon Musk” (Culhane) to address it: “Elon, you’ve been in the news because you wasted half a billion dollars on the midterms.” Said “Elon,” attempting to change the subject: “No, I’m in the news because my car did a flip. My car did a flip. It was like a freaking Hot Wheel. It was like, and then pop, but I was like totally chill. I was like thug life. Imagine.” Jost then asked “Elon” about halting production on Tesla’s Cybertruck, another major piece of news coming out of Texas this week. “Do you have anything to say about that?,” Jost asked. Responded Elon: “Hey, remember when my car did a flip? It was like, but everyone was like, ‘Whoa!’ But I was just like, ‘Hold my beer.'” “Elon” continued to ramble: “Then like, you, me, and Che, we’re just like there. We’re just like hanging out, doing like epic vulgar roast of each other. And then these girls are like, ‘Can we hang?’ And we’re like, ‘No, you know, we’re good.’ And then like, imagine my leather jacket becomes like a suit of armor, like, ‘Shing, shing,’ and everybody’s like, ‘Elon, Elon, Elon!’ That would be amazing, man. Like, imagine?” Responded Jost: “I cannot believe you are the richest person in the world.” Jost them recapped for Musk: “You moved to Texas because California was run by Democrats. You moved all your companies to Texas because you didn’t want to pay taxes. You even built your own town in Texas. And now Texas is run by Democrats. So now you’re going to have to pay taxes. So how does that make you feel?” Said “Elon”: “Bad.” “I guess that’s what I thought. I mean, I would feel bad too,” Jost said. That is another epic vulgar roast from Colin Jost, my poorest friend.” So what is an “epic vulgar roast”? “It’s my AI Grok’s most epic hardcore feature,” “Elon” said. “It’s so vulgar and hilariously funny.” Then Elon asked Grok to make a few “epic vulgar roasts” at his own expense, and the roasts, admittedly, were pretty epic: “Elon Musk, you’re the worst thing South Africa has ever done.” “When you’re on TV, it feels like an episode of ‘Hate on the Spectrum.'” “If you have 100 more kids, one of them will talk to you.” Ouchie Wouchie! “Shut it down, Grok, shut it down!” Elon screamed as he left the “Weekend Update” desk.

entry.title: King Charles' 'short fuse' on display in viral downpour as Queen Camilla gets umbrella first: expert - Fox News
entry.body: King Charles III was left royally soaked — and his patience appeared to dry up faster than his suit. The British monarch was caught without an umbrella as the skies opened on Nov. 1 during a celebration at Sir Vivian Richards Stadium marking Antigua and Barbuda's 45th anniversary of independence. Charles and his wife, Queen Camilla, were attending the parade during their royal tour of the Caribbean when the weather took a sudden turn. As heavy rain pelted the royal couple, Camilla was quickly handed an umbrella and hurried toward shelter. Charles, however, was left exposed to the elements, getting more drenched by the second and appearing increasingly exasperated. KING CHARLES’ ‘JUST GIVE US A RING!’ QUIP LEADS VIRAL MOMENTS FROM ROYAL US TOUR WITH QUEEN CAMILLA After spotting his wife walking away beneath an umbrella, the 77-year-old threw his hands into the air and repeatedly waved at royal aides, apparently calling for an umbrella of his own as rain soaked his suit. Help eventually arrived, but not before Charles was drenched. By the time an aide handed him an umbrella, the king was already soaking wet. "King Charles has historically had a short fuse," royal commentator Meredith Constant told Fox News Digital. "What we see is that when he is under immense pressure and something seemingly small goes awry, like the pen incident, he loses his cool. In the situation with the umbrella, King Charles had every right to be annoyed with his aides. He's in his late 70s, living with cancer; his wife was immediately handed an umbrella; this was a downpour, not a light drizzle." WATCH: KING CHARLES CAUGHT IN DOWNPOUR DURING ROYAL TOUR "One of the reasons Charles and Camilla work is that she balances him out," Constant said. "She can laugh it off, share a funny aside; she has the ability to let things roll off her shoulders in a way Charles never has. Charles and Camilla function much more like a unit, particularly because Camilla never tries to compete for the limelight." Camilla couldn't hold back her laughter when she rejoined her husband on the dais after the rain eased. The couple chuckled at the mishap. "I've started growing watercress on my trousers," Charles joked, according to the Evening Standard. "The umbrella incident was in stark contrast to the public composure, restraint and emotional discipline demonstrated by Queen Elizabeth," British royal expert Hilary Fordwich told Fox News Digital. "Yet 'all's well that ends well’ as the giggles King Charles and Queen Camilla displayed after the rain saved the day." "The humor King Charles displayed at the moment, without any advice or counsel from courtiers, was immensely significant as it demonstrated he can handle challenges with grace, dignity and deflect with humor," she said. But Constant said the soaking threatened more than Charles' carefully tailored suit. "There's a lot of consideration as to what his legacy will look like," she said. "He certainly doesn't want images of him looking like a drowned rat in the archives, especially when there are large discussions happening about the future of the Commonwealth. This situation should never have happened." "Queen Elizabeth II maintained a firmer distinction between her private reactions and her public responsibilities," Fordwich said, referring to the king's late mother. "She was from the generation which placed emphasis on public reserve. The immediacy of modern social media means unexpected incidents like this rocket around the world in minutes. The king is more visibly expressive, at times impatient, occasionally humorous and way more willing to let audiences see his immediate reactions than his mother." Christopher Andersen, author of "The King," previously told Fox News Digital that sources had described Charles as having a short fuse in his younger years. "He's very moody, very temperamental," Andersen said. "He has a volcanic temper. Camilla has always been a calming influence, and since he became king, Charles has mellowed considerably. That doesn't mean he's lost his edge entirely, by any means. When he is displeased by something, he lets his staff know it in no uncertain terms. They feel the royal heat." Following his mother's death in September 2022, Charles appeared frustrated with a leaking pen during a visit to Northern Ireland. He told an aide, "I can't bear this bloody thing! Every stinking time." A pen was quickly handed to Camilla to complete the signing during the royal ceremony. These moments stand out because they are in such stark contrast to Queen Elizabeth. King Charles is very aware that he is viewed as a transitional monarch, and he wants to leave his mark." entry.title: ‘SNL’: Druski Impersonates ‘Crazy’ Elizabeth Holmes in Meta-Documentary
entry.body: ‘SNL’: Druski Impersonates ‘Crazy’ Elizabeth Holmes in Meta-Documentary Saturday Night Live host, actor and comedian Druski starred in a sketch that imagined a prelude to You Can See Everything, the metadocumentary about Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes. In the sketch, it is revealed that before the tech fraudster had Nathan Fielder interview her, she talked to Druski. Druski was immediately skeptical of Holmes (Jane Wickline) and her partner, Billy Evans (Ben Marshall). “Y’all have some of the weirdest, freakiest vibes I’ve ever seen,” he says, before whispering just to the camera: “Whatever they say this bitch did, she done did that s–t.” Then, during their close-up interview, Druski thinks Holmes is trying to seduce him, so he goes to shut her eyes with his fingers—but they pop right back open. When Holmes shows Druski a product she is working on, he calls it out: “Okay, listen white girl: I’m gonna say this with all love, right: this is the most Temu-ass piece of s–t I’ve ever seen in my life.” In the sketch, Druski also uses a technique that Fielder deployed: reenactments. “I just need to find somebody who can truly embody her character,” he says to himself in the mirror. Cue the cut to him as Holmes. “I’m always being real,” he says eerily to Holmes, who repeats it back to him. They exchange those lines once more. “I could do this all day, bitch,” Druski says at last.
entry.summary: The comedian unveils a new impression in his SNL debut

entry.title: ‘The Undertaker’ Director Thiti Srinuan Reveals He Defecated on Camera for Real as an Actor in Thailand’s Taibaan Universe
entry.body: Thiti “Tongte” Srinuan, director of Thai blockbuster “The Undertaker,” put up a photo of himself defecating on camera for real during a session at Taiwan Creative Content Fest in Taipei. The scene dates from his days as a supporting actor with Taibaan Studio. “I was a supporting actor, and I played a crazy person,” Srinuan said. “Because he’s crazy, he relieves himself wherever he likes.” Rather than use a prop, the production had him actually do it on set. “Forty or 50 people were sitting there watching me, and I felt like I couldn’t go,” he said. The session was moderated by Mr. Knee, senior public relations manager at Vieshow Cinemas and the Taiwan Film Critics Society’s founding chair. Knee noted that the photo was a surprise to organizers too, who had only seen it that morning. Srinuan said the episode showed him how far the studio went for realism, and that realism is what makes its universe flexible. Because every character feels like a real resident of the same village, any of them can be pulled out to lead a film, whether the studio wants a ghost story or a romance. Srinuan, who wrote and directed “The Undertaker” and its sequel for Taibaan Studio, was the sole panelist at the TCCF forum on how user-generated content is turning into a route to theatrical features. Much of his talk was about money. Before “The Undertaker” grossed more than THB700 million ($20.8 million) in Thailand, much of the Taibaan universe was bankrolled with revenue from online music videos. The 2023 film, the sixth feature in the Taibaan universe, became the highest-grossing Thai film in nine years. The franchise is rooted in the language and culture of Thailand’s northeastern Isan region. Its sequel arrived this year. Srinuan came into the business as an extra and supporting player in Taibaan Studio’s films. The crew was a small group from rural Thailand with little formal training, so he volunteered to write scripts and then to assist on directing, working on five films in those roles. Those films played almost entirely to Isan audiences, he said. A music video he made that went viral across the country convinced him a film from the region could cross over, and when no one else would take on his script, he directed it himself. The first Taibaan film raised THB2 million ($59,000), or THB4 million ($119,000) including marketing, and grossed THB35 million ($1 million), in a market where a typical Thai feature costs THB30 million ($891,000) or more. “The Undertaker” was budgeted at THB10 million ($297,000), though Srinuan said only THB8 million ($238,000) was spent. The other THB2 million was there to make it a round number. Raising money for a follow-up proved harder. “If we were still nobodies with no name, they couldn’t invest in us,” Srinuan said. The team turned to building a following online instead. “Believe it or not, after the first film, the second, third and fourth films were funded by what we built online,” he said. “We earned money from music videos. The views kept running and running until we could take that money and make films.” Because a Thai film can take a year to come together, Srinuan said he took on music videos to fill the months between shoots. His videos have now passed 4 billion views combined. Rather than accept flat fees, he asked clients for a share of the view revenue, which meant a video that flopped earned him nothing and pushed him to learn marketing. He has carried the same terms into features, asking to be paid from ticket sales instead of a fixed fee. Music videos also shaped how he writes. He builds features out of segments of four to five minutes, the length of a music video, and lays them end to end until they reach two hours, an approach he said suits audiences raised on short-form and vertical content. “The downside is people comment that the film swings and the emotions don’t connect. You’re laughing, then you’re made to cry, then you’re laughing again,” he said. “But to me, life is like that. You laugh sometimes, you cry sometimes. So I like it this way.” Comments matter more to the studio than likes or shares, Srinuan said. A trailer is expected to reach roughly 20,000 shares and 2 million views with no paid advertising, and when viewers fixate on an unexpected character in the comments, the marketing shifts toward that character. After the first Taibaan film, Srinuan borrowed Marvel’s habit of announcing a slate, declaring a universe before any scripts existed to push himself to keep working. The title of “The Undertaker” came first. Srinuan said he picked the profession because he figured no one sees more ghosts, but early drafts were all ghosts and had little to do with the job. He then drew on his own childhood in the countryside, when he had no money and was paid to be ordained as a novice monk for funerals, watching undertakers at close range. The film turned from horror into drama, though it was still marketed in Thailand as a ghost film because that genre sells. When the first film played in Taiwan two to three years ago, it did not catch on. “I’d like to ask the market now: does Taiwan still want blood-splattered Thai films?” Srinuan said. He suggested Taiwanese viewers had expected gory, frightening Thai horror, while his ghosts are played for laughs. The moderator, who described the film as closer to a comedy, pointed to “Shutter” as the title that first won Taiwanese audiences over to Thai horror. Isan is Thailand’s most populous region, but its local beliefs did not travel to the country’s other three regions, Srinuan said. For “The Undertaker,” he studied Charlie Chaplin and leaned on visual storytelling over dialogue. Traveling overseas with the first film, he found the comedy landed but the local culture often did not, and he called reaching a global audience a challenge he is still working on. Having already handled writing, directing, acting, editing and sound, Srinuan took marketing classes after finishing the first “Undertaker.” The film opened only in Isan, playing to core fans first, and word of mouth pulled it into cinemas across the rest of the country, a strategy he likened to “the forest surrounding the city.” The moderator cited “Backrooms” and “Milk & Serial,” both from directors who came up on YouTube, as signs of the shift. Srinuan said he saw parallels with his own path and argued that ideas count for more than budgets. “If you don’t create work, miracles won’t happen,” he said. He said the success of “The Undertaker” has also drawn a wave of Thai YouTubers into features. “They think, ‘I have 1 million followers on YouTube. I make a film, so all 1 million people who follow me have to watch it, right?’” Srinuan said. “In reality, the first person goes in and says they didn’t like it, and the other 999,999 start deciding whether to watch or not. Then the second person goes in and says it’s not OK, and 900,000 people are gone.”

entry.title: Taiwan’s Content Agency and Partners Put $180 Million Into 27 Projects, From an ‘Our Blues’ Remake to an Off-Broadway Musical
entry.body: The Taiwan Creative Content Agency (TAICCA) and its partners have invested in 27 projects, backed by NT$5.64 billion ($180 million) in total, including NT$740 million ($23.7 million) from the agency and NT$4.9 billion ($157 million) in private capital, TAICCA chair Sue Wang said at the Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF). TAICCA brought together its four joint ventures – Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund, Enjoy Entertainment Limited Partnership, momomini Kids Content Fund and Joint Journey Creative – to present their slates. The partnerships span nine countries, and Wang said the joint-venture model allows for more professional and precise investment assessments. Enjoy Entertainment, a partnership between TAICCA and Taiwanese telecom Far EasTone, said it had invested in 15 projects in its first 10 months: eight in film and TV and seven in music and live events. They include horror film “The Rope Curse 4: Kuntilanak,” which took NT$80 million ($2.6 million) at the Taiwanese box office, a franchise record, and VMTheatre Company’s “Don’t Cry, Dancing Girls the Musical,” billed at the event as the first Taiwanese musical to reach Off-Broadway. On the music side, Enjoy developed the ID. Music Festival with Spotify, which brought 14 Taiwanese acts to two stages in the streamer’s first collaboration with a Taiwanese music event. It also highlighted “Her Voice,” a concert featuring five female performers from Taiwan and South Korea, and indie band Shallow Levée’s “Speak in Silence” project, which pairs the band’s 10th-anniversary album with collaborations with Japanese and Korean musicians and a planned tour of about 50 shows across Taiwan and eight other Asian countries. Enjoy is also behind an immersive project marking 25 years of work by Taiwanese picture-book artist Jimmy Liao. Gary Tsai, general manager of Enjoy Entertainment and COO of Far EasTone’s FET Entertainment Service, said the company aims to take Taiwanese original content to international audiences while adapting international IP for local viewers. Through Far EasTone’s streaming service friDay Video, investment and cross-border partnerships, it hopes to help Taiwanese productions expand overseas and create more opportunities for local talent. Launched in December 2025, momomini Kids Content Fund has made six investments: three in animation, two in live-action and one in drama. COO Phoebe Tsai said the fund weighs each project’s potential impact on the industry alongside content production, talent development and commercial viability. It focuses on children’s content, which Phoebe Tsai said had not previously been treated as a distinct investment category in Taiwan. Its projects include “Who’s Our Sub Today?,” a comedy-adventure series for children ages 8 to 12; “Feifei,” a picture-book adaptation in development as an animated children’s sitcom; and “Mogu & Perol,” which pairs a French IP with Taiwanese talent. The 39-episode series includes six or seven episodes featuring the culture of Taiwan’s Hakka people, one of the island’s main ethnic groups. The fund also backed “Mountain Adventure Squad 2,” a children’s outdoor reality show slated to launch in the first quarter of 2027, and “Hello, Mr. President!,” which received an Excellent Screenplay Award from Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture. Joint Journey Creative’s slate includes Taiwanese films “The Damp,” “All Money Back My Home” and “Suffocation,” as well as Season 6 of Japanese series “Midnight Diner,” an international production it is participating in. The Chunghwa Digital Cultural and Creative Fund totals NT$1 billion ($32 million). Chunghwa Telecom holds 64%, TAICCA 30% through the National Development Fund, E.Sun Financial Holding 5% and fund manager CDCC Capital 1%. The fund backs film, TV and other programs at the project level. It also takes equity stakes in companies working in content development and production, international distribution and business integration, and new uses for IP across cultural technology, games and music. Its equity investments include DaMou Entertainment, the production company behind “The World Between Us,” and Horiza Creations, which focuses on international IP operations, data-driven business models and crowdfunding. Its project slate includes “Call of Lobster,” an action comedy spanning Taiwan and South Korea that won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF’s 2024 pitching competition, and “C’est la Vie,” an eight-episode drama executive produced by and starring Esther Liu, with Tu Cheng-che as screenwriter and director. The fund is also an investor in Shallow Levée’s “Speak in Silence.” Enjoy Entertainment’s slate also includes “Our Blues,” a Taiwanese remake of the 2022 Korean series, which launches globally on Netflix on Dec.

entry.title: Indonesian Horror Hit ‘Pabrik Gula’ Gets 2028 Sequel
entry.body: Indonesian studio giant MD Entertainment will release a sequel to its 2025 horror smash “Pabrik Gula” in early 2028 and has Imax films planned for 2027, Astrid Wienardi, the company’s head of content licensing and global business, said Sunday at Taiwan Creative Content Fest (TCCF) in Taipei. Wienardi delivered a presentation on how MD ties its film and series library to broadcast and streaming. The company took control of free-to-air channel NET TV in a deal worth up to $105 million and has brought in investment from Korea’s SBS. “Pabrik Gula” sold more than 5 million tickets in Indonesia before traveling to Vietnam, Cambodia, Singapore, Malaysia, Brunei, the U.S. Its hooks and popularity persuaded MD to commit to a second installment. The Imax relationship started with “Badarawuhi,” the prequel to “KKN di Desa Penari” and the first Southeast Asian film shot for the format. One of the upcoming Imax titles will draw on “Dhot Design,” a YouTube animated series about four friends that pulls between 8 million and 10 million views an episode. Lionsgate and CJ are also among MD’s strategic partners. Active for more than two decades across film, series, animation, music publishing and talent management, MD has more than 200 features to its name and plans 12 to 13 releases in 2027, led by horror alongside comedy and drama. “KKN di Desa Penari” sold 10.7 million tickets at home, an Indonesian record at the time. “Ivanna 2” is due early next year. The original is a spinoff from MD’s “Danur” horror universe about a headless Dutch woman. “‘Ivanna’ was moderately accepted in Indonesia market, but it did fascinatingly well in Vietnam,” Wienardi said. “It actually broke records in the theatrical Vietnamese market.” Feedback from platform partners, along with fan comments on social media, decides whether MD extends a series, spins off a title or grows a franchise. Netflix drama “Ipar Adalah Maut,” which Wienardi translated as “Brother-in-Law Is Death,” topped the streamer’s trending list in its first week and stayed in the top 10 for seven straight weeks. A second season is in the works and could launch on Netflix next year. MD has eight titles on Netflix and three on WeTV, where seven of the platform’s top 20 titles were MD productions, including “Layangan Putus,” which trended in 25 countries. A deal with iQIYI, unveiled in mid-October, will see two titles roll out by December and a third in the first quarter of 2027. Music is part of the playbook too. Netflix series “Suara Hati,” whose two lead actresses are dangdut singers, generated 100,000 first-week downloads across Spotify and YouTube Music, while “Bakti,” a song from “Danyang: Mahar Tukar Nyawa,” which opened Nov. 5, has passed 200,000 downloads on Spotify. “The golden rule for us is that the universal appeal should never mean stripping away local identity,” Wienardi said. “Local identity is very important for MD. Without local identity, we lose the soul of the story.” She added that CEO Manoj Punjabi demands that soul at every greenlight meeting, and that MD wants folklore-rooted horror rather than “watered-down thrillers or any Hollywood-like thrillers.” When an audience member asked how Indonesian films command around 65% of local moviegoing while Taiwanese films account for just 10%-12% at home, Wienardi cited Indonesia’s population of roughly 280 million and a deep well of haunting folklore that parents pass to their children. “We are surrounded by a lot of mountainous areas where the spiritual taboos are actually discussed on family dinners,” she said. Horror, MD’s specialty for more than 20 years, is the genre that crosses borders most easily, according to Wienardi, who said it has at times reached the U.S. “When it comes to drama, it’s a bit different because then, you know, there’s a lot of sayings in Indonesia that probably are not translated or culturally translated well,” she said. The traffic runs both ways. MD released adaptations of Thai and Korean properties this year, partnered with Korea’s Barunson on “Sorop” and has fielded co-production inquiries from U.S. Wienardi said the studio sees strong potential in bringing Taiwanese and East Asian IP to Indonesia, and wants pitches that arrive with proof of concept, a clear fit for Indonesian viewers and a track record in their home market. “When we’re talking about NET TV, data is number one,” Wienardi said. Free-to-air and pay-TV ratings land daily at 10 a.m. and determine whether a program is extended or changed, while MD series simulcast on the channel help widen its reach. The channel’s goal is a place in Indonesia’s top five. Wienardi said she hopes MD will one day work with Taiwanese directors and producers and “share probably a common ground of storytelling.”

entry.title: House poised to impeach Pete Hegseth after GOP midterm defeat
entry.body: House Republican leaders are bracing for enough GOP defections to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth when the measure comes to a vote this week. Why it matters : Republicans who were defeated in Tuesday's election-night bloodbath have little left to lose and could be more willing to back impeaching Hegseth, whose overall support has eroded since the start of the Iran war. Hegseth doesn't have "a lot of love" on Capitol Hill, retiring Rep. Don Bacon (R-Neb.) told Fox News. Bacon told Axios he's undecided on this week's vote. Driving the news: Rep. Thomas Massie (R-Ky.) is planning to force a vote on his resolution to impeach Hegseth for allegedly defying Congress and illegally continuing the U.S. war in Iran. Republican leaders avoided the measure before Election Day after Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.) canceled votes and sent lawmakers home early. Johnson has denied his decision to send members home was related to the impeachment vote, but it would have been a politically difficult vote for Republicans just weeks before the midterms. The political calculus has now shifted dramatically since Tuesday, with the GOP's crushing defeat fueling anger within the conference and increasing the number of Republicans willing to back impeachment. The big picture: The blame game is already in full swing among House Republicans, with the Iran war emerging as a top target of their ire. "Iran, Iran, Iran ... We should have never done the war before the midterms," a GOP lawmaker told Axios. Hegseth is the face of the war for many on Capitol Hill, putting him in the crosshairs of frustrated Republicans. Another GOP lawmaker told Axios that Hegseth's tone and rhetoric have been "very damaging to our ability to get the facts out to the American people on why the strikes targeting Iran's nuclear facilities, and the additional military actions, were necessary." Zoom in: Hegseth is also on "thin ice" with the Trump administration, with some officials pushing for his ouster, Axios' Marc Caputo and Alex Isenstadt reported . Trump defended Hegseth on Wednesday, telling reporters he has every intention to "keep him" in his post. If Hegseth is still around come January, the new Democratic majority will have the power to pursue investigations and impeachment proceedings. The other side: Hegseth is fighting back, calling the impeachment effort a "sham" led by a "disgruntled, defeated congressman" in a video posted on X Thursday. Massie, who lost his primary to a Trump-backed opponent, fired back, urging Trump to replace Hegseth while Republicans still control the Senate. "There is one contingency in which I won't reintroduce the articles of impeachment: Hegseth resigns," Massie wrote . Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said in a statement to Axios: "Secretary Hegseth will not back down or be deterred by politicians seeking to score partisan points or launch phony investigations where no wrongdoing exists. The Department of War has followed the law, and our Secretary will continue to stand and fight every single day to support and defend the Constitution, lead our troops, and protect America." "We will continue to drive President Trump's agenda at the Department of War — despite threats of sham witch hunts from Democrats — and Secretary Hegseth is 100% committed to leading the Department until the end of President Trump's term in office." Reality check: Even if the House impeaches Hegseth, removing him from office would require a two-thirds vote in the Senate, a threshold that would be difficult to achieve, even when Democrats take control of the chamber in January.
