entry.title: Box Office: ‘Heated Rivalry’ Fans Drive Show’s Theatrical Release to $1.4 Million
entry.body: Nearly a year after “Heated Rivalry” debuted on streaming, fans are venturing to movie theaters to rewatch the steamy romance between hockey superstars Shane Hollander (Hudson Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Connor Storrie). The limited theatrical release, which is scheduled from Nov. 30, has generated $1.4 million from 945 theaters, according to distributor Regal Entertainment. Moviegoers were able to choose between three paired screenings (episodes 1 and 2: “Rookies” and “Olympians”, episodes 3 and 4: “Hunter” and “Rose,” and episodes 5 and 6: “I’ll Believe in Anything” and “The Cottage”), with tickets for each showtime costing $9.99. That’s less than the average movie price, which is $12.87 for standard screenings, according to research firm EntTelligence. It’s an impressive haul for a show that’s widely available to stream at home. There aren’t many points of comparison at the box office. When television shows like Netflix’s “Stranger Things” series finale or the Christian drama “The Chosen” have played on the big screen, they aired new, never-before-seen episodes. Although Netflix didn’t report grosses for “Stranger Things,” the Season 5 series finale was estimated to have earned a massive $25 million to $28 million around New Year’s Eve. However, that’s not a fair reference given the super-sized, two-hour finale was the much-anticipated conclusion to the streamer’s biggest series of all time. In any case, theatrical releases or (re-releases) of popular TV shows are all gravy for cinema operators, who are enjoying the biggest year at the box office since the onset of the pandemic. Gen Z, the target demographic for shows like “Heated Rivalry,” has been driving the movie theater resurgence. “This could become a really interesting trend, not only as a way to bring fans together but also to keep popular series top of mind during gaps between seasons, when maintaining momentum can be a challenge,” says Rentrak’s head of marketplace trends Paul Dergarabedian. “We initially thought this might be something largely confined to the faith-based space, but clearly the potential extends to virtually any series with a passionate fan base.” He adds, “Of course, not every television series is going to translate into a successful big-screen event, but for the right show with the right audience, movie theaters could become an exciting extension of the television experience rather than simply an alternative to it.” “Heated Rivalry,” based on Rachel Reid’s “Game Changers” book series, is gearing up for a second season. The Canadian-produced show was released in the U.S. on HBO Max in November 2025, although it didn’t become a word-of-mouth sensation until early 2026, when episodes reached an average viewership of more than 10 million and made instant stars out of Williams and Storrie. “When a series connects with audiences the way ‘Heated Rivalry’ has, we look for ways to bring it to the big screen and give fans a reason to experience it together,” Regal’s senior VP of U.S. content Brooks LeBoeuf said prior to the re-release. “It’s a chance to celebrate the story, its creators and its performances before Season 2 arrives in 2027.”

entry.title: ‘Avedon’ Review: Ron Howard’s Thrilling Documentary About Richard Avedon, the Great Photographer Who Turned Head-On Portraits Into an Art Form
entry.body: “Avedon,” Ron Howard’s documentary about the legendary photographer, is a fantastic movie. It’s the best documentary Ron Howard has made (my favorite before this: “The Beatles: Eight Days a Week”), and it’s been edited in a way that’s so supple and artful that its technique should be studied in filmmaking classes. (The film’s editor is Andrew Morreale.) Woven through the movie are hundreds of photographs that were shot by Richard Avedon, and there’s no question that the images are stunning, but the way the movie layers them into your consciousness is nearly musical in its finesse. And that helps to tell the very large story “Avedon” is telling: how Richard Avedon changed the metaphysics of photography, shifting the way we see the world. There’s a paradox running down the center of Avedon’s work that feels as epic and tingly as the 20th century, and that is this: He was a paragon of high fashion — the world of glamour and impossible beauty — but he was also, as a maker of images, the ultimate democratic humanist. The beauty of “Avedon” is that it explains that paradox and makes those images sing. Howard interpolates old clips and interviews, placing Avedon, with his sleek command, at the center of the movie. He also talks to models and critics and media and art-world luminaries who have a great deal of import to say. They include Tina Brown, Larry Gagosian, John Lahr, Twiggy, Adam Gopnik, Hilton Als, Calvin Klein, and Avedon’s lovingly insightful son, John Avedon. James Martin, the executive director of the Richard Avedon Foundation, takes us deep into the labyrinth of Avedon’s archives, where we see the work that resulted from the 16,000 sittings he did from 1944 until his death in 2004. That’s a long time, but it still averages out to one sitting per day, Monday through Friday, for 60 years. The movie also tells the tragic story of his mentally ill sister, whom he revered, and traces his troubled marriages. “Avedon” opens with an old clip of Richard Avedon, fixing that piercing bird-eye look of his into the camera as he explains, “I can say very little about photography. I follow no rules, no laws, and no advice.” He’s totally serious about that. We then get a montage, set to the funky martial beat of Spoon’s “I Turn My Camera On,” of Avedon portraits of the famous. Marilyn Monroe lovingly embracing Arthur Miller. All the images look timeless. (Avedon’s lighting makes it look as if each one was taken yesterday.) Every subject looks like what we imagine them looking like, and also different from how you’ve ever seen them. More direct and unfiltered, more intimately themselves. That’s the Avedon touch, but the magic element is that we can’t see how he achieved it. There’s a part of one that thinks, “Okay, just set up a camera and put some black-and-white film in it. Place a famous person in front of it. Encourage them to relax and ‘be themselves.’ And voilà! I could be Richard Avedon.” He probably would have said you’re not wrong. He wasn’t very interested in the technique of photography. Talk to him about f-stops and he would glaze over. His technique was in the way he approached a session. In the film, Isabella Rossellini says that other photographers tend to shoot and shoot and shoot, but Avedon would shoot an image every so often, then tell you to think of something, then shoot again, and end up with a total of maybe 10 shots. He himself explains that if you’ve booked someone for an hour, you don’t have to shoot for an hour. He says that he wastes half an hour having coffee, and then, maybe five minutes before the hour is over, he and the subject will go over to the white paper background, and the magic happens. It has its source in a remarkable story. Avedon was born in New York in 1923, and when he was a kid he says that walking down a street he would blink for a moment and keep his eyes closed, to keep what he saw alive in his head. It was his way of taking pictures before he’d even gotten a camera. Merchant Marines when he was 19, securing a place in the photographic department, where he took maybe 100,000 portraits of enlisted men and other workers, all to use for ID cards. This was the photographer’s equivalent of peeling potatoes on KP duty. But Avedon began to notice something. Shooting these military mug shots against a white background, he encountered “thousands of baffled faces looking into the camera,” and he saw how the photographs revealed these people. That’s one of the startling things about police mug shots. (John Waters: “Everybody looks better under arrest.”) We see a handful of the ID photos that Avedon took, and there it is: the Avedon style. He saw that each face was different, and needed nothing else to be different. So he took what fate handed him — a thankless military assignment — and turned it into a vision. The white background equalized everything. It became his way of making each individual stand out as an individual, with literally nothing to get in the way. He became a head-on existential classicist, one who echoed Diane Arbus’s eye for highlighting the aspect of a person that was somehow off. The famous Avedon shot of the model Lauren Hutton with her head thrown back and her breast popping out looks as perfectly composed as a Picasso sculpture. But it was totally spontaneous; it just happened. And that’s true of all the famous and iconic gazes Avedon’s portrait subjects gave him. Those looks weren’t planned (how could they have been?). At the tail-end of a session in 1953, Charlie Chaplin pranked the camera by holding devil horns over his grinning face, and that became one of the most famous images Avedon ever shot. Images like that happened…and then became frozen in the hive mind’s eye. But as “Avedon” explains, part of what he was always recording was the ineffable dance between subject and artist, using each subject to express something that there was there in himself. (Chaplin wouldn’t have made those devil horns for anyone else.) By the time of the 1957 Hollywood musical “Funny Face,” which paired Audrey Hepburn with Fred Astaire as a magazine photographer pointedly based on Avedon, he was already becoming a legend, and he began to use his power as part of his method as an artist. In his 1957 shoot with Marilyn Monroe, pegged to “The Prince and the Showgirl,” the trick was: How could you photograph Marilyn — or, rather, how could you photograph her the way Avedon wanted to photograph her — when she had come prepared, more than anyone else alive, to be photographed? The shoot took an entire day, and it’s full of joyous photographs of Marilyn in full splendor, but the iconic shot that emerged from it was taken at the end of the day, when she let down her guard for 10 seconds, and kind of drooped, and looked a bit sad, and we glimpse, in that photograph, the real Marilyn — not necessarily the forlorn Marilyn, but the full woman behind the image. You see Norma Jean grown up. “Avedon” is full of great stories and privileged glimpses into how Avedon created some of his most famous images. And, of course, he also photographed the unfamous, like the Oklahoma oil workers he shot in 1980. He used his impish nature to coax fashion models into leaping through the air for his models-in-motion photographs. He waited around for seven weeks in Vietnam to photograph the war’s American generals, and devised singular ways to shoot the Chicago 7 and the denizens of the Warhol Factory and the residents of the new American West, in a series that was so raw and authentic no museum in New York wanted anything to do with it. (He was that far ahead of the curve.) We also hear the story of how he photographed his aging father and used that process to reconcile with him. Avedon supported his own ritzy lifestyle by doing advertising work (including the Obsession perfume TV spots that were like surrealist mini-films), but for him it was never a compromise. And we see how that could be the case. There is, over 60 years, a breathtaking continuity between his portrait work and his fashion work and his commercial work that makes it all inseparable. That’s because every photograph Richard Avedon ever took was striving for the same thing: to open your eyes.
entry.summary: "Avedon," Ron Howard’s documentary about the legendary photographer, is a fantastic movie. It’s the best documentary Ron Howard has made (my favorite before this: "The Beatles: Eight Days a Week — The Touring Years"), and it’s been edited in a way that’s so supple and artful that its technique should be studied in filmmaking classes. (The film’s editor is Andrew Morreale.) Woven through the movie are hundreds of images that were shot by Richard Avedon, and there’s no question that the images are stunning, but the way the movie layers them into your consciousness is nearly musical in its finesse. And that helps to tell the very large story that "Avedon" is telling: how Richard Avedon changed photography in a way that shifted how we see the world.

entry.title: Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — ‘Being Heumann’ and ‘La Bola Negra’ Found the Year’s Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them?
entry.body: Oscar Predictions: Best Casting — ‘Being Heumann’ and ‘La Bola Negra’ Found the Year’s Boldest Discoveries. Will the Academy Reward Them? Variety Awards Circuit section is the home for all awards news and related content throughout the year, featuring the following: the official predictions for the upcoming Oscars, Emmys, Grammys and Tony Awards ceremonies, curated by Variety chief awards editor Clayton Davis. The prediction pages reflect the current standings in the race and do not reflect personal preferences for any individual contender. As other formal (and informal) polls suggest, competitions are fluid and subject to change in response to buzz and events. Predictions are updated every Thursday. Best Casting Predictions Commentary (Updated: Nov. 8, 2026): Casting is only in its second year as an Oscar category and if voters just default to whichever best picture front-runner had the splashiest ensemble, the whole point of the award might be flawed. One of the two films that stand out in this category sense, are “Being Heumann,” Siân Heder’s Apple drama about Judy Heumann and the 1977 San Francisco sit-in that forced the government to enforce disability rights and “La Bola Negra,” Los Javis’ Netflix epic that threads three gay men across three eras of Spain. For Heder’s film, casting directors Bernie Telsey and Adam Caldwell put more than 20 disabled actors on screen around breakout Ruth Madeley’s Judy, a lot of them with little or no acting experience, which is a bigger swing than any other star-studded ensemble. Over in Spain, Eva Leira and Yolanda Serrano delivered Javier Calvo and Javier Ambrossi a cast where the pop singer Guitarricadelafuente makes his acting debut alongside newcomers Milo Quifes and Carlos González, then surrounded them with legends like Penélope Cruz and a Spanish-speaking Glenn Close. We’ll see what other films can pop in the phase one period. The list of predictions in all categories can be found here. entry.title: Andy Serkis Says He Was ‘Evangelical’ About Performance Capture After Playing Gollum in ‘Lord of the Rings’ but Now Accepts It’s ‘Misunderstood’: ‘If You Get It? Great’
entry.body: Now I just think, ‘If you get it? “Performances like Gollum are authored by an actor in the same way a prosthetics team engineered John Hurt in ‘The Elephant Man.’ But, for some reason, a performance underneath a physical mask is more understandable to some than this, which is a digital mask.” In May, “Lord of the Rings” filmmaker Peter Jackson weighed in on the motion-capture conversation, saying the mounting debate over AI in film is one reason Serkis hasn’t — and likely never will — win awards for playing Gollum. “A lot of the current environment, everyone’s so worried about AI … I don’t think a Gollum-type character or a generated character has any hope for winning any awards,” he said at the time. “Which is a bit unfair, especially in the Andy Serkis case where it’s not an AI-generated performance. It’s a human-generated performance 100% of the way.” Serkis returns as the character for “The Lord of the Rings: The Hunt for Gollum,” which he is also directing. The film is scheduled to open in theaters on Dec.

entry.title: Andy Richter Claims U2’s the Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel Screenplay
entry.body: Andy Richter Claims U2’s the Edge Wrote an ‘Elf’ Sequel Screenplay Andy Richter, who had a small role in the 2003 Christmas classic Elf, revealed in a new interview that U2’s the Edge wrote a screenplay for the sequel to the Will Ferrell-starring film. For over two decades, Elf fans have clamored for a sequel to the film, and while an Elf 2 came close to happening in 2013, Ferrell ultimately decided against reprising the role of Buddy. At some point after the film’s release and rise to holiday favorite, as Richter told Obsessed: The Podcast, Elf producer Shauna Robertson received a phone call from an unlikely screenwriter pitching a meeting about Elf 2. “Somebody reached out to her and said, ‘The Edge from U2 has written a sequel to Elf, and he wants to talk to you about it,’” Richter said. “It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written somewhere in the world. There is an Edge-penned Elf 2 out there.” Richter added that the meeting “never happened.” “It’s one of those things where she’s like, ‘All right, sure, I’ll meet him,’ and then it just petered out and never happened,” Richter said. While the Edge has hundreds of credits on his IMDB page thanks to his work with U2, “Screenwriter” is not among “Composer,” “Soundtrack,” and “Actor” (as himself) in his filmography. However, the Edge has served as a producer on a handful of occasions on non-U2 projects, including documentaries and short films. The Edge has not commented, ever, on his Elf 2 script. U2, however, will gives fans an early Christmas present next week with the arrival of their new album Carnaval de Luz.
entry.summary: "It’s the weirdest story, but apparently it was fully written somewhere in the world," actor says. "There is an Edge-penned Elf 2 out there"

entry.title: ‘Passing Strange’ Comes to Pasadena Playhouse: Creators Stew and Heidi Rodewald on the Rock Musical Reaching L.A. Almost Two Decades After Tony-Winning Broadway Run
entry.body: So they’ve always a loyal audience of rock fans in SoCal eagerly waiting for the show to take root here, too, on top of Angeleno theater buffs who never got to see the show back east. Now it’s finally happening, thanks to director Zhailon Levingston, who won the Tony this year for best direction of a musical for “Cats: The Jellicle Ball.” When he sat down with the top folks at Pasadena Playhouse to discuss what he might like to do here, giving “Passing Strange” its proper SoCal premiere was at the top of his list. Stew and Rodewald will not be performing in the show in Pasadena, as they did throughout its entire Broadway and pre-Broadway runs. (Neither will Colman Domingo, who had a supporting role, pre-fame, on Broadway. You can see all of those performances in the film version Spike Lee directed.) Vintage Trouble singer Ty Taylor stars in this production as the Stew stand-in known only as Narrator, along with Brittany Campbell (pictured above), Britton Smith and Saycon Sengbloh. Stew and Rodewald are as eager as anyone to see what Levingston has done with a project that takes elements of Stew’s real coming-of-age and sets them to rock ‘n’ roll.

entry.title: Blanche dismisses Means allegations as GOP's MAHA feud deepens
entry.body: Attorney General Todd Blanche on Sunday dismissed former Trump health adviser Calley Means' corruption allegations against senior White House officials, even as a former FDA commissioner described pressure from tobacco lobbyists and a Republican congressman called for scrutiny. Why it matters: The feud inside President Trump's coalition raises a central question about Trump's health agenda: Were his advisers undermining it, as Means alleges, or were they carrying out the president's wishes? The latest: Asked on CNN's "State of the Union" whether the DOJ would investigate Means' allegations, Blanche responded: "Something that someone says on a podcast? No, I do not listen to that. Absolutely not." Blanche called Means a "disgruntled former administration official" and praised former White House chief of staff Susie Wiles , who Trump announced Friday would be replaced by Stephen Miller . On "Fox News Sunday," Blanche said allegations about Wiles' financial dealings did not concern him. But Rep. Marlin Stutzman (R-Ind.) told CNN that "any allegation of any impropriety like this should be looked at." Driving the news: Means, who alleged widespread corruption in a Friday interview with Joe Rogan, told CBS' "Face the Nation" that he had wanted Wiles removed. Means accused Wiles of blocking an initiative to examine children's sugar consumption because she wanted sugar-industry donations for the midterms. He also alleged that Wiles' deputies pushed policies favorable to the flavored-vaping and kratom industries over the objections of officials working on the Make America Healthy Again agenda. Means accused Trump pollster Tony Fabrizio of advising against defining ultra-processed foods while receiving money from PepsiCo. The White House and the Justice Department did not respond to Axios' request for comment. What they're saying: Former FDA Commissioner Marty Makary backed up part of Means' account in a statement to CBS. "Big tobacco exploited their connections to administration and HHS officials," Makary said, alleging repeated pressure to approve fruit-flavored vapes. Makary said kratom lobbyists similarly tried to undermine his attempts to restrict the substances. He did not identify which officials pressured him. The other side: Former White House adviser James Blair, one of Wiles' allies that Means has accused of wrongdoing, disputed Means' allegations in messages to Axios. "I didn't promote flavored vaping specifically at all," Blair said, adding that he never weighed in on individual applications or which flavors should be approved. Blair said he was following Trump's instructions to ensure the FDA made timely decisions on applications, whether approving or denying them. "The voters elected President Trump. Not me, and not Calley Means," Blair told Axios. He said he never dealt with kratom policy and is reviewing his legal options. When speaking to Axios, Fabrizio called Means' allegation that he was "in the pocket of Big Pharma" "ridiculous" and "demonstrably false," citing his firm's polling showing support for lower prescription drug prices and policies that would cut into pharmaceutical profits. Fabrizio also said he encouraged Republican lawmakers to campaign on Trump's "most favored nation" drug-pricing proposal. In a statement on X, the lobbying firm Ballard Partners took exception to Means' "false" accusations about its interactions with Wiles, who had worked at the company seven years ago. Ballard Partners said it did not lobby Wiles or anyone in the White House on fruit-flavored vapes or another issue Means mentioned, glyphosate, the active ingredient in the weedkiller Roundup, owned by Bayer. In February, Trump outraged MAHA activists by signing an executive order to grant "immunity" to glyphosate producers as Bayer struggled under the weight of lawsuits over roundup. In June, the Supreme Court ruled 7–2 that federal law preempts state lawsuits concerning pesticide sales, thereby making it tougher for people to sue for cancer claims regarding Roundup use. Between the lines: Means has portrayed Trump as unaware of decisions his advisers made. But the Wall Street Journal reported in May that Trump personally pressured Makary to approve flavored vaping products. Pressed by CBS' Margaret Brennan, Means said he did not know whether Trump had called Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. after meeting with tobacco-industry representatives. Means argued advisers manipulated what reached the president and invoked Trump's authority to advance their own priorities. Blair rejected that characterization, telling Axios: "In the White House, I implemented the President's agenda always." Editor's note: This story has been updated with a statement from Ballard Partners.

entry.title: MAGA castoffs plot 2028 spoiler bid
entry.body: An unusual coalition wants to recruit outgoing Rep. Thomas Massie as the Libertarian Party's 2028 presidential nominee, betting that MAGA fractures can turn a third-party candidacy into a spoiler for the Republican nominee. Why it matters: Organizers see a fighter in Massie, a frequent critic of President Trump who pushed hard on releasing the Epstein files and lost a bitter primary rather than quietly walking away. Massie raised almost $10 million in the process and has a large online donor list and base. For his parting act in Congress, Massie is pushing an impeachment vote against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth . Driving the news: For months, Libertarian Party operatives and MAGA defectors have been privately and publicly encouraging Massie to run under a rebranded party. "Libertarian Jesus is Ron Paul, and one of our saints is Thomas Massie," Larry Sharpe, a perennial Libertarian candidate and longtime third-party operative, told Axios. Sharpe has spoken with Massie several times about a potential presidential run. Aside from playing GOP spoiler, organizers believe the Libertarian Party's existing ballot access and infrastructure could help them win 5% of the national vote — which would qualify its next presidential nominee for federal funding. Massie didn't respond to several requests for comment. The big picture: The plan is for libertarians to claim dibs on the "America First" agenda, mainly focusing on anti-war sentiment. Organizers believe they can build consensus among supporters of the MAGA wing that's closer to Tucker Carlson, former Trump official Joe Kent and former Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene (R-Ga.), as well as disillusioned "Make America Healthy Again" activists and populist-inclined voters on the right and left. "A party that would speak clearly about the disaster of the war in Iran, that would speak clearly about the mistake to continue to give military aid, taxpayer-funded military aid, to Israel — that would perk up a lot of ears among young people," said James Fishback, a former GOP gubernatorial candidate in Florida who met with the organizers in October. "The idea is if one can take 5, 10, 15% of the vote from one of these parties, then that party has to listen and cave to interest of the people," Bret Weinstein, a lead organizer of this effort, said on his podcast last week. Zoom in: LP operative Michael Heise, a leader and founder of the Mises Caucus, is a main organizer for this rebranded party. Heise's caucus took over the LP in 2022. The LP picks its presidential nominee at conventions by delegates voting on the floor. Those who bring the most delegates can take over a convention. Heise is also a skilled fundraiser — by third party standards. The Mises PAC, which is bankrolling this "draft Massie" operation, according to the website, raised $394,000 in 2024's election cycle. The PAC has previously received donations from Kimbal and Christina Musk, Elon's brother and sister-in-law; Abigail Rockefeller, a former Robert F. Kennedy Jr. campaign and Democratic-leaning donor; and Patricia Duggan, a MAGA Inc mega-donor and longtime LP contributor, according to FEC records. Heise declined to comment.

entry.title: Scoop: Trump asked Netanyahu to move on Gaza peace plan in post-election call
entry.body: President Trump told Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu during a phone call Thursday that he wants him to take steps to implement his Gaza peace plan , according to two sources with knowledge of the matter. Why it matters: The roadmap calls for disarming Hamas and demilitarizing Gaza, as well as transferring responsibility for governing the enclave to a new Palestinian technocratic government. But it has been on hold for months because of the Israeli elections held on Oct. 27. The Trump administration did not want implementation of the plan to become a politically explosive issue during the Israeli election campaign. Trump endorsed Netanyahu shortly before the election. Now that it's over, the president wants to forge ahead with his Gaza plan, regardless of whether Netanyahu or his opposition forms a new government. Catch up quick: A year ago, Israel and Hamas agreed to the first phase of Trump's 20-point plan, which led to a ceasefire in the Gaza war and the release of the last 20 living hostages taken during the Oct. 7, 2023 attacks. Trump's Board of Peace, which was established as part of the Gaza agreement, has been working for months on an implementation plan that includes the establishment of a Palestinian technocratic government and an International Stabilization Force. Last July, the Board of Peace reached an agreement with Hamas on a 15-point plan to disarm the armed groups in Gaza and transfer civilian and security control to the new Palestinian technocratic government. Since then, Netanyahu's government has largely refused to move forward with implementing it, mostly for domestic political reasons. In an August visit to Israel, Trump adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner told Netanyahu that Hamas for the first time had agreed to disarm. He urged the Israeli prime minister to take steps to test whether that commitment was real. Netanyahu was and still is extremely skeptical that Hamas will ever demilitarize. He says the group is reconstituting and rearming in Gaza. Zoom in: Over the past three months, Trump's Board of Peace has been working with the Israeli government and military to refine details of the plan and address Israeli concerns about demilitarization in Gaza. A U.S. official said the process would be gradual. Reconstruction would only begin after progress in disarming Hamas had been verified. Trump's Board of Peace unveiled a six-month, $2.45 billion initial recovery plan for Gaza during the U.N. General Assembly in September. The 66-project proposal offers one of the most comprehensive roadmaps yet for what the early months of post-war recovery and governance in Gaza would look like. But for the plan to move forward, the Board of Peace needs Israel and Hamas to cooperate. A source with knowledge of the details said the Trump administration, Board of Peace and Israel agree that the plan remains the best way forward and that there is no credible alternative. Behind the scenes: Secretary of State Marco Rubio as well as Kushner and Trump envoy Steve Witkoff also participated in the call between the president and Netanyahu. A source with knowledge of the details described the call, which Netanyahu initiated, as constructive. It also addressed the war in Iran. The White House and the Israeli prime minister's office did not immediately respond to requests for comment. State of play: A day after the call, former British Prime Minister Tony Blair, who is a member of the Board of Peace, visited Israel. He met with Netanyahu and his opponent Gadi Eisenkot, who's been tasked with trying to form a new government to replace Netanyahu's. A source with knowledge of the visit said Blair urged Netanyahu and other Israeli political leaders to give the plan a chance. What they're saying: "The implementation will be difficult but we believe it is a good plan for Israel. Nevertheless we can't do it with one hand tied behind our back," the U.S. official said. "We want to move forward collaboratively and we need full cooperation and partnership from the Israeli government," the person added.
